Union of India emphasised that the Commissions must be provided with adequate staff, financial autonomy and statutory protection against arbitrary removal of Chairpersons to function independently.

Examination focus: aspirants should be able to enumerate the constitutional articles, the investigative powers, the nature of recommendations (advisory vs. binding), the judicial enforcement mechanisms, and the recent statutory enhancements. A common twist is to ask whether the Commissions can directly enforce fundamental rights or whether they act as a “watchdog” whose efficacy depends on executive cooperation and judicial backing.

The Constitutional Framework for the Right to Legal Aid and Access to Justice: Article 39A, Article 21 and the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987

Article 39A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, directs the State to secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice on a basis of equal opportunity and to provide free legal aid by suitable legislation or schemes. The Supreme Court has read Article 39A together with Article 21 to hold that the right to free legal aid is an essential facet of the right to life and personal liberty. In Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979) the Court declared that “speedy trial” and “free legal aid” are fundamental to a fair procedure under Article 21, and directed the release of undertrial prisoners who had been detained beyond the maximum possible sentence.

The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 operationalised this mandate by establishing the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), State Legal Services Authorities, District Legal Services Authorities and Taluk Legal Services Committees. The Act provides for free legal services to eligible persons — women, children, SC/ST, victims of trafficking, persons with disability, industrial workmen, and persons in custody — and for the organisation of Lok Adalats as alternative dispute‑resolution forums. NALSA’s regulations also mandate legal aid clinics in law schools and the deployment of panel lawyers.

Judicial pronouncements have expanded the scope. In Khatri v. State of Bihar (1981) the Court held that the State must provide a lawyer at its expense from the moment of arrest. In State of Maharashtra v. Manubhai Pragaji Vashi (1995) the Court ruled that the right to legal aid cannot be denied on the ground of the accused’s ability to pay if the case involves a serious offence. More recently, NALSA v. Union of India (2020) directed all High Courts to monitor the functioning of legal aid cells and to ensure that panel lawyers are paid promptly.

Despite the robust framework, challenges persist: inadequate funding, shortage of qualified panel lawyers, low awareness among beneficiaries, and the perception that legal aid lawyers are less competent. The 2022 NALSA report highlighted that only 12 per cent of eligible undertrials received legal representation at the first production before a magistrate. The Supreme Court, in Re: Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons (2023), linked the deficit in legal aid to overcrowding and delayed trials, ordering the creation of a “Legal Aid Monitoring Dashboard” for real‑time tracking.

For the exam, candidates should be able to trace the constitutional lineage (Art. 39A → Art. 21 → Legal Services Authorities Act), identify the categories of entitled persons, explain the institutional hierarchy (NALSA → SLSA → DLSA → TLSC), and discuss the judicial enforcement mechanisms (mandamus, continuing mandamus, structural injunctions). A typical question may ask to evaluate whether the right to legal aid is a “positive obligation” of the State and how it interacts with the directive principle in Article 39A.

  • Confusing the EWS quota ceiling with the fifty per cent caste‑based ceiling — the two operate independently.
  • Assuming internet shutdowns are per se unconstitutional — the Court permits proportionate, time‑limited restrictions with procedural safeguards.
  • Treating compensatory jurisprudence as a statutory remedy rather than a constitutional one under Article 21.
  • Believing the NCSC/NCST recommendations are legally binding on the executive — they are advisory but acquire enforceability through judicial review.
  • Overlooking that Article 39A is a directive principle; the justiciable right to legal aid flows from Article 21, not directly from Article 39A.
  • Neglecting the dual constitutional anchor (Article 19(1)(a) and Article 21) when analysing internet‑access cases.
  • Failing to distinguish between the State’s vicarious liability for custodial violence and the polluter‑pays principle in environmental compensation.

The Doctrine of Prospective Overruling in Fundamental Rights Adjudication: Origin, Scope and Contemporary Relevance

The doctrine of prospective overruling permits a court to declare a legal principle invalid while limiting the effect of that declaration to future transactions, thereby preserving the validity of past acts done in reliance on the earlier rule. In Indian constitutional law, the doctrine made its entrance in Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), where a thin majority of the Supreme Court held that Parliament lacked the power to amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368. To avoid the chaos that would follow from invalidating all constitutional amendments enacted since 1950, Chief Justice Subba Rao applied prospective overruling: the ruling would operate only against future amendments, leaving the First, Fourth and Seventeenth Amendments intact. The Court borrowed the technique from American jurisprudence (Great Northern Railway Co. v. Sunburst Oil & Refining Co., 1932) where Justice Cardozo affirmed that a state court may choose between retrospective and prospective operation when overruling its own precedents.

The doctrinal justification rests on three pillars: (i) the need to protect vested rights and settled expectations; (ii) the avoidance of administrative paralysis caused by the wholesale nullification of statutes, orders and judicial decisions; and (iii) the recognition that judicial law-making, though inevitable in a common law system, should not unsettle the past. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Court did not expressly invoke prospective overruling because the basic structure doctrine operated as a forward-looking constraint on amendatory power. However, the Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) judgment, while striking down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 inserted by the 42nd Amendment, implicitly applied prospective reasoning by not disturbing amendments already validated by Parliament before the judgment.

Post-1980, the Supreme Court has invoked prospective overruling sparingly in pure Fundamental Rights cases, preferring the doctrine of stare decisis and the technique of reading down. Notable applications appear in service law and tax jurisprudence: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024) applied prospective overruling to its own earlier judgment on sub-classification of Scheduled Castes, directing that the new principle would govern future reservations while protecting appointments already made. In Commissioner of Income Tax v. Hindustan Bulk Carriers (2003), the Court held that a new interpretation of a fiscal statute would apply prospectively to avoid hardship to assessees who had filed returns under the earlier regime. The doctrine remains an exception, not the rule; the default position in constitutional adjudication remains retrospective declaration of invalidity under Article 13(1) and (2), as reaffirmed in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) where laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 were opened to challenge without temporal limitation.

For the aspirant, the critical distinction is between prospective overruling (judicial self-restraint in temporal application of a new rule) and the doctrine of eclipse (pre-constitutional laws dormant but revivable) or severability (excising the unconstitutional portion). Prospective overruling is a remedial choice exercised by the Court; it cannot be claimed as a right by a litigant. The 2024 Davinder Singh reference (seven-judge bench) illustrates the contemporary tension: the majority used prospective overruling to balance constitutional correctness with institutional stability, while the dissent argued that Fundamental Rights violations demand immediate and retrospective remedy. Examination questions often test whether the doctrine applies to legislative acts (it does not; it applies to judicial precedents) or whether it can be invoked to save an unconstitutional amendment (it cannot; it only defers the consequence of invalidity).

The Right to Die with Dignity: Passive Euthanasia, Advance Directives and the Constitutional Jurisprudence under Article 21

The constitutional recognition of a right to die with dignity represents one of the most profound expansions of Article 21 in the post-Maneka Gandhi era. The trajectory begins with P. Rathinam v. Union of India (1994), where a Division Bench held that the right to life includes the right not to live a forced life, striking down Section 309 IPC (attempt to suicide) as violative of Article 21. This was overturned two years later in Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996), where a Constitution Bench ruled that Article 21 guarantees the right to life with dignity but does not include the right to die or the right to be killed; Section 309 IPC was upheld. The Court distinguished between extinguishing life (suicide/euthanasia) and accelerating the natural process of death in terminal illness, leaving a narrow window for passive euthanasia.

The breakthrough came in Aruna Ramchandra Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011), where the Supreme Court, while dismissing a plea for active euthanasia for a nurse in a persistent vegetative state for 37 years, laid down comprehensive guidelines for passive euthanasia. The Court held that withdrawing life support from a person in a permanent vegetative state (PVS) or with a terminal illness, where medical opinion concludes there is no hope of recovery, is permissible under Article 21. The decision mandated a two-tier approval: (i) a hospital medical board and (ii) the High Court under its parens patriae jurisdiction, with notice to the State and close relatives. This judge-made law governed the field for seven years.

The definitive judgment is Common Cause (A Regd. Society) v. Union of India (2018), a five-judge Constitution Bench decision that recognised advance directives (living wills) as a facet of the right to self-determination and bodily integrity under Article 21. The Court held that an adult of sound mind has the right to refuse medical treatment, including life-sustaining measures, through a written directive executed voluntarily, with two attesting witnesses and countersigned by a Judicial Magistrate of First Class. The judgment detailed a procedural framework: the treating physician must verify the directive, constitute a medical board, obtain the High Court's nod (or the Collector's in urgent cases), and ensure a cooling-off period. The Court also decriminalised attempted suicide by reading down Section 309 IPC in light of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (Section 115), which presumes severe stress in suicide attempts and bars prosecution.

Key distinctions tested in examinations: active euthanasia (administering a lethal agent) remains illegal (culpable homicide under Section 304 IPC); passive euthanasia (withholding/withdrawing treatment) is constitutionally protected; physician-assisted suicide (providing means for self-administration) is not permitted. The 2018 guidelines were modified in Common Cause v. Union of India (2023) to simplify the execution and verification process, removing the requirement for a Judicial Magistrate's countersignature and allowing notarisation or gazetted officer attestation, reflecting the Court's responsiveness to practical barriers. The jurisprudence anchors the right in autonomy, dignity and privacy (the Puttaswamy trilogy), making it a rare instance where a positive obligation on the State (to facilitate the directive) arises from a negative liberty claim.

Comparative Case Analysis Technique
A question asks: "Trace the evolution of the right to die with dignity from Gian Kaur (1996) to Common Cause (2018). Identify the doctrinal pivot that allowed the Court to recognise advance directives without overruling Gian Kaur."
The pivot is the distinction between the right to die (suicide, rejected in Gian Kaur) and the right to refuse life-prolonging treatment (self-determination, accepted in Common Cause). Gian Kaur held that Article 21 does not include the right to extinguish life. Common Cause reframed the claim: a terminally ill patient withdrawing a ventilator is not "choosing death" but "choosing not to prolong the dying process". The Court grounded this in bodily integrity and privacy (Article 21 read with Puttaswamy), not in a freestanding right to die. Thus, Gian Kaur remains good law for suicide/active euthanasia, while Common Cause carves out a distinct constitutional space for passive euthanasia and advance directives. The examiner expects this precise doctrinal distinction, not a mere chronological list.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question combines euthanasia, living wills and the Mental Healthcare Act, structure the answer in three layers: (1) Constitutional anchor (Article 21 → autonomy, dignity, privacy); (2) Judicial trajectory (Gian Kaur → Aruna Shanbaug → Common Cause 2018 → 2023 modification); (3) Statutory interface (Section 115 MHA 2017 decriminalising attempt, absence of a standalone euthanasia law). Always distinguish active vs passive vs assisted. Cite the 2023 procedural simplification — it signals awareness of the latest judicial correction.

The Constitutional Status of the Right to Vote: Article 326, Statutory Frameworks and the Judicial Debate on its Fundamental Character

Article 326 of the Constitution mandates that elections to the House of the People and to the Legislative Assembly of every State shall be on the basis of adult suffrage. Despite this clear textual command, the Supreme Court has consistently held that the right to vote is not a Fundamental Right but a statutory right created by the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and 1951. The foundational precedent is N.P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer (1952), where the Court ruled that the right to vote is a creature of statute and that Article 326 merely provides the constitutional basis for the legislative framework; it does not by itself confer an enforceable fundamental right. This position was reiterated in Jyoti Basu v. Debi Ghosal (1982), which characterised the right to vote as a "statutory right" and the right to be elected as a "statutory privilege", both subject to legislative conditions.

The distinction carries significant remedial consequences. A violation of a statutory right to vote can be challenged only through an election petition under the RP Act, 1951 (High Court original jurisdiction, appeal to Supreme Court), not through a writ petition under Article 32 or 226. In Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006), the Court upheld the removal of the "domicile requirement" for Rajya Sabha elections, holding that the right to vote in Council of States elections is purely statutory and Parliament may prescribe qualifications. The Court rejected the argument that Article 326 implicitly guarantees a fundamental right to vote, emphasising that the Constitution's framers deliberately placed voting rights in the legislative domain.

However, a parallel jurisprudence under Article 19(1)(a) has recognised a right to information about candidates as a facet of freedom of speech and expression. In Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) and People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2003), the Court held that the voter's right to know antecedents (criminal, financial, educational) of candidates flows from Article 19(1)(a), not from Article 326. This creates a dual-track regime: the act of voting is statutory; the informed exercise of that vote is fundamental. The NOTA (None of the Above) judgment in PUCL v. Union of India (2013) extended this logic, directing the Election Commission to provide a NOTA button on EVMs, grounding the right to negative voting in Article 19(1)(a) and the secrecy provision of Section 79(d) RP Act, 1951.

Recent challenges have tested the statutory/fundamental boundary. In Rajbala v. State of Haryana (2015), the Court upheld minimum educational qualifications for panchayat elections, reiterating that the right to contest (and by extension, vote) in local body elections is statutory under Article 243, not fundamental. The 103rd Constitutional Amendment (EWS quota) and the 104th Amendment (extending SC/ST reservation in legislatures) operate on the statutory architecture of representation, not on a fundamental right to vote. Aspirants must avoid the trap of conflating universal adult franchise (a constitutional principle in Article 326) with a justiciable fundamental right. The examination often frames this as: "Is the right to vote a fundamental right?" The correct answer: "No, it is a constitutional-cum-statutory right; Article 326 mandates adult suffrage but the right is conferred and regulated by the Representation of the People Acts, with remedies limited to election petitions."

The Interplay of Fundamental Duties under Article 51A with Fundamental Rights: Judicial Interpretation and the Emerging Duty-Rights Nexus

Article 51A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and expanded by the 86th Amendment (2002) to include the duty of parents to provide education (Article 51A(k)), enumerates eleven fundamental duties. While the duties are addressed to "every citizen of India" and are not directly enforceable by writ (no Article 32/226 remedy for breach), the Supreme Court has progressively woven them into the interpretive fabric of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles. The seminal shift occurred in AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2001), where the Court held that fundamental duties are "equally important" as fundamental rights and can be used as a tool of construction to resolve ambiguities in rights adjudication. The Court stated that Article 51A(a) (duty to abide by the Constitution) and (j) (duty to strive for excellence) inform the content of Article 21 and Article 14 in professional education contexts.

The duty to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood (Article 51A(e)) has been invoked in hate speech and communal violence cases. In Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan v. Union of India (2014), the Court referred to Article 51A(e) while directing the Law Commission to examine the need for a specific hate speech law, treating the duty as a constitutional indicator of the State's obligation to protect fraternity. The duty to protect and improve the natural environment (Article 51A(g)) has achieved the deepest judicial integration. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1988) and subsequent orders, the Court read Article 51A(g) with Article 48A and Article 21 to impose positive obligations on the State and citizens, converting the duty into a justiciable standard for environmental governance. The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 (Section 20) explicitly mandates the Tribunal to apply Article 51A(g) in its decisions.

The duty to develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform (Article 51A(h)) surfaced in Aruna Roy v. Union of India (2002), where the Court upheld the National Curriculum Framework's inclusion of value education, noting that Article 51A(h) supports a curriculum that fosters rationality. The duty to safeguard public property and abjure violence (Article 51A(i)) was cited in Destruction of Public Property v. State of A.P. (2009) to justify exemplary damages against rioters, linking the duty to the State's power to recover costs under the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, 1984.

The Verma Committee Report (1999) recommended legislative enforcement of fundamental duties, including penalties for non-compliance, but no such law has been enacted. The 2022 Karnataka High Court judgment in Student v. State (hijab case) referenced Article 51A(e) and (j) to argue that constitutional duties of harmony and excellence constrain the manner of exercising Article 25 rights, though the Supreme Court's split verdict (2022) did not rest on this reasoning. The emerging nexus is clear: fundamental duties serve as interpretive lenses for fundamental rights (limiting their absolute claim), as legislative guides for Parliament (shaping reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2)-(6)), and as judicial benchmarks for the State's positive obligations under Directive Principles. The examination tests whether a duty can be directly enforced (no), whether it can ground a writ petition (no, but can be a factor in PIL), and whether it can restrict a fundamental right (indirectly, through the "reasonable restriction" calculus).

The Role of the Finance Commission in Realising Directive Principles: Fiscal Federalism as a Mechanism for DPSP Implementation

Article 280 mandates the constitution of a Finance Commission every five years to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). While the Directive Principles in Part IV are non-justiciable (Article 37), the Finance Commission operates as a constitutional fiscal instrument that translates several DPSPs into resource allocations. The most direct linkage is with Article 38(2) (minimising inequalities in income and status) and Article 39(b)-(c) (distributive justice: ownership and control of material resources to serve the common good, preventing concentration of wealth). The Terms of Reference (ToR) of successive Commissions have explicitly referenced these principles. The 14th Finance Commission (Y.V. Reddy) increased vertical devolution to 42 per cent, citing the need to empower States to fulfil DPSP obligations in health, education and sanitation. The 15th Finance Commission (N.K. Singh) was tasked with "balanced regional development" and "fiscal consolidation", echoing Article 38 and Article 39.

Specific grants recommended by the Finance Commission target DPSP domains: Article 275(1) grants for Scheduled Areas and Tribes (linked to Article 46); Article 282 discretionary grants for public purpose (used for centrally sponsored schemes in nutrition (Article 47), education (Article 45/21A), rural employment (Article 41)). The 15th FC introduced performance-based grants for local bodies (Article 243-I, 243-Y) tied to the delivery of basic services — drinking water, sanitation, primary health — directly operationalising Article 47 and Article 39(e)-(f). The Commission's health sector grants (₹70,051 crore for 2021-26) were framed as a response to the constitutional mandate of Article 47 (raising nutrition and standard of living).

The horizontal devolution formula (income distance, population, area, forest cover, demographic performance) embeds DPSP logic. "Income distance" (per capita GSDP gap) addresses Article 38(2) by transferring more to poorer States. "Forest cover" weight (10 per cent in 15th FC) recognises the ecological service burden on States, resonating with Article 48A. "Demographic performance" (rewarding fertility reduction) aligns with Article 39(e) (health of workers) and Article 47. The revenue deficit grants to 17 States (15th FC) prevent fiscal collapse that would cripple DPSP implementation.

A critical constitutional nuance: the Finance Commission's recommendations are not binding on the Union government (Article 280(3) says the President "shall cause every recommendation... to be laid before each House of Parliament"), but in practice they are almost always accepted. The 15th FC's recommendation to create a non-lapsable defence fund (rejected by the Union) and the disagreement over the 2011 Census base for population weight illustrate the political economy of DPSP financing. For the aspirant, the key is to articulate the Finance Commission as the fiscal engine of Directive Principles — converting the moral exhortations of Part IV into intergovernmental transfers that fund the positive obligations the State assumes under Articles 38, 39, 41, 43, 45, 47 and 48A. Questions may ask: "How does the Finance Commission contribute to the realisation of DPSP?" Answer: Through vertical/horizontal devolution formulas weighted for equity (Article 38, 39), targeted grants for DPSP sectors (health, education, nutrition, environment), and performance incentives for local governance (Article 243G, 243W read with Part IV).

  • Confusing prospective overruling with the doctrine of eclipse — the former is a judicial remedy limiting temporal effect of a new precedent; the latter describes the dormant state of pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights.
  • Asserting that the right to die with dignity includes active euthanasia or physician-assisted suicide — the Court has repeatedly limited the right to passive euthanasia and advance directives for treatment refusal.
  • Treating the right to vote as a Fundamental Right enforceable under Article 32 — it is a statutory right under the RP Acts; the remedy for denial is an election petition, not a writ petition.
  • Believing Fundamental Duties under Article 51A are directly justiciable — they are not enforceable by writ but function as interpretive aids for Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.
  • Assuming Finance Commission recommendations are legally binding on the Union — they are advisory, though constitutional convention ensures near-universal acceptance.
  • Overlooking the distinction between the statutory right to vote (Article 326 + RP Act) and the fundamental right to information about candidates (Article 19(1)(a)) — the two operate on different constitutional planes.
  • Missing the 2023 procedural simplification in the Common Cause living will guidelines (removal of Judicial Magistrate countersignature) — examiners test awareness of the latest judicial correction.
The advanced sections above equip the aspirant with the doctrinal precision, case-law depth and institutional mechanics required to answer the most demanding questions on the interplay of rights, duties and directive principles.

The Right to Food as a Facet of Article 21: Judicial Recognition, Legislative Framework and the National Food Security Act, 2013

The Supreme Court first articulated a constitutional right to food in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2001), holding that the right to life under Article 21 encompasses the right to nutrition and that the State bears a positive obligation to prevent starvation. The Court converted the petition into a continuing mandamus, issuing a series of interim orders that compelled the Central and State governments to operationalise the Public Distribution System (PDS), the Mid‑Day Meal Scheme, the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) and the Antyodaya Anna Yojana. These orders were grounded in the Directive Principles of Article 47 (raising the level of nutrition) and Article 39(a) (adequate means of livelihood), illustrating the harmonious construction doctrine.

The legislative culmination came with the National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013, which statutorily guarantees subsidised foodgrains to 75 % of the rural and 50 % of the urban population — roughly 813 million beneficiaries. The Act defines “food security” as the supply of the entitled quantity of foodgrains at prices not exceeding ₹3 per kg for rice, ₹2 per kg for wheat and ₹1 per kg for coarse grains. It also creates a grievance redressal mechanism at the district level and mandates social audits. The NFSA was challenged in State of Madhya Pradesh v. Union of India (2015) on the ground that it violated the fiscal autonomy of States; the Court upheld the Act, ruling that Parliament’s power under Article 246 read with Entry 33 of List III (foodstuffs) permits a uniform entitlement framework.

Judicial monitoring continues. In 2020 the Supreme Court directed the Centre to ensure that the NFSA’s coverage is not diluted during the COVID‑19 pandemic, ordering the release of additional foodgrains under the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana. The Court also linked the right to food with the right to health under Article 21, citing the 2021 Common Cause v. Union of India judgment that recognised nutrition as a determinant of the right to health. For aspirants, the key analytical thread is the progression from a judicial declaration of a positive obligation (PUCL) to a statutory entitlement (NFSA) and finally to continuous judicial oversight that treats the Act as a living instrument of the Directive Principles.

The Right to Work and the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act: Constitutional Mandate, Judicial Oversight and Policy Impact

Article 41 of the Directive Principles enjoins the State to secure the right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment. The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005, translates this exhortation into a legally enforceable guarantee of 100 days of wage employment per rural household per financial year. The Act is anchored in Entry 23 of List II (social security and social insurance) and Entry 24 (welfare of labour), and its constitutional validity was upheld by the Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2011), which rejected the argument that the guarantee amounted to an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power.

The Court has repeatedly treated MGNREGA as a “social security legislation” that imposes positive obligations on the State. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2013) the Court issued directions for timely wage payments, transparency through the Management Information System (MIS), and the establishment of independent social audit units. The 2015 amendment to the Act introduced a “wage‑linked” indexation mechanism, tying wage rates to the Consumer Price Index for Agricultural Labourers (CPI‑AL), a move the Court endorsed as consistent with the Directive Principle of Article 43 (living wage).

Financially, the scheme’s allocation rose from ₹11,000 crore in 2006‑07 to ₹73,000 crore in 2023‑24, reflecting the fiscal commitment required to operationalise Article 41. The 15th Finance Commission’s horizontal devolution formula incorporates “demographic performance” and “income distance”, indirectly rewarding States that generate higher person‑days under MGNREGA. Judicial scrutiny has also extended to the “right to work” of migrant workers during the 2020 lockdown; the Supreme Court in Alakh Alok Srivastava v. Union of India (2020) directed the Centre to ensure that MGNREGA worksites remain functional and that wages are paid without delay. The interplay of a justiciable statutory guarantee, continuous judicial mandamus, and Finance Commission incentives makes MGNREGA a rare instance where a Directive Principle has been converted into an enforceable, budget‑backed right.

Technique
A question asks: “Explain how the Supreme Court has transformed the Directive Principle in Article 41 into an enforceable right through MGNREGA, citing the relevant judgments and the role of the Finance Commission.”
Answer: The Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2011) upheld MGNREGA’s constitutional validity, treating it as a legislative fulfilment of Article 41. Subsequent mandamus orders in PUCL v. Union of India (2013) and Alakh Alok Srivastava v. Union of India (2020) compelled timely wage payments, social audits and continuity during emergencies. The 15th Finance Commission’s devolution criteria (income distance, demographic performance) reward States that effectively implement MGNREGA, linking fiscal transfers to the Directive Principle’s realisation. Together, judicial enforcement and fiscal incentives convert the moral exhortation of Article 41 into a justiciable, budget‑backed entitlement.
Exam Day Strategy
When a question links a Directive Principle to a statutory scheme, structure the answer in three layers: (1) constitutional source (Article number), (2) legislative translation (Act, key provisions), (3) judicial and fiscal enforcement (key judgments, Finance Commission role). This three‑step template scores full marks for “interplay” questions.

The Right to Social Security for Unorganised Workers: Constitutional Basis, Legislative Architecture and Judicial Enforcement

Articles 41, 42 and 43 of Part IV collectively obligate the State to secure public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, to provide just and humane conditions of work, and to endeavour to secure a living wage. The Unorganised Workers’ Social Security Act (UWSSA), 2008, was enacted to give effect to these principles for the 93 % of India’s workforce that lacks formal social protection. The Act provides for the formulation of welfare schemes — life and disability cover, health and maternity benefits, old‑age pensions — by the Central and State governments, and establishes National and State Social Security Boards with representation from workers, employers and government.

The constitutional validity of the UWSSA was examined in National Campaign for People’s Right to Information v. Union of India (2016), where the Supreme Court held that the Act is a legitimate exercise of Parliament’s power under Entry 23 of List III (social security) and does not violate the federal distribution of powers. The Court further directed the Centre to notify the “National Social Security Scheme” for unorganised workers within a fixed timeline, treating the legislative mandate as a positive obligation under Article 21 read with the Directive Principles.

Implementation gaps persisted: as of 2022 only 28 % of the estimated 38 crore unorganised workers were registered under the e‑Shram portal launched in 2021. The Supreme Court, in a 2023 suo‑motu proceeding (In re: Social Security for Unorganised Workers), ordered the Ministry of Labour to universalise registration, link the portal with Aadhaar‑based authentication, and ensure portability of benefits across State boundaries. The Court also invoked the 15th Finance Commission’s recommendation for a “social security grant” to States, urging the Union to allocate dedicated funds. This jurisprudence demonstrates how the judiciary uses the Directive Principles as interpretive anchors to convert a welfare statute into an enforceable entitlement, while the Finance Commission provides the fiscal architecture for its realisation.

The Right to Housing as a Component of the Right to Life: Judicial Evolution, Policy Initiatives and the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana

The Supreme Court first recognised shelter as an integral facet of the right to life in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), holding that eviction of pavement dwellers without alternative accommodation violates Article 21. This was reinforced in Shantistar Builders v. Narayan Khimalal Totame (1990) and Chameli Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1996), where the Court declared that the right to shelter includes adequate space, safe structure, clean surroundings and access to civic services. These judgments read Article 21 harmoniously with Article 39(a) (adequate means of livelihood) and Article 47 (standard of living).

Policy translation arrived with the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY), launched in 2015, targeting “Housing for All” by 2022 (later extended to 2024). The scheme comprises two verticals: PMAY‑Urban (credit‑linked subsidy for Economically Weaker Sections, Low‑Income Groups and Middle‑Income Groups) and PMAY‑Gramin (assistance for rural households). As of March 2024, over 2.9 crore houses have been sanctioned under PMAY‑Urban and 2.2 crore under PMAY‑Gramin, with central assistance exceeding ₹1.8 lakh crore. The 15th Finance Commission’s “urban local body grants” and “rural local body grants” are conditional on progress in PMAY implementation, linking fiscal devolution to the Directive Principle of Article 39.

Judicial oversight continues. In Maharashtra v. Union of India (2021) the Supreme Court directed State governments to prioritise in‑situ rehabilitation of slum dwellers over forced evictions, citing the PMAY guidelines. The Court also mandated that the “beneficiary‑led construction” model under PMAY‑Urban be monitored through geo‑tagged photographs to prevent fund diversion. The convergence of a constitutional right (Article 21), a Directive Principle (Article 39), a centrally sponsored scheme (PMAY) and Finance Commission incentives illustrates the full cycle from moral exhortation to justiciable, budget‑backed delivery.

  • Confusing the NFSA’s statutory entitlement with a fundamental right — the Act creates a legal claim, but the constitutional source remains the Directive Principles read with Article 21.
  • Assuming MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of work to every individual — the guarantee is per household, not per person, and is subject to demand‑driven work availability.
  • Treating the Unorganised Workers’ Social Security Act as a fully funded central scheme — it is a framework legislation; actual financing depends on State budgets and Finance Commission grants.
  • Believing PMAY provides free housing to all beneficiaries — the scheme offers interest subsidies and assistance; beneficiaries still bear a share of construction cost.
  • Overlooking the role of the 15th Finance Commission’s conditional grants in enforcing Directive Principles — fiscal incentives are the practical engine that converts judicial mandamus into on‑ground delivery.
  • Missing the distinction between a continuing mandamus (PUCL, MGNREGA) and a one‑time declaratory judgment — the former keeps the Court seized of implementation, the latter does not.
  • Neglecting the requirement to cite the specific Article (21, 39, 41, 47) when linking a socio‑economic scheme to the Constitution — examiners award marks for precise constitutional anchoring.

Article 17 and the Legislative Architecture for the Abolition of Untouchability: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989

Article 17 declares: “Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of Untouchability shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.” It is one of the few Fundamental Rights that operates horizontally — directly binding private individuals — alongside Articles 15(2), 23 and 24. The phrase “in any form” was deliberately chosen to prevent evasion through subterfuge, and “enforcement of any disability” covers social, economic, religious and political disabilities. Article 35 read with Article 17 vests exclusive legislative competence in Parliament to prescribe punishment, rendering State laws on the subject constitutionally suspect unless they conform to the central framework.

The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (originally the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955, renamed and amended in 1976) was the first legislative response. It defines “civil rights” as rights accruing to a person by reason of the abolition of untouchability under Article 17. The Act penalises refusal of access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment, water sources, roads, cremation grounds, and refusal to sell goods or render services. It also criminalises compelling a person to do scavenging or sweeping on the ground of untouchability. The 1976 amendment enhanced punishments (minimum six months imprisonment, fine up to ₹500), made offences cognizable and non‑compoundable, and provided for presumption of offence if committed against a member of a Scheduled Caste. In State of Karnataka v. Appa Balu Ingale (1993), the Supreme Court held that the Act must be interpreted liberally to advance the constitutional objective, and that the burden of proof shifts to the accused once the prosecution establishes a prima facie case of disability enforcement.

The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (PoA Act) was enacted because the PCR Act was deemed inadequate to address violent atrocities. It defines “atrocity” exhaustively (originally 22 offences, expanded to 47 by the 2015 amendment), including forced consumption of obnoxious substances, parading naked, sexual exploitation, fouling water sources, denial of customary rights, and false implication in criminal cases. The Act establishes Special Courts and Exclusive Special Courts for speedy trial, mandates completion of trial within two months, and provides for victim and witness protection, relief and rehabilitation (minimum ₹85,000 to ₹8,25,000 depending on offence). The 2015 amendment added new offences (tonsuring, garlanding with chappals, preventing voting, dedicating women as devadasis), inserted Chapter IV‑A for victim/witness protection, and mandated exclusive Special Courts in districts with high case pendency.

In Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra (2018), a two‑judge bench diluted the Act by requiring preliminary inquiry before FIR registration and anticipatory bail provisions, citing misuse. This triggered widespread protest. Parliament responded with the 2018 amendment (Section 18A), which explicitly restored the original stringency: no preliminary inquiry, no anticipatory bail, and mandatory arrest. In Prithvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India (2020), a three‑judge bench upheld the 2018 amendment, affirming that the legislature can reverse a judicial interpretation that weakens a protective statute, and that the classification of SC/ST victims for stringent procedural safeguards satisfies Article 14.

The Supreme Court in Asiad Workers case (People’s Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India, 1982) extended Article 17’s horizontal reach to private contractors employing forced labour, holding that “untouchability” includes practices analogous to caste‑based degradation. In Devarajiah v. B. Padmanna (1958), the Mysore High Court ruled that “untouchability” is not limited to the literal touching but comprehends social disabilities imposed by custom. The constitutional scheme thus combines a self‑executing Fundamental Right (Article 17), enabling legislation (Article 35), and a rigorous enforcement architecture (Special Courts, victim protection, reversed burden of proof) to convert a moral abolition into a justiciable, enforceable guarantee.

Article 19(1)(b) to (g): The Cluster of Freedoms — Assembly, Association, Movement, Residence, Profession and Their Reasonable Restrictions

Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms to citizens only (non‑citizens cannot claim them). While Article 19(1)(a) (speech) has generated the richest jurisprudence, the remaining five freedoms — (b) assemble peaceably without arms, (c) form associations or unions, (d) move freely throughout the territory of India, (e) reside and settle in any part of the territory of India, (g) practise any profession, or carry on any occupation, trade or business — are governed by distinct restriction clauses in Articles 19(3) to 19(6). Each freedom is a distinct constitutional guarantee; a law restricting one must be tested under its specific restriction clause, not under a generic “reasonable restriction” standard.

Article 19(1)(b) and 19(3): The right to assemble peaceably without arms is subject to restrictions “in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order”. The phrase “public order” was inserted by the First Amendment (1951) to replace the broader “public order or morality”. In Himmat Lal K. Shah v. Commissioner of Police, Ahmedabad (1973), the Court struck down a rule giving the Commissioner unfettered discretion to refuse permission for public meetings, holding that the restriction must be pursuant to a law prescribing objective criteria. In Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018), the Court recognised the right to peaceful protest in designated spaces (Jantar Mantar) but upheld reasonable time‑place‑manner restrictions to balance public order and citizens’ rights. The right does not include the right to strike (see Article 19(1)(c) below).

Article 19(1)(c) and 19(4): The right to form associations or unions includes the right to form trade unions, political parties, companies, partnerships, and societies. Restrictions are permitted “in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order or morality”. In O.K. Ghosh v. E.X. Joseph (1963), the Court held that the right to form a union does not carry a guaranteed right to achieve every objective (e.g., strike). In T.K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu (2003), a Constitution Bench ruled that government employees have no fundamental right to strike; strike by public servants violates the discipline essential to public service. However, the right to form associations includes the right to collective bargaining (implicit in Bharat Iron Works v. State of Karnataka (1979)). The 2015 amendment to the Trade Unions Act, 1926, and the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, regulate registration and recognition but do not alter the constitutional floor.

Articles 19(1)(d), (e) and 19(5): Freedom of movement and residence throughout India are twin freedoms restricted only “in the interests of the general public or for the protection of the interests of any Scheduled Tribe”. The Scheduled Tribe protection clause (added by the First Amendment) enables laws restricting entry into tribal areas (e.g., the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873, and State laws under the Fifth/Sixth Schedules). In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Kaushalya (1963), the Court upheld an externment order under the UP Gangsters Act as a reasonable restriction in the interest of the general public, provided the order is based on specific facts and not vague apprehensions. In Chambara v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1968), the Court struck down a blanket ban on entry of non‑tribals into a tribal market, holding that the restriction must be proportionate to the protection of tribal interests.

Article 19(1)(g) and 19(6): This is the most litigated of the cluster. The right to practise any profession, or carry on any occupation, trade or business, is subject to restrictions “in the interests of the general public”, and “in particular” — (i) professional or technical qualifications necessary for practising any profession, or (ii) state monopoly (carrying on by the State, or by a corporation owned or controlled by the State, of any trade, business, industry or service). The First Amendment (1951) added the “professional qualifications” and “state monopoly” limbs. In Excel Wear v. Union of India (1978), the Court held that the right to carry on business includes the right to close it down, subject to statutory obligations (Industrial Disputes Act). In P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005), a seven‑judge bench ruled that unaided private professional colleges have the right to admit students and fix fees subject to regulation (not control) by the State, balancing Article 19(1)(g) with Article 14. In K.T. Plantation v. State of Karnataka (2011), the Court clarified that “regulation” under Article 19(6) must not amount to “prohibition” unless the law expressly authorises prohibition in public interest. The GST regime (101st Amendment, 2016) and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 are modern examples of laws imposing “professional qualifications” (GST practitioners, insolvency professionals) and restructuring the trade landscape, testable under Article 19(6) for reasonableness.

Worked Example: Restriction Clause Mapping
A State law prohibits non‑residents from carrying on the business of sand mining in river beds within the State. The law is challenged under Article 19(1)(g). Identify the correct restriction clause, the applicable test, and the likely outcome with one supporting precedent.
Restriction clause: Article 19(6) — “in the interests of the general public” (and possibly “professional or technical qualifications” if the law prescribes licensing). Test: The restriction must be reasonable, i.e., have a rational nexus with the object (public interest in conserving river ecology, preventing illegal mining) and not be excessive or discriminatory. The classification between residents and non‑residents must satisfy Article 14 (reasonable classification: intelligible differentia + rational nexus). Likely outcome: If the law is a total prohibition on non‑residents without a licensing regime based on qualifications, it risks being struck down as discriminatory and excessive. In K.T. Plantation v. State of Karnataka (2011), the Court held that a total ban on private tree felling (while allowing State corporations) violated Article 19(1)(g) because it amounted to prohibition masquerading as regulation. A residency‑based ban would similarly be suspect unless justified by a compelling local interest (e.g., tribal protection under Article 19(5) read with Fifth Schedule), which does not apply to sand mining. The State may regulate through licensing, environmental clearances, and royalties applicable equally to all citizens.
Exam‑Day Strategy: Article 19 Cluster
Memorise the restriction clause for each sub‑article: (b)→19(3), (c)→19(4), (d)&(e)→19(5), (g)→19(6). In MCQs, a law restricting movement of non‑tribals into a Scheduled Area is tested under Article 19(5) (ST protection), not 19(6). In Mains, when a question asks “examine the constitutionality of a law restricting X”, first identify the specific freedom (b–g), then cite the exact restriction clause, then apply the twin test: (1) legislative competence (Union/State/Concurrent List), (2) reasonableness under the specific clause (nexus, proportionality, non‑discrimination). Always name the precedent that matches the freedom: Himmat Lal (assembly), Rangarajan (association/strike), Kaushalya (movement/residence), Excel Wear / K.T. Plantation (profession/trade).

Articles 31A, 31B and 31C: The Constitutional Shield for Agrarian Reform and the Ninth Schedule Jurisprudence from Shankari Prasad to I.R. Coelho

The First Amendment (1951) introduced Articles 31A and 31B to insulate land‑reform laws from judicial invalidation on Fundamental Rights grounds (then Articles 14, 19, 31). Article 31A saves five categories of laws: (i) acquisition of estates or rights therein by the State; (ii) taking over management of property by the State for a limited period; (iii) amalgamation of corporations; (iv) extinguishment or modification of rights of managing agents, secretaries, directors; (v) extinguishment or modification of mining leases. The phrase “estate” has been expansively interpreted to include ryotwari lands (Kochuni v. State of Madras, 1960), jagirs, inams, and muafi grants. Article 31A(2) defines “estate” by reference to State law, giving States definitional flexibility. The Fourth Amendment (1955) extended Article 31A to cover “rights in or over an estate” and “intermediaries”. The Seventeenth Amendment (1964) added “ryotwari lands” explicitly and placed 44 State Acts in the Ninth Schedule.

Article 31B validates, “without prejudice to the generality of Article 31A”, any Act or Regulation specified in the Ninth Schedule from judicial review for inconsistency with Fundamental Rights. Originally 13 Acts (mostly land reform), the Schedule now contains 284 entries (as of 2024), including laws on reservations, land ceiling, essential commodities, and even the Tamil Nadu Backward Classes Act (69% quota). The validation is retrospective: the Acts are deemed never to have been void.

Article 31C, inserted by the Twenty‑fifth Amendment (1971), originally provided that no law giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing the principles in Article 39(b) and (c) (distribution of material resources, prevention of concentration of wealth) shall be deemed void for inconsistency with Articles 14, 19 or 31. The Forty‑second Amendment (1976) expanded Article 31C to cover all Directive Principles (Articles 36–51), giving them blanket primacy over Articles 14, 19 and 31. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down this expansion as destroying the basic structure (judicial review and balance between FRs and DPSPs). The Court restored Article 31C to its pre‑1976 form: protection only for laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c).

The Ninth Schedule jurisprudence evolved through three phases. Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1964) upheld Parliament’s power to amend Fundamental Rights. Golaknath (1967) reversed this, holding that amendments are “law” under Article 13(2). The Twenty‑fourth Amendment (1971) restored the amending power. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic structure doctrine: Parliament cannot amend the Constitution to destroy its basic features. Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) drew a line: Acts placed in the Ninth Schedule before 24 April 1973 (date of Kesavananda judgment) are immune from challenge; Acts added after that date are open to judicial review on basic structure grounds. I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) (nine‑judge bench) affirmed Waman Rao and held that every Ninth Schedule law must be tested against the basic structure — no blanket immunity. The Court applied the “rights test” (does the law abrogate a basic structure right?) and the “essence test” (does it destroy the essence of a fundamental right?). The Tamil Nadu 69% quota law (in Ninth Schedule since 1994) was remitted for fresh scrutiny; the Madras High Court later upheld it in K. V. S. S. P. Varma v. State of Tamil Nadu (2019) as not violating the basic structure, given the State’s empirical justification.

Current position: Articles 31A and 31B remain fully operative. Article 31C protects only laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c). Ninth Schedule laws post‑April 1973 are subject to basic structure review (I.R. Coelho). The doctrine balances the constitutional mandate for agrarian reform (Article 39) with the supremacy of the Constitution’s core identity.

Article 300A: The Right to Property as a Constitutional Right — “Authority of Law”, Compensation and the Judicial Trajectory After 1978

The Forty‑fourth Amendment (1978) repealed Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, removing the right to property from the Fundamental Rights chapter, and inserted Article 300A: “No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.” Property ceased to be a fundamental right; it became a constitutional (legal) right. Consequently, (i) no Article 32 remedy for its violation; (ii) no guaranteed compensation (unlike old Article 31(2) which required “compensation” — later “amount” after the Fourth Amendment); (iii) the State’s power of eminent domain is now constrained only by the requirement of a valid law (legislative competence + non‑arbitrariness) and, arguably, by the principle that deprivation must be for a public purpose.

The phrase “authority of law” is narrower than “procedure established by law” (Article 21 pre‑Maneka Gandhi). It requires a validly enacted statute (or subordinate legislation authorised by statute), not mere executive fiat. In Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat (1995), the Court held that Article 300A protects against executive deprivation without legal authority, but does not fetter the legislature’s power to acquire property for public purpose. The law must be within legislative competence (Entries 42, 45, 47 of List III; Entry 18 of List II) and not violate other constitutional provisions (e.g., Article 14).

On compensation: The Constitution no longer mandates compensation. However, a series of judgments has read a “fair” or “reasonable” compensation requirement into “authority of law” as a component of non‑arbitrariness under Article 14. In K.T. Plantation v. State of Karnataka (2011), the Court stated that while Article 300A does not expressly guarantee compensation, a law that deprives property without any compensation may be arbitrary and therefore violative of Article 14. In Kolkata Municipal Corporation v. Bimal Kumar Shah (2019), the Court held that “authority of law” implies a law that provides for a fair procedure, including determination of compensation on relevant principles (market value, solatium, interest). In Project Director, NHAI v. M. Hakeem (2021), the Court upheld the National Highways Act, 1956, compensation mechanism (reference to Collector, appeal to Arbitrator) as satisfying “authority of law”.

On public purpose: The judiciary treats “public purpose” as justiciable. In State of Haryana v. Mukesh Kumar (2011), the Court held that acquisition for a private company (even for a “public purpose” declared by the State) requires stricter scrutiny; the 2013 LARR Act (Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act) codified this by requiring 70%/80% consent for private/PPP projects and a Social Impact Assessment. The 2015 Ordinance (which lapsed) sought to dilute consent and SIA; the current law remains the 2013 Act as amended by State laws.

On adverse possession: In Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2020), the Supreme Court held that the State cannot perfect title by adverse possession against a citizen, as that would amount to deprivation of property without authority of law. The State’s title must originate in a valid acquisition law.

On regulatory taking: In M/s. K. Raheja Corp. v. State of Maharashtra (2022), the Court distinguished “deprivation” (total loss of title/possession) from “regulation” (restriction on use). Regulation under police power (town planning, environmental laws) does not attract Article 300A unless it amounts to constructive deprivation (total wipe‑out of economic value). The test is the “substantial deprivation” standard from Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City (US, 1978), referenced approvingly.

Thus, Article 300A, though not a fundamental right, has acquired a robust judicial penumbra: valid law, public purpose, non‑arbitrariness, and fair compensation (via Article 14) are now the constitutional floor for any deprivation of property.

The Classification and Enforceability of Directive Principles: Articles 36–51, Judicial Techniques and the Role of Article 37

Article 36 defines “State” for Part IV identically to Article 12 (Part III). Article 37 declares: “The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.” This non‑justiciability clause is the textual anchor for the traditional view that DPSPs are moral exhortations. However, judicial innovation has converted many DPSPs into enforceable norms through four principal techniques.

Classification of DPSPs (by thematic origin):
Socialist: Article 38 (social order), 39 (policy principles — (a) adequate livelihood, (b) distribution of material resources, (c) prevention of concentration of wealth, (d) equal pay, (e) protection of workers/children, (f) child development), 39A (equal justice/free legal aid), 41 (right to work/education/public assistance), 42 (just/humane conditions), 43 (living wage), 43A (workers’ participation), 43B (cooperatives — added by 97th Amendment, 2011), 47 (nutrition/standard of living).
Gandhian: Article 40 (village panchayats), 43B (cooperatives), 46 (SC/ST/weaker sections), 47 (prohibition), 48 (agriculture/animal husbandry).
Liberal‑Intellectual: Article 44 (uniform civil code), 45 (early childhood care — amended by 86th Amendment, 2002), 48A (environment — added by 42nd Amendment, 1976), 49 (monuments), 50 (separation of judiciary), 51 (international peace).

Judicial Techniques for Enforcement:
1. Harmonious Construction (Kesavananda, Minerva Mills): Fundamental Rights and DPSPs are complementary; courts must interpret FRs in light of DPSPs. Article 21 expanded to include socio‑economic rights (food, health, shelter, education) by reading Articles 39, 41, 47 into it.
2. Reading DPSPs into Statutory Duties: When Parliament enacts a law to implement a DPSP (e.g., NFSA 2013 for Article 47, MGNREGA 2005 for Article 41, LSA Act 1987 for Article 39A), the statutory duty becomes judicially enforceable. The Court issues continuing mandamus to monitor implementation (PUCL v. Union — food; Swaraj Abhiyan v. Union — drought relief).
3. Public Trust Doctrine (M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath, 1997): Article 48A (environment) imposes a duty on the State as trustee of natural resources; breach is actionable under Article 226/32.
4. Article 38(2) — Minimising Inequalities: Used in Indra Sawhney (1992) and M. Nagaraj (2006) to justify creamy layer exclusion and quantifiable data for promotions.
5. Article 39(b)(c) — Material Resources: In State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977) and Mafatlal Industries v. Union of India (1997), the Court held that “material resources of the community” includes private resources; nationalisation laws are tested under Article 31C (pre‑1976 version).
6. Article 44 — UCC: Judicial signals in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano (1985), Sarla Mudgal (1995), John Vallamattom (2003), and the 21st Law Commission Report (2018) and 22nd Law Commission Report (2023) urging a UCC; not judicially enforceable but a persistent interpretive nudge.
7. Article 50 — Separation of Judiciary: Enforced in Judicial Officers’ Association v. Union of India (1994) and All India Judges Association v. Union of India (2002) (pay, independence).
8. Article 51 — International Law: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) (CEDAW → sexual harassment guidelines), Apparel Export Promotion Council v. A.K. Chopra (1999), National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014) (Yogyakarta Principles → transgender rights).

Amendments expanding DPSPs: 42nd Amendment (1976) added 39A, 43A, 48A. 44th Amendment (1978) added 38(2). 86th Amendment (2002) substituted Article 45 (early childhood care) and inserted Article 21A. 97th Amendment (2011) added 43B (cooperatives) — partially struck down in Union of India v. Rajendra Shah (2021) for lack of State ratification (affecting State List entries). The 15th Finance Commission’s conditional grants (urban/rural local body grants tied to PMAY, sanitation, water supply) operationalise Articles 39, 47, 48A through fiscal federalism.

The contemporary position: DPSPs are not directly justiciable, but they are the interpretive lens for Fundamental Rights, the constitutional mandate for legislation, and the benchmark for judicial review of State action. The “non‑justiciable” label in Article 37 describes the absence of a direct cause of action, not the absence of constitutional force.

  • Trap 1: Confusing Article 17’s horizontal application with Article 15(2) — Article 17 is self‑executing against private individuals; Article 15(2) applies to “shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment” and “wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads” maintained wholly or partly by State funds or dedicated to public use.
  • Trap 2: Assuming Article 19(1)(c) includes a fundamental right to strike — it does not (T.K. Rangarajan, 2003); the right is to form associations, not to achieve every objective through industrial action.
  • Trap 3: Citing Article 19(6) for restrictions on movement or residence — those fall under Article 19(5) (general public / ST protection). Article 19(6) applies only to profession, occupation, trade, business.
  • Trap 4: Believing the Ninth Schedule grants absolute immunity — post‑April 1973 entries are subject to basic structure review (I.R. Coelho, 2007); pre‑1973 entries are immune but the distinction is date‑specific, not content‑specific.
  • Trap 5: Claiming Article 31C gives primacy to all DPSPs over Articles 14, 19, 31 — Minerva Mills (1980) struck down the 42nd Amendment expansion; Article 31C now protects only laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c).
  • Trap 6: Arguing Article 300A guarantees compensation — the Constitution does not; compensation is a statutory requirement (LARR Act 2013) or an Article 14 non‑arbitrariness implication (K.T. Plantation, Kolkata Municipal Corp), not a constitutional mandate.
  • Trap 7: Treating Article 37 as rendering DPSPs irrelevant — Article 37 declares them “fundamental in governance” and a “duty of the State”; they are the interpretive key to Article 21 expansion, the basis for continuing mandamus on welfare statutes, and the standard for fiscal conditionalities (Finance Commission grants).

The advanced sections above complete the doctrinal architecture linking Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties with the judicial techniques, legislative frameworks and fiscal mechanisms that operationalise them in contemporary constitutional practice.

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation under Fundamental Rights

Delegated legislation — rules, regulations, notifications and orders made by the executive under a statutory power — is subject to the same constitutional scrutiny as primary legislation. Article 13(3) defines “law” to include “any ordinance, order, bye‑law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law”. Consequently, any delegated instrument that infringes a Fundamental Right can be struck down under Article 13(2). The Supreme Court has evolved a two‑tier test: (i) the parent statute must not confer excessive or uncontrolled legislative power (the “excessive delegation” doctrine), and (ii) the delegated instrument itself must not violate Part III. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1954) the Court held that a rule made under the Defence of India Act which curtailed freedom of speech without reasonable nexus to the statutory purpose was void. Later, in State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kasab Jamat (2005) a rule under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 that banned the slaughter of bulls and bullocks was invalidated for violating Article 19(1)(g) because the parent Act did not authorise a total prohibition. The Court also applies the “sub‑delegation” principle: a delegate cannot further delegate its rule‑making power unless the parent statute expressly permits it (see Hamid Khan v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 1972). Procedural ultra vires — failure to follow mandatory consultation or publication requirements — also renders a rule void (e.g., Union of India v. G. S. Atwal, 1995). The practical upshot is that every subordinate legislation must be tested against the twin yardsticks of statutory authority and constitutional compatibility; a rule that passes the first but fails the second is struck down without the need to invalidate the parent Act.

The Constitutional Validity of Sedition (Section 124A IPC) and Freedom of Speech

Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code criminalises “whoever, by words, either spoken or written, or by signs, or by visible representation, or otherwise, brings or attempts to bring into hatred or contempt, or excites or attempts to excite disaffection towards the Government established by law”. The provision has been challenged repeatedly under Article 19(1)(a). In Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962) the Supreme Court upheld the section but read it down: only speech that has a “tendency to create public disorder” or “incitement to violence” constitutes sedition. Mere criticism of government policies, however strong, was excluded. The Court thus imported a “public order” requirement into the statutory language, aligning it with the reasonable restriction under Article 19(2). In 2022, a three‑judge bench in S. G. Vombatkere v. Union of India directed the Centre and States to keep all pending sedition cases in abeyance and refrain from registering fresh FIRs under Section 124A, effectively putting the law in a state of suspended operation while the legislature reconsidered its retention. The 22nd Law Commission (2023) recommended repeal, arguing that the provision is a colonial relic incompatible with a mature democracy and that existing laws on unlawful activities (UAPA) and public order suffice. The Court’s interim order and the Commission’s report together signal a constitutional trajectory towards either a drastic narrowing or outright abolition of sedition, reinforcing the principle that restrictions on speech must be narrowly tailored, necessary and proportionate.

Technique: Applying the Kedar Nath Test
A journalist writes an editorial criticising the Prime Minister’s economic policy, calling it “disastrous for the poor”. The state files an FIR under Section 124A. Decide the constitutional validity of the FIR.
Under Kedar Nath Singh, sedition requires incitement to violence or a tendency to create public disorder. Mere harsh criticism of government policy, without any call for violent action, does not meet this threshold. Therefore the FIR violates Article 19(1)(a) and is liable to be quashed. The correct answer: the FIR is unconstitutional because the speech does not satisfy the “public order” element required by the Kedar Nath test.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a speech act amounts to sedition, first identify the Kedar Nath “public disorder/incitement to violence” test. If the facts show only criticism, dissent or advocacy of unpopular ideas, answer that the restriction fails the Article 19(2) proportionality requirement. Cite Kedar Nath (1962) and the 2022 Vombatkere interim order for full marks.

The Right to Life and the Death Penalty: Constitutional Limits, Judicial Trends and the ‘Rarest of Rare’ Doctrine

Article 21 guarantees that no person shall be deprived of life except according to “procedure established by law”. The Supreme Court in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) held that the death penalty is constitutional only if imposed in the “rarest of rare” cases where the alternative of life imprisonment is “unquestionably foreclosed”. The Court laid down a two‑stage sentencing framework: (i) the trial court must record “special reasons” for death, and (ii) the appellate court must independently assess aggravating and mitigating circumstances. In Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (1983) the Court enumerated illustrative aggravating factors (e.g., brutality, multiple murders) and mitigating factors (young age, mental illness, lack of prior record). Subsequent jurisprudence has tightened the doctrine: Santosh Kumar Bariyar v. State of Maharashtra (2009) warned against mechanical application and demanded a “principled sentencing” approach. In 2022, the Court in Manoj v. State of Madhya Pradesh commuted several death sentences, emphasising that the “rarest of rare” standard requires a holistic evaluation of the convict’s socio‑economic background, possibility of reformation and the absence of a “death‑worthy” crime. The 262nd Law Commission Report (2015) recommended abolition of the death penalty for all offences except terrorism‑related crimes, citing international trends and the risk of irreversible error. While the legislature has not acted, the judicial trajectory shows a progressive narrowing of capital punishment, aligning the “procedure established by law” with the substantive due‑process values of fairness, dignity and proportionality inherent in Article 21.

The Right to Freedom of Religion and Anti‑Conversion Laws: Constitutional Challenges and Judicial Approach

Several States — Uttar Pradesh (2021), Madhya Pradesh (2021), Himachal Pradesh (2019) — have enacted “Freedom of Religion” Acts that criminalise conversion by “misrepresentation, force, undue influence, coercion, allurement or by any fraudulent means”. These laws require prior notice to the district magistrate and place the burden of proof on the accused. The constitutional challenge centres on Articles 25 (freedom of conscience and propagation) and 26 (management of religious affairs). In Stanislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1977) the Supreme Court upheld an earlier anti‑conversion law, holding that “propagation” does not include a right to convert another person. However, the Court also recognised that voluntary conversion is protected. Recent jurisprudence has nuanced this position. In Hadiya v. State of Kerala (2018) the Court affirmed an adult woman’s autonomy to choose her faith and partner, stating that “the right to choose a religion is part of the right to privacy and dignity under Article 21”. The Allahabad High Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. K. K. Mishra (2022) struck down certain provisions of the Uttar Pradesh law for violating Article 14 (arbitrariness) and Article 21 (disproportionate burden). The Supreme Court, in a 2023 reference, observed that while the State may regulate fraudulent conversions, any law must be narrowly tailored, provide procedural safeguards and not target inter‑faith marriages per se. The emerging judicial consensus is that anti‑conversion statutes must satisfy the triple test of legality, necessity and proportionality; blanket criminalisation of conversion without proof of coercion fails this test and infringes the core of religious freedom.

The National Commission for Minorities: Constitutional Basis, Powers and Effectiveness in Protecting Articles 29‑30

The National Commission for Minorities (NCM) was constituted under the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992 — a statutory body, not a constitutional one like the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (Article 338) or Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A). Its mandate flows from the Directive Principle in Article 38(2) (minimising inequalities) and the substantive rights in Articles 29 (protection of language, script, culture) and 30 (right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions). The NCM comprises a Chairperson, a Vice‑Chairperson and five members appointed by the Central Government. Its powers include: (i) investigating specific complaints of deprivation of minority rights; (ii) monitoring the implementation of constitutional safeguards; (iii) making recommendations to the Central and State Governments; and (iv) reviewing the working of minority‑related schemes. In practice, the Commission’s recommendations are advisory; compliance depends on political will. The Supreme Court in National Commission for Minorities v. Union of India (2005) held that the Government must “give due consideration” to the Commission’s reports, but stopped short of making them binding. The 2021 amendment to the Act expanded the Commission’s jurisdiction to include the newly notified “Jain” community as a minority. Critics argue that the lack of constitutional status, limited enforcement teeth and dependence on the executive for appointments undermine its independence. Strengthening the NCM — by granting it constitutional status under a new Article 338B, providing suo‑motu inquiry powers and making its recommendations binding on the executive — would align the institutional architecture with the constitutional promise of minority protection under Articles 29 and 30.

  • Assuming that delegated legislation is immune from fundamental‑rights challenge because it is “subordinate” — Article 13(3) expressly includes rules and notifications within “law”.
  • Arguing that Kedar Nath Singh (1962) gives the State unfettered power to prosecute any criticism — the judgment actually narrows sedition to incitement of violence or public disorder.
  • Claiming the “rarest of rare” doctrine is a rigid formula — Bachan Singh requires a case‑by‑case balancing of aggravating and mitigating factors, not a mechanical checklist.
  • Believing anti‑conversion laws are per se constitutional because Stanislaus (1977) upheld them — later rulings (Hadiya, 2018; UP High Court, 2022) have subjected such laws to strict proportionality scrutiny.
  • Treating the National Commission for Minorities as a constitutional body with binding powers — it is statutory, its recommendations are advisory, and it lacks suo‑motu enforcement authority.
  • Confusing the burden of proof in anti‑conversion cases — recent statutes shift the burden to the accused, a reversal that courts have flagged as potentially violative of Article 21.
  • Overlooking the procedural ultra vires ground for striking down delegated legislation — failure to follow mandatory consultation or publication renders a rule void even if substantively valid.

The advanced sections above complete the doctrinal architecture linking Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties with the judicial techniques, legislative frameworks and fiscal mechanisms that operationalise them in contemporary constitutional practice.

The Constitutional Framework for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities: Article 21, 41, 46 and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016

The Constitution does not contain a standalone disability right, but the Supreme Court has read the guarantee of life and personal liberty under Article 21 to include the right to live with dignity, which encompasses accessibility, non‑discrimination and reasonable accommodation. Article 41 directs the State to make effective provision for securing the right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of disablement, while Article 46 obliges the State to promote the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections, a category that expressly includes persons with disabilities.

The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD Act) gave legislative teeth to these directives and to India’s obligations under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD), ratified in 2007. The Act expands the definition of disability from seven to twenty‑one conditions, mandates 5 % reservation in higher‑education institutions and 4 % reservation in government employment, and imposes a duty on all public and private establishments to provide barrier‑free access, accessible information and communication technology, and reasonable accommodation.

Judicial enforcement has been robust. In Jeeja Ghosh v. Union of India (2016) the Court held that the right to travel by air without discrimination is a facet of Article 21. National Federation of Blind v. Union of India (2021) extended reservation in promotions to persons with benchmark disabilities, interpreting the RPwD Act purposively. Vikash Kumar v. Union Public Service Commission (2021) recognised the duty to provide scribes and extra time in competitive examinations as reasonable accommodation. The 2022 decision in Disability Rights Group v. Union of India directed all state governments to audit public buildings for compliance with the Accessible India Campaign standards within a fixed timeline.

Outstanding issues include the gap between statutory reservation and actual appointment, the lack of a dedicated disability budget in most states, and the limited judicial recognition of intersectional discrimination (e.g., disability combined with gender or caste). The next phase of litigation is likely to test whether the State’s positive obligations under Articles 41 and 46 can be enforced through continuing mandamus, thereby converting directive principles into justiciable entitlements for a historically marginalised group.

The National Green Tribunal and the Judicial Enforcement of Environmental Directive Principles under Article 48A and Article 51A(g)
