The National Green Tribunal (NGT), constituted under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, is a specialised environmental court vested with original and appellate jurisdiction over substantial questions relating to the enforcement of environmental laws. Its mandate flows directly from Article 48A (the State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment) and Article 51A(g) (it shall be the duty of every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment). The NGT applies the principles of sustainable development, polluter pays, and precautionary principle — doctrines that the Supreme Court elevated to constitutional status in Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) and M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1997).

Unlike ordinary civil courts, the NGT can grant restitutionary relief (restoration of ecology), impose exemplary damages, and issue continuing mandamus to monitor compliance. Landmark NGT orders include the Yamuna Pollution case (2015) where the Tribunal directed a time‑bound cleanup plan and constituted a monitoring committee; the Bellandur Lake case (2018) imposing heavy penalties on defaulting industries and municipal bodies; and the Western Ghats case (2020) restricting mining and construction in ecologically sensitive zones. The Tribunal’s decisions are appealable only to the Supreme Court, ensuring a streamlined appellate route.

The NGT has also interpreted Article 21 to include the right to a clean environment, thereby bridging fundamental rights and directive principles. In Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991) the Supreme Court had already recognised this link; the NGT operationalises it by providing a forum where citizens can enforce the duty under Article 51A(g) against both State and private polluters. However, challenges persist: limited benches, vacancies, and the lack of suo‑motu power to initiate proceedings on its own motion (a power the Supreme Court possesses) constrain its reach. The 2021 amendment to the NGT Act, which expanded the Tribunal’s jurisdiction to include disputes under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and the Forest Rights Act, 2006, signals a legislative intent to strengthen this institutional mechanism.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The NGT can take suo‑motu cognisance of environmental disputes under the NGT Act, 2010.” True or False?
False. The NGT Act, 2010 does not confer suo‑motu jurisdiction on the Tribunal. It can entertain only applications or appeals filed by aggrieved persons, the Central Government, State Governments, or statutory authorities. The Supreme Court, under Article 32, retains suo‑motu power, but the NGT does not.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links a specialised tribunal to a directive principle, first identify the constitutional source (Article 48A/51A(g)), then recall the enabling statute (NGT Act, 2010) and the specific powers (restitution, exemplary damages, continuing mandamus). Distinguish between the Tribunal’s statutory jurisdiction and the Supreme Court’s constitutional jurisdiction — this distinction is a favourite trap.

The Doctrine of Substantive Due Process in Indian Constitutional Law: Myth or Emerging Reality?

The Indian Constitution originally adopted the phrase “procedure established by law” in Article 21, deliberately rejecting the American “due process of law” clause. In A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) the Court held that any procedure enacted by a competent legislature satisfied Article 21, irrespective of its fairness. The turning point came in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where a seven‑judge bench read “procedure” as “fair, just and reasonable”, thereby importing procedural due process into Indian jurisprudence.

Whether this evolution amounts to substantive due process — the power to strike down legislation for violating fundamental values beyond procedural fairness — remains contested. The Supreme Court has consistently declined to adopt the label. In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) the Court recognised privacy as an intrinsic part of liberty under Article 21, but grounded the reasoning in the “reasonable expectation of privacy” test and the proportionality standard under Article 14, not in a freestanding substantive due process doctrine. Similarly, Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) and Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) invalidated colonial‑era provisions on dignity and autonomy grounds, yet the opinions emphasised constitutional morality and the basic structure rather than a substantive due process clause.

Scholars such as Upendra Baxi and Gautam Bhatia argue that the cumulative effect of Article 14 (equality), Article 19 (freedoms), and the expanded Article 21 creates a functional equivalent of substantive due process, allowing the Court to review the substantive reasonableness of laws affecting life, liberty, and dignity. The counter‑view, articulated by Justice Chandrachud in his Puttaswamy concurrence, warns that importing an unenumerated substantive due process standard would undermine legislative supremacy and the basic structure doctrine. As of 2024, the Court’s technique remains “procedural due process plus proportionality”, a pragmatic synthesis that achieves substantive protection without formally adopting the American doctrine.

The Role of the Election Commission of India in Safeguarding Political Rights under Article 324 and its Link to Fundamental Rights

Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice‑President in the Election Commission of India (ECI). This constitutional mandate is the institutional backbone of the political rights guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech and expression), Article 19(1)(b) (peaceful assembly), Article 19(1)(c) (formation of associations), and Article 326 (universal adult suffrage). The ECI’s powers include the preparation and revision of electoral rolls, the recognition and registration of political parties, the enforcement of the Model Code of Conduct, and the monitoring of election expenditure.

In Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner (1978) the Supreme Court described the ECI’s powers as “plenary” and “untrammelled” within the constitutional scheme, subject only to judicial review for mala fides or arbitrariness. The Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2000) upheld the Model Code as a legitimate exercise of the Commission’s authority to ensure a level playing field. In Subramaniam Balaji v. State of Tamil Nadu (2013) the Court restrained the distribution of freebies during elections, linking the ECI’s regulatory role to the purity of the electoral process under Article 324.

Recent developments include the Election Commission (Conditions of Service of Election Commissioners and Transaction of Business) Act, 2023, which seeks to insulate the appointment and tenure of Election Commissioners from executive interference, thereby strengthening the Commission’s independence — a prerequisite for the effective enforcement of political rights. The ECI’s directive to political parties to disclose criminal antecedents of candidates (2020) and its use of the cVIGIL mobile app for real‑time violation reporting illustrate the operationalisation of Article 324 in the digital age. The Commission’s ability to de‑register parties that fail to contest elections or that violate the Constitution’s secular ethos further connects its statutory functions to the fundamental rights of citizens to fair representation and political participation.

The Constitutional Implications of the Anti‑Defection Law (Tenth Schedule) on the Freedom of Speech and Association under Article 19

The Tenth Schedule, inserted by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment (1985), disqualifies a legislator who voluntarily gives up membership of his party or votes contrary to the party whip. While aimed at curbing political defections, the law directly implicates Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech) and Article 19(1)(c) (freedom of association) because it penalises a legislator’s dissenting vote or speech in the House.

In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) a Constitution Bench upheld the Tenth Schedule’s validity but struck down the provision barring judicial review of the Speaker’s decision, rendering it subject to Article 136 and Article 226/227. The Court held that the Speaker acts as a tribunal and must decide disqualification petitions within a reasonable time. Subsequent rulings refined the framework: Rajendra Singh Rana v. Swami Prasad Maurya (2007) clarified that a “split” in a party requires at least one‑third of its legislators to constitute a separate group; Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur Legislative Assembly (2023) imposed a three‑month outer limit for the Speaker to decide disqualification petitions, failing which the matter may be referred to the Election Commission.

The tension persists. Critics argue that the whip system reduces legislators to party delegates, eroding the deliberative function of legislatures and the individual’s right to conscience. Proponents contend that stable governments and party accountability outweigh individual dissent. The Supreme Court has so far balanced the competing interests by insisting on procedural fairness (timely decision, reasoned order) while leaving the substantive policy choice to Parliament. A future challenge may test whether the anti‑defection law, as applied to voting on a no‑confidence motion or constitutional amendment bills, constitutes an unreasonable restriction on Article 19(1)(a) and (c) under the proportionality standard articulated in Modern Dental College v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2016).

  • Assuming the RPwD Act, 2016 automatically guarantees reservation in private sector jobs — the Act mandates reservation only in government establishments; private employers are encouraged but not compelled.
  • Believing the NGT possesses suo‑motu jurisdiction — the NGT Act, 2010 does not confer such power; only the Supreme Court can initiate environmental proceedings on its own motion.
  • Equating procedural due process under Article 21 with substantive due process — Indian jurisprudence has adopted “fair, just and reasonable procedure” plus proportionality, not a freestanding substantive due process doctrine.
  • Thinking the Election Commission can deregister a political party solely for ideological reasons — deregistration is permissible only for failure to contest elections or for violating the Constitution’s secular and democratic principles, not for policy disagreements.
  • Treating the Speaker’s disqualification decision under the Tenth Schedule as final and non‑reviewable — Kihoto Hollohan (1992) expressly subjected it to judicial review for mala fides, perversity, or violation of natural justice.
  • Overlooking the three‑month deadline for Speaker’s decision on disqualification petitions — the 2023 Manipur Assembly judgment made this timeline mandatory; non‑compliance invites judicial intervention.
  • Confusing the Model Code of Conduct with statutory law — the Code is an executive instruction issued by the ECI; its violation attracts ECI sanctions but not criminal liability unless backed by a specific statute.

These advanced sections complete the doctrinal architecture linking Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties with the judicial techniques, legislative frameworks and institutional mechanisms that operationalise them in contemporary constitutional practice.

Article 17 and the Legislative Architecture Against Untouchability: From Constitutional Prohibition to the Atrocities Act

Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. The enforcement of any disability arising out of untouchability is an offence punishable in accordance with law. Unlike most fundamental rights which operate vertically against the State, Article 17 operates horizontally — it binds private individuals and creates a positive obligation on the State to enact penal legislation. The Constitution itself does not define "untouchability"; the Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Appa Balu Ingale (1993) held that the term must be understood in its historical and social context, referring to the social disabilities imposed on certain castes by reason of their birth in the traditional caste hierarchy. The Court emphasised that Article 17 is not a mere declaration but a mandatory directive to the State to eradicate the practice root and branch.

The first legislative response was the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955, renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act (PCR Act) in 1976. The PCR Act prescribed punishment for enforcing religious, social, and occupational disabilities — such as denial of entry to temples, shops, hotels, hospitals, or refusal to sell goods or render services. However, the Act suffered from low conviction rates, compoundable offences, and inadequate deterrence. The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (PoA Act) was enacted to address these gaps. It defined specific "atrocities" — including forced consumption of inedible substances, parading naked, sexual exploitation, fouling water sources, and social boycott — and established Special Courts, mandatory minimum punishments, and the presumption of offence if the accused was acquainted with the victim. The 2015 amendment (effective 2016) expanded the list of atrocities to include tonsuring of head, garlanding with footwear, preventing candidates from filing nominations, and damaging property. It also added Chapter IVA on rights of victims and witnesses, and mandated exclusive Special Courts and Special Public Prosecutors.

Judicial interpretation has been pivotal. In State of M.P. v. Ram Krishna Balothia (1995), the Supreme Court held that the PoA Act creates a distinct offence not subsumed by the IPC, and the two can run concurrently. In Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra (2018), a two-judge bench diluted the mandatory arrest provision (Section 18) and allowed anticipatory bail, citing misuse. This triggered widespread protest and a review petition. In Prithvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India (2020), a three-judge bench restored the pre-2018 position: no anticipatory bail under Section 18, and arrest does not require prior approval, though the Court read in a preliminary inquiry by a DSP-level officer in "appropriate cases" to prevent harassment. The Court reiterated that the legislative intent of the PoA Act is to protect the dignity of SC/ST communities and that judicial activism cannot dilute statutory safeguards. The 2018 amendment to the PoA Act (Section 18A) subsequently nullified the Mahajan guidelines by statutory command, and its constitutional validity was upheld in Prithvi Raj Chauhan.

Implementation challenges persist. The National Crime Records Bureau data consistently shows high pendency and low conviction rates (hovering around 30-35%). The Supreme Court in National Campaign for Dalit Human Rights v. Union of India (2023) directed States to fill vacancies in Special Courts, ensure time-bound trials, and submit compliance reports. The Court also flagged the non-application of the PoA Act in cases of intersectional discrimination — for instance, against SC/ST women facing sexual violence — urging prosecutors to invoke both the PoA Act and the IPC/POCSO Act. The constitutional mandate of Article 17 thus remains a work in progress, requiring not merely statutory text but institutional capacity, prosecutorial diligence, and judicial sensitivity to translate the abolition of untouchability into lived reality.

Article 18: Abolition of Titles — Scope, Exceptions and the National Awards Jurisprudence

Article 18 prohibits the State from conferring any title, except military or academic distinctions. It also bars citizens of India from accepting any title from a foreign State, and prohibits any person holding an office of profit or trust under the State from accepting any present, emolument, or office from a foreign State without the President's consent. The provision reflects the republican ethos of the Constitution — equality of status and the rejection of feudal hierarchies. The term "title" has been interpreted narrowly by the Supreme Court. In Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996), a Constitution Bench upheld the validity of the National Awards — Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, and Padma Shri — ruling that they do not constitute "titles" within the meaning of Article 18(1). The Court reasoned that these awards are not hereditary, carry no special privileges or precedence in official warrant, and are merely recognition of excellence in various fields. The prefix or suffix to the name (e.g., "Padma Shri X") is a description, not a title. The Court also laid down guidelines: the awards should not be used as prefixes or suffixes in official correspondence, and a high-level committee should screen recommendations to avoid political patronage.

The exception for "military or academic distinctions" covers honours such as the Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra, Vir Chakra, and degrees conferred by universities. The distinction hinges on functional necessity: military decorations recognise valour in defence of the nation, while academic degrees certify professional competence. Neither creates a social hierarchy akin to feudal titles. Article 18(2) prohibits Indian citizens from accepting titles from foreign States. This was tested when certain Indian nationals accepted honours from foreign governments (e.g., knighthoods before 1947, or contemporary awards like the Legion of Honour). The Ministry of Home Affairs issues guidelines requiring prior permission; acceptance without consent may attract departmental action for government servants, though no penal consequence is prescribed for private citizens. Article 18(3) and (4) extend the restriction to non-citizens holding office under the State — a safeguard against foreign influence on public functionaries. The provision has rarely been litigated but gained attention when judges or bureaucrats received foreign honours; the government has generally required prior presidential consent.

A recurring controversy concerns the use of honorifics like "Sir" or "Lord" by Indians who received British honours before 1947. The Constitution does not retrospectively strip such titles, but Article 18(1) prevents the Indian State from recognising them. In practice, the government does not accord official precedence to such titles. The larger constitutional point is that Article 18 operationalises the Preamble's promise of "equality of status" by denying the State the power to create new hierarchies of honour. The Balaji Raghavan judgment struck a balance: it permitted the State to recognise merit without violating the republican principle, provided the recognition remains non-hereditary, non-privileged, and transparent. The judgment also underscored that the power to confer awards is executive, not legislative, and must be exercised fairly — a principle later invoked in challenges to the selection process for Padma awards. The Court's refusal to treat national awards as "titles" has been criticised by some scholars as formalistic, but it has stood the test of time and remains the governing precedent.

Worked Application: Article 17 and the PoA Act in a Hypothetical Scenario
A dominant-caste landlord prevents a Dalit agricultural labourer from drawing water from a common village well, threatens him with eviction, and forces him to dispose of animal carcasses. The labourer files an FIR. The landlord moves the High Court for anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC, arguing the PoA Act does not apply because the well is not a "public place" and carcass disposal is a traditional occupation, not an atrocity. How should the Court decide?
The Court should reject the anticipatory bail application. First, the PoA Act, 1989 (as amended in 2015) explicitly includes "preventing a member of SC/ST from using common water sources" (Section 3(1)(i)) and "forcing to dispose of carcasses" (Section 3(1)(j)) as atrocities. The definition of "public place" is not a limiting factor; the Act covers acts committed in any place. Second, Section 18 of the PoA Act expressly bars anticipatory bail for offences under the Act, a position restored by the 2018 amendment (Section 18A) and upheld in Prithvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India (2020). The Subhash Kashinath Mahajan (2018) guidelines permitting anticipatory bail were legislatively overridden. Third, the offence is cognizable and non-bailable; the Court cannot import CrPC provisions to dilute the special law. The preliminary inquiry safeguard read in by Prithvi Raj Chauhan applies only to prevent "frivolous" cases, not where a prima facie case exists on the FIR. The Court must direct registration of the FIR under Sections 3(1)(i), (j) and relevant IPC sections, and deny anticipatory bail.
Exam Strategy: Article 17/18 and the PoA Act
Memorise the key atrocities added by the 2015 amendment (tonsuring, garlanding with footwear, election interference, social boycott). Know the procedural hierarchy: PoA Act > CrPC on anticipatory bail (Section 18/18A). For Article 18, remember the Balaji Raghavan test: non-hereditary, no official precedence, no privileges = not a "title". Distinguish military/academic distinctions (exempt) from national awards (upheld as non-titles). A frequent trap: the PoA Act applies to offences by non-SC/ST against SC/ST; offences among SC/ST are not covered. Another: Article 17 is self-executing for horizontal application — no State action required for the prohibition, but State action is required for punishment.

Articles 31A, 31B and 31C: Constitutional Immunity for Land Reform and Social Welfare Legislation

Articles 31A, 31B and 31C form a triad of "saving clauses" inserted to insulate specific categories of legislation from fundamental rights challenges, particularly Articles 14, 19 and 31 (before its repeal). Article 31A, introduced by the First Amendment (1951) and expanded by the Fourth (1955), Seventeenth (1964) and Thirty-ninth (1975) Amendments, saves laws providing for acquisition of estates, extinguishment of rights therein, or modification of such rights, from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31. The term "estate" has been broadly interpreted to include jagirs, inams, muafis, and any land held under a revenue settlement (Kochuni v. State of Madras, 1960). Article 31A(2) defines "estate" by reference to local land tenure laws, giving States wide latitude. However, the protection is not absolute: the law must provide for compensation at market value if it acquires land held under personal cultivation within the ceiling limit (Waman Rao v. Union of India, 1981).

Article 31B, also inserted by the First Amendment, creates the Ninth Schedule. Any law included in the Ninth Schedule is immune from judicial review for violation of fundamental rights. Initially, 13 land reform acts were placed in the Schedule; the number grew to 284 by the 76th Amendment (1994). The Supreme Court in Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) upheld Parliament's power to amend the Constitution to curtail fundamental rights. Golaknath (1967) reversed this, but the 24th Amendment (1971) restored it. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic structure doctrine, holding that while Parliament can amend fundamental rights, it cannot destroy the basic structure. In Waman Rao (1981), the Court drew a line: laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before 24 April 1973 (the date of Kesavananda) are immune; laws added after are open to challenge on basic structure grounds. This "doctrine of prospective overruling" balanced legislative reform with constitutional supremacy.

Article 31C, inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971) and expanded by the 42nd Amendment (1976), originally saved laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c) — distribution of material resources and prevention of concentration of wealth — from Articles 14, 19 and 31. The 42nd Amendment extended this to all Directive Principles. In Minerva Mills (1980), the Court struck down the 42nd Amendment's expansion as violating the basic structure, restoring Article 31C to its pre-1976 form: protection only for laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c). The Court also held that judicial review is part of the basic structure; a law claiming Article 31C protection must be scrutinised to ensure it genuinely implements Article 39(b) or (c) and is not a colourable exercise. In State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Abu Kavur Bai (1984), the Court upheld a land ceiling law under Article 31C. In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine-judge bench reaffirmed Waman Rao: Ninth Schedule laws post-1973 are testable on basic structure, including the "rights test" (whether they violate Articles 14, 19, 21) and the "structure test" (whether they damage constitutional identity). The Court also held that the validity of a Ninth Schedule law must be judged on its own merits, not by the mere fact of inclusion.

These provisions illustrate the constitutional tension between transformative social legislation and individual rights. Article 31A reflects a targeted compromise for agrarian reform. Article 31B created a legislative "safe harbour" that became a repository for diverse laws — including reservation acts, tax laws, and election laws — prompting judicial gatekeeping. Article 31C embodies the DPSP-FR harmonisation project, judicially confined to Article 39(b)(c) to prevent the Directive Principles from swallowing the Fundamental Rights. Together, they map the evolving boundary of legislative power in a welfare State committed to both equity and liberty.

Article 19(1)(b) to (g): The Cluster of Freedoms Beyond Speech — Assembly, Association, Movement, Residence and Profession

Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms to citizens: (a) speech and expression, (b) assembly peaceably and without arms, (c) formation of associations or unions, (d) movement throughout the territory of India, (e) residence and settlement in any part of India, and (f) practice of any profession, or carrying on any occupation, trade or business. While Article 19(1)(a) dominates jurisprudence, the remaining five freedoms have generated substantial case law defining the architecture of civil liberty in a federal polity. Each freedom is subject to reasonable restrictions under clauses (2) to (6) respectively, and the grounds differ — reflecting the distinct social interests each freedom engages.

Article 19(1)(b) — assembly — is restricted only on grounds of "sovereignty and integrity of India" and "public order" (Article 19(3)). The Supreme Court in Himat Lal K. Shah v. Commissioner of Police (1973) struck down a rule giving the Police Commissioner unfettered discretion to deny permission for public meetings, holding that prior restraint must be guided by objective criteria. In Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018), the Court recognised the right to protest in designated spaces but upheld reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions. The "without arms" qualifier excludes armed processions; the Arms Act, 1959 regulates this. Article 19(1)(c) — association — includes the right to form trade unions, political parties, companies, and societies. In T.K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu (2003), the Court held that government employees have no fundamental right to strike, though they have a right to form associations. The right to recognition of a union is statutory, not constitutional. Article 19(1)(d) and (e) — movement and residence — are restricted on grounds of "public interest" and "protection of interests of any Scheduled Tribe" (Article 19(5)). The tribal protection ground enables States to restrict entry into Scheduled Areas (Fifth/Sixth Schedule) to preserve tribal culture and land rights. In Satwant Singh v. Assistant Passport Officer (1967), the Court held that the right to travel abroad is part of "personal liberty" under Article 21, not Article 19(1)(d), because the latter covers movement within India.

Article 19(1)(g) — profession, occupation, trade, business — is the economic freedom most litigated after speech. It is restricted by Article 19(6) on grounds of "public interest", professional/technical qualifications, and State monopolies. The Supreme Court in Chintaman Rao v. State of M.P. (1950) established that restrictions must be reasonable and not arbitrary. In Excel Wear v. Union of India (1978), the Court held that the right to close a business is included in Article 19(1)(g), but the State can regulate closure in public interest (Industrial Disputes Act, Chapter V-B). The liquor trade cases (Cooverjee B. Bharucha v. Excise Commissioner, 1954; State of A.P. v. McDowell, 1996) established that there is no fundamental right to trade in intoxicants — the State may prohibit or regulate it strictly. The 2017 GST regime and the Internet shutdown cases (Anuradha Bhasin, 2020) have tested Article 19(1)(g) in the digital economy: the Court held that indefinite suspension of internet affects the right to carry on trade and must satisfy the proportionality test under Article 19(6). The interplay between Article 19(1)(g) and Article 301 (freedom of trade, commerce, intercourse) is significant: Article 301 applies to all persons (not just citizens) and covers inter-State and intra-State trade, while Article 19(1)(g) is citizen-specific and individual. Restrictions under Article 302-304 (Parliament/State legislative competence) must also satisfy Article 19(6) reasonableness when they impinge on the citizen's right.

A critical doctrinal point: the six freedoms are not mutually exclusive. A protest march engages (b) and (d); a trade union strike engages (c) and (g); a professional's right to practice across State borders engages (d), (e) and (g). The Supreme Court in Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1962) (minority view) and later in Maneka Gandhi (1978) adopted a "cluster theory" — fundamental rights are not watertight compartments but overlapping guarantees of human dignity. The proportionality standard from Modern Dental College (2016) now governs all Article 19 restrictions: legitimate aim, suitability, necessity, and balancing. This unified approach prevents the State from fragmenting a single act of repression into multiple "reasonable" restrictions across sub-clauses.

Article 50 and the Separation of Judiciary from Executive: Constitutional Mandate, Judicial Enforcement and Institutional Practice

Article 50, a Directive Principle, directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State. Unlike most DPSPs, Article 50 addresses the internal structure of governance rather than socio-economic outcomes. Its placement in Part IV makes it non-justiciable (Article 37), but the Supreme Court has treated judicial independence as a basic structure feature, rendering the separation effectively enforceable. The historical context: at Independence, district magistrates and collectors exercised both executive and judicial functions (e.g., trying criminal cases under the CrPC 1898). The Law Commission (14th Report, 1958) recommended separation. The CrPC 1973 implemented this by creating Judicial Magistrates under the control of the High Court (Section 6, 11) and Executive Magistrates under the State Government (Section 20). The judicial magistracy handles trials; the executive magistracy handles preventive functions (Section 107, 144, 145 CrPC).

Judicial enforcement has been iterative. In State of West Bengal v. Nripendra Nath Bagchi (1966), the Court held that the separation is a constitutional mandate, not a mere administrative convenience. In Union of India v. Sankalchand Sheth (1977), the Court linked Article 50 to Article 217 (independence of High Courts) and Article 124 (Supreme Court), holding that the "judiciary" in Article 50 includes the subordinate judiciary. The landmark All India Judges Association v. Union of India (1993, 2002) series of cases transformed Article 50 into a justiciable standard for judicial infrastructure, pay, and career progression. The Court directed the creation of a National Judicial Pay Commission, time-bound promotions, and the separation of judicial and executive functions at the district level. In Kumar Padma Prasad v. Union of India (1992), the Court struck down the appointment of a district judge who was a serving administrative officer, violating the separation principle.

Despite formal separation, functional overlaps persist. Executive magistrates (DMs, SDMs) continue to exercise quasi-judicial powers under Section 144 CrPC (curfew), Section 107 (security for keeping peace), and the National Security Act, 1980. The Supreme Court in Madhu Limaye v. SDM Monghyr (1971) upheld Section 144 as a preventive, not judicial, power. However, in Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Court required that Section 144 orders be published, reasoned, and subject to judicial review — narrowing executive discretion. The Police Act, 1861 and State Police Acts also vest executive officers with powers affecting liberty (arrest, detention) that intersect with judicial functions. The 2006 Prakash Singh directives on police reforms sought to insulate investigation from political interference, indirectly reinforcing Article 50.

Contemporary challenges include the tribunalisation of justice — where executive-branch tribunals (e.g., NGT, SAT, CAT) perform adjudicatory functions. The Supreme Court in R. Gandhi v. Union of India (2010) and Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2014, 2021) held that tribunals must have judicial dominance (majority judicial members) and independence from the sponsoring ministry to satisfy Article 50 read with basic structure. The Finance Act, 2017 tribunal merger and tenure rules were struck down in Madras Bar Association (2021) for violating judicial independence. Article 50 thus operates as a structural constraint on the fusion of power, enforceable not through its own text but through the basic structure doctrine and Article 21's guarantee of fair procedure. The separation is not a binary achievement but a continuous institutional project requiring vigilance against executive encroachment on adjudicatory space.

  • Confusing Article 17 (untouchability) with Article 15(2) (access to public places) — Article 17 is a specific prohibition with penal consequences; Article 15(2) is a non-discrimination guarantee. The PoA Act creates distinct offences not subsumed by the IPC.
  • Assuming national awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma awards) are "titles" prohibited by Article 18 — Balaji Raghavan (1996) held they are not titles because they are non-hereditary, carry no official precedence or privileges.
  • Believing the Ninth Schedule provides absolute immunity — post-Kesavananda (24 April 1973) inclusions are subject to basic structure review (Waman Rao, I.R. Coelho). Pre-1973 laws are immune.
  • Thinking Article 31C protects laws implementing any Directive Principle — Minerva Mills (1980) restricted it to Article 39(b) and (c) only; the 42nd Amendment's expansion was struck down.
  • Equating the right to strike with Article 19(1)(c) — T.K. Rangarajan (2003) held government employees have no fundamental right to strike; the right to form associations does not include the right to strike.
  • Treating Article 19(1)(d) (movement) as covering the right to travel abroad — Satwant Singh (1967) located the right to travel abroad under Article 21 (personal liberty), not Article 19(1)(d).
  • Assuming Article 50 is non-justiciable because it is a DPSP — while Article 37 declares DPSPs non-enforceable, the Supreme Court has read judicial independence (which Article 50 protects) into the basic structure and Article 21, making separation effectively justiciable.

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation and Its Bearing on Fundamental Rights

Delegated legislation — rules, regulations, notifications and orders made by the executive under a statutory power — forms the bulk of operative law in India. The Constitution does not expressly mention delegated legislation, but Article 13(2) read with the doctrine of ultra vires makes any subordinate law that contravenes a fundamental right void to the extent of the contravention. The Supreme Court has consistently held that the parent statute must contain adequate legislative guidance; otherwise the delegation itself is an excessive abdication of legislative function and violates Article 14 (arbitrariness) and Article 21 (procedure established by law). In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1954) the Court struck down a rule made under the Essential Commodities Act because the enabling provision gave the executive unguided discretion to fix prices, thereby violating Article 14. In Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (1985) a notification under the Press Council Act that imposed pre‑censorship on newspapers was held void for violating Article 19(1)(a). The Court applied the “reasonable classification” test to the delegated norm, requiring that the classification be founded on an intelligible differentia and have a rational nexus with the object of the parent Act.

The judicial toolkit includes three distinct grounds of review: (i) substantive ultra vires — the rule exceeds the scope of the enabling provision; (ii) procedural ultra vires — mandatory consultation, publication or laying‑before‑Parliament requirements are not complied with; and (iii) constitutional ultra vires — the rule infringes a fundamental right. The last ground has gained prominence after Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) expanded “procedure established by law” to mean a fair, just and reasonable procedure. Consequently, a delegated norm that authorises arbitrary detention, unreasonable restriction on speech, or discriminatory licensing is liable to be struck down even if the parent statute is constitutionally valid. The Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (1993) held that a rule made under the Income‑Tax Act which imposed a penalty without a hearing violated Article 21. The principle of proportionality — now entrenched in Modern Dental College v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2016) — is also applied to delegated legislation: the restriction must be suitable, necessary and balanced.

Parliamentary oversight operates through the “laying” requirement (Articles 118 and 208) and the Committee on Subordinate Legislation. However, the Committee’s recommendations are advisory; the real check remains judicial. The 2018 amendment to the General Clauses Act, 1897 introduced a mandatory “sunset clause” for certain delegated powers, but its constitutional efficacy is yet untested. Aspirants should note that the doctrine does not permit courts to rewrite rules; they can only declare them void. The remedy is usually a declaration of invalidity coupled with a direction to the legislature to enact a proper law, as seen in State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) where the Court gave Parliament six months to replace an ultra vires notification under the Defence of India Rules.

Constitutional Constraints on the Executive Ordinance‑Making Power under Articles 123 and 213 and Its Impact on Fundamental Rights

Articles 123 (President) and 213 (Governor) empower the executive to promulgate ordinances when Parliament or the State Legislature is not in session. The power is conditional: (a) the legislature must be out of session; (b) the President/Governor must be satisfied that circumstances exist which render immediate action necessary; and (c) the ordinance must be laid before the legislature at its reassembly and ceases to operate after six weeks unless approved. The Supreme Court has treated these conditions as justiciable. In R. C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) the Court held that an ordinance cannot be used to bypass legislative debate on a matter of profound public importance — the Bank Nationalisation Ordinance was upheld only because the urgency of the economic crisis satisfied the “immediate action” test. In D. C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) the Court struck down a series of repromulgated ordinances on the ground that repromulgation without legislative approval amounted to a “fraud on the Constitution”. The principle was reiterated in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017) where a seven‑judge bench declared that repeated repromulgation of the same ordinance without legislative sanction violates the separation of powers and the basic structure.

Ordinances that curtail fundamental rights attract heightened scrutiny. In A. K. Roy v. Union of India (1982) the Court examined the National Security Ordinance, 1980 (later Act) and held that preventive detention provisions must conform to Article 22 safeguards; an ordinance cannot dilute the procedural guarantees of Article 22(4)–(7). The Court also ruled that an ordinance cannot amend the Constitution — the 42nd Amendment’s attempt to extend the life of ordinances was struck down in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980). The “satisfaction” of the President/Governor is not immune from judicial review; in State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) the Court held that the satisfaction must be based on objective material and not be a mere colourable exercise of power. The 2015 amendment to the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules introduced a requirement that the Cabinet note accompanying an ordinance must contain a “statement of urgency”, but the constitutional adequacy of this procedural safeguard remains untested.

From a fundamental‑rights perspective, the ordinance route is often used to enact laws affecting Article 19(1)(a) (speech), Article 21 (personal liberty) and Article 300A (property). The Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) noted that Section 66A of the IT Act, originally introduced by an ordinance, suffered from vagueness and overbreadth, violating Article 19(1)(a). The judgment underscores that the temporary nature of an ordinance does not lower the constitutional threshold for reasonableness. Aspirants should remember that an ordinance lapses automatically if not approved; however, rights violations occurring during its operative period can be challenged retrospectively, and the State may be liable for compensation under the compensatory jurisprudence of Article 21.

Examiner's Twist
A State Governor promulgates an ordinance imposing a blanket ban on all public assemblies for 30 days citing “public order”. The State Legislative Assembly is in session at the time. The ordinance is challenged. Decide the constitutional validity.
The ordinance is unconstitutional on two grounds. First, Article 213 requires that the Legislature be not in session; since the Assembly is in session, the precondition fails, making the ordinance void ab initio (Krishna Kumar Singh, 2017). Second, a blanket ban on assemblies is a disproportionate restriction on Article 19(1)(b) and fails the test of reasonable restriction under Article 19(3) (Anuradha Bhasin, 2020). The Governor’s satisfaction is not immune from review; the Court will examine whether objective material justified the urgency. Consequently, the ordinance is struck down and any arrests made under it are illegal, attracting State liability under Article 21 compensatory jurisprudence.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes ordinance‑making power with fundamental rights, first check the textual preconditions (legislature not in session, immediate necessity). Then apply the proportionality/reasonable‑restriction framework to the substantive restriction. Cite Krishna Kumar Singh for repromulgation and Anuradha Bhasin for proportionality on speech/assembly. This two‑step approach fetches full marks.

The Comptroller and Auditor General as a Guardian of Directive Principles: Fiscal Accountability and the Realisation of Socio‑Economic Rights

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) occupies a unique constitutional position under Articles 148–151. While the CAG’s primary mandate is audit of government accounts, the Supreme Court has repeatedly treated CAG reports as credible evidence in public interest litigation concerning Directive Principles, especially Article 39(b)–(c) (distribution of material resources) and Article 47 (nutrition and public health). In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2004) the Court relied on the CAG’s 2002 report on the Public Distribution System to issue directions for universalising food entitlements, effectively converting a DPSP into an enforceable right under Article 21. The 2013 National Food Security Act was subsequently enacted, and the CAG’s 2018 performance audit of the Act highlighted leakages, prompting further judicial monitoring.

The CAG’s audit of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) in 2012 exposed large‑scale fund diversion. In Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2019) the Supreme Court used the CAG’s findings to direct the Ministry of Rural Development to strengthen social audit mechanisms, linking the audit function to the realisation of the right to work under Article 41 read with Article 21. The Court observed that the CAG’s independence — secured by the removal procedure akin to a Supreme Court judge (Article 148(1)) — makes its reports a “constitutional check” on executive fiscal behaviour that directly impacts socio‑economic rights.

At the State level, the CAG’s reports on the implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY) and the Jal Jeevan Mission have been cited in High Court PILs to enforce the right to housing (Article 21) and the right to clean water (Article 21). The 2021 CAG report on the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Package revealed delays in cash transfers; the Delhi High Court in Delhi Rozi Roti Adhikar Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022) treated the report as prima facie evidence of violation of Article 21 and ordered immediate disbursement. The emerging jurisprudence thus treats the CAG not merely as an accountant but as an institutional sentinel for DPSP implementation. Aspirants should note that while CAG reports are not binding, courts accord them high evidentiary value because of the constitutional safeguards surrounding the office.

Fundamental Duties and the Emerging Jurisprudence of Constitutional Citizenship in Environmental and Social Governance

Article 51A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and expanded by the 86th Amendment (2002), enumerates eleven fundamental duties. For decades they were regarded as moral exhortations, non‑justiciable under Article 37. However, the Supreme Court has progressively woven them into the fabric of enforceable constitutional law. In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) (Oleum gas leak) the Court held that the duty under Article 51A(g) to protect and improve the natural environment imposes a corresponding positive obligation on the State under Article 21, making environmental degradation actionable. The principle was reinforced in Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) where the Court declared that “the fundamental duties are not merely pious declarations; they are enforceable through public interest litigation”.

The duty to develop scientific temper [Article 51A(h)] was invoked in K. M. Chinnappa v. Union of India (2020) to uphold the validity of the National Education Policy’s emphasis on evidence‑based curriculum, linking the duty to the State’s obligation under Article 45 (early childhood care) and Article 21A (right to education). The duty to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood [Article 51A(e)] has been cited in Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K. M. (2018) (Hadiya case) to underscore that the State must protect inter‑faith marriages from vigilante violence, thereby converting a duty into a positive right to personal liberty under Article 21. The 2023 judgment in K. S. Puttaswamy (Privacy) v. Union of India (the second privacy reference) referred to Article 51A(j) (strive towards excellence) while interpreting the right to data protection as a facet of informational self‑determination.

Legislatively, the 2019 amendment to the Environment (Protection) Act introduced a “citizen’s duty” clause mirroring Article 51A(g), enabling the National Green Tribunal to impose costs on private polluters for breach of the duty. The 2022 Supreme Court decision in Sher Singh v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2014) (re‑affirmed 2022) held that the State’s failure to enforce forest conservation duties under Article 51A(g) attracts liability under the public trust doctrine. The emerging “constitutional citizenship” framework thus treats fundamental duties as a bridge between individual responsibility and State accountability, allowing courts to fashion remedies that simultaneously enforce DPSPs (Articles 48A, 51A(g)) and fundamental rights (Article 21). Aspirants should be ready to argue that a breach of a fundamental duty by a private actor can be the basis for a PIL seeking State action, and that the State’s own failure to promote duties (e.g., scientific temper) can be challenged as a violation of Article 14 (arbitrariness) and Article 21.

  • Confusing the justiciability of fundamental duties with that of directive principles — duties are not directly enforceable against the State, but courts use them to interpret and expand fundamental rights.
  • Assuming the CAG’s audit reports are binding judicial precedents — they are high‑value evidence but not stare decisis.
  • Believing that an ordinance can amend a fundamental right — ordinances are subject to the same constitutional limits as ordinary legislation (Minerva Mills).
  • Thinking delegated legislation cannot be challenged on proportionality grounds — post‑Modern Dental College, proportionality applies to subordinate norms as well.
  • Overlooking the “legislature not in session” precondition for ordinances — a common factual trap in problem‑type questions.
  • Treating Article 51A(g) as a standalone source of liability for private polluters without invoking the State’s positive obligation under Article 21.
  • Missing the distinction between “repromulgation” (void) and “re‑enactment after legislative approval” (valid) in ordinance jurisprudence.
The advanced sections above equip aspirants with the doctrinal depth, case‑law precision and exam‑oriented traps necessary to tackle the toughest GS II questions on Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties.

Article 13(3) – The Constitutional Definition of ‘Law’ and Its Reach Over Fundamental Rights

Article 13(3) supplies an inclusive definition: “law includes any Ordinance, order, bye‑law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law in the territory of India.” This definition determines the universe of norms that can be struck down under Article 13(2) for inconsistency with fundamental rights. The Supreme Court has repeatedly interpreted each component. In Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951) the Court held that a constitutional amendment under Article 368 is not “law” within Article 13(3), a position reversed in Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967) where amendments were treated as law for the purpose of Article 13(2). The Kesavananda Bharati (1973) majority restored the amendment‑as‑law view but limited it through the basic‑structure doctrine, making only those amendments that destroy the basic structure vulnerable. Subsequent jurisprudence clarified that ordinances promulgated under Article 123 or 213 are “law” (see State of Karnataka v. Union of India, 1977). Delegated legislation — rules, regulations, bye‑laws — falls squarely within the definition; the Court in Modern Dental College v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2016) applied the proportionality test to such subordinate norms. Personal laws, customs and usages having the force of law are also covered, as affirmed in Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) where the practice of instant triple talaq was examined as a “custom or usage” under Article 13(3). The practical consequence is that any State action — whether primary legislation, subordinate rule, executive order, or even a long‑standing custom — must survive the Article 13(2) filter. Aspirants should note the distinction: a constitutional amendment is not ordinary “law” for Article 13(2) but is subject to basic‑structure review; an ordinance, though temporary, is fully justiciable; and a custom loses its immunity once it is codified or recognised by a statute.

Article 19(1)(g) – Freedom of Trade, Business and Profession: The Architecture of Reasonable Restrictions under Article 19(6)

Article 19(1)(g) guarantees every citizen the right to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business. The right is not absolute; Article 19(6) permits the State to impose “reasonable restrictions” in the interest of the general public, and also to prescribe professional or technical qualifications. The Supreme Court has evolved a two‑pronged test: (i) the restriction must be authorised by a law that is itself constitutionally valid, and (ii) the restriction must be reasonable, a determination that involves a proportionality analysis balancing the public interest against the severity of the encroachment. In Chintaman Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1950) the Court struck down a total ban on the manufacture of bidis as excessive. Excel Wear v. Union of India (1978) upheld a closure notice for a textile mill only after finding that the government had considered less drastic alternatives. The State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab (2005) decision refined the test: a restriction must be “necessary” and “proportionate” to the object sought, and the State must demonstrate that the measure is the least restrictive means. Professional qualifications — such as those for medical practitioners under the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956, or for advocates under the Advocates Act, 1961 — are expressly saved by Article 19(6). However, the Court in P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005) held that the State cannot, under the guise of prescribing qualifications, create a monopoly that excludes private unaided institutions from imparting professional education. The 2020 judgment in K. M. Chinnappa v. Union of India linked the duty to develop scientific temper (Article 51A(h)) with the reasonableness of curriculum regulations, illustrating the growing interplay between fundamental duties and the Article 19(6) calculus. For examination purposes, remember that “reasonable” is a judicial question; the Court examines the object, the nexus, the extent of the restriction, and the availability of less intrusive alternatives.

Examiner's Trap
A question asks: “The State enacts a law requiring all private coaching centres for engineering entrance exams to obtain a licence from a State‑appointed board, failing which they shall be closed. The law is challenged under Article 19(1)(g). Decide.”
The law imposes a restriction on the right to carry on an occupation. Under Article 19(6) the restriction must be reasonable. The Court will ask: (1) Is the licensing law a valid law? Yes, if enacted by the legislature. (2) Does the licensing scheme serve a legitimate public interest (e.g., quality control, consumer protection)? If yes, the Court proceeds to proportionality. (3) Is a total closure for non‑licensing the least restrictive means? Likely not; the Court in Excel Wear and Mirzapur Moti Kureshi insisted on less drastic alternatives such as penalties, suspension, or conditional licensing. Therefore, the provision mandating automatic closure is disproportionate and violates Article 19(1)(g). The licensing requirement itself may survive if it is coupled with a fair hearing and graded sanctions.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question on Article 19(1)(g) appears, first identify the restriction, then run the three‑step test: (a) legislative competence, (b) legitimate public interest, (c) proportionality/least restrictive means. Cite Chintaman Rao, Excel Wear, Mirzapur Moti Kureshi and Inamdar to show doctrinal depth. Avoid the trap of treating “reasonable” as a mere policy opinion; the Court treats it as a justiciable standard.

Article 21 – Right to Speedy Trial and Fair Trial as Facets of Life and Personal Liberty

Article 21 declares that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. The Supreme Court has read “procedure established by law” to mean a fair, just and reasonable procedure, thereby importing the due‑process values of the American Constitution. Two critical facets are the right to a speedy trial and the right to a fair trial. In Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979) the Court held that “speedy trial” is an essential part of the fundamental right to life and liberty under Article 21, and that undue delay in the disposal of criminal cases violates this right. The Court issued directions for the release of undertrial prisoners who had been detained beyond the maximum possible sentence. In Kadra Pahadiya v. State of Bihar (1982) the principle was extended to require the State to provide adequate judicial infrastructure. The right to a fair trial encompasses the presumption of innocence, the right to be heard, the right to legal representation, and protection against media trials. Zahira Habibullah Sheikh v. State of Gujarat (2004) affirmed that a fair trial is a constitutional mandate and that the State must ensure witness protection and prevent intimidation. The Court in State of Rajasthan v. Balchand (1977) articulated the “bail not jail” principle, holding that denial of bail without reasonable grounds infringes Article 21. More recently, Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) laid down guidelines to prevent arbitrary arrests under Section 41A CrPC, reinforcing the liberty interest. The cumulative effect is that any procedural law — whether the Code of Criminal Procedure, special statutes like the UAPA, or preventive detention laws — must be tested against the twin pillars of speed and fairness. Aspirants should be ready to argue that systemic delays, lack of legal aid, or prejudicial pre‑trial publicity constitute Article 21 violations, and that the State bears a positive obligation to create conditions for timely and impartial adjudication.

Articles 31A, 31B and 31C – The Ninth Schedule, Judicial Review and the Basic‑Structure Test

Articles 31A, 31B and 31C form a triad designed to insulate certain socio‑economic legislation from fundamental‑rights challenges. Article 31A saves laws providing for the acquisition of estates or rights therein, and laws for the extinguishment or modification of such rights, from Articles 14 and 19. Article 31B validates all Acts and Regulations included in the Ninth Schedule, irrespective of any inconsistency with fundamental rights. Article 31C, originally inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971), gave primacy to laws implementing the directive principles in Article 39(b) and (c) over Articles 14, 19 and 31. The Supreme Court’s engagement with this triad has been pivotal. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the majority struck down the portion of Article 31C that ousted judicial review entirely, holding that judicial review is part of the basic structure. Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) further limited Article 31C, ruling that the protection extends only to laws genuinely implementing Article 39(b) and (c), and that the Court retains the power to examine whether a law falls within that category. The Ninth Schedule, originally a shield for land‑reform laws, became a repository for a wide array of statutes. In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) the Court held that amendments to the Ninth Schedule made after 24 April 1973 (the date of Kesavananda) are open to challenge on basic‑structure grounds. This principle was decisively affirmed in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), where a nine‑judge bench ruled that every law placed in the Ninth Schedule after Kesavananda must be tested against the basic structure, particularly the fundamental rights forming part of it. The Court clarified that the “basic structure” includes the supremacy of the Constitution, the rule of law, separation of powers, and the core of fundamental rights. Consequently, the Ninth Schedule is no longer a blanket immunity; it is a legislative device that still bows to constitutional supremacy. For examination, remember the chronological line: pre‑1973 Ninth Schedule entries are largely immune; post‑1973 entries are subject to basic‑structure scrutiny; Article 31C protection is conditional and reviewable; and Article 31A’s shield is limited to acquisition‑type laws and does not extend to arbitrary deprivation.

Article 35 – Parliament’s Exclusive Power to Legislate for Giving Effect to Fundamental Rights

Article 35 empowers Parliament, and not State Legislatures, to make laws for giving effect to certain fundamental rights. The provision lists specific matters: (a) prescribing residence requirements for public employment under Article 16(3); (b) empowering courts other than the Supreme Court and High Courts to issue directions, orders or writs under Article 32; (c) regulating the right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(2); (d) providing for preventive detention under Article 22; and (e) any other matter which may be prescribed. The rationale is to ensure uniformity in the implementation of these rights across the Union. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977) the Court upheld the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 as a valid exercise of Parliament’s power under Article 35 read with Article 22. The Court emphasised that the power under Article 35 is not a general legislative power but a specific enabling provision tied to the enumerated rights. In R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) (the Bank Nationalisation case) the Court discussed Article 35 in the context of Article 31(2) (now Article 300A) and held that Parliament’s law must still conform to the constitutional limitations on property acquisition. The 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property from Part III, but Article 35 remains relevant for the other enumerated rights. A common confusion is to treat Article 35 as a source of legislative competence independent of the Union List; however, the Supreme Court in Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (1971) clarified that Article 35 operates as a “supplementary” power, allowing Parliament to legislate on State‑list subjects only to the extent necessary for implementing the specified fundamental rights. Aspirants should distinguish Article 35 from Article 245 (general legislative competence) and from Article 246 (distribution of legislative powers). The key takeaway: Article 35 is a targeted, rights‑based legislative conduit, not a general plenary power.

  • Confusing the definition of “law” in Article 13(3) with the amendatory power under Article 368 — amendments are not ordinary law but are subject to basic‑structure review.
  • Treating every restriction on Article 19(1)(g) as automatically reasonable because it is “in the public interest” — the Court demands proportionality and least‑restrictive‑means analysis.
  • Assuming that the right to speedy trial under Article 21 is merely aspirational — it is enforceable and has led to release of undertrials (Hussainara Khatoon).
  • Believing the Ninth Schedule provides absolute immunity — post‑1973 entries are testable on basic‑structure grounds (I.R. Coelho).
  • Thinking Article 35 gives Parliament unlimited legislative authority — it is a specific, rights‑linked enabling provision, not a general competence.
  • Overlooking that Article 31C protection is conditional on genuine implementation of Article 39(b) and (c) — the Court examines the law’s nexus with those directives (Minerva Mills).
  • Neglecting the interplay between fundamental duties (Article 51A) and the reasonableness test under Article 19(6) — recent judgments (K.M. Chinnappa) show duties informing the proportionality calculus.

Article 15: Special Provisions for Advancement of Backward Classes — The Complete Architecture

Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth, but its clauses (3) to (6) carve out a layered architecture of affirmative action that has evolved through constitutional amendments and judicial interpretation. Clause (3), original to the Constitution, permits special provisions for women and children. In Yusuf Abdul Aziz v. State of Bombay (1954), the Court upheld a law punishing only men for adultery under Section 497 IPC as a valid special provision for women under Article 15(3), reasoning that the classification was based on sex and favoured women. Clause (4) was inserted by the First Amendment (1951) after State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) struck down caste-based reservations in educational institutions as violative of Article 15(1) and 29(2). Article 15(4) enables the State to make special provisions for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes (SEBCs) or for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The seminal judgment in M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore (1963) capped reservations at 50 per cent, held that backwardness must be both social and educational, and ruled that caste alone cannot be the sole criterion. This was refined in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), where the nine-judge bench upheld 27 per cent OBC reservations in central services, mandated the creamy layer exclusion, and declared that Article 15(4) is an enabling provision, not an exception to Article 15(1).

Clause (5) was inserted by the 93rd Amendment (2005) to enable reservations in private unaided educational institutions (except minority institutions under Article 30(1)). In Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India (2008), the Court upheld the 93rd Amendment and the Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006, applying the 50 per cent ceiling and creamy layer exclusion to Article 15(5) admissions. The Court clarified that Article 15(5) is a separate enabling provision, not an exception to Article 19(1)(g), and that the State’s power under it is subject to judicial review for arbitrariness. Clause (6), inserted by the 103rd Amendment (2019), provides up to 10 per cent reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) in educational institutions, including private unaided ones, over and above the 50 per cent ceiling. In Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022), a 3:2 majority upheld Article 15(6), holding that economic criteria alone can constitute a valid classification, that the 50 per cent ceiling is not inflexible for affirmative action benefiting non-backward classes, and that the exclusion of SC/ST/OBC from EWS quota does not violate the basic structure. The dissent (Justices Bhat and Lalit) argued that excluding historically disadvantaged groups from a purely economic quota perpetuates structural inequality. The current architecture thus comprises four distinct enabling clauses: 15(3) for women and children; 15(4) for SEBCs, SCs, STs in State-aided institutions; 15(5) for the same categories in private unaided non-minority institutions; and 15(6) for EWS across all institutions, each with its own judicial guardrails.

Article 16: Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment — The Reservation Jurisprudence Beyond Creamy Layer

Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. Clause (1) lays down the general rule; clause (2) prohibits discrimination on specified grounds; clause (3) permits Parliament to prescribe residence requirements; and clauses (4), (4A), (4B), (5), and (6) constitute the reservation architecture. Article 16(4), original to the Constitution, allows the State to make provision for reservation of appointments in favour of any backward class of citizens which, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services. In Devadasan v. Union of India (1964), the Court struck down the “carry forward rule” that allowed unfilled reserved vacancies to be carried forward indefinitely, holding it violated the 50 per cent ceiling. The 77th Amendment (1995) inserted Article 16(4A) to permit consequential seniority in promotions for SCs and STs. In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006), a five-judge bench upheld 16(4A) but imposed three conditions: the State must demonstrate backwardness, inadequacy of representation, and maintenance of administrative efficiency. The 85th Amendment (2001) made consequential seniority retrospective to 1995. In Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018), a five-judge bench held that the creamy layer exclusion applies to SC/ST promotions under Article 16(4A) and that the State need not collect quantifiable data on backwardness for SCs/STs (distinguishing them from OBCs), but must show inadequacy of representation.

Article 16(4B), inserted by the 81st Amendment (2000), permits the State to treat unfilled reserved vacancies of a year as a separate class of vacancies to be filled in succeeding years, exempting them from the 50 per cent ceiling. This effectively overruled Devadasan for the limited purpose of clearing backlogs. Article 16(5) preserves the right of religious or denominational institutions to appoint persons professing a particular religion. Article 16(6), inserted by the 103rd Amendment (2019), provides up to 10 per cent reservation for EWS in public employment, over and above the 50 per cent ceiling. In Janhit Abhiyan (2022), the majority upheld 16(6) applying the same reasoning as for Article 15(6). The Court has also developed the “roster system” for implementing reservations: in R.K. Sabharwal v. State of Punjab (1995), it mandated the 100-point roster for direct recruitment, treating each cadre as a unit. In Union of India v. Ramesh Ram (2010), the Court held that the roster applies to promotions as well. The “adequacy of representation” test requires the State to review representation at regular intervals; in Mukesh Kumar v. State of Uttarakhand (2020), the Court directed States to conduct such reviews for SC/ST promotions. The interplay of Articles 15 and 16 is critical: Article 15(4) and (5) govern educational reservations; Article 16(4), (4A), (4B), and (6) govern employment reservations; both are subject to the 50 per cent rule (except EWS quota and 16(4B) backlog vacancies), creamy layer exclusion (for OBCs, and now for SC/ST promotions), and the requirement of quantifiable data for OBCs.

Examiner's Trap: Conflating Article 15(4) and Article 16(4) Standards
A question asks: "The creamy layer exclusion applies identically to OBC reservations in education under Article 15(4) and in public employment under Article 16(4)." True or False? Explain the constitutional basis.
False. While Indra Sawhney (1992) mandated creamy layer exclusion for OBCs under Article 16(4), the extension to Article 15(4) came later through Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008) which applied it to Article 15(5) admissions in central educational institutions. The constitutional basis differs: Article 16(4) is read with the "adequacy of representation" test for services; Article 15(4) and (5) are read with the "advancement" standard for education. The 103rd Amendment's EWS quota under Articles 15(6) and 16(6) explicitly excludes creamy layer concept for the new class, but the OBC creamy layer remains operative under both articles. The trap lies in assuming textual symmetry where judicial evolution created functional symmetry at different times.
Exam-Day Strategy: The Four-Clause Map
Memorise a 2×2 matrix: Rows = Education (Art. 15) vs Employment (Art. 16); Columns = Traditional Beneficiaries (SC/ST/OBC) vs New Beneficiaries (EWS). Fill each cell: 15(4)/(5) for traditional education; 15(6) for EWS education; 16(4)/(4A)/(4B) for traditional employment; 16(6) for EWS employment. Tag each with ceiling rule (50% applies to traditional, not EWS), creamy layer (OBC yes, SC/ST in promotions yes post-Jarnail Singh, EWS no), and quantifiable data (OBC yes, SC/ST no for backwardness but yes for inadequacy). This matrix solves 80% of reservation comparison questions.

Article 31C: The Directive Principles–Fundamental Rights Balancing Clause — From 25th Amendment to Minerva Mills to Present

Article 31C is the Constitution’s explicit mechanism for resolving conflicts between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles. Inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971) to insulate land reform laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c) from challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31, the original Article 31C had two limbs: first, a law giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing the principles in Article 39(b) and (c) shall not be deemed void on the ground of inconsistency with Articles 14, 19, or 31; second, no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Court upheld the first limb as a valid exercise of constituent power but struck down the second limb as violating the basic structure by ousting judicial review. The 42nd Amendment (1976) radically expanded Article 31C: it replaced “Article 39(b) and (c)” with “all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV”, and reinstated the ouster of judicial review by declaring that no such law shall be called in question in any court. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), a five-judge bench struck down the 42nd Amendment’s expansion. The Court held that giving primacy to all Directive Principles over Articles 14 and 19 destroys the basic structure because it removes the constitutional balance between Parts III and IV. The Court restored the pre-1976 position: Article 31C protects only laws genuinely implementing Article 39(b) and (c), and such laws remain subject to judicial review to determine whether they actually further those directives. The judgment established that the harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself a basic structure feature.

Post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C operates as a conditional shield. In State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Abu Kavur Bai (1984), the Court held that a law nationalising bus routes was protected under Article 31C as it served Article 39(b) (distribution of material resources). In Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Co. v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. (1983), the Court upheld the nationalisation of coking coal mines under Article 31C. However, in D.S. Nakara v. Union of India (1983), the Court refused Article 31C protection to a pension scheme that discriminated between pre- and post-1979 retirees, holding it lacked nexus with Article 39(b) and (c). The current test requires: (i) the law must be enacted to give effect to Article 39(b) or (c); (ii) there must be a real and substantial nexus between the law’s provisions and those directives; (iii) the law is not immune from challenge under other basic structure features (e.g., rule of law, separation of powers). Article 31C does not protect laws implementing other Directive Principles such as Article 38 (social order), 39A (legal aid), 41 (right to work), 43 (living wage), or 48A (environment). Those laws must satisfy the ordinary reasonable restriction tests under Articles 14, 19, and 21. The 44th Amendment (1978) did not alter Article 31C, leaving the Minerva Mills framework intact. Aspirants must distinguish Article 31C (conditional protection for Article 39(b)/(c) laws) from Article 31A (acquisition of estates) and Article 31B (Ninth Schedule), each with distinct scopes and judicial review standards.

Article 31A and 31B: The Agrarian Reform Shield — Estate Acquisition, Ninth Schedule, and Basic Structure Limits

Articles 31A and 31B, inserted by the First Amendment (1951), were the Constitution’s original response to judicial invalidation of zamindari abolition laws. Article 31A saves laws providing for the “acquisition of any estate” or “extinguishment or modification of rights” therein from challenge under Articles 14, 19, and 31 (now 300A). The term “estate” has been expansively interpreted: in K.K. Kochuni v. State of Madras (1960), the Court held it includes any land held under a permanent settlement or ryotwari settlement; in Maharao Sahib Sri Bhim Singhji v. Union of India (1981), it included jagirs and muafis; in Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector (1965), it covered land held by religious institutions. However, Article 31A does not protect arbitrary deprivation — the acquisition must be for a public purpose and provide compensation (though the 44th Amendment removed the “adequate compensation” requirement for non-minority institutions, the requirement of “compensation” not being illusory remains per Kesavananda). Article 31B validates, without judicial review, any Act or Regulation specified in the Ninth Schedule. The Ninth Schedule originally contained 13 land reform Acts. By the 42nd Amendment (1976), it had grown to 64 entries; by the 76th Amendment (1994), to 284 entries, including laws on reservations, land ceilings, urban land ceiling, and even the Tamil Nadu Backward Classes Act.

The critical jurisprudential turn came in Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981), where the Court held that Ninth Schedule amendments made after 24 April 1973 (the Kesavananda date) are open to challenge on basic structure grounds. This was decisively affirmed in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) by a nine-judge bench: every law placed in the Ninth Schedule after Kesavananda must be tested against the basic structure, particularly the fundamental rights forming part of it (Articles 14, 19, 21). The Court clarified that the “basic structure” includes the supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, separation of powers, and the core of fundamental rights. Consequently, the Ninth Schedule is no longer a blanket immunity; it is a legislative device that still bows to constitutional supremacy. For Article 31A, the protection is limited to laws that genuinely relate to acquisition of estates or modification of rights therein; it does not extend to arbitrary regulatory measures masquerading as agrarian reform. In K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011), the Court held that a law converting leasehold to freehold without acquisition was not protected by Article 31A. The chronological line for examination is: pre-1973 Ninth Schedule entries are largely immune; post-1973 entries are subject to basic structure scrutiny; Article 31C protection is conditional on genuine implementation of Article 39(b) and (c) and is reviewable; Article 31A’s shield is limited to acquisition-type laws and does not extend to arbitrary deprivation. The 44th Amendment’s conversion of property right into a constitutional right under Article 300A did not alter Articles 31A, 31B, or 31C, but it means that any acquisition under Article 31A must now satisfy Article 300A’s requirement of “authority of law” and non-arbitrariness.

The Classification and Enforceability of Directive Principles: Socialistic, Gandhian, Liberal‑Intellectual — Judicial Treatment of Non‑Justiciable Rights

Part IV (Articles 36–51) contains Directive Principles of State Policy, expressly declared non-justiciable by Article 37. However, judicial practice has transformed many into enforceable obligations through creative interpretation of Article 21 and Article 32. The Principles are conventionally classified into three categories.
