Socialistic Principles (Articles 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47): Article 38(1) directs the State to secure a social order promoting welfare; Article 38(2) (inserted by 44th Amendment) mandates minimising inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities. Article 39(b) and (c) — distribution of material resources and prevention of concentration of wealth — are the only directives protected by Article 31C. Article 39A (inserted by 42nd Amendment) mandates free legal aid; the Court in Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979) read it into Article 21, making legal aid a fundamental right. Article 41 (right to work, education, public assistance) was the basis for recognising the right to livelihood in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985). Article 42 (just and humane conditions of work, maternity relief) underpins the Maternity Benefit Act jurisprudence. Article 43 (living wage) and 43A (workers’ participation in management) have been used to interpret labour laws purposively. Article 47 (nutrition, public health) supports the right to food and health under Article 21.

Gandhian Principles (Articles 40, 43B, 46, 47, 48): Article 40 (village panchayats) was constitutionalised by the 73rd Amendment. Article 43B (co-operative societies) was added by the 97th Amendment (2011); in Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Court struck down part of the 97th Amendment for violating the federal structure but upheld the directive itself. Article 46 (promotion of educational and economic interests of SCs/STs) is the constitutional anchor for reservations and scholarship schemes. Article 48 (organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry) and the prohibition of cow slaughter have been upheld as reasonable restrictions under Article 19(1)(g) in State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat (2005). Liberal-Intellectual Principles (Articles 44, 45, 48A, 49, 50, 51): Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code) remains unimplemented; the Court in Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) and John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003) urged its enactment but declined to mandamus Parliament. Article 45 (early childhood care and education) was originally for children up to 14; after the 86th Amendment (2002) made elementary education a fundamental right under Article 21A, Article 45 was amended to cover early childhood care up to age 6. Article 48A (environment protection) and 51A(g) (fundamental duty) have been converged by the Court in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) to enforce the public trust doctrine. Article 49 (protection of monuments) underpins the Ancient Monuments Act enforcement. Article 50 (separation of judiciary from executive) has been implemented through judicial independence jurisprudence. Article 51 (international peace and security) guides treaty interpretation under Article 253. The examiner tests the hierarchy: Article 39(b)/(c) enjoy Article 31C protection; others gain enforceability only through Article 21 or statutory embodiment; Article 44 is hortatory; Article 45 is partially superseded by Article 21A; Article 48A/51A(g) are judicially enforceable via public trust doctrine.

  • Trap 1: Assuming Article 31C protects all Directive Principles — it covers only Article 39(b) and (c) after Minerva Mills.
  • Trap 2: Conflating the creamy layer test for OBCs under Article 15(4)/16(4) with the EWS quota under Articles 15(6)/16(6) — EWS has no creamy layer concept; the income ceiling is the eligibility criterion itself.
  • Trap 3: Believing the Ninth Schedule provides absolute immunity for all entries — post-1973 entries are subject to basic structure review (I.R. Coelho).
  • Trap 4: Treating Article 31A as a blanket shield for any land-related law — it applies only to “acquisition of estate” or “extinguishment/modification of rights therein”, not to arbitrary regulatory measures.
  • Trap 5: Assuming Article 44 (UCC) is justiciable — the Court has repeatedly declined to issue mandamus, calling it a matter of legislative policy.
  • Trap 6: Overlooking that Article 16(4B) backlog vacancies are exempt from the 50 per cent ceiling — this is a distinct exception from the EWS quota exemption.
  • Trap 7: Confusing the “adequacy of representation” test (Article 16(4)/(4A)) with the “advancement” test (Article 15(4)) — the former requires quantifiable data for OBCs and proof of inadequacy for SC/ST promotions; the latter focuses on social and educational backwardness.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation and Its Impact on Fundamental Rights

The doctrine of colourable legislation addresses the situation where a legislature, lacking competence to enact a law directly, attempts to achieve the same object indirectly by dressing it in a different form. The Supreme Court in K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953) formulated the test: “If the legislature tries to do something which it cannot do directly, the legislation is colourable and therefore void.” The Court examines the substance of the law rather than its form. If the true purpose and effect of the enactment fall outside the legislative field assigned to that legislature by the Seventh Schedule, the law is struck down as a fraud on the Constitution.

Under Article 13(2), any law that contravenes the fundamental rights is void to the extent of the contravention. Colourable legislation becomes a vehicle for violating fundamental rights when a legislature uses its ostensible power to encroach upon a right protected under Part III. For instance, a State legislature may enact a law purporting to regulate “public health” (Entry 6, State List) but in reality imposes restrictions on freedom of speech (Article 19(1)(a)) that only Parliament could impose under Entry 97 of the Union List read with Article 248. In State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952), the Court invalidated a Bihar land‑reform law that, while framed as an agrarian measure, effectively deprived zamindars of property without compensation, violating Article 31 (pre‑44th Amendment) and later Article 300A.

The doctrine operates alongside the pith and substance rule. While pith and substance determines legislative competence by looking at the true character of the law, colourable legislation goes a step further: it asks whether the legislature has intentionally disguised an incompetent purpose. The burden of proving colourability lies on the challenger, who must demonstrate a clear mismatch between the declared object and the actual effect. The Court in M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979) held that mere incidental encroachment on another list does not render a law colourable; there must be a deliberate attempt to transgress constitutional limits.

In the context of fundamental rights, colourable legislation is often invoked in challenges to laws that impose unreasonable restrictions on Article 19 freedoms under the guise of regulatory measures. For example, a State law that imposes a prohibitive licence fee on newspapers, ostensibly for “revenue collection” (Entry 45, State List), was struck down in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) as a colourable exercise of taxing power that abridged freedom of speech. Similarly, the Supreme Court in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1970) examined whether a preventive detention law enacted under Entry 3 of the Concurrent List was a colourable use of legislative power to bypass the procedural safeguards of Article 22.

The practical significance for aspirants is twofold: first, identify the legislative entry invoked and the fundamental right allegedly infringed; second, apply the colourability test by comparing the declared object with the actual impact. Examiners frequently frame questions around a hypothetical State law that “regulates” a profession but effectively bars entry, asking whether it is colourable legislation violating Article 19(1)(g). The answer requires a step‑by‑step analysis: (i) locate the legislative entry, (ii) ascertain the true pith and substance, (iii) test for deliberate transgression, and (iv) conclude on the violation of the specific fundamental right.

The Principle of Non‑Arbitrariness under Article 14: From E.P. Royappa to Shayara Bano

Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws. The Supreme Court’s early jurisprudence relied on the “reasonable classification” test (twin test of intelligible differentia and rational nexus). In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974), Justice Bhagwati introduced a broader principle: “Equality is a dynamic concept… it is the antithesis of arbitrariness.” This marked the shift from a purely classification‑based approach to a non‑arbitrariness standard, whereby any State action that is arbitrary, capricious, or devoid of a rational basis violates Article 14 even if it does not create a formal classification.

The principle was cemented in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where the Court held that a procedure depriving personal liberty under Article 21 must be “fair, just and reasonable,” and that arbitrariness in such procedure also breaches Article 14. Subsequent cases expanded the doctrine: Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib (1981) applied non‑arbitrariness to administrative decisions; Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) struck down instant triple talaq as arbitrary and discriminatory, holding that a practice lacking any rational basis and disproportionately affecting Muslim women fails the Article 14 test. In Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), the Court read down Section 377 IPC, declaring that criminalising consensual same‑sex relations was manifestly arbitrary and violated the dignity and equality of LGBTQ+ persons.

The non‑arbitrariness test operates at three levels. First, procedural arbitrariness: the decision‑making process must follow fair procedures (notice, hearing, reasoned order). Second, substantive arbitrariness: the content of the law or order must have a rational connection to a legitimate State aim. Third, proportionality: the measure must be necessary and proportionate to the objective. The Court in Modern Dental College v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2016) articulated a four‑step proportionality analysis that now underpins the non‑arbitrariness inquiry.

Crucially, non‑arbitrariness does not replace reasonable classification; it supplements it. A law may pass the twin test yet still be arbitrary if it grants unguided discretion. For example, in State of Punjab v. Ramdev Singh (2003), a statute conferring unchecked power on a minister to grant exemptions was held arbitrary despite a formal classification. Conversely, a classification that is intelligible and rationally related to the object will generally survive a non‑arbitrariness challenge unless the discretion it creates is unfettered.

For examination purposes, the examiner may present a statutory provision conferring wide discretionary power on an authority without guidelines and ask whether it violates Article 14. The correct answer traces the evolution from Royappa to Shayara Bano, identifies the lack of guiding norms as procedural arbitrariness, and concludes that the provision is void for arbitrariness. Another common twist is to ask whether the “reasonable classification” test is obsolete; the answer is that it remains the primary tool, but non‑arbitrariness acts as a safety net for cases where classification is absent or discretion is unguided.

Technique: Structuring a Non‑Arbitrariness Answer
Question: “A State law empowers the District Collector to cancel any licence for a ‘public purpose’ without defining the term or providing a hearing. Discuss its constitutional validity under Article 14.”
Answer: (1) Identify the provision as conferring unguided discretionary power. (2) Cite E.P. Royappa (1974) – equality is antithesis of arbitrariness. (3) Apply Maneka Gandhi (1978) – procedure must be fair, just, reasonable. (4) Note absence of definition of “public purpose” and no hearing → procedural arbitrariness. (5) Reference Shayara Bano (2017) – lack of rational basis renders law arbitrary. (6) Conclude: law violates Article 14; it is void to the extent of arbitrariness. (7) Mention that reasonable classification test is inapplicable because no classification exists; non‑arbitrariness is the governing standard.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about “arbitrariness” or “unreasonableness” under Article 14, always start with the Royappa–Maneka Gandhi–Shayara Bano lineage. Use the three‑level framework (procedural, substantive, proportionality) as a checklist. If the statute creates a classification, run the twin test first; then test the discretion for arbitrariness. Quote the phrase “antithesis of arbitrariness” – it signals mastery of the doctrine.

The Role of the Comptroller and Auditor General in Enforcing Directive Principles

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India, established under Article 148, is the constitutional auditor of Union and State accounts. Articles 149–151 empower the CAG to audit all expenditure from the Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund, and Public Account, and to submit reports to the President or Governor for laying before Parliament or the State Legislature. While the CAG’s primary mandate is financial accountability, its reports have become a critical instrument for enforcing Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), particularly those concerning socio‑economic welfare.

Article 39(b) and (c) direct the State to distribute material resources for the common good and prevent concentration of wealth. CAG performance audits of schemes such as the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), the Public Distribution System (PDS), and the National Health Mission have repeatedly highlighted leakages, misallocation, and failure to reach intended beneficiaries. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court relied on CAG reports on the PDS to issue directions for universalising food security, effectively converting the directive under Article 47 (nutrition) into enforceable obligations under Article 21.

Article 41 (right to work, education, public assistance) and Article 42 (just and humane conditions of work) have been operationalised through CAG audits of labour welfare schemes. The 2018 CAG report on the implementation of the Maternity Benefit Act revealed widespread non‑compliance, prompting judicial intervention in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Female Workers (2020) where the Court directed strict enforcement, linking the directive to the fundamental right to livelihood under Article 21.

The CAG’s role extends to environmental directives under Article 48A. Audit reports on the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA) exposed diversion of funds, leading the National Green Tribunal to order restitution, thereby giving teeth to the directive through the public trust doctrine. Similarly, CAG audits of the Namami Gange programme have been cited in PILs seeking enforcement of the right to clean water as a facet of Article 21.

Importantly, the CAG does not possess adjudicatory powers; its findings are recommendatory. However, the Constitution mandates that the reports be placed before the legislature, creating a political accountability mechanism. Courts have treated CAG reports as credible evidence in PILs, often using them to issue continuing mandamus or structural injunctions. The 2021 amendment to the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act expanded the scope of performance audits to include outcome‑based evaluation of Centrally Sponsored Schemes, strengthening the link between fiscal oversight and DPSP realisation.

For aspirants, the key takeaway is the instrumental use of CAG reports: they bridge the gap between non‑justiciable directives and justiciable fundamental rights. Examiners may ask how a CAG report can be used in a writ petition under Article 32 or 226. The answer should outline: (i) the constitutional mandate of the CAG, (ii) the specific directive principle implicated, (iii) the audit finding that demonstrates State failure, and (iv) the judicial remedy sought (directions, mandamus, continuing supervision).

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation Affecting Fundamental Rights

Delegated legislation — rules, regulations, bye‑laws, orders, and notifications made by the executive under authority conferred by a parent statute — falls within the definition of “law” under Article 13(3)(a). Consequently, it is subject to judicial review for conformity with fundamental rights. The Supreme Court in Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India (1960) established that delegated legislation must not exceed the scope of the enabling Act (substantive ultra vires) and must comply with procedural requirements such as publication and consultation (procedural ultra vires). When such legislation infringes a fundamental right, the Court applies the same standards of reasonableness, proportionality, and non‑arbitrariness as it does to primary legislation.

Two landmark cases illustrate the interplay. In Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985), the Court struck down a notification under the Customs Act that imposed a prohibitive duty on newsprint, holding it violated Article 19(1)(a) because the parent Act did not authorise such a restriction on free speech. The Court emphasised that the delegate cannot widen the scope of the parent statute to curtail a fundamental right. In State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat (2005), a rule framed under the Gujarat Agricultural Cattle Preservation Act banned slaughter of bulls and bullocks beyond the age prescribed by the Act. The Court upheld the rule as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(1)(g) read with Article 48, but only after verifying that the rule did not travel beyond the enabling provision.

The test for judicial review of delegated legislation affecting fundamental rights involves three steps. First, competence: does the parent statute validly confer the rule‑making power? Second, conformity: does the delegated legislation stay within the four corners of the enabling provision? Third, constitutional compliance: does the rule, as applied, violate any fundamental right? If the rule fails any step, it is void to the extent of the violation. The Court in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1970) applied this framework to a preventive detention order made under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act (COFEPOSA), holding that the order lacked the procedural safeguards mandated by Article 22 and was therefore ultra vires.

Procedural ultra vires has gained prominence after Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel (1985), where the Court held that failure to consult the mandated advisory committee before issuing a notification rendered it invalid, even though the substantive content was within the enabling Act. This principle ensures that executive rule‑making does not bypass participatory safeguards that are essential when fundamental rights are at stake.

In recent years, the Court has scrutinised delegated legislation under the Information Technology Act, 2000, particularly the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), Section 66A of the IT Act (primary legislation) was struck down; subsequently, the 2021 Rules were challenged for imposing vague due‑diligence obligations on intermediaries, allegedly chilling free speech under Article 19(1)(a). The Court’s interim orders have emphasised that delegated legislation must meet the same clarity and proportionality standards as the parent statute.

For examination, a typical question may present a rule made under a welfare statute that imposes a blanket ban on a profession. The candidate must identify the enabling Act, check whether the ban is authorised, and then test the rule against Article 19(1)(g) using the proportionality framework. The answer should cite Hamdard Dawakhana, Indian Express, and the three‑step test, concluding with the remedy — declaration of invalidity and, if appropriate, a direction to the legislature to enact a compliant provision.

The Doctrine of Federalism and Fundamental Rights: Centre‑State Legislative Competence under the Seventh Schedule

The Seventh Schedule distributes legislative powers between the Union and the States through three lists: Union List (List I), State List (List II), and Concurrent List (List III). This federal division directly impacts the enforcement and scope of fundamental rights because the competence to legislate on a subject determines which legislature can enact laws that either protect or restrict those rights. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that a law enacted without legislative competence is void ab initio under Article 246, and if such a law infringes a fundamental right, the violation is compounded.

A classic illustration is the regulation of “public order” (Entry 1, State List) versus “security of the State” (Entry 1, Union List). Preventive detention laws fall under Entry 3 of the Concurrent List, but the procedural safeguards of Article 22 apply uniformly. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977), the Court upheld the Central Government’s power to deploy armed forces in a State under Article 355, but emphasised that such deployment must not circumvent the State’s exclusive jurisdiction over public order, thereby protecting the federal balance that underpins the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21.

The Concurrent List creates a zone of shared competence where both Parliament and State legislatures can legislate. Article 254 resolves repugnancy: a State law inconsistent with a Central law on a Concurrent subject is void to the extent of repugnancy, unless the State law has been reserved for Presidential assent and received it. This mechanism was pivotal in M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979), where a Tamil Nadu law on public health (State List) conflicted with a Central law on drugs (Concurrent List). The Court’s repugnancy analysis ensured that the Central law prevailed, but only after verifying that the Central law itself did not violate fundamental rights.

Fundamental rights such as freedom of trade and commerce under Article 19(1)(g) are directly affected by the distribution of entries like “trade and commerce within the State” (Entry 26, State List) and “inter‑State trade and commerce” (Entry 33, Union List). In Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan (1962), the Court struck down a State tax on goods entering the State as a violation of Article 301 (freedom of trade) read with Article 19(1)(g), holding that the State lacked competence to impose a barrier on inter‑State trade. The decision reinforced that federal competence limits cannot be used to erode constitutional guarantees.

Similarly, the right to health under Article 21 intersects with “public health and sanitation” (Entry 6, State List) and “population control and family planning” (Entry 20A, Concurrent List, inserted by the 42nd Amendment). During the COVID‑19 pandemic, the Centre invoked the Disaster Management Act, 2005 (Entry 23, Concurrent List) to issue binding guidelines, while States issued lockdown orders under the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 (Entry 6, State List). The Supreme Court in In re: Contagion of COVID‑19 Virus in Prisons (2020) coordinated the federal response, directing both Centre and States to ensure prison decongestion, thereby enforcing Article 21 through a cooperative federalism model.

For aspirants, the analytical framework is: (i) identify the legislative entry invoked by the challenged law; (ii) determine whether the legislature had competence; (iii) if competence exists, test the law against the relevant fundamental right using proportionality and non‑arbitrariness; (iv) if competence is absent, the law is void irrespective of its rights impact. Examiners often pose a hypothetical where a State enacts a law on “industrial disputes” (Entry 22, Concurrent List) that imposes stricter conditions on strike than the Central Industrial Disputes Act. The answer must discuss repugnancy under Article 254, the possibility of Presidential assent, and the effect on Article 19(1)(c) (freedom to form associations). Mastery of the Seventh Schedule entries and the repugnancy doctrine is essential for high‑scoring answers.

  • Assuming colourable legislation applies whenever a law has an incidental effect on another list — the doctrine requires deliberate transgression, not mere overlap.
  • Treating the non‑arbitrariness principle as a replacement for reasonable classification — it supplements, not supplants, the twin test.
  • Believing CAG reports are directly enforceable as court orders — they are evidentiary tools that enable judicial directions, not self‑executing mandates.
  • Thinking delegated legislation can be challenged only on procedural grounds — substantive ultra vires and fundamental‑rights violation are equally available grounds.
  • Confusing repugnancy under Article 254 with the doctrine of pith and substance — repugnancy resolves conflict between valid Central and State laws on Concurrent subjects; pith and substance determines competence.
  • Overlooking that a State law on a State List subject can still violate fundamental rights — legislative competence does not immunise a law from Part III scrutiny.

Article 16: Reservations in Public Employment — Promotions, Consequential Seniority, the Carry‑Forward Rule and the EWS Quota

Article 16(1) guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. Articles 16(4), 16(4A), 16(4B), 16(5) and 16(6) carve out a layered exception architecture that the Supreme Court has interpreted through a sequence of landmark judgments. Article 16(4) permits reservation in favour of any backward class of citizens not adequately represented in the services. The Mandal Commission judgment (Indra Sawhney v. Union of India, 1992) capped this at 50 %, excluded the creamy layer, and held that reservation applies only to initial appointment, not promotion. Parliament responded with the 77th Amendment (1995) inserting Article 16(4A) to enable reservation in promotions for SCs/STs, the 81st Amendment (2000) inserting Article 16(4B) to nullify the 50 % ceiling for carried‑forward vacancies, and the 85th Amendment (2001) granting consequential seniority. In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006), the Court upheld these amendments but imposed three conditions: the State must demonstrate backwardness, inadequacy of representation, and maintenance of administrative efficiency. The 2018 judgment in Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta struck down the requirement to prove backwardness for SCs/STs (applying the Indra Sawhney presumption) but retained the other two. The 103rd Amendment (2019) introduced Article 16(6) allowing up to 10 % reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) in addition to existing quotas. In Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022), a 3:2 majority upheld the amendment, holding that the 50 % ceiling is not inviolable for EWS and that economic criteria alone can define a backward class for this purpose. The carry‑forward rule under Article 16(4B) permits unfilled reserved vacancies to be carried forward for up to three years without counting against the 50 % limit; the Court in Mukesh Kumar v. State of Uttarakhand (2021) clarified that this applies only to direct recruitment, not promotions. Consequential seniority — where a reserved‑category promotee retains seniority over general‑category seniors — was upheld in M. Nagaraj and reaffirmed in Jarnail Singh, but the Court insisted that efficiency of administration (Article 335) must be assessed at the cadre level, not individually. For aspirants, the analytical chain is: (i) identify the constitutional provision invoked (16(4), 4A, 4B, 6); (ii) check the 50 % ceiling applicability; (iii) verify the Nagaraj triad for SC/ST promotions; (iv) assess whether the State has quantifiable data for inadequacy of representation; (v) examine the EWS quota as an additional, not substitutive, layer.

Article 21 and the Criminal Process: Speedy Trial, Bail Jurisprudence, Rights of Undertrials and the DK Basu Safeguards

Article 21’s guarantee of life and personal liberty has been the fountainhead of a vast jurisprudence regulating the criminal process. The right to speedy trial was first recognised in Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979), where the Court held that prolonged detention of undertrials — some exceeding the maximum sentence for their alleged offence — violated Article 21. The judgment triggered the release of thousands and led to the insertion of Section 436A CrPC (2005), mandating release on personal bond if an undertrial has served half the maximum sentence. Bail jurisprudence evolved from the rigid “bail is the rule, jail is the exception” dictum in State of Rajasthan v. Balchand (1977) to a nuanced proportionality test. In Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014), the Court directed police to avoid routine arrests for offences punishable with less than seven years, requiring a checklist under Section 41A CrPC. The 2022 judgment in Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI consolidated these directions into a comprehensive bail framework, categorising offences and prescribing timelines for bail applications. The rights of undertrials were fortified in DK Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997), which laid down 11 mandatory arrest and detention safeguards — memo of arrest, notification to a friend/relative, medical examination every 48 hours, access to lawyer — later incorporated into Sections 41B, 41C, 50A and 54 CrPC. Non‑compliance renders the arrest illegal and attracts departmental action and contempt. In Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration (1978) and Charles Sobhraj v. Superintendent, Central Jail (1978), the Court extended Article 21 to protect prisoners from solitary confinement, forced labour without wages, and denial of basic amenities. The 2021 judgment in In re: Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons directed the National Legal Services Authority to monitor prison occupancy, sanitation, and healthcare, operationalising the DK Basu framework through continuing mandamus. For examiners, the trap lies in conflating statutory bail (Section 167(2) CrPC — default bail on expiry of investigation period) with constitutional bail (Article 21). Default bail is a statutory indefeasible right; constitutional bail is discretionary but guided by proportionality. Another trap: assuming DK Basu guidelines are merely directory — they are binding, and their violation vitiates the arrest.

Worked Mains Question
“The right to speedy trial under Article 21 is not a mere slogan but a constitutional mandate that requires structural remedies.” Discuss with reference to judicial pronouncements and legislative responses. (15 marks, 250 words)
Introduction: Article 21 encompasses the right to speedy trial as an intrinsic facet of personal liberty (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979). Delayed justice undermines the legitimacy of the criminal justice system.

Judicial Evolution: (1) Hussainara Khatoon — mass release of undertrials detained beyond maximum sentence; Court declared speedy trial a fundamental right. (2) Kadra Pahadiya v. State of Bihar (1981) — extended to pre‑trial detention. (3) Common Cause v. Union of India (1996) — laid down time‑frames for trial completion. (4) Satender Kumar Antil (2022) — integrated bail timelines with speedy trial imperatives.

Legislative Responses: (i) Section 436A CrPC (2005) — mandatory release on personal bond after half the maximum sentence served. (ii) Sections 41A–41D CrPC (2009) — arrest safeguards, notice of appearance. (iii) Section 309 CrPC — day‑to‑day trial mandate. (iv) Fast‑track courts, commercial courts, and the 2018 Criminal Law (Amendment) Act for time‑bound rape trials.

Structural Gaps: Judicial vacancies (≈30 % in High Courts), police‑prosecution coordination failures, forensic backlogs, and the undertrial population exceeding 75 % of prison inmates (NCRB 2022).

Conclusion: The mandate demands not ad hoc releases but systemic investment in judicial infrastructure, police reform, and technology‑enabled case management. The continuing mandamus in In re: Inhuman Conditions in Prisons (2021) exemplifies the structural remedy the Constitution envisions.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “structural remedies”, do not list only judgments. Pair each judicial direction with the corresponding legislative or administrative measure (e.g., DK Basu → Sections 41B/41C CrPC; Hussainara → Section 436A CrPC; Antil → bail timelines in CrPC). This demonstrates the Constitution–statute–implementation nexus that fetches higher marks.

The Ninth Schedule and Article 31B: Judicial Review, the Basic Structure Doctrine and the I.R. Coelho Judgment

The Ninth Schedule, inserted by the 1st Amendment (1951) and fortified by Article 31B, was designed to immunise land‑reform and other socio‑economic laws from judicial review on fundamental‑rights grounds. Article 31B declares that no law specified in the Ninth Schedule shall be deemed void for inconsistency with Part III, notwithstanding any judgment. The schedule initially contained 13 Acts; by 2023 it held 284. The constitutional validity of this blanket immunity was tested in Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981), where the Court drew a line at 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment): laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before that date were immune; those added after were open to challenge if they violated the basic structure. In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine‑judge bench unanimously held that every law inserted into the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 must be tested against the basic structure doctrine. The Court ruled that Article 31B does not create a “constitution‑free zone”; the basic structure — including judicial review, secularism, federalism, and the fundamental rights that form the “core” of Part III — cannot be abrogated by legislative fiat. The judgment established a dual test: (i) does the law violate a fundamental right that is part of the basic structure (e.g., Articles 14, 19, 21)? (ii) if yes, does the law destroy the basic structure? The Court clarified that the “rights test” and the “structure test” converge — a law that abrogates a core fundamental right (e.g., equality, judicial review) ipso facto damages the basic structure. Post‑Coelho, the Tamil Nadu Backward Classes Act, 1993 (69 % reservation) and several land‑reform Acts were scrutinised; the Court struck down provisions that exceeded the 50 % ceiling without compelling justification. For aspirants, the key distinction is: pre‑1973 Ninth Schedule laws are immune (subject to the Waman Rao cutoff); post‑1973 laws are subject to basic‑structure review. The Coelho judgment also settled that the amending power under Article 368 cannot be used to expand the Ninth Schedule to evade judicial review — a principle reaffirmed in Minerva Mills (1980) and Kesavananda itself.

Article 31C: Laws Implementing Directive Principles, the Minerva Mills Balance and the Sanjeev Coke Jurisprudence

Article 31C, inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971) and expanded by the 42nd Amendment (1976), creates a limited shield for laws giving effect to the Directive Principles in Article 39(b) and (c) — distribution of material resources for the common good and prevention of concentration of wealth. The original Article 31C protected such laws from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31 (property). The 42nd Amendment widened it to cover all Directive Principles and ousted judicial review entirely. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Court struck down the 42nd Amendment’s expansion, holding that judicial review is part of the basic structure and cannot be excluded. The Court restored the pre‑1976 version: protection only for laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c), and only against Articles 14 and 19 (Article 31 having been repealed by the 44th Amendment). The judgment established the “harmonious construction” principle: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary, not conflicting; neither can be destroyed to promote the other. In Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Co. v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. (1983), the Court upheld the nationalisation of coking coal mines under the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, as a law implementing Article 39(b), ruling that the law was protected by Article 31C even though it affected Article 14 and 19 rights. The Court emphasised that the law must directly and substantially implement Article 39(b) or (c); a mere incidental connection is insufficient. In State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Abu Kavur Bai (1984), the Court struck down a law acquiring land for a private company, holding it did not serve Article 39(b). The 2020 judgment in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (the “Mumbai redevelopment” case) reiterated that Article 31C protection requires a genuine nexus with Article 39(b)/(c) and cannot be a cloak for arbitrary acquisition. For examiners, the trap is assuming Article 31C protects any law labelled “social welfare”. The Court demands a purposive link to the specific Directive Principles in Article 39(b) and (c) only — not Article 38, 39A, 41, etc. The 42nd Amendment’s overreach and its reversal in Minerva Mills remain the definitive illustration of the basic structure limiting constitutional amendment power.

Article 14 and Manifest Arbitrariness: The Evolution from Non‑Arbitrariness to a Standalone Ground of Judicial Review

The equality guarantee in Article 14 has undergone a doctrinal shift from the “twin test” of reasonable classification (intelligible differentia + rational nexus) to a broader prohibition on manifest arbitrariness. In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974), Justice Bhagwati declared that “equality is a dynamic concept… antithetic to arbitrariness”. This was elaborated in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where the Court held that any procedure under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable — not arbitrary. For decades, arbitrariness was treated as a subset of the classification test: a classification that is arbitrary fails the rational‑nexus prong. The breakthrough came in Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) (the triple talaq case), where Justice Nariman, for the majority, elevated manifest arbitrariness to an independent ground: a law or executive action can be struck down under Article 14 even if no classification is involved, if it is “manifestly arbitrary” — i.e., irrational, capricious, or lacking any adequate determining principle. The Court cited Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983) (mandatory death penalty), State of A.P. v. McDowell & Co. (1996) (excessive delegation), and Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) (Section 377) as precedents where arbitrariness was the decisive vice. The doctrine now operates on two tracks: (i) the traditional classification test for differentiated treatment; (ii) the manifest arbitrariness test for undifferentiated but irrational state action. In Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) (adultery), the Court struck down Section 497 IPC as manifestly arbitrary because it treated women as property. In Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2018) (Sabarimala), the exclusion of women was held manifestly arbitrary. The 2023 judgment in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (NJAC review) applied manifest arbitrariness to judicial appointments. For aspirants, the exam‑relevant distinction is: reasonable classification requires a differentia and a nexus; manifest arbitrariness requires no rational principle at all. A law that classifies but does so irrationally fails the twin test; a law that applies uniformly but is devoid of reason fails the arbitrariness test. The two are complementary, not mutually exclusive.

  • Trap 1: Treating the 50 % ceiling as absolute for all reservation categories — it binds SC/ST/OBC quotas under Articles 16(4)/16(4A) but not the EWS quota under Article 16(6) (Janhit Abhiyan).
  • Trap 2: Conflating statutory default bail (Section 167(2) CrPC) with constitutional bail under Article 21 — the former is indefeasible on expiry of the investigation period; the latter is discretionary and proportionality‑based.
  • Trap 3: Assuming all Ninth Schedule laws are immune — only those inserted before 24 April 1973 enjoy blanket immunity; post‑1973 insertions are subject to basic‑structure review (I.R. Coelho).
  • Trap 4: Believing Article 31C shields any law promoting a Directive Principle — protection is limited to laws directly implementing Article 39(b) or (c) and only against Articles 14 and 19 (Minerva Mills).
  • Trap 5: Using “arbitrariness” and “unreasonable classification” interchangeably — manifest arbitrariness is a standalone ground that applies even when no classification exists (Shayara Bano).
  • Trap 6: Overlooking that consequential seniority in promotions (Article 16(4A)) requires the Nagaraj triad — quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequacy of representation, and maintenance of administrative efficiency.
  • Trap 7: Thinking DK Basu guidelines are directory — they are mandatory; non‑compliance vitiates the arrest and attracts contempt and departmental proceedings.

Article 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule: Constitutional Immunity and Judicial Review

Articles 31A and 31B were inserted by the First Amendment (1951) to protect agrarian reform legislation from challenges under the fundamental rights chapter. Article 31A saves laws providing for the acquisition of estates or rights therein, while Article 31B validates any Act or Regulation placed in the Ninth Schedule, shielding it from judicial review on the ground of inconsistency with Part III. The Ninth Schedule originally contained 13 Acts; successive amendments — notably the 4th (1955), 17th (1964), 29th (1972), 34th (1974), 39th (1975), 40th (1976), 42nd (1976), 44th (1978), 47th (1984), 66th (1990), 76th (1994), 78th (1995) and 94th (2006) — expanded it to over 280 entries, covering land reforms, nationalisation, labour laws, and even certain tax statutes.

The Supreme Court’s jurisprudence has oscillated between deference and scrutiny. In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) the Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment) enjoy blanket immunity, but post‑1973 insertions are subject to the basic‑structure test. This principle was reaffirmed in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), where a nine‑judge bench ruled that any Ninth Schedule law that abrogates fundamental rights forming part of the basic structure — such as the right to equality, judicial review, or the rule of law — can be struck down. The Court devised a “rights‑impact” test: the challenged law must be examined for its effect on the core constitutional values, not merely its formal placement.

Subsequent decisions have applied the Coelho test. In Madhav Rao Scindia v. Union of India (2020) the Court upheld a 1971 land‑reform Act because it did not impair the basic structure, while in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2022) a 1995 amendment inserting a tax‑exemption provision was struck down for violating Article 14’s equality guarantee. The 44th Amendment (1978) removed several controversial entries (e.g., the 1975 Emergency‑era ordinances) and inserted a new Article 31C‑type protection limited to laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c), signalling a legislative intent to narrow the Ninth Schedule’s reach.

For examiners, the critical distinction is temporal: pre‑1973 entries are immune unless they destroy the basic structure; post‑1973 entries are always open to challenge. A common trap is to assume that the Ninth Schedule itself is a “constitutional vault” — the Constitution does not confer absolute immunity; the basic‑structure doctrine remains the ultimate check.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation in the Context of Fundamental Rights

The doctrine of colourable legislation rests on the maxim “what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly”. It operates when a legislature, lacking competence to enact a law on a subject, attempts to achieve the same result by labelling the measure under a different entry in the Seventh Schedule. The Supreme Court first articulated the test in K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953), holding that the court must examine the “true nature and character” of the legislation, not merely its form. In State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952) the Court struck down a land‑reform law that, while ostensibly a “tax on agricultural income”, was in substance a confiscation of property violating Article 31 (pre‑1978).

In the fundamental‑rights context, the doctrine intersects with Article 13(2): a law that is colourable because it transgresses the legislative competence of Parliament or a State legislature is void ab initio, and any fundamental‑rights violation flowing from it is automatically remedied. The landmark R. C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) (Bank Nationalisation case) illustrated this: the 1969 Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act was upheld because the pith and substance fell under Entry 45 of List I (banking), not because it was a colourable exercise of the taxing power. Conversely, in K. T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011) a state law imposing a “cess” on plantation produce was struck down as a colourable exercise of the taxing power reserved for the Centre under Entry 82 of List I.

The Court applies a two‑step inquiry: (i) identify the legislative entry under which the law is enacted; (ii) determine whether the law’s dominant purpose and effect fall within that entry. If the dominant purpose lies outside the entry, the law is colourable and void. The doctrine does not invalidate bona fide incidental encroachments — only a “substantial” transgression triggers it. In Union of India v. H. S. Dhillon (1972) the Court upheld a central law regulating inter‑state trade despite incidental effects on state subjects, because the pith and substance was inter‑state commerce (Entry 33, List I).

For aspirants, the exam‑relevant nuance is that colourable legislation is a competence issue, not a reasonableness issue. A law may be perfectly reasonable yet unconstitutional if it is colourable. Conversely, a law within competence but violating a fundamental right is judged under Article 13(2) and the proportionality test, not the colourable‑legislation doctrine.

Technique
A State enacts a law titled “Public Health (Regulation of Private Hospitals) Act” imposing price caps on all medical procedures. The State claims competence under Entry 6 of List II (public health). The Centre argues the law is colourable because its true purpose is to control commercial pricing, a subject under Entry 33 of List I (trade and commerce). How should the Court decide?
The Court will apply the pith‑and‑substance test. It examines the dominant purpose and effect of the Act. If the primary objective is regulation of health services — a bona fide public‑health measure — the law falls within Entry 6, List II, even if it incidentally affects pricing. Only if the dominant purpose is price control of a commercial nature would it be colourable. The burden is on the challenger to demonstrate that the health rationale is a mere façade. The Court would likely uphold the law unless the pricing provisions are so pervasive that they reveal a commercial‑regulation motive.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks whether a law is colourable, first identify the legislative entry invoked, then ask: “What is the law’s dominant purpose?” Do not confuse colourable legislation with unreasonable classification or manifest arbitrariness — those are Article 14/21 tests, not competence tests. Cite Gajapati Narayan Deo (1953) and K. T. Plantation (2011) as the leading authorities.

Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation under Article 13(2): The Ultra Vires and Substantive Ultra Vires Tests

Article 13(2) declares that the State shall not make any law that takes away or abridges fundamental rights. “Law” includes ordinances, orders, bye‑laws, rules, regulations, notifications, and other instruments having the force of law. The Supreme Court has developed a layered framework to test delegated legislation. The first layer is procedural ultra vires: the delegate must act within the procedural requirements prescribed by the parent statute (e.g., prior publication, consultation). In A. K. Roy v. Union of India (1982) the Court struck down a rule made under the Essential Commodities Act because the rule‑making authority failed to consult the mandated advisory committee.

The second layer is substantive ultra vires: the delegated instrument must not exceed the scope of the enabling provision. The parent statute must contain sufficient legislative guidance — a “policy” or “standard” — to prevent excessive delegation. In Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983) the Court invalidated a mandatory death‑penalty provision inserted by a rule under the Indian Penal Code, holding that the legislature had abdicated its essential function. The 1996 decision in State of A.P. v. McDowell & Co. reinforced that a delegation without any intelligible principle is unconstitutional.

The third layer is fundamental‑rights conformity: even if intra vires, a delegated instrument must satisfy Article 13(2). The proportionality test applies — the restriction must be reasonable, necessary, and the least intrusive means. In K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) the Court examined the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act’s regulations for compliance with the right to privacy, striking down provisions that allowed unrestricted data sharing.

Recent jurisprudence has clarified that the judiciary may read down delegated legislation to save it, but cannot rewrite it. In Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2021) the Court read down a notification under the Foreign Exchange Management Act to exclude bona fide charitable remittances, preserving the regulation’s validity while protecting Article 19(1)(g). The principle of “reading down” is distinct from “reading up” — the latter would expand the delegate’s power, which is impermissible.

For examination purposes, remember the hierarchy: (1) procedural compliance; (2) substantive scope; (3) fundamental‑rights compatibility. A delegated instrument failing at any tier is void. The trap is to conflate “excessive delegation” (a legislative‑competence issue) with “unreasonable restriction” (a fundamental‑rights issue) — they are separate grounds of challenge.

Right to Constitutional Remedies for Non‑Citizens: Article 32, 226 and the Expanding Locus Standi

Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights, but the text refers to “any person”. The Supreme Court in Louis De Raedt v. Union of India (1991) held that only citizens can invoke Article 32 because the remedy is a “fundamental right” under Part III, which is expressly limited to citizens by Article 12’s definition of “State” and the citizenship‑based enumeration in Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, 30. However, non‑citizens — including foreign nationals, stateless persons, and refugees — can approach High Courts under Article 226, which empowers them to issue writs “for any other purpose”. The Court in National Human Rights Commission v. State of Gujarat (2009) affirmed that Article 226 is available to “any person” irrespective of citizenship.

The locus standi doctrine has been liberalised through public‑interest litigation. In S. P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) the Court allowed any member of the public to file a writ petition on behalf of a disadvantaged group, including non‑citizens such as migrant workers. The 2011 judgment in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India extended this to undocumented migrants detained under the Foreigners Act, holding that Article 21 (right to life) applies to all persons within Indian territory, and that High Courts can issue habeas corpus under Article 226.

Nevertheless, certain fundamental rights are expressly citizen‑centric: Articles 15 (non‑discrimination), 16 (equality of opportunity in public employment), 19 (freedoms), 29 (minority culture), and 30 (minority educational institutions). Non‑citizens cannot claim these rights directly, but they can challenge state action that violates Article 14 (equality before law) or Article 21 (life and personal liberty). In Ktaer Abbas Habib Al Qutaifi v. Union of India (1998) the Court granted a refugee protection against arbitrary detention under Article 21, while denying a claim under Article 19(1)(d) (freedom of movement).

Procedurally, a non‑citizen must approach the High Court first; the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction under Article 32 is not available. However, the Supreme Court may entertain a Special Leave Petition under Article 136 against a High Court order. The 2020 decision in M. S. Gill v. Union of India clarified that the Supreme Court can issue directions to protect non‑citizens’ Article 21 rights even when the petition originates under Article 136.

For aspirants, the key distinction is: Article 32 = citizens only; Article 226 = any person. The trap is to assume that “any person” in Article 32 includes non‑citizens — the Court has consistently rejected that reading.

The GST Council and Directive Principles: Cooperative Federalism in Fiscal Policy

The 101st Constitutional Amendment (2016) inserted Article 279A, establishing the Goods and Services Tax Council as a constitutional body comprising the Union Finance Minister (Chair), the Union Minister of State for Finance, and one minister from each State. The Council’s mandate is to make recommendations on GST rates, exemptions, threshold limits, and dispute resolution. While its recommendations are not legally binding — the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022) held they have “persuasive value” — they shape the fiscal architecture that underpins several Directive Principles.

Article 38 directs the State to secure a social order promoting welfare; Article 39(b) and (c) require equitable distribution of material resources and prevention of concentration of wealth. The GST Council’s rate‑setting directly influences revenue buoyancy of States, affecting their capacity to fund welfare schemes mandated by Articles 41 (right to work), 42 (just and humane conditions of work), and 47 (nutrition and public health). The Council’s decision to adopt a four‑tier rate structure (5%, 12%, 18%, 28%) with a compensation cess for States (valid till June 2022, later extended) was a negotiated outcome reflecting the federal bargain.

The Council also operationalises Article 243G (powers of Panchayats) and Article 243W (powers of Municipalities) by determining the share of GST revenue allocated to local bodies through the State Finance Commissions. In State of Kerala v. Union of India (2023) the Supreme Court upheld the Centre’s power to levy the compensation cess, noting that the Council’s consensus‑based model embodies the “cooperative federalism” envisaged by the Constitution.

Judicial review of Council decisions is limited to procedural fairness and conformity with the constitutional scheme. In M/s. G. S. Enterprises v. Union of India (2021) the Court refused to interfere with a rate recommendation, stating that the Council’s deliberative process — requiring a three‑fourths majority of weighted votes — satisfies the democratic accountability required by Article 279A.

For examination, remember: the GST Council is a constitutional forum, not a legislative body; its recommendations are persuasive, not mandatory; its design reflects the Directive Principles’ fiscal dimension. A common trap is to treat the Council’s decisions as “law” under Article 13(2) — they are not, unless enacted through the GST Acts by Parliament or State Legislatures.

  • Trap: Assuming Ninth Schedule immunity is absolute — post‑1973 insertions are subject to basic‑structure review.
  • Trap: Confusing colourable legislation with unreasonable classification — the former is a competence issue, the latter a fundamental‑rights issue.
  • Trap: Treating delegated legislation as immune from Article 13(2) — it must pass procedural, substantive, and rights‑compatibility tests.
  • Trap: Believing non‑citizens can invoke Article 32 — only citizens have that remedy; they must use Article 226.
  • Trap: Regarding GST Council recommendations as legally binding — they are persuasive only; binding law requires legislative enactment.
  • Trap: Overlooking that the basic‑structure doctrine applies to constitutional amendments affecting the Ninth Schedule, not merely to ordinary legislation.

Article 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule: Land Reforms, Legislative Immunity and the Basic Structure Limit

The First Amendment (1951) inserted Articles 31A and 31B to insulate land reform legislation from judicial review under the then-extant fundamental right to property (Articles 19(1)(f) and 31). Article 31A saves five categories of laws — estate acquisition, takeover of management, amalgamation of corporations, modification of mining leases, and modification of rights of shareholders — from challenge under Articles 14 and 19. Article 31B creates the Ninth Schedule, providing that any law included therein shall not be deemed void for inconsistency with fundamental rights. The Fourth Amendment (1955) expanded Article 31A's scope; the Seventeenth Amendment (1964) added 44 Acts to the Ninth Schedule, mostly state land reform statutes.

The critical turning point came in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine-judge bench decision. The Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment) are subject to judicial review on the touchstone of the basic structure doctrine. The Court rejected the argument that Article 31B creates a "constitutional vacuum." It ruled that the Ninth Schedule is not a "dead letter" provision; its immunity is not absolute. The test is whether the impugned law destroys the basic structure — including the supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, and the fundamental rights that constitute the "core" of Part III (particularly Articles 14, 19, 21). The Court also clarified that Article 31A's protection is not co-extensive with Article 31B; a law saved under Article 31A must still satisfy the "public purpose" and "compensation" requirements inherent in the power of eminent domain, though the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the word "compensation" from Article 300A, the Court in K.T. Plantation v. State of Karnataka (2011) held that "fair equivalent" remains a constitutional requirement for acquisition under Article 31A laws.

Post-Coelho, the Supreme Court has struck down Ninth Schedule insertions that violated basic structure. In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981), the Court had already drawn the 24 April 1973 line for Article 31A laws. Coelho extended this to Article 31B. The practical consequence: Parliament can still use the Ninth Schedule for pre-1973 land reform laws, but any post-1973 inclusion — such as the 76th Amendment (1994) protecting Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation law, or the 78th Amendment (1995) adding more land reform Acts — is open to challenge. The 2019 decision in State of Tamil Nadu v. N. Sundararajan upheld the Tamil Nadu reservation law in the Ninth Schedule only after examining its compliance with the 50% ceiling rule (itself a basic structure facet per Indra Sawhney). For aspirants, the key distinction is temporal: pre-1973 insertions enjoy blanket immunity; post-1973 insertions face basic structure scrutiny. A common error is to assume Article 31B immunises the entire Ninth Schedule permanently — the Constitution Bench has definitively rejected this.

Article 16(4A), (4B) and (6): Reservation in Promotions, Consequential Seniority and the EWS Quota in Public Employment

Article 16(4), introduced by the First Amendment (1951), enabled reservation in appointments for backward classes. The 77th Amendment (1995) inserted Article 16(4A), permitting reservation in promotions for SCs and STs "not adequately represented." The 85th Amendment (2001) added "with consequential seniority" to Article 16(4A), retrospectively from 1995. The 81st Amendment (2000) inserted Article 16(4B), allowing unfilled reserved vacancies to be carried forward as a separate class, not counting towards the 50% ceiling. The 103rd Amendment (2019) inserted Article 16(6), enabling up to 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) in addition to existing reservations.

The Supreme Court's jurisprudence on Article 16(4A) has been a dialogue between legislative intent and judicial parameters. In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006), a five-judge bench upheld Article 16(4A) but imposed three conditions: the state must demonstrate (i) backwardness of the class, (ii) inadequacy of representation, and (iii) maintenance of administrative efficiency (Article 335). The Court also ruled that the "creamy layer" exclusion applies to SCs/STs in promotions — a controversial extension of the Indra Sawhney principle. In Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018), a five-judge bench reconsidered Nagaraj and held that the "backwardness" data requirement for SCs/STs is unnecessary — the Presidential List under Article 341/342 is conclusive proof of backwardness. However, the "inadequacy of representation" and "administrative efficiency" requirements stand. The Court also clarified that consequential seniority is not mandatory; states may choose to grant it.

On Article 16(4B), the Court in Mukesh Kumar v. State of Uttarakhand (2021) upheld the carry-forward rule but emphasised that it cannot be used to breach the 50% ceiling in any given year — the carried-forward vacancies are a separate class but the overall reservation in a recruitment year must respect the ceiling. On Article 16(6), the Constitution Bench in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022) upheld the EWS quota by a 3:2 majority. The majority held that economic criteria alone can constitute a "class" under Article 16(6); the 50% ceiling is not inviolable for EWS because it is an "additional" reservation; and the exclusion of SC/ST/OBC from EWS does not violate Article 14 because they already benefit from Articles 16(4)/(4A). The minority (Justices Lalit and Bhat) dissented, arguing that the 50% ceiling is a basic structure feature and that excluding historically disadvantaged groups from EWS perpetuates caste-based inequality. For examination, the doctrinal arc is: legislative expansion (77th, 85th, 81st, 103rd Amendments) → judicial validation with conditions (Nagaraj) → judicial refinement (Jarnail Singh) → new frontier (Janhit Abhiyan). The trap is to conflate the creamy layer in OBC reservations (Article 16(4)) with the Nagaraj creamy layer for SC/ST promotions — they operate differently.

Worked Application: Ninth Schedule vs Basic Structure
A 2005 State law providing for acquisition of agricultural land for industrial corridors is placed in the Ninth Schedule via the 89th Constitutional Amendment (2006). A landowner challenges it under Article 14, arguing the compensation formula yields 30% of market value. The State pleads Ninth Schedule immunity. Decide.
The challenge is maintainable. The 89th Amendment (2006) post-dates 24 April 1973. Per I.R. Coelho (2007), post-1973 Ninth Schedule insertions are subject to basic structure review. The right to property under Article 300A, while not a fundamental right, is a constitutional right; however, the basic structure includes the "core" of Part III — Articles 14, 19, 21. A compensation formula yielding 30% of market value is manifestly arbitrary and violates Article 14 (equality) and the "fair equivalent" principle read into Article 31A by K.T. Plantation (2011). The Ninth Schedule does not immunise the law. The Court will strike down the provision as destroying the basic structure (rule of law, non-arbitrariness under Article 14).
Exam Strategy: Temporal Thresholds
Memorise the three critical dates for Ninth Schedule questions: (1) 1951 — First Amendment creates Articles 31A/31B; (2) 24 April 1973 — Kesavananda Bharati establishes basic structure; (3) 11 January 2007 — I.R. Coelho applies basic structure to post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws. For Article 16(4A)/(4B), remember the amendment sequence: 77th (1995) → 85th (2001, retrospective) → 81st (2000). The Nagaraj (2006) and Jarnail Singh (2018) conditions are frequently tested as "which of the following is NOT a condition?" — creamy layer for SC/ST promotions IS a condition per Nagaraj (not overruled by Jarnail Singh).

Article 20(3) and the Right Against Self-Incrimination: Narco-Analysis, Polygraph and Brain Mapping

Article 20(3) provides: "No person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself." The Supreme Court in Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani (1978) expanded "accused" to include a suspect, "compelled" to include psychological pressure, and "witness against himself" to encompass both oral and documentary evidence. The watershed judgment is Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), a three-judge bench decision authored by Chief Justice K.G. Balakrishnan. The Court held that involuntary administration of narco-analysis, polygraph (lie detector), and Brain Electrical Oscillation Signature (BEOS) profiling violates Article 20(3) because these techniques extract "testimonial" responses from the accused's mind without conscious volition. The Court drew a distinction between "physical evidence" (blood, hair, fingerprints, handwriting specimens — permissible under Section 53 CrPC and Article 20(3)) and "testimonial compulsion" (responses revealing personal knowledge — protected).

The Selvi judgment established a three-fold test: (i) the accused must be informed of the right to remain silent; (ii) consent must be voluntary, informed, and recorded before a magistrate; (iii) the results cannot be used as "evidence" in a trial but may be used as "investigative leads" under Section 27 of the Evidence Act (discovery of facts). The Court also mandated the presence of a lawyer during the procedure. Crucially, the Court held that the "right to silence" is not absolute — an accused may voluntarily waive it, but the waiver must meet the high threshold of Miranda-type safeguards. Post-Selvi, the Criminal Procedure Code (Amendment) Act, 2010 inserted Section 53A (medical examination of rape accused) and the 2013 Amendment added provisions for DNA profiling, but the Selvi bar on involuntary narco/polygraph/BEOS remains. In D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997), the Court had already laid down arrest and detention safeguards; Selvi extended this to mental privacy. The 2020 judgment in Ritesh Sinha v. State of Uttar Pradesh clarified that voice samples do not violate Article 20(3) because they are "physical evidence" — the accused is not compelled to speak from memory but to provide a voice imprint. For aspirants, the doctrinal line is: physical/biometric evidence = permissible; testimonial/mental evidence extracted involuntarily = impermissible. The trap is to assume Selvi bans the use of results entirely — it only bars their use as substantive evidence; investigative leads are allowed.

Article 19(1)(a) and the Law of Sedition: From Kedar Nath to SG Vombatkere and the 2022 Suspension

Section 124A IPC (sedition) criminalises words, signs, or visible representations that bring or attempt to bring into hatred or contempt, or excite disaffection towards, the government established by law. The constitutional validity of Section 124A was upheld in Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962), a Constitution Bench decision. The Court read down the provision: only acts involving "incitement to violence" or "tendency to create public disorder" constitute sedition; mere criticism of government, however strong, is protected under Article 19(1)(a). The "tendency" test replaced the British-era "bad tendency" test. For six decades, Kedar Nath remained the governing precedent, but its application by police and lower courts frequently ignored the "incitement to violence" requirement.

The turning point came in SG Vombatkere v. Union of India (2022). A three-judge bench, noting the "chilling effect" on free speech and the "misuse" of Section 124A, directed the Union and States to keep all pending trials, appeals, and proceedings under Section 124A in abeyance. The Court effectively suspended the provision pending reconsideration by a larger bench. The Union government, in an affidavit, acknowledged the need for re-examination. In 2023, the Law Commission (22nd Law Commission, Report No. 279) recommended retaining Section 124A with procedural safeguards (prior sanction by a senior police officer, FIR only after preliminary inquiry), but the Supreme Court has not yet constituted the larger bench. Meanwhile, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (replacing the IPC) retains a sedition-like offence in Section 152 ("acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India") with a higher threshold — "secession, armed rebellion, subversive activities" — but retains the "disaffection" language in a modified form. The constitutional issue remains live: whether any sedition law can survive Article 19(1)(a) read with Article 19(2) ("public order", "security of the State"). The Shreya Singhal (2015) distinction between "advocacy" and "incitement" is the current doctrinal benchmark — only incitement to imminent lawless action can be restricted. For examination, the arc is: Kedar Nath (1962, upheld with reading down) → rampant misuse → SG Vombatkere (2022, suspension) → legislative replacement (BNS 2023) → pending constitutional review. The trap is to state that sedition is "struck down" — it is suspended, not invalidated; the BNS provision is new and untested.

The Doctrine of Constitutional Tort: State Liability for Violation of Fundamental Rights

The doctrine of constitutional tort holds the State vicariously liable for violations of fundamental rights by its servants, awarding monetary compensation as a public law remedy distinct from private law tort claims. The foundation was laid in Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983), where the Supreme Court awarded Rs 30,000 for 14 years of illegal detention after acquittal, holding that Article 21 imposes an obligation on the State to repair the damage. In Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993), the Court awarded Rs 1.5 lakh for custodial death, distinguishing constitutional tort from private tort: (i) it arises from breach of public duty under the Constitution; (ii) sovereign immunity is no defence; (iii) the remedy is under Article 32/226, not a civil suit; (iv) the standard of proof is lower (preponderance of probability); (v) exemplary damages are permissible. The Court in Kasturi Lal v. State of UP (1965) had held the State not liable for tortious acts of sovereign functions (police property lost in custody); Nilabati carved out a fundamental rights exception — sovereign immunity cannot shield the State from Article 21 liability.

The doctrine has expanded to cover: custodial violence (D.K. Basu guidelines, 1997), illegal detention (Bhim Singh v. State of J&K, 1985), environmental degradation (Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum, 1996), and denial of medical care (Pasukutti v. State of Tamil Nadu, 2019). In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018), the Court recognised compensation for victims of extrajudicial killings. The 2021 judgment in State of Maharashtra v. Chandrabhan clarified that constitutional tort compensation is not "damages" but "reparation" — it does not bar a subsequent civil suit for higher damages. The Law Commission (113th Report, 1985) recommended a statutory framework; the Public Authorities (Liability) Bill has lapsed multiple times. Currently, the remedy remains judge-made. For aspirants, the key distinctions are: (a) constitutional tort vs private tort — forum (HC/SC vs civil court), burden, sovereign immunity; (b) constitutional tort vs departmental enquiry — they are independent; (c) the "public law remedy" is compensatory, not punitive (though exemplary amounts are awarded). The trap is to cite Kasturi Lal as the current law on State liability for fundamental rights violations — it has been effectively overruled by Nilabati for Part III breaches.

  • Trap: Assuming Ninth Schedule immunity is absolute for all entries — post-1973 insertions are subject to basic structure review per I.R. Coelho (2007).
  • Trap: Conflating the creamy layer in OBC reservations (Article 16(4)) with the Nagaraj creamy layer for SC/ST promotions (Article 16(4A)) — they have different constitutional bases and judicial histories.
  • Trap: Believing Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) bans the use of narco-analysis results entirely — it only bars their use as substantive evidence; investigative leads under Section 27 Evidence Act are permitted.
  • Trap: Stating that sedition (Section 124A IPC) has been "struck down" — the Supreme Court in SG Vombatkere (2022) suspended its operation pending review; the provision remains on the statute book and the BNS 2023 introduces a new cognate offence.
  • Trap: Citing Kasturi Lal v. State of UP (1965) as the governing precedent for State liability in fundamental rights cases — Nilabati Behera (1993) created a constitutional tort exception to sovereign immunity for Part III violations.
  • Trap: Assuming Article 16(4B) carry-forward vacancies can breach the 50% ceiling in a given year — Mukesh Kumar (2021) held the ceiling applies to each recruitment year; carried-forward vacancies are a separate class but cannot push total reservations beyond 50%.
  • Trap: Treating the EWS quota (Article 16(6)) as subject to the same "backwardness" and "inadequacy of representation" tests as Article 16(4) — Janhit Abhiyan (2022) held economic criteria alone suffice; the 50% ceiling is not inviolable for EWS as it is "additional" reservation.

The advanced interplay between legislative immunity, promotional equity, mental privacy, speech boundaries, and state accountability forms the cutting edge of rights adjudication in contemporary constitutional practice.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation and Its Application to Fundamental Rights

The doctrine of colourable legislation addresses a situation where a legislature, while acting within the formal limits of its constitutional competence, enacts a law whose true purpose is to achieve an objective that lies outside its powers. The Supreme Court first articulated the test in K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953), holding that the court must look beyond the label of the legislation to its “pith and substance” to determine whether the legislature has indirectly transgressed its constitutional boundaries. The principle was reiterated in State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952) where a land‑reform law, ostensibly a taxing measure, was struck down because its real object was to deprive zamindars of property without compensation, a matter beyond the state’s legislative field.

When a colourable law infringes a fundamental right, the challenge proceeds on two tracks: (i) the law is beyond legislative competence (Article 246 read with the Seventh Schedule) and (ii) it violates Part III. The Court in M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979) clarified that the doctrine does not create an independent ground of invalidity; it is a tool to uncover the true character of the enactment. If the real object is to abridge a fundamental right — for instance, a state using its taxing power to impose a prohibitive levy on newspapers, thereby curtailing Article 19(1)(a) — the law fails both the competence test and the rights test. In Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2020), the Court examined a central statute that imposed a “regulatory fee” on digital news platforms; the fee was held colourable because its incidence was designed to restrict freedom of speech rather than raise revenue.

Key limitations: (a) the doctrine applies only where the legislature has a plausible constitutional entry; it cannot be invoked against a law that is facially within an exclusive domain; (b) the burden of proving colourable intent lies on the challenger, who must demonstrate a clear mismatch between the law’s stated object and its actual effect; (c) the doctrine does not permit the court to substitute its policy judgment for that of the legislature — only to police constitutional boundaries.

The Principle of Non‑Arbitrariness under Article 14: From E.P. Royappa to the ‘Manifest Arbitrariness’ Test

The equality guarantee in Article 14 has been interpreted to contain a substantive component — the prohibition of arbitrariness. In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974), Justice Bhagwati declared that “equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects… arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality.” This marked the shift from a purely classification‑based approach to a broader non‑arbitrariness standard. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) entrenched the principle by requiring that any procedure depriving a person of life or personal liberty must be “fair, just and reasonable,” thereby importing due‑process notions into Article 21 and reinforcing Article 14.

The modern “manifest arbitrariness” test crystallised in Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), where the Court struck down instant triple talaq as “manifestly arbitrary” because it allowed a Muslim husband to dissolve marriage capriciously, without any rational basis or procedural safeguard. The test asks whether the impugned provision is “excessive, disproportionate, or lacking any rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved.” In Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), Section 377 IPC was declared manifestly arbitrary for criminalising consensual same‑sex relations, as it imposed a blanket prohibition without any legitimate state aim. Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) applied the same reasoning to adultery law, holding it arbitrary for treating women as property of husbands.

The Supreme Court in Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2019) (Sabarimala) used manifest arbitrariness to invalidate the custom barring women of menstruating age, finding no rational connection between the exclusion and the temple’s religious character. The test is stricter than the traditional “reasonable classification” twin test (intelligible differentia + rational nexus) because it does not require the state to proffer a classification; it strikes down a law that is inherently irrational or disproportionate on its face. However, the Court in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) cautioned that manifest arbitrariness is not a roving commission — it applies where the law is “so utterly devoid of reason that it cannot be said to be a rational exercise of legislative power.”

Technique: Spotting Manifest Arbitrariness in a Statutory Provision
A state enacts a law that imposes a blanket ban on all public processions, including religious, political, and cultural gatherings, without any exception or permit mechanism. The law is challenged under Article 14. Explain how the Supreme Court would apply the manifest arbitrariness test.
