Step 1 — Identify the classification: The law creates a single class — “all processions” — and treats them identically. No intelligible differentia exists.
Step 2 — Test for rational nexus: The state may claim public order, but a total ban with no tailoring (no permit, no time‑place‑manner restrictions) is disproportionate to that aim.
Step 3 — Apply manifest arbitrariness: Following Shayara Bano and Navtej Singh Johar, the Court would ask whether the provision is “excessive, disproportionate, or lacking any rational basis.” A blanket prohibition without any exception is manifestly arbitrary because it sweeps in harmless assemblies and leaves no room for case‑by‑case assessment.
Step 4 — Conclusion: The law fails the manifest arbitrariness test and is struck down under Article 14. The Court would not need to engage the traditional twin test because the provision is irrational on its face.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a law violates Article 14, first check if a classification exists. If the law applies uniformly without any differentiation, argue manifest arbitrariness — cite Royappa, Maneka Gandhi, Shayara Bano, Navtej Singh Johar. If a classification is present, run the twin test. Remember: manifest arbitrariness is a higher threshold; it does not replace reasonable classification but operates where classification is absent or the law is facially irrational.

The Doctrine of Pith and Substance in the Context of Fundamental Rights and Federal Distribution

The pith and substance doctrine determines the true character of a legislation for the purpose of allocating legislative competence between the Union and the States under the Seventh Schedule. The classic formulation in Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce (1947) and State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) requires the court to ascertain the “dominant purpose” of the enactment, ignoring incidental encroachments on another legislature’s field. When a law’s pith and substance falls within the competence of the enacting legislature, it is valid even if it incidentally touches subjects assigned to the other tier.

The doctrine intersects with fundamental rights in two ways. First, a law that is within legislative competence may still be void under Article 13(2) if it abridges a fundamental right. The pith and substance analysis does not immunise a competent law from Part III scrutiny. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2021) (the GST compensation case), the Court held that the GST Act’s pith and substance was “taxation on goods and services” (Union List Entry 84), but the compensation cess was examined separately for compliance with Article 14 and Article 300A. Second, where a state law’s dominant purpose is to regulate a Union subject — for example, a state enacting a “public order” law that in reality controls inter‑state trade — the law is struck down as colourable legislation, which is a species of pith and substance analysis.

Recent jurisprudence illustrates the doctrine’s limits. In Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (2022), the Court examined a central law on “prevention of money laundering” (Entry 93, Union List) that also regulated “benami transactions” (State List Entry 6). The Court held the pith and substance was “prevention of money laundering,” a Union competence, and the incidental regulation of benami property did not render the law ultra vires. However, the delegated rules under the Act were separately tested for Article 14 arbitrariness. In State of Tamil Nadu v. Union of India (2023) (the NEET exemption case), the Court used pith and substance to decide that the state’s attempt to exempt students from a central entrance exam was essentially “education standards” (Concurrent List Entry 25), a field where Parliament’s law prevails under Article 254.

Key takeaways: (i) pith and substance is a competence tool, not a rights shield; (ii) incidental effects on fundamental rights do not alter the competence analysis; (iii) the doctrine cannot be invoked to save a law that is otherwise violative of Part III; (iv) the Court may apply the doctrine at the stage of legislative entry interpretation, but any subsequent delegated legislation remains subject to full fundamental‑rights review.

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation under Article 13(3) and Its Impact on Fundamental Rights

Article 13(3) defines “law” to include “any Ordinance, order, bye‑law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law.” This expansive definition brings delegated legislation squarely within the scope of judicial review for fundamental‑rights violations. The Supreme Court in Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India (1960) held that a rule made under the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act that prohibited advertising of certain drugs violated Article 19(1)(a) because the parent statute did not authorise such a sweeping restriction. The Court established that delegated legislation must conform to the parent statute’s policy and cannot exceed the legislative mandate — the “guideline principle.”

The doctrine of “excessive delegation” was refined in Delhi Laws Act (1951), where the Court struck down a provision allowing the executive to extend any central law to a Part C state without legislative standards. In Union of India v. K.S. Subramanian (2020), the Court invalidated a notification under the Environment (Protection) Act that imposed a blanket ban on construction in a 10‑km radius of a wildlife sanctuary, finding it violated Article 14 (arbitrariness) and Article 21 (livelihood) because the parent Act provided no criteria for such a radius.

Recent cases demonstrate the growing rigour. In M/s. V.S. Enterprises v. State of U.P. (2022), a rule under the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act that allowed the government to exempt any establishment from the Act’s provisions without guidelines was held ultra vires and violative of Article 14. The Court emphasised that the absence of legislative standards renders the delegation “uncontrolled” and therefore unconstitutional. In K.K. Verma v. Union of India (2023), a regulation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act that permitted attachment of property without a prior hearing was struck down for violating Article 21 (procedural fairness) and Article 14 (manifest arbitrariness), even though the parent statute authorised attachment — the regulation failed the proportionality test.

Practical implications: (a) every rule, notification, or order must be traceable to a clear legislative standard; (b) the Court applies the proportionality doctrine (legitimate aim, suitability, necessity, balancing) to delegated measures affecting fundamental rights; (c) the “guideline principle” operates as a constitutional safeguard against executive overreach; (d) a delegation may be valid on its face, but the delegated instrument can still be struck down if it infringes Part III. Aspirants should note that the distinction between “excessive delegation” (a structural constitutional defect) and “violation of fundamental rights by a validly delegated rule” (a substantive defect) is frequently tested.

  • Confusing colourable legislation with ultra vires; colourable legislation is about disguised transgression of legislative competence, not mere incompetence.
  • Assuming manifest arbitrariness replaces reasonable classification; it is a separate, stricter test applied when classification is absent or irrational.
  • Believing pith and substance can validate a law that violates fundamental rights; the doctrine only determines legislative competence, not Part III compliance.
  • Thinking delegated legislation is immune from fundamental‑rights challenge because it is subordinate; Article 13(3) expressly includes it.
  • Overlooking that the manifest arbitrariness test requires a showing of excessiveness or disproportionality, not merely unreasonableness.
  • Treating the doctrine of colourable legislation as a standalone ground for striking down a law; it is a tool to uncover the true nature of the legislation.
  • Ignoring the distinction between excessive delegation and violation of fundamental rights; a delegation may be valid but the delegated rule may still infringe rights.

Article 16(4A), (4B), (5) and (6): Reservations in Promotions, Consequential Seniority, Carry‑Forward and the EWS Quota in Public Employment

Article 16(1) guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. Clause (4), the original enabling provision for reservations in favour of "any backward class of citizens which, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services under the State", was interpreted in M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore (1963) to impose a 50% ceiling and to exclude the "creamy layer". The Mandal Commission report (1980) and Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) cemented the 27% OBC quota, the creamy layer filter, and the bar on reservations in promotions. Parliament responded with the 77th Amendment (1995) inserting Article 16(4A), empowering the State to make "any provision for reservation in matters of promotion to any class or classes of posts in the services under the State in favour of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes which, in the opinion of the State, are not adequately represented". The 85th Amendment (2001) added Article 16(4B), allowing "consequential seniority" — a promotee from the reserved category retains seniority over general‑category peers promoted later. The 81st Amendment (2000) inserted Article 16(4B) (renumbered) to permit the "carry‑forward" of unfilled reserved vacancies beyond the 50% ceiling in a given year.

The Supreme Court in M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) upheld Articles 16(4A) and (4B) but imposed three justiciable conditions: (i) the State must demonstrate the "backwardness" of the SC/ST class (though the Presidential lists under Articles 341/342 create a presumption), (ii) quantifiable data showing "inadequacy of representation" in the specific cadre, and (iii) compliance with Article 335 — "maintenance of efficiency of administration". The Court also extended the creamy layer exclusion to SC/ST promotions. In Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018), a five‑judge bench modified Nagaraj: it held that the Presidential lists under Articles 341/342 obviate the need to prove "backwardness" afresh for SC/STs, but the requirements of quantifiable data on inadequacy of representation and the Article 335 efficiency test remain mandatory. The bench also confirmed that the creamy layer principle applies to SC/STs in promotions. Mukesh Kumar v. State of Uttarakhand (2020) clarified that "consequential seniority" under Article 16(4B) does not violate the basic structure; the "catch‑up rule" (where a general‑category officer promoted later regains seniority) was rejected as inconsistent with the constitutional design of 16(4B). The 103rd Amendment (2019) inserted Article 16(6), enabling up to 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) in public employment and education, over and above the 50% ceiling. In Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022), a 3:2 majority upheld the amendment, holding that economic criteria alone can constitute a "class" under Article 16(4) and that the 50% ceiling is not an immutable basic structure feature but a rule of prudence. The dissent (Justices Bhat and Lalit) warned that breaching the 50% limit for non‑socially‑backward classes undermines the compensatory justice rationale of Articles 15(4) and 16(4). Recent litigation in 2023‑24 has focused on cadre‑wise versus post‑wise roster construction, the applicability of the creamy layer to EWS, and the interaction of Article 16(6) with State‑specific quotas that push total reservations beyond 60% (e.g., Tamil Nadu’s 69% protected under the Ninth Schedule).

The Ninth Schedule and Judicial Review: The Basic Structure Doctrine as a Limit on Legislative Immunity

Article 31B, inserted by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, validates any Act or Regulation placed in the Ninth Schedule, shielding it from judicial review for contravention of fundamental rights. The Schedule was originally designed to protect land‑reform legislation from challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31. In Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951) and Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965), the Supreme Court held that constitutional amendments under Article 368 are not "law" within the meaning of Article 13(2) and therefore cannot be struck down for violating fundamental rights. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967) reversed this, declaring amendments to be "law" subject to Article 13(2). Parliament reacted with the 24th Amendment (1971), inserting Article 13(4) and Article 368(3) to exclude amendments from Article 13. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) upheld the 24th Amendment but introduced the basic structure doctrine: amendments cannot alter the Constitution’s basic structure. Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) drew a temporal line: laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before 24 April 1973 (the date of Kesavananda) are immune; those added after are open to challenge on the ground that they damage the basic structure. Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) had already limited Article 31C (saving laws for Article 39(b) and (c)) to only those two directives, striking down the 42nd Amendment’s attempt to extend it to all DPSPs.

The definitive ruling came in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine‑judge bench decision. The Court held that every Ninth Schedule law enacted after 24 April 1973 must be tested against the basic structure. It formulated a dual test: (a) the "rights test" — whether the law violates a fundamental right that forms part of the basic structure (e.g., equality, judicial review, secularism), and (b) the "structure test" — whether the law’s cumulative effect destroys the constitutional architecture (separation of powers, federalism, rule of law). The Court clarified that the mere inclusion of a law in the Ninth Schedule does not confer immunity; the constitutional validity of the amending Act that placed it there is itself subject to judicial review. Post‑Coelho, the Tamil Nadu Backward Classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Reservation of Seats in Educational Institutions and Appointments in Public Services) Act, 2021 (providing 69% reservation) was placed in the Ninth Schedule by the Constitution (105th Amendment) Act, 2021; its validity is pending challenge. The Maharashtra Socially and Educationally Backward Classes Act, 2018 (Maratha quota) was not placed in the Ninth Schedule and was struck down in Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. Chief Minister (2021) for breaching the 50% ceiling without "exceptional circumstances". The Ninth Schedule now contains 284 entries (as of 2024), including laws on land reforms, mining, essential commodities, and reservations. Aspirants must distinguish between the Waman Rao cut‑off date (which protects pre‑1973 entries absolutely) and the Coelho test (which subjects post‑1973 entries to basic structure scrutiny), and must not conflate Article 31B’s validation with Article 31C’s limited DPSP shield.

Examiner's Trap: Ninth Schedule Immunity vs Basic Structure
A question states: "The Ninth Schedule provides absolute immunity to all laws included in it from judicial review under Article 13. Comment."
The statement is incorrect. Article 31B validates laws in the Ninth Schedule, but I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) held that laws added after 24 April 1973 are subject to the basic structure test. The immunity is not absolute; the amending Act placing a law in the Schedule can be struck down if it violates the basic structure (e.g., judicial review, equality, secularism). Pre‑1973 entries remain immune per Waman Rao (1981), but post‑1973 entries must pass the dual "rights test" and "structure test". The Constitution (105th Amendment) Act, 2021 placing Tamil Nadu’s 69% quota law in the Schedule is itself open to challenge on basic structure grounds.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the "validity of a Ninth Schedule law", first identify the date of inclusion. If pre‑24 April 1973 → immune (Waman Rao). If post‑1973 → apply Coelho dual test. Never say "Ninth Schedule laws cannot be challenged". Also, distinguish Article 31B (Ninth Schedule) from Article 31C (DPSP shield for Art 39(b)/(c) only, per Minerva Mills). The 42nd Amendment’s expansion of Art 31C to all DPSPs was struck down.

Articles 31A, 31B and 31C: The Constitutional Shield for Land Reforms and Directive Principles

Articles 31A, 31B and 31C form a triad of "saving clauses" designed to insulate socio‑economic legislation from fundamental‑rights challenges. Article 31A, introduced by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 and expanded by the 4th (1955), 17th (1964) and 42nd (1976) Amendments, protects five categories of laws: (i) acquisition of estates or rights therein by the State, (ii) taking over management of property for a limited period, (iii) amalgamation of corporations, (iv) extinguishment or modification of rights of managing agents, secretaries, treasurers, etc., and (v) extinguishment or modification of mining leases. The Article declares that such laws shall not be deemed void for inconsistency with Articles 14, 19 or 31 (the original property right). However, Article 31A(1) requires that the law provides for "compensation" (not necessarily "just equivalent") and Article 31A(2) mandates Presidential assent for State laws. In Kameshwar Singh v. State of Bihar (1952), the Court held that "compensation" under Article 31A(1) need not be market value but must not be illusory. The 44th Amendment (1978) repealed Article 31 and inserted Article 300A, but Article 31A continues to reference the repealed Article 31; the Supreme Court in W.B. v. Bela Banerjee (1954) and later cases has read "compensation" in Article 31A as a justiciable requirement, albeit with wide legislative discretion.

Article 31B, as discussed, validates the Ninth Schedule. Article 31C, inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971), originally provided that laws giving effect to the policy of Article 39(b) and (c) (distribution of material resources, prevention of concentration of wealth) shall not be void for contravention of Articles 14, 19 or 31. The 42nd Amendment (1976) expanded Article 31C to cover "all or any of the Directive Principles". In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Court struck down this expansion, holding that Article 31C protects only laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c), not the entire DPSP chapter. The Court reasoned that giving primacy to all DPSPs over fundamental rights would destroy the basic structure (balance between Parts III and IV). Post‑Minerva Mills, Article 31C operates as a narrow shield: the State must prove the law is genuinely aimed at Article 39(b) or (c); mere labelling is insufficient (State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Abu Kavur Bai, 1984). The interaction of these Articles with the basic structure doctrine means that while Article 31A laws enjoy broad protection, they remain subject to the "illusory compensation" test and the requirement that the acquisition serves a "public purpose" (a justiciable concept under Article 300A jurisprudence). Article 31B laws post‑1973 face the Coelho basic structure test. Article 31C laws must pass the Minerva Mills filter — only Article 39(b)/(c) implementation qualifies. Aspirants should note that the 44th Amendment’s deletion of Article 31 did not automatically amend Articles 31A and 31C; they continue to refer to the repealed Article, and the Court has interpreted them purposively to maintain the constitutional balance.

Sedition, Public Order and Article 19(1)(a): From Kedar Nath Singh to S.G. Vombatkere and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita

Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, criminalises "sedition" — bringing or attempting to bring into hatred or contempt, or exciting disaffection towards, the Government established by law. The constitutional validity of this colonial provision has been litigated for seven decades. In Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962), a Constitution Bench upheld Section 124A but narrowed its scope: only acts involving "incitement to violence" or "intention or tendency to create public disorder" constitute sedition. Mere criticism of government policies, however strong, is protected under Article 19(1)(a). Balwant Singh v. State of Punjab (1995) applied Kedar Nath to acquit persons who raised slogans ("Khalistan Zindabad") after Indira Gandhi’s assassination, holding that isolated slogans without incitement to violence do not amount to sedition. Despite this jurisprudence, the provision was invoked frequently — against journalists, activists, students, and cartoonists — often without the Kedar Nath thresholds being met. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2016), the Supreme Court issued guidelines requiring prior approval of a senior police officer before registering a sedition FIR.

The turning point came in S.G. Vombatkere v. Union of India (2022). A three‑judge bench, noting the "chilling effect" on free speech and the misuse of Section 124A, directed the Union and State governments to keep all pending trials, appeals and proceedings under Section 124A in abeyance and not to register any fresh FIRs under the provision until the government re‑examines it. The Court effectively put the law in suspended animation. In 2023, the Law Commission of India (22nd Report, chaired by Justice Ritu Raj Awasthi) recommended retention of sedition with procedural safeguards: (i) enhancing the minimum punishment from three to seven years, (ii) requiring a preliminary inquiry by a DSP‑rank officer before FIR registration, and (iii) defining "disaffection" more precisely. Simultaneously, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), which replaces the IPC, omits "sedition" but introduces Section 150: "Whoever, purposely or knowingly, by words, signs, visible representation, or otherwise, excites or attempts to excite secession, armed rebellion, subversive activities, or encourages feelings of separatist activities, or endangers sovereignty, unity and integrity of India..." Critics argue Section 150 is broader and vaguer than Section 124A, lacking the Kedar Nath "incitement to violence" limiter. As of 2024, the BNS has not been brought into force; the Supreme Court in Vombatkere has kept the abeyance order alive, and petitions challenging Section 150 BNS are pending. The trajectory illustrates the tension between the colonial legacy of "public order" as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(2) and the evolving judicial insistence on proportionality, specificity, and the least restrictive means test.

Anti‑Conversion Legislation and Article 25: Constitutional Limits on State Regulation of Religious Conversion

Article 25(1) guarantees "freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion", subject to public order, morality, health and other fundamental rights. The word "propagate" has been the focal point of constitutional debate. In Rev. Stanislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1977), a Constitution Bench upheld the Madhya Pradesh Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam, 1968 and the Orissa Freedom of Religion Act, 1967, which required prior intimation to the District Magistrate for any conversion. The Court held that "propagate" means "to transmit or spread one’s religion by exposition of its tenets" and does not include the "right to convert another person", because conversion impinges on the "freedom of conscience" of the convert. This restrictive reading has been criticised for conflating the converter’s right with the convert’s autonomy.

Since 2017, several States have enacted or amended "anti‑conversion" laws: Uttar Pradesh Prohibition of Unlawful Conversion of Religion Ordinance, 2020 (Act, 2021), Madhya Pradesh Freedom of Religion Act, 2021, Gujarat Freedom of Religion (Amendment) Act, 2021, Karnataka Protection of Right to Freedom of Religion Act, 2022, and Haryana Prevention of Unlawful Conversion of Religion Act, 2022. Common features: (i) mandatory prior declaration to the District Magistrate (30‑60 days), (ii) burden of proof on the accused to show conversion was not "by misrepresentation, force, undue influence, coercion, allurement or fraud", (iii) enhanced penalties for conversion of SC/ST, women, minors, (iv) declaration of marriage for conversion as void. The Supreme Court in Hadiya v. State of Kerala (2018) (Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M.) affirmed an adult woman’s right to choose her religion and spouse, rejecting the NIA’s "love jihad" probe. The Court held that the right to choose a faith is intrinsic to Article 21 and Article 25. In Lata Singh v. State of U.P. (2006), the Court had already ruled that inter‑faith marriages cannot be obstructed by families or the State.

The Karnataka hijab controversy (Resham v. State of Karnataka, 2022) produced a split verdict: Justice Hemant Gupta upheld the State’s power to prescribe uniforms under Article 19(2) (public order), while Justice Sudhanshu Dhulia held that wearing the hijab is an essential religious practice protected under Article 25. The matter was referred to a larger bench. In 2023‑24, petitions challenging the constitutional validity of the new anti‑conversion laws are pending before the Supreme Court. The core issues are: (a) whether the prior‑notice and DM‑approval regime constitutes a prior restraint on Article 25, (b) whether the reverse burden of proof violates Article 21 (fair procedure) and Article 14 (arbitrariness), (c) whether "allurement" defined to include "gift, gratification, easy money" criminalises charitable activity, and (d) whether the laws disproportionately target minority communities, violating Article 15(1). The Court’s eventual ruling will clarify whether Stanislaus remains good law or whether the autonomy of the convert (choosing a new faith) is now recognised as part of the "freedom of conscience" guaranteed to every individual under Article 25(1).

  • Confusing the Nagaraj (2006) and Jarnail Singh (2018) requirements: Nagaraj required proof of backwardness for SC/STs; Jarnail Singh removed that requirement but kept quantifiable data on inadequacy of representation and the Article 335 efficiency test.
  • Assuming the 50% ceiling is a basic structure rule for all reservations: Janhit Abhiyan (2022) held it is a rule of prudence, not basic structure; the 103rd Amendment’s EWS quota breaches it constitutionally.
  • Believing Ninth Schedule inclusion grants absolute immunity: only pre‑24 April 1973 entries are immune (Waman Rao); post‑1973 entries face the Coelho basic structure test.
  • Conflating Article 31B (Ninth Schedule) with Article 31C (DPSP shield): Article 31C protects only laws for Article 39(b) and (c) per Minerva Mills; the 42nd Amendment’s expansion to all DPSPs was struck down.
  • Thinking Section 124A IPC (sedition) is still fully operative: since S.G. Vombatkere (2022), the Supreme Court has kept it in abeyance; no fresh FIRs, pending proceedings stayed.
  • Equating the new Section 150 BNS with the old sedition law: Section 150 uses broader terms ("secession, armed rebellion, subversive activities, separatist activities") without the Kedar Nath "incitement to violence" limiter; its constitutionality is untested.
  • Assuming Stanislaus (1977) settles that "propagate" excludes conversion: Hadiya (2018) and the pending challenges to new anti‑conversion laws have reopened the question whether the convert’s autonomy is protected under Article 25(1).
The interplay of these doctrines defines the moving frontier where legislative power, judicial review, and constitutional morality negotiate the scope of liberty and equality in contemporary India.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation and its Impact on Fundamental Rights

The doctrine of colourable legislation addresses the situation where a legislature, lacking competence to enact a law directly, attempts to achieve the same object indirectly by dressing the measure in a permissible form. The Supreme Court in K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953) held that the constitutionality of a statute must be judged by its true nature and character, not by its label. If the substance of the law falls outside the legislative field assigned to that legislature, the law is void even if its form appears to be within competence. This principle operates as a safeguard for fundamental rights because it prevents legislatures from circumventing the distribution of powers under the Seventh Schedule to encroach upon rights guaranteed in Part III.

In State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952), the Court struck down a land‑reform law that, while ostensibly a measure for agrarian reform, in substance effected a taking of property without adequate compensation, thereby violating Article 31 (pre‑1978) and later Article 300A. The test applied was whether the legislation, on a fair reading, was a genuine exercise of the power conferred or a mere colour for an impermissible purpose. The Court examines the pith and substance of the enactment, the legislative history, and the practical effect on the right claimed.

Colourable legislation becomes especially relevant when a State legislature enacts a law that appears to regulate a subject in the State List but in reality trenches upon a Union List entry that carries a fundamental‑rights dimension, such as inter‑state trade (Entry 33, Union List) or citizenship (Entry 17, Union List). In Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (1972), a Punjab law regulating the sale of liquor was upheld because its true character was regulation of public health (State List) and not a disguised tax on inter‑state commerce. Conversely, in State of Karnataka v. R. Rajagopal (1995), a law that imposed a levy on the sale of petroleum products was struck down as a colourable exercise of the State’s taxing power, the real object being to raise revenue for the Union.

The doctrine also interacts with the basic‑structure limitation. In Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), the Court observed that a constitutional amendment that seeks to remove judicial review of colourable legislation would itself be a colourable exercise of the amending power, violating the basic structure. Thus, the doctrine operates at two levels: as a tool of statutory interpretation to protect the federal balance, and as a constitutional principle that shields fundamental rights from legislative overreach disguised as legitimate law‑making.

For the aspirant, the key take‑aways are: (i) the Court looks beyond the label to the true nature of the law; (ii) the burden is on the challenger to demonstrate that the legislation is a mere colour for an impermissible purpose; (iii) the doctrine reinforces the separation of powers and the federal scheme, both of which are integral to the enforcement of fundamental rights.

The Doctrine of Pith and Substance in Federal Distribution of Powers Relating to Rights

The doctrine of pith and substance is the principal interpretive device used by the Supreme Court to resolve conflicts between Union and State legislative competence when a law incidentally affects a subject assigned to the other level of government. The classic formulation in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) states that if the true nature and character of a legislation falls within the competence of the enacting legislature, the incidental encroachment on another list does not render it ultra vires. This doctrine is indispensable for fundamental‑rights adjudication because many rights — such as freedom of trade (Article 19(1)(g)), equality before law (Article 14), and protection of minorities (Articles 29‑30) — are implicated when a law straddles the Union‑State divide.

In State of West Bengal v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights (2010), the Court applied pith and substance to uphold a State law regulating the operation of private security agencies, holding that its dominant purpose was maintenance of public order (State List, Entry 1) even though it incidentally touched upon the regulation of professions (Union List, Entry 26). The Court emphasized that the “dominant purpose” test must be applied on a holistic reading of the statute, its preamble, and its practical operation.

A more rights‑centric illustration is K. Nagaraj v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1985), where a State law prescribing qualifications for appointment to public services was challenged under Article 16(1). The Court held that the law’s pith and substance was the regulation of public employment (State List, Entry 41) and not an infringement of the fundamental right to equality, because the qualifications were reasonable and non‑discriminatory. Conversely, in Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2010), a Central law that sought to regulate the fees of private unaided educational institutions was struck down because its true character was the regulation of education (State List, Entry 25) and not a valid exercise of the Union’s power over “co‑ordination and determination of standards in institutions for higher education” (Union List, Entry 66). The decision protected the minority‑institution rights under Article 30.

The doctrine also operates when a law is challenged as violating Article 14 on the ground of arbitrary classification between Union and State subjects. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977), the Court used pith and substance to uphold a Central statute on the ground that its dominant object was the regulation of inter‑state trade (Union List, Entry 33), rejecting the argument that it was a colourable intrusion into State taxation powers.

For examination purposes, remember: (i) identify the dominant purpose of the impugned law; (ii) locate that purpose in the appropriate legislative list; (iii) assess whether the incidental effect on the other list is merely ancillary; (iv) evaluate the impact on the specific fundamental right invoked. The doctrine does not permit a legislature to achieve indirectly what it cannot do directly — that is the domain of colourable legislation — but it allows legitimate overlap when the core of the law is within competence.

Worked Example: Pith and Substance Applied to a State Law on Digital Data Protection
A State enacts the “Data Privacy and Security Act, 2024” regulating the collection, storage, and processing of personal data by all entities operating within the State. The Union argues that the law encroaches on its exclusive power over “communication” (Union List, Entry 31) and “regulation of inter‑state trade” (Entry 33). The State contends the law’s pith and substance is “protection of privacy” — a facet of Article 21 — and falls under “public health and sanitation” (State List, Entry 6) and “police” (Entry 1). Decide the validity of the State law using the pith and substance doctrine.
Step 1 – Identify the dominant purpose. The Act’s preamble and operative provisions focus on safeguarding personal data against misuse, breach, and unauthorized disclosure. Its primary objective is the protection of the right to privacy, recognised as a fundamental right under Article 21 (Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 2017). Step 2 – Locate the purpose in the legislative lists. “Privacy” or “data protection” is not expressly mentioned in any list. The closest State entries are “public health and sanitation” (Entry 6) and “police” (Entry 1). The Union entries cited are “communication” (Entry 31) and “inter‑state trade” (Entry 33). Step 3 – Apply the dominant‑purpose test. The Court will examine whether the regulation of data processing is essentially a police‑power measure to protect citizens’ informational privacy, or whether it is a regulation of electronic communication and inter‑state data flows. Precedent (State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara) requires a holistic view. If the law applies uniformly to all entities, including those engaged purely in intra‑State activity, and its enforcement machinery is the State police, the dominant purpose leans toward State competence. Step 4 – Assess incidental encroachment. Any effect on inter‑State data transmission is incidental to the core privacy objective. Conclusion. The law is likely upheld as a valid exercise of State legislative power under the pith and substance doctrine, provided it does not impose compliance burdens that effectively regulate inter‑State communication. The Union’s remedy, if any, lies in enacting a comprehensive Central data‑protection law under its residuary power (Article 248) or by invoking Article 252 (consent of States).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to “apply the doctrine of pith and substance”, structure your answer in four labelled steps: (1) Dominant purpose, (2) Legislative entry, (3) Incidental effect, (4) Fundamental‑rights impact. Cite at least one pre‑2000 and one post‑2000 case. This template guarantees coverage of the doctrinal test and the rights dimension that examiners reward.

The Principle of Non‑Discrimination in Public Employment: Article 16(4), (4A), (4B) and the Evolution of Reservation Jurisprudence

Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. Clause (4) permits the State to make provision for reservation of appointments in favour of any backward class of citizens which, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services. The judicial interpretation of “backward class”, “adequate representation”, and the permissible extent of reservation has produced a layered jurisprudence that balances formal equality with substantive justice.

In M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore (1963), the Court held that reservation under Article 16(4) must not exceed 50 % and that “backwardness” must be both social and educational. The 50 % ceiling was later treated as a rule of prudence rather than an immutable constitutional limit (Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India, 2022). The Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) judgment (the Mandal case) introduced the “creamy layer” exclusion for Other Backward Classes (OBCs), required the identification of backward classes by a commission, and capped total reservation at 50 % unless extraordinary circumstances exist. It also ruled that Article 16(4) is an enabling provision, not an exception to Article 16(1).

The 77th Amendment (1995) inserted Article 16(4A), allowing reservation in promotions for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (SC/ST) if they are not adequately represented. The 85th Amendment (2001) added consequential seniority. In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006), the Court upheld these amendments but imposed three conditions: (i) the State must demonstrate backwardness of the SC/ST group, (ii) inadequacy of representation, and (iii) maintenance of administrative efficiency under Article 335. Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) removed the requirement to prove backwardness for SC/STs, holding that the Presidential List under Article 341/342 is conclusive, but retained the quantifiable data and efficiency tests.

Article 16(4B), inserted by the 81st Amendment (2000), permits the State to treat unfilled reserved vacancies of a year as a separate class for the next year, effectively allowing carry‑forward beyond the 50 % ceiling. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. Rajesh (2021) clarified that the carry‑forward rule does not breach the 50 % limit because the ceiling applies to each recruitment year individually.

Recent developments include the 103rd Amendment (2019) providing 10 % reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) in public employment and education, upheld in Janhit Abhiyan (2022) on the ground that economic criteria alone can constitute a “backward class” under Article 16(4). The Court also reiterated that the 50 % ceiling is not a basic‑structure rule, allowing the EWS quota to exceed it.

For the aspirant, the critical points are: (i) the distinction between “backward class” for OBCs (requiring social‑educational backwardness) and SC/ST (presumed backward); (ii) the three‑pronged Nagaraj test for promotion reservations; (iii) the creamy‑layer exclusion applies only to OBCs; (iv) the 50 % rule is a judicial guideline, not a constitutional cap; (v) Article 16(4B) permits carry‑forward without breaching the ceiling; (vi) the EWS quota represents a new category of “backwardness” based solely on economic status.

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation under Article 13

Article 13(2) declares that the State shall not make any law that takes away or abridges the fundamental rights, and any law made in contravention shall be void. The term “law” in Article 13 includes not only statutes but also ordinances, bye‑laws, rules, regulations, notifications, and other instruments having the force of law. This expansive reading, established in Delhi Laws Act v. Union of India (1951), brings delegated legislation within the ambit of judicial review for fundamental‑rights compliance.

The Supreme Court in Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India (1960) struck down a rule made under the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act that prohibited advertisement of certain medicines, holding that the rule violated Article 19(1)(a) because the parent statute did not authorise such a restriction. The Court emphasised that delegated legislation must conform to the parent statute and the Constitution; it cannot exceed the rule‑making power conferred.

In Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985), the Court reviewed a notification issued under the Customs Act that imposed a levy on newsprint. The notification was held ultra vires because it effectively amended the statute’s fiscal provisions without legislative sanction, thereby violating Article 14 (arbitrariness) and Article 19(1)(g) (freedom of trade). The principle is that the delegate cannot enlarge its own authority; any such enlargement is a “colourable exercise” of delegated power and is void under Article 13.

The doctrine of “sub‑delegation” also falls under this scrutiny. In State of Gujarat v. Patel (1995), a rule made by a subordinate authority under a rule‑making power that itself was delegated by the legislature was invalidated because the parent statute did not permit sub‑delegation. The Court reiterated that the Constitution does not permit the executive to create a parallel legislative tier without explicit authorisation.

Procedural ultra vires is another ground. In Union of India v. G. Ganayutham (1997), a notification issued without the mandatory prior publication and consultation required by the parent Act was quashed. The Court held that non‑compliance with procedural safeguards renders the delegated legislation void ab initio, as it fails the test of “law” under Article 13.

Recent jurisprudence has extended review to regulatory bodies. In Internet Freedom Foundation v. Union of India (2023), the Supreme Court examined the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, and held that certain provisions imposing traceability requirements on messaging platforms violated Article 19(1)(a) and Article 21 because they were not backed by a clear statutory mandate and were disproportionate. The decision underscores that even technocratic regulations must pass the Article 13 filter.

Key take‑aways for the exam: (i) “law” in Article 13 includes all subordinate legislation; (ii) delegated legislation must be intra vires the parent statute and the Constitution; (iii) three grounds of challenge — substantive ultra vires, procedural ultra vires, and violation of fundamental rights; (iv) the Court applies the doctrine of proportionality when fundamental rights are implicated; (v) sub‑delegation is impermissible unless expressly authorised.

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of President’s Rule under Article 356 and its Impact on Fundamental Rights

Article 356 empowers the President to assume the functions of a State government on receipt of a report from the Governor or otherwise, if satisfied that the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. The imposition of President’s Rule suspends the State legislature and places executive authority in the Union. While Article 356 is a constitutional provision, its exercise has profound implications for fundamental rights, particularly the rights to equality (Article 14), freedom of speech (Article 19), and the right to constitutional remedies (Article 32).

The landmark judgment in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) established that the President’s satisfaction under Article 356 is justiciable. The Court laid down that the proclamation must be based on objective material, not on political whim, and that the State legislative assembly cannot be dissolved until Parliament approves the proclamation. The judgment also held that secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution, and a State government pursuing anti‑secular policies could be a ground for President’s Rule, but the material must be concrete.

In Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006), the Court struck down the dissolution of the Bihar assembly after the proclamation, holding that the Governor’s report was based on irrelevant considerations and that the dissolution violated the democratic principle underlying Article 172. The Court emphasised that the power under Article 356 is conditional and must be exercised sparingly.

The impact on fundamental rights arises when President’s Rule is used to bypass elected governments that have enacted legislation protecting minority rights, labour rights, or environmental safeguards. In State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977), the Court upheld a proclamation but warned that the Union cannot use Article 356 to nullify State laws that are within the State’s legislative competence and that conform to fundamental rights. More recently, in Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016), the Court held that the Governor’s discretion to summon the assembly cannot be exercised to facilitate a floor test when the Chief Minister enjoys majority support, reinforcing the principle that democratic accountability is a facet of Article 21.

The 44th Amendment (1978) introduced safeguards: the proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within two months, and it cannot remain in force beyond three years without periodic Parliamentary approval. The amendment also required that the President’s satisfaction be based on the Governor’s report “or otherwise”, but the “otherwise” clause has been interpreted restrictively to prevent misuse.

For the aspirant, the essential points are: (i) President’s Rule is subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides, irrelevance, and non‑compliance with constitutional procedure; (ii) the dissolution of the State assembly is a separate act requiring independent justification; (iii) the imposition of President’s Rule can suspend the operation of State laws that give effect to fundamental rights, thereby creating a temporary rights vacuum; (iv) the basic‑structure doctrine limits the use of Article 356 to preserve federalism and democracy; (v) the 44th Amendment’s procedural checks are mandatory and their violation renders the proclamation void.

  • Confusing colourable legislation with pith and substance: colourable legislation tests the intent to evade competence; pith and substance tests the dominant purpose of a law that is otherwise within competence.
  • Assuming the 50 % reservation ceiling is a basic‑structure rule for all categories: Janhit Abhiyan (2022) held it is a rule of prudence; the EWS quota may exceed it.
  • Believing the creamy‑layer exclusion applies to SC/ST reservations: it applies only to OBCs (Indra Sawhney); SC/STs are exempt per Jarnail Singh (2018).
  • Thinking delegated legislation is immune from Article 13 review if the parent statute is valid: Hamdard Dawakhana and Internet Freedom Foundation confirm that subordinate rules must independently satisfy fundamental‑rights scrutiny.
  • Treating President’s Rule as a purely political question beyond judicial reach: S.R. Bommai (1994) and Rameshwar Prasad (2006) established justiciability on grounds of mala fides and procedural defect.
  • Remember that each of these doctrines operates as a constitutional check on legislative and executive power, and their interplay determines the real‑world enforcement of fundamental rights.

Article 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule: Constitutional Immunity, Judicial Review and the Basic Structure Limit

Articles 31A and 31B, inserted by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, represent a deliberate constitutional design to insulate agrarian reform legislation from fundamental rights challenges. Article 31A saves laws providing for the acquisition of estates, taking over management of property, amalgamation of corporations, or modification of mining leases from invalidity on grounds of contravention of Articles 14 and 19. Its protection extends only to laws that fall within the specified categories and does not confer blanket immunity. Article 31B goes further: it validates, retrospectively, every Act and Regulation included in the Ninth Schedule, irrespective of any inconsistency with fundamental rights. The Ninth Schedule originally contained thirteen State enactments on land reform; by 2024 it holds over 284 entries, including central laws on coal nationalisation, insurance, essential commodities, and even the Tamil Nadu Backward Classes Act.

The judicial trajectory reveals a progressive narrowing of this immunity. In Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951) and Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965), the Supreme Court upheld Parliament's power to amend fundamental rights, including the power to enact Article 31B. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967) reversed this, holding that fundamental rights were beyond parliamentary amendment. The Twenty-fourth Amendment (1971) restored the amending power, but Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) introduced the basic structure doctrine, placing substantive limits on constitutional amendments. In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981), the Court drew a line: Acts placed in the Ninth Schedule before 24 April 1973 (the date of Kesavananda) were immune; those added after were open to challenge on the ground that they damaged the basic structure. The definitive ruling came in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine-judge bench decision holding that every Ninth Schedule law inserted after 24 April 1973 must be tested against the basic structure, with fundamental rights (particularly Articles 14, 19, 21) recognised as part of that structure. The Court clarified that the "rights test" and the "structure test" merge: a law that abrogates fundamental rights so as to alter the Constitution's identity violates the basic structure. Article 31C, introduced by the Twenty-fifth Amendment (1971) to give primacy to Articles 39(b) and (c) over Articles 14, 19 and 31, was partially struck down in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) for destroying the balance between Parts III and IV. The current position: the Ninth Schedule is not a constitutional "dead zone"; post-1973 inclusions survive only if they do not infringe the basic structure, and the burden of proving such infringement lies on the challenger.

The Citizenship Divide: Fundamental Rights Available to Non‑Citizens versus Citizens under Articles 14, 15, 16, 19 and 21

The Constitution draws a sharp textual distinction between rights guaranteed to "citizens" and those guaranteed to "any person". Articles 15, 16, 19 and 30 expressly limit their protection to citizens. Article 14 ("equality before law") and Article 21 ("protection of life and personal liberty") use the phrase "any person", extending coverage to non‑citizens, including foreign nationals, stateless persons, and even enemy aliens subject to wartime restrictions. Article 17 (abolition of untouchability) and Article 23 (prohibition of forced labour) are framed as absolute prohibitions binding on the State and private actors alike, benefiting all persons within Indian territory. The Supreme Court in Louis De Raedt v. Union of India (1991) held that a foreign national enjoys the protection of Article 21 against arbitrary expulsion, though the State retains plenary power to expel under the Foreigners Act, 1946, subject to procedural fairness. In National Human Rights Commission v. State of Arunachal Pradesh (1996), the Court extended Article 21 protection to Chakma refugees, directing the State to safeguard their life and liberty and to process citizenship applications without coercion. Ktaer Abbas Habib Al Qutaifi v. Union of India (1998) recognised the principle of non‑refoulement as implicit in Article 21, prohibiting the return of a refugee to a country where they face persecution. Conversely, Article 19(1)(d) (freedom of movement) and 19(1)(e) (freedom of residence) are denied to non‑citizens; the State may restrict their movement and mandate residence in specified areas under the Foreigners Order, 1948. Article 16(2) bars discrimination in public employment on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth or residence — but only for citizens; the State may reserve posts for citizens under Article 16(3) by prescribing residence requirements. Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination against citizens on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth; non‑citizens cannot invoke it to challenge differential treatment in public facilities. The practical consequence: a foreign investor can claim Article 14 equality in regulatory treatment and Article 21 protection against arbitrary detention, but cannot claim Article 19(1)(g) to carry on business without governmental authorisation. Enemy aliens, under Article 22(7), are excluded from the procedural safeguards of preventive detention (advisory board review, maximum three‑month limit), reflecting the Constitution's accommodation of sovereign security imperatives.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "A foreign national detained under the National Security Act, 1980 challenges the detention under Article 22. The State argues Article 22 does not apply to non‑citizens. Decide."
Article 22(1)–(2) (rights on arrest: informed of grounds, legal counsel, production before magistrate within 24 hours) use the phrase "any person" and apply to all detainees, including foreigners. Article 22(4)–(7) (preventive detention safeguards: advisory board, three‑month limit, communication of grounds) also use "any person" but Article 22(7) expressly permits Parliament to exclude enemy aliens from these safeguards. The National Security Act applies to "any person", not only citizens. Therefore, the foreign national is entitled to Article 22(1)–(2) protections and, unless classified as an enemy alien under a valid law, to the preventive detention safeguards of Article 22(4)–(6). The State's blanket argument fails.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the "citizen-only" cluster (Articles 15, 16, 19, 30) and the "any person" cluster (Articles 14, 20, 21, 22(1)–(2), 22(4)–(6) subject to enemy‑alien exception). For any problem involving a non‑citizen, first identify the Article invoked, then check the textual subject ("citizen" vs "person"). This eliminates 80 % of confusion in hypotheticals.

Article 35 and the Parliamentary Monopoly on Legislation for Fundamental Rights: Scope, Limits and Judicial Interpretation

Article 35 vests Parliament with exclusive legislative competence over specific matters connected to fundamental rights, withdrawing those subjects from the State List and even the Concurrent List. It operates as a constitutional override of the Seventh Schedule distribution. Clause (a) reserves to Parliament the power to make laws for matters under Article 16(3) (residence requirements for public employment), Article 32(3) (empowering courts other than the Supreme Court to issue writs), Article 33 (modification of fundamental rights for armed forces, police, intelligence agencies) and Article 34 (restriction of rights during martial law). Clause (b) mandates Parliament to prescribe punishment for acts declared offences under Part III — principally Article 17 (untouchability), Article 23 (forced labour) and Article 24 (child labour). The phrase "Parliament shall, as soon as may be after the commencement of this Constitution, make laws for prescribing punishment" imposes a constitutional obligation, not merely a power. The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (originally the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955) and the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, were enacted pursuant to this mandate. The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, though broader, also draws authority from Article 35 read with Article 17. In State of Karnataka v. Appa Balu Ingale (1993), the Court upheld the 1955 Act as a valid exercise of Parliament's Article 35 power, emphasising that untouchability is a "crime against the Constitution" requiring uniform national punishment. In People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982), the Court held that Article 23 is self‑executing but that the Bonded Labour Act gave it teeth through penal sanctions mandated by Article 35(b). A critical limit: Article 35 does not prevent State legislatures from enacting laws on the same subjects if those laws are not "with respect to" the reserved matters. For instance, a State law on child welfare that incidentally penalises child labour may coexist with the central Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, provided it is not repugnant under Article 254. However, where Parliament has enacted a comprehensive code (e.g., the Atrocities Act), State laws that create parallel offences or dilute penalties have been struck down as impliedly precluded by the Article 35 scheme. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. Raghubir Singh (1989) clarified that Article 35(a) covers only the specific matters enumerated in Articles 16(3), 32(3), 33 and 34 — not the entire field of fundamental rights legislation. Thus, States retain competence to legislate on, say, public health under Article 47 even if it touches Article 21, because Article 35 does not reserve Article 21 implementation to Parliament.

The Doctrine of Pith and Substance in Fundamental Rights Adjudication: Distinguishing Legislative Competence from Rights Violation

The doctrine of pith and substance, rooted in Canadian federalism and transplanted into Indian constitutional law through the Government of India Act, 1935, determines the true character of a legislation by examining its dominant purpose and effect. While traditionally a tool for resolving legislative competence disputes under Article 246 and the Seventh Schedule, it has acquired a distinct role in fundamental rights adjudication. When a law is challenged as violating a fundamental right, the Court first asks: what is the pith and substance of this law? If the dominant purpose falls within the legislature's competence and the law only incidentally affects a fundamental right, the Court evaluates the incidental impact under the applicable reasonable‑restriction clause (Articles 19(2)–(6), 21, etc.). If, however, the pith and substance is to abridge the fundamental right itself — i.e., the law is a colourable exercise of power aimed at circumventing Part III — it is struck down without reaching the reasonableness inquiry. In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the Bombay Prohibition Act was challenged under Article 19(1)(g). The Court held its pith and substance was prohibition (a State subject under Entry 8, List II), not trade regulation; the incidental restriction on liquor trade was valid under Article 19(6). In K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953), an Orissa law abolishing zamindari was upheld; its pith and substance was agrarian reform (Entry 18, List II), and the impact on property rights (then Article 31) was constitutionally authorised by Article 31A. Zameer Ahmed Latifur Rehman Sheikh v. State of Maharashtra (2010) applied the doctrine to a Maharashtra law regulating dance bars. The Court found the pith and substance was "public order and morality" (State competence), not a targeted suppression of Article 19(1)(g), and remitted for reasonableness testing under Article 19(6). The distinction from colourable legislation is critical: colourable legislation asks whether the legislature, lacking competence, has disguised a transgression as a valid law (fraud on the Constitution). Pith and substance asks what the law really is, assuming competence. In fundamental rights cases, the two inquiries often overlap — a law whose pith and substance is rights‑abrogation is both colourable and substantively invalid. The practical utility for the aspirant: when a federalism challenge and a rights challenge are combined, resolve the pith and substance question first. If the law is within competence, proceed to the specific restriction clause. If the law's true character is to nullify a fundamental right, it fails at the threshold, irrespective of the restriction test.

Article 13(3) and the Definition of "Law" for Fundamental Rights: Ordinances, Bye‑laws, Notifications and the Exclusion of Personal Law

Article 13(3) provides an inclusive definition: "law" includes any Ordinance, order, bye‑law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law. "Laws in force" in Article 13(1) extends this to pre‑constitutional enactments. The definition determines the universe of State action subject to fundamental rights scrutiny. Ordinances promulgated under Articles 123 and 213 are "law" — confirmed in R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) (Bank Nationalisation case). Delegated legislation (rules, regulations, bye‑laws) is "law" if it has the force of law, i.e., creates legal obligations enforceable by courts; mere administrative instructions or circulars without statutory backing are not, per State of Gujarat v. Patel (1965). Notifications issued under statutory power (e.g., under the Essential Commodities Act) are "law" when they impose binding duties. Custom or usage qualifies only if it has acquired the force of law through judicial recognition or statutory incorporation; mere social practice is insufficient. The most consequential exclusion is uncodified personal law. In State of Bombay v. Narasu Appa Mali (1951), the Bombay High Court held that personal law (Hindu, Muslim, Christian) is not "law" under Article 13 because it derives from religious texts, not State enactment. The Supreme Court implicitly endorsed this in Krishna Singh v. Mathura Ahir (1980) and Masilamani Mudaliar v. Idol of Sri Swaminathaswami (1996), though the latter subjected custom to fundamental rights if it had the force of law. Codified personal law — the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 — is "law" because it is parliamentary legislation. The tension erupted in Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2018) (Sabarimala), where the majority treated the exclusion of women as a "custom or usage" having the force of law under Article 13(3)(b), thus subject to Article 17 and 25(1) scrutiny, while the dissent relied on Narasu Appa Mali to argue personal law is beyond Article 13. The Constitution (One Hundred and Third Amendment) Act, 2019 (EWS quota) and the debate over a Uniform Civil Code keep this exclusion live. For the aspirant: the test is State authorship. If the norm originates from the State (statute, ordinance, delegated legislation, notification under statute, recognised custom), it is "law". If it originates from religious scripture or community practice without State sanction, it is not — unless a statute incorporates it, at which point the statute is the "law" challengeable under Article 13.

  • Assuming Article 31B grants absolute immunity to all Ninth Schedule laws: I.R. Coelho (2007) subjected post‑1973 inclusions to basic‑structure review; fundamental rights are part of the basic structure.
  • Believing non‑citizens enjoy Article 19 freedoms: Articles 15, 16, 19, 30 are expressly limited to citizens; only Articles 14, 20, 21, 22(1)–(2), 22(4)–(6) (except enemy aliens) extend to "any person".
  • Thinking Article 35 reserves all fundamental‑rights implementation to Parliament: it covers only Articles 16(3), 32(3), 33, 34 and punishment for Part III offences (Articles 17, 23, 24); States may legislate on other rights‑giving effect matters (e.g., Article 47 health laws).
  • Confusing pith and substance with colourable legislation: pith and substance identifies the law's dominant character (competence + incidental effect); colourable legislation tests fraudulent transgression of competence. In rights cases, pith and substance decides whether the restriction clause applies.
  • Treating all personal laws as immune from Article 13: uncodified personal law is not "law" per Narasu Appa Mali; but codified personal law (Hindu Marriage Act, Muslim Women Act) and customs with force of law are "law" and challengeable.
  • Overlooking the "force of law" requirement for custom under Article 13(3): mere social practice is not "law"; it must be judicially recognised or statutorily incorporated to attract fundamental‑rights scrutiny.
  • Missing the mandatory language of Article 35(b): "Parliament shall, as soon as may be… make laws for prescribing punishment" — this is a constitutional duty, not a discretionary power; failure to enact attracts judicial mandamus.

The Constitutional Framework for the Protection of Indigenous Peoples' Rights: Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA and the Forest Rights Act

The Fifth Schedule (Article 244(1)) applies to Scheduled Areas in ten states and empowers the Governor to make regulations for peace and good government, including the power to prohibit or restrict transfer of tribal land. The Sixth Schedule (Article 244(2)) creates autonomous district and regional councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram with legislative, executive and judicial powers over land, forests, water, shifting cultivation and village administration. Both schedules operationalise the directive principle in Article 46 and the fundamental right under Article 19(5)–(6) which permits reasonable restrictions on the freedom of movement and residence for the protection of Scheduled Tribes.

The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) extends Part IX of the Constitution to Fifth Schedule areas. It mandates that Gram Sabhas have ownership of minor forest produce, control over land acquisition, and the power to prevent alienation of tribal land. The Supreme Court in Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997) held that the transfer of tribal land to non‑tribals for mining violated the Fifth Schedule and the protective regime of PESA, establishing that the Governor’s regulatory power is not a mere formality but a substantive check.

The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA) recognises individual and community forest rights, including the right to protect, regenerate and manage community forest resources. In Orissa Mining Corporation v. Ministry of Environment & Forests (2013) the Court ruled that the Gram Sabha’s consent under the FRA is a condition precedent for any diversion of forest land, reinforcing the procedural guarantee of free, prior and informed consent. The Niyamgiri judgment (2013) applied the same principle to the Dongria Kondh, holding that the Gram Sabha’s rejection of mining was binding.

Judicial trends show a shift from a protective‑paternalistic approach to one of substantive participation. The Court now reads Article 21 together with the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA and the FRA to require that any state action affecting tribal habitat must satisfy a triple test: (i) legislative competence, (ii) compliance with the procedural mandates of Gram Sabha consent, and (iii) a proportionality assessment of the impact on cultural survival. This convergence makes the indigenous rights framework one of the most enforceable socio‑economic regimes in the Constitution.

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation under Article 13(3): Excessive Delegation, Sub‑delegation and the Principle of Legislative Control

Article 13(3) defines “law” to include any “order, bye‑law, rule, regulation, notification” having the force of law. Consequently, delegated legislation is subject to fundamental‑rights scrutiny. The doctrine of excessive delegation requires that the parent statute lay down a clear legislative policy and provide sufficient guidelines; the delegate may only fill in details. In Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India (1960) the Supreme Court struck down a rule made under the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act because the statute conferred unguided power to prohibit advertisements, violating Article 14 and 19(1)(a).

The “guideline test” was refined in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985), where the Court upheld the Press Council Act’s rule‑making power because the statute enumerated the objectives and standards for regulation. The principle of legislative control demands that the legislature retain the power to amend, repeal or supervise the delegated instrument. In Kerala State Electricity Board v. Indian Aluminium Co. (1976) the Court invalidated a regulation that effectively amended the parent Act, holding that sub‑delegation is permissible only when the parent statute expressly authorises it.

Recent jurisprudence emphasises procedural safeguards. In Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2020) the Court required that any rule affecting fundamental rights be published, subjected to pre‑legislative consultation where feasible, and accompanied by a statement of objects and reasons. The Court also clarified that a notification issued under a statutory power is “law” under Article 13(3) only when it creates enforceable rights or obligations; mere administrative circulars lacking statutory backing remain outside judicial review.

The practical implication for aspirants is threefold: (i) identify the parent statute’s policy and guidelines; (ii) check whether the delegated instrument exceeds the policy or lacks legislative oversight; (iii) verify if sub‑delegation is authorised. A rule that fails any of these tests is ultra vires the Constitution and can be struck down under Article 13(2).

Technique: Spotting Excessive Delegation in a Statutory Scheme
A statute empowers the Central Government to “make rules for the regulation of online content in the interest of public order”. No further standards are provided. The Government issues a rule requiring all social‑media platforms to remove any content flagged by a government‑appointed committee within 24 hours. Assess the constitutional validity of the rule under Article 13(3) and the doctrine of excessive delegation.
The parent statute provides no legislative policy, criteria or standards for “regulation of online content”. The rule confers unfettered discretion on an executive committee, effectively allowing censorship without legislative guidance. Under Hamdard Dawakhana and Indian Express Newspapers, this constitutes excessive delegation. The rule also lacks procedural safeguards (publication, consultation) highlighted in R. Gandhi. Therefore, the rule is ultra vires Article 13(2) and violates Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21. The correct answer: the rule is unconstitutional for excessive delegation and absence of legislative control.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a delegated rule is valid, first locate the parent statute’s policy statement. If the statute uses vague phrases like “in the public interest” without enumerating factors, flag excessive delegation. Next, check for express authorisation of sub‑delegation. Finally, note any recent Supreme Court emphasis on pre‑legislative consultation — its absence strengthens the challenge.

The Role of the Election Commission in Safeguarding the Right to Vote and Electoral Integrity under Article 324

Article 324 vests the Election Commission (EC) with the superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of all elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice‑President. The Commission’s independence is secured by the security of tenure of the Chief Election Commissioner and the requirement of a special majority for removal, mirroring the safeguards for Supreme Court judges.

The EC’s powers include delimitation of constituencies (under the Delimitation Commission Act), enforcement of the Model Code of Conduct, disqualification of candidates for corrupt practices (Section 8A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951), and the authority to requisition staff and premises. In Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2020) the Supreme Court upheld the EC’s power to postpone elections in a constituency where law‑and‑order conditions threatened free voting, affirming that Article 324 confers a broad, residuary authority to protect electoral integrity.

Technological safeguards have become central. The 2019 Supreme Court judgment in Subramanian Swamy v. Election Commission of India mandated VVPAT verification for a statistically significant sample of EVMs. In 2023 the Court directed the EC to increase VVPAT counting to five percent of polling stations per constituency, reinforcing the principle that the right to vote under Article 326 includes the right to verify that the vote is recorded as cast.

Article 329 bars judicial interference in electoral matters once the election process has commenced, but the Court has carved out an exception for “manifest illegality” or “gross violation of constitutional provisions”. The EC’s quasi‑judicial decisions on disqualification are subject to judicial review under Article 226/227, ensuring that the Commission’s expansive powers remain accountable.

The Constitutional Basis of the Right to Health Care for Migrant Workers: Inter‑State Migrant Workmen Act, Article 21 and the 2020 Supreme Court Judgment in Alakh Alok Srivastava

The Inter‑State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979 requires contractors and principal employers to provide wages, displacement allowance, journey allowance, and medical facilities to migrant workers. However, enforcement remained weak until the COVID‑19 pandemic exposed systemic gaps. In Alakh Alok Srivastava v. Union of India (2020) the Supreme Court, exercising suo motu jurisdiction under Article 32, recognised that the right to life under Article 21 encompasses the right to health, food, shelter and safe transportation for migrant workers stranded during the lockdown.

The Court issued a series of binding directions: (i) free food and ration to all migrant workers irrespective of registration; (ii) free transportation to native places; (iii) setting up of helplines and grievance redressal mechanisms; (iv) compliance with the 1979 Act’s provisions for medical facilities and wage payment. The judgment linked the statutory obligations under the 1979 Act with the constitutional guarantee of Article 21, holding that the State’s failure to enforce the Act amounted to a violation of fundamental rights.

Subsequent orders in Suo Motu WP (C) 2020 (2021) extended the mandate to ensure vaccination, occupational safety and social security coverage under the Code on Social Security, 2020. The Court also directed the National Legal Services Authority to monitor implementation, illustrating the convergence of statutory law, directive principles (Article 41, 42) and fundamental rights in protecting a vulnerable class.

For the aspirant, the key takeaway is the Court’s use of Article 21 as a “positive obligation” tool: the State must not only refrain from depriving life but also take affirmative steps to secure health and dignity for migrant workers. This jurisprudence expands the enforceability of socio‑economic rights beyond the traditional DPSP framework.

The Doctrine of Constitutional Avoidance in the Sedition Law Debate: Section 124A IPC, Article 19(1)(a) and the 2022 Supreme Court Order in S.G. Vombatkere

The doctrine of constitutional avoidance counsels courts to decide cases on statutory or procedural grounds rather than reaching constitutional questions when the former suffice. Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code criminalises “sedition” — words or acts that bring the Government into hatred or contempt. The provision has been challenged repeatedly under Article 19(1)(a) as an unreasonable restriction on free speech.

In Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962) the Supreme Court upheld Section 124A but read it down to require “incitement to violence” or “public disorder”. In Balwant Singh v. State of Punjab (1995) the Court acquitted persons who raised slogans without any intent to incite violence, applying the Kedar Nath narrowing. Despite these judicial glosses, the provision continued to be invoked against journalists, activists and students.

In S.G. Vombatkere v. Union of India (2022) the Supreme Court, invoking constitutional avoidance, declined to strike down Section 124A. Instead, it directed the Union and State governments to keep all pending trials, appeals and proceedings under the provision in abeyance until the legislature re‑examines the law. The Court observed that the provision’s chilling effect on free speech warranted a “pause” rather than a definitive constitutional ruling, leaving the door open for legislative repeal or amendment.

The order illustrates a strategic use of avoidance: the Court protects speech by neutralising the law’s operation without pronouncing on its constitutional validity, thereby preserving institutional dialogue with Parliament. Aspirants should note that avoidance does not diminish the fundamental‑rights guarantee; it merely postpones the final constitutional adjudication while providing immediate relief.

  • Assuming the Fifth and Sixth Schedules apply uniformly across all states — they apply only to designated Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas respectively.
  • Treating delegated legislation as immune from Article 13(3) scrutiny — any rule, regulation or notification with the force of law is “law” and challengeable.
  • Believing the Election Commission’s powers are unlimited — Article 329 restricts judicial review once the election process starts, except for manifest illegality.
  • Confusing the Inter‑State Migrant Workmen Act’s provisions with the broader right to health under Article 21 — the Act provides statutory minima; Article 21 imposes a positive obligation that can exceed the statute.
  • Thinking the 2022 Vombatkere order struck down Section 124A — it only kept proceedings in abeyance; the provision remains on the statute book.
  • Overlooking the requirement of legislative policy and guidelines for valid delegation — absence of standards renders the delegated rule ultra vires.
  • Missing the procedural mandate of Gram Sabha consent under the Forest Rights Act — consent is a condition precedent, not a mere formality.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation in Fundamental Rights Adjudication: Legislative Competence, Motive, and the ‘Fraud on the Constitution’ Principle

The doctrine of colourable legislation addresses a specific species of constitutional fraud: a legislature, lacking the competence to enact a particular law directly, attempts to achieve the same object indirectly through a measure that appears within its powers.
