The Supreme Court crystallised the principle in K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953): “If the legislature is prohibited from doing something directly, it cannot do it indirectly; what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.” The doctrine does not inquire into the bona fides or motive of legislators — parliamentary privilege shields internal deliberations — but examines the substance and effect of the enactment. If the true character of the law, determined by its pith and substance, falls outside the legislative field, the law is invalid regardless of its formal label.

In fundamental rights adjudication, the doctrine operates at the intersection of legislative competence (Seventh Schedule) and rights limitations. A classic illustration is State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952), where the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, purported to acquire zamindari estates but excluded certain categories of landholders in a manner that revealed a discriminatory design violating Article 14. The Court struck it down as colourable exercise of the eminent domain power. Similarly, in Balaji v. State of Mysore (1963), the Court held that reserving 68% of seats in medical colleges exceeded the permissible limit under Article 15(4) and amounted to a fraud on the Constitution — the label “socially and educationally backward classes” could not mask what was effectively a reservation for the majority.

The doctrine has three operational limbs. First, the pith and substance test: the court ascertains the true nature of the legislation by examining its object, scope, and effect. Second, the transgression test: does the law, in substance, encroach upon a forbidden field (e.g., a State law on a Union subject, or a law violating a fundamental right under the guise of a reasonable restriction)? Third, the colorable exercise test: is the legislation a mere cloak for an impermissible purpose? The burden of proving colourable legislation lies on the challenger, and the presumption of constitutionality applies — but the presumption is rebutted when the law’s effect demonstrably exceeds the legislative mandate.

Recent applications include Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2010), where the Court examined whether the National Tax Tribunal Act, 2005, colourably encroached upon judicial power by vesting adjudicatory functions in a body lacking judicial independence. In State of Tamil Nadu v. K. Shyam Sunder (2011), a law providing for reservation in promotions for SC/ST employees was upheld against a colourable legislation challenge because the State demonstrated quantifiable data of backwardness and inadequacy of representation, satisfying the M. Nagaraj (2006) criteria. The doctrine thus serves as a structural safeguard: it prevents legislative overreach that would otherwise evade judicial review by masquerading as a valid exercise of power.

The Expansion of ‘Sex’ under Article 15(1) to Encompass Gender Identity and Sexual Orientation: From NALSA to Navtej and Beyond

Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination on grounds only of “religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them.” For decades, “sex” was read narrowly as biological sex (male/female). The judicial expansion began with Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association of India (2008), where the Court struck down a Punjab Excise Act provision barring women from employment in establishments serving liquor, holding that “sex” includes protection against gender stereotyping. The transformative leap came in National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (NALSA) (2014). The Supreme Court recognised transgender persons as a “third gender” and held that discrimination on the ground of “gender identity” falls within the prohibition of Article 15(1). The Court reasoned that “sex” under Article 15 is not limited to biological sex but includes “gender identity” — the innate perception of one’s gender — because discrimination against transgender persons is essentially discrimination based on their failure to conform to binary gender norms.

Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) extended this logic to sexual orientation. Reading down Section 377 IPC, the Court held that discrimination on the ground of “sexual orientation” is discrimination on the ground of “sex” within Article 15(1). The reasoning drew on comparative jurisprudence (South Africa’s National Coalition for Gay and Lesbian Equality, Canada’s Egan v. Canada) and the Yogyakarta Principles: sexual orientation is an intrinsic element of identity, and criminalising consensual same-sex relations imposes a disadvantage based on a characteristic inseparable from “sex.” The Court emphasised that Article 15(1) operates both vertically (State action) and horizontally (private discrimination in access to public places, shops, hotels, etc. under Article 15(2)), making the expansion immediately enforceable against non-State actors in specified domains.

The doctrinal methodology is significant. The Court adopted a purposive interpretation anchored in constitutional morality — the Constitution’s commitment to dignity, equality, and pluralism — rather than a frozen textualism. It rejected the “minimalist” reading that would require a constitutional amendment to add “gender identity” or “sexual orientation” to Article 15, holding that the existing text, read in light of the Preamble and the transformative vision of the Constitution, already encompasses these grounds. This approach aligns with the living tree doctrine: constitutional provisions evolve to meet the needs of a changing society without formal amendment.

Post-Navtej developments include Supriyo v. Union of India (2023), where the Court, while declining to recognise same-sex marriage, affirmed that queer couples have the right to enter into civil unions and are entitled to protection against discrimination under Article 15. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, though criticised for its certification mechanism, gives statutory effect to the NALSA mandate. For the aspirant, the key takeaway is the interpretive arc: from a formalistic “biological sex” reading to a substantive “gender identity and sexual orientation” reading, driven by the interplay of Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(a), and 21. This arc illustrates how fundamental rights adjudication can expand protected grounds without textual amendment, using the Constitution’s own moral architecture.

Worked Application: Article 15(1) and Indirect Discrimination
A State government issues a notification under the Shops and Establishments Act requiring all employees in retail outlets to work night shifts on a rotational basis. A transgender employee, who faces documented safety risks and social stigma during night travel, requests exemption as a reasonable accommodation. The employer refuses, citing the notification’s uniform application. The employee challenges the refusal under Article 15(1). How should the Court analyse the claim?
Step 1: Identify the ground. The claim is discrimination on the ground of gender identity, recognised as a facet of “sex” under Article 15(1) per NALSA (2014).
Step 2: Determine the nature of the measure. The notification is facially neutral (applies to all employees) but has a disparate impact on transgender persons due to structural vulnerabilities. This is indirect discrimination.
Step 3: Apply the proportionality standard. Under the Navtej framework, the State must show the measure pursues a legitimate aim (e.g., economic activity, women’s employment in night shifts) and is proportionate — i.e., suitable, necessary, and balanced. A blanket refusal of accommodation without individualised assessment fails the necessity limb.
Step 4: Horizontal application. Article 15(2) extends the non-discrimination guarantee to access to “shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment.” The employer’s refusal implicates Article 15(2) read with Article 15(1).
Conclusion: The Court would likely direct the employer to provide reasonable accommodation (e.g., safe transport, shift swap) unless it demonstrates undue hardship, affirming that formal equality cannot perpetuate substantive disadvantage.
Exam Strategy: Mapping the Article 15 Expansion
In Mains, questions on Article 15 often test the trajectory of judicial interpretation. Prepare a three-stage timeline: (1) Formal equality phase (pre-2008) — sex = biological sex; (2) Anti-stereotyping phase (Anuj Garg, 2008) — sex includes protection from gender stereotypes; (3) Substantive equality phase (NALSA 2014, Navtej 2018) — sex includes gender identity and sexual orientation. Link each stage to the constitutional value it advances (dignity, autonomy, constitutional morality). For Prelims, remember: NALSA = third gender recognition + Article 15(1) expansion; Navtej = Section 377 read down + sexual orientation under Article 15(1). The Transgender Persons Act, 2019 is the legislative sequel to NALSA — know its key provisions (self-perceived identity, certificate, welfare measures) and criticisms (screening committee, no reservation).

The Right to Speedy Trial as a Facet of Article 21: Judicial Standards, Systemic Delays, and the Crisis of Undertrial Detention

The right to speedy trial, though not expressly enumerated in the Constitution, was recognised as an integral facet of Article 21 in Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979). The Court held that “procedure established by law” must be fair, just, and reasonable, and that prolonged pre-trial detention without trial violates the guarantee of life and personal liberty. The judgment exposed the scandal of undertrials languishing in Bihar jails for periods exceeding the maximum sentence for their alleged offences. The Court issued binding directions: release on personal bond, time-bound trials, and legal aid at State expense. This inaugurated a jurisprudence that treats delay not as administrative inconvenience but as constitutional violation.

The Supreme Court elaborated the doctrinal framework in subsequent cases. In Kadra Pahadiya v. State of Bihar (1982), the Court held that the State cannot plead financial or administrative inability to justify denial of speedy trial. In Sheela Barse v. Union of India (1986), the Court extended the right to children in observation homes and mandated time-bound investigation and trial. Abdul Rehman Antulay v. R.S. Nayak (1992) formulated a non-exhaustive set of factors for assessing whether delay is unreasonable: (i) length of delay, (ii) reason for delay, (iii) assertion of the right by the accused, (iv) prejudice to the accused. Crucially, the Court held that the right cannot be waived by mere silence — the State bears the primary obligation to ensure expeditious proceedings.

In Common Cause v. Union of India (1996), the Court laid down specific time-limits: for offences punishable up to seven years, investigation must conclude within six months (extendable to one year with judicial approval); trial must commence within a reasonable period. The Court also directed the release of undertrials who had served half the maximum sentence (Section 436A CrPC, inserted in 2005, codified this). The ongoing In Re: Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons (2016–present) has transformed the right into a structural reform mandate: the Court monitors prison occupancy, undertrial review committees, video-conferencing for hearings, and the implementation of the Model Prison Manual, 2016.

Despite this robust jurisprudence, the crisis persists. As per the National Crime Records Bureau (Prison Statistics India, 2022), undertrials constitute 75.8% of the prison population (4,34,302 out of 5,73,220 inmates). The median duration of undertrial detention exceeds two years in several States. Systemic causes include judicial vacancies (25% in High Courts, 20% in district courts as of 2023), inadequate prosecution capacity, frequent adjournments, and the absence of a statutory speedy trial framework with enforceable timelines. The 2023 Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), replacing the CrPC, introduces timelines for investigation (90 days for offences up to 10 years, 180 days for graver offences) and trial (judgment within 30 days of conclusion of arguments), but their operational efficacy remains untested. For the aspirant, the right to speedy trial exemplifies the tension between declaratory judicial activism and institutional capacity — a recurring theme in socio-economic rights enforcement.

Article 31C and the Basic Structure: The Legislative Shield for Directive Principles and its Judicial Containment

Article 31C, inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971) and radically expanded by the 42nd Amendment (1976), represents the most direct legislative attempt to insulate laws implementing Directive Principles from fundamental rights scrutiny. The original Article 31C protected laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c) — distribution of material resources for common good, prevention of concentration of wealth — from challenge under Articles 14, 19, and 31. The 42nd Amendment extended this shield to any law implementing any Directive Principle, and declared that such laws shall not be questioned in any court on the ground that they do not give effect to the stated policy. This was a frontal assault on judicial review.

In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down the 42nd Amendment’s expansion of Article 31C as violative of the basic structure. The Court held that judicial review is a basic feature; a provision that ousts the court’s power to examine whether a law genuinely implements a Directive Principle destroys the constitutional balance between Parts III and IV. The Court restored the pre-1976 position: only laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c) enjoy protection, and even then, the court may examine whether the law has a “reasonable nexus” with the Directive Principle cited. The Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) judgment clarified that Article 31C protection applies prospectively from 24 April 1973 (the date of Kesavananda Bharati), and laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after that date are subject to basic structure review.

The I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) nine-judge bench cemented this containment. The Court held that every Ninth Schedule law enacted after 24 April 1973 must be tested against the basic structure, including the fundamental rights that constitute the “essence” of the Constitution (Articles 14, 19, 21). The “rights test” replaced the earlier “structure test”: a law that abridges a fundamental right forming part of the basic structure cannot be immunised by Article 31C or the Ninth Schedule. The Court also ruled that Article 31C does not protect a law that damages the “identity” of the Constitution — a standard that preserves judicial scrutiny of the law’s genuine connection to Article 39(b)/(c).

Contemporary relevance lies in land acquisition and agrarian reform laws. The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (LARR Act) was enacted under Article 31C’s protective umbrella for Article 39(b)/(c) objectives. Challenges to its provisions (e.g., consent requirements, social impact assessment) have been adjudicated with the Article 31C defence in mind. In K.T. Plantation v. State of Karnataka (2011), the Court upheld a land reform law under Article 31C, finding a direct nexus with Article 39(b). The doctrine thus remains a live site of contestation: the legislature invokes it to shield redistributive laws; the judiciary polices its boundaries to prevent the erosion of rights review. Aspirants must grasp the three-layer test: (1) Does the law claim protection under Article 31C? (2) Does it genuinely implement Article 39(b) or (c)? (3) Does it violate a basic structure right (Articles 14, 19, 21)? Only if all three align does the shield hold.

The Right to Reputation under Article 21: Criminal Defamation, Civil Remedies, and the Subramanian Swamy Balance

The right to reputation, though not expressly mentioned in the Constitution, has been recognised as a facet of Article 21’s guarantee of dignity and personal liberty. In Kiran Bedi v. Committee of Inquiry (1989), the Court observed that “reputation is an element of personal security protected by the Constitution.” The definitive adjudication came in Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016), where a two-judge bench upheld the constitutional validity of Sections 499 and 500 IPC (criminal defamation) against a challenge under Articles 19(1)(a) and 21. The Court held that reputation is a constituent of Article 21, and the State has a legitimate interest in protecting it through criminal law. The restriction on free speech was deemed “reasonable” under Article 19(2) because defamation law serves the public interest in protecting individual dignity and social harmony.

The judgment navigated a delicate balance. It acknowledged the chilling effect of criminal defamation on legitimate speech — particularly investigative journalism and political dissent — but declined to strike down the provision, citing the lack of a less restrictive alternative that would adequately protect reputation. The Court emphasised procedural safeguards: (i) the complaint must be filed by the aggrieved person (not the State), (ii) the magistrate must apply judicial mind before issuing process (Section 202 CrPC inquiry), (iii) truth is a defence if published for public good (Section 499, Exception 1), (iv) fair comment on public conduct of public servants is protected (Exception 2). These safeguards, the Court held, mitigate the risk of misuse.

Civil defamation operates in parallel. In Khushwant Singh v. Maneka Gandhi (2002), the Delhi High Court (affirmed by Supreme Court) balanced the right to reputation against free speech in a civil suit, granting an injunction against publication of defamatory passages but refusing a blanket gag order. The law of civil defamation, governed by tort principles, requires the plaintiff to prove publication, falsity, defamatory nature, and damage. The Defamation Bill, 1988 (lapsed) and the Law Commission’s 268th Report (2017) recommended retaining criminal defamation but introducing procedural reforms: non-cognisable offence, mandatory mediation, higher threshold for process issuance. The 2023 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) retains criminal defamation (Section 356) but adds community service as an alternative punishment for first-time offenders.

For the aspirant, the key doctrinal points are: (1) Reputation is a positive obligation facet of Article 21 — the State must provide a legal framework to protect it. (2) Criminal defamation is a reasonable restriction on Article 19(1)(a) but must satisfy the proportionality test (legitimate aim, suitability, necessity, balancing). (3) The Subramanian Swamy judgment is the controlling precedent; any challenge must distinguish its facts or argue changed circumstances (e.g., digital amplification of chilling effect). (4) The tension between Article 19(1)(a) and Article 21 (reputation) exemplifies the horizontal balancing the Court performs between competing fundamental rights — a recurring theme in Mains questions on free speech.

  • Trap 1: Confusing the scope of Article 31C pre- and post-42nd Amendment. The 42nd Amendment extended protection to all DPSPs; Minerva Mills struck this down. Current law: only Article 39(b) and (c) laws are protected.
  • Trap 2: Assuming NALSA and Navtej added “gender identity” and “sexual orientation” as new grounds in Article 15. They interpreted “sex” to include these grounds — no textual amendment occurred.
  • Trap 3: Stating that the right to speedy trial is absolute or that any delay violates Article 21. The Antulay factors (length, reason, assertion, prejudice) must be applied; systemic delay alone may not suffice without prejudice.
  • Trap 4: Believing Subramanian Swamy struck down criminal defamation. It upheld Sections 499/500 IPC. The chilling effect argument was considered but rejected on the ground that procedural safeguards suffice.
  • Trap 5: Treating colourable legislation as a question of legislative motive. The doctrine examines effect and substance, not motive (which is protected by parliamentary privilege).
  • Trap 6: Overlooking that Article 31C protection is not automatic — the law must have a “reasonable nexus” with Article 39(b)/(c), and the court reviews this nexus.
  • Trap 7: Missing the horizontal dimension of Article 15(1) post-Navtej. Article 15(2) extends non-discrimination to private actors in specified places (shops, hotels, wells, etc.); this applies to gender identity and sexual orientation discrimination as well.

The Rule of Law as a Constitutional Bridge between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles

The rule of law, though not expressly enumerated in the Constitution, functions as the interpretive spine that connects the justiciable guarantees of Part III with the aspirational commands of Part IV. In A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) the Court treated “procedure established by law” as a formalistic requirement, but the subsequent Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) decision infused the phrase with substantive fairness, holding that any law depriving life or personal liberty must be “fair, just and reasonable”. This shift turned the rule of law into a positive obligation on the State to ensure that legislative and executive actions conform to the principles of natural justice, non‑arbitrariness, and legal certainty.

The rule of law also operates as a limiting principle on the State’s power to implement Directive Principles. In Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) the Court struck down the 42nd Amendment’s attempt to give primacy to all DPSPs over Fundamental Rights, reasoning that such a move would destroy the “basic structure” of the Constitution, of which the rule of law is an essential component. The judgment clarified that while the State may pursue socio‑economic goals, it cannot do so by enacting laws that abrogate the core guarantees of Articles 14, 19 and 21 without satisfying the proportionality test.

Judicial pronouncements have repeatedly invoked the rule of law to read Directive Principles into Fundamental Rights. In Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) the Court held that the right to education, though originally a Directive Principle under Article 45, had become enforceable through Article 21 because the rule of law demands that the State provide a minimum level of education to make the right to life meaningful. Similarly, in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (1997) the Court linked the right to food (Article 47) to Article 21, stating that the rule of law obliges the State to prevent starvation.

The rule of law also underpins the doctrine of “positive obligations” — the State must not merely refrain from violating rights but must actively create conditions for their enjoyment. This was articulated in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) where the Court, relying on the rule of law and international conventions, laid down guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace, effectively converting a Directive Principle (Article 39 (e)) into a justiciable right.

For the aspirant, the key take‑aways are: (1) the rule of law is the constitutional bridge that allows courts to enforce Directive Principles indirectly through Fundamental Rights; (2) any legislative measure that seeks to implement a DPSP must satisfy the “fair, just and reasonable” standard of Article 21; (3) the basic‑structure doctrine, rooted in the rule of law, prevents Parliament from giving blanket immunity to DPSP‑implementing laws; (4) the rule of law also mandates procedural safeguards — notice, hearing, reasoned orders — before the State can curtail a Fundamental Right in pursuit of a Directive Principle.

Judicial Independence and the Collegium System: Impact on Rights Adjudication

Judicial independence is the institutional guarantee that courts can interpret Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles without executive or legislative pressure. The Constitution secures this through security of tenure (Article 124(2)), fixed salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund (Article 125), and a removal process requiring a two‑thirds parliamentary majority (Article 124(4)). However, the manner of appointment has been the most contested aspect.

The “First Judges Case” S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) held that the executive’s opinion in judicial appointments was not binding, but the “Second Judges Case” Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (1993) reversed this, establishing the collegium system: the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and the four senior‑most judges of the Supreme Court collectively recommend appointments and transfers. The “Third Judges Case” (1998) refined the collegium to the CJI plus the four senior‑most judges for Supreme Court appointments, and the CJI plus two senior‑most judges for High Court appointments.

This judge‑led appointment mechanism has direct consequences for rights adjudication. A collegium composed of judges with a proven record of expansive rights interpretation tends to elevate like‑minded jurists, reinforcing a jurisprudential trajectory that favours transformative constitutionalism. Empirical studies of Supreme Court benches from 1993‑2020 show a correlation between collegium‑appointed judges and a higher rate of decisions expanding Article 21 (e.g., right to privacy, right to health, right to clean environment).

The 99th Constitutional Amendment (2014) attempted to replace the collegium with the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC), comprising the CJI, two senior judges, the Law Minister and two “eminent persons”. In Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (2015) the Court struck down the NJAC, holding that judicial primacy in appointments is part of the basic structure. The judgment underscored that any appointment body in which the executive holds a veto would compromise the independence necessary for impartial rights adjudication.

Critics argue that the collegium lacks transparency and accountability. The 2017 “Memorandum of Procedure” (MoP) negotiations between the government and the judiciary sought to introduce criteria such as merit, diversity and integrity, but the MoP remains unresolved. The absence of a formal, public criteria framework raises concerns about nepotism and the potential for ideological homogeneity, which could narrow the interpretive space for Directive Principles that require progressive judicial activism.

For examination purposes, remember: (1) judicial independence is a basic‑structure feature; (2) the collegium system, though not textually mandated, has been judicially entrenched as the constitutional method of appointment; (3) the NJAC judgment (2015) is the controlling precedent on the unconstitutionality of executive‑dominated appointment bodies; (4) the composition of the collegium influences the doctrinal direction of Fundamental Rights and DPSP jurisprudence; (5) ongoing MoP negotiations are a live constitutional issue — questions may ask about the balance between independence and accountability.

Technique: Applying the Collegium‑Independence Link to a Hypothetical
A 2024 amendment proposes a “Judicial Appointments Commission” where the executive nominates three members, the CJI nominates two, and Parliament ratifies. The amendment is challenged. Using the NJAC judgment, explain whether the amendment violates the basic structure.
The NJAC judgment (2015) held that judicial primacy in appointments is an essential feature of the basic structure because it safeguards judicial independence, which in turn is indispensable for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. The proposed commission gives the executive a majority (three out of five) and subjects appointments to parliamentary ratification, effectively granting the political branches a veto over judicial selection. This replicates the defect the Court identified in the NJAC: the executive’s dominant role undermines the judiciary’s institutional autonomy. Therefore, the amendment would be struck down as violating the basic structure, irrespective of the presence of a CJI nominee, because the overall architecture does not preserve judicial primacy.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to “critically examine” a judicial appointment reform, structure the answer in three steps: (i) state the constitutional provision and the basic‑structure principle (judicial independence); (ii) summarise the NJAC ratio decidendi; (iii) apply the ratio to the specific reform, highlighting the executive’s share of power and any parliamentary override. Conclude with a one‑sentence verdict. This template works for both 10‑mark and 15‑mark questions.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation in the Context of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles

Colourable legislation refers to a law that, while ostensibly enacted within legislative competence, in substance transgresses constitutional limits — either by infringing Fundamental Rights or by masquerading a Directive Principle implementation as a valid exercise of power. The classic formulation comes from K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953): “If the legislature enacts a law which it has no power to enact, the law is void, even though it may be clothed in the language of a permissible entry.” The doctrine focuses on the effect and substance of the statute, not the motive of the legislators (which is protected by parliamentary privilege).

In the Fundamental Rights arena, the doctrine operates when a law purports to be a “reasonable restriction” under Article 19(2)‑(6) but in reality imposes a blanket prohibition. For instance, in State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952) the Court struck down a land‑reform law that, though framed as a measure for agrarian reform (a DPSP under Article 39), effectively deprived zamindars of property without compensation, violating the then‑existing Article 31. The Court held that the law’s true colour was confiscation, not reform.

Post‑Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the doctrine gained a basic‑structure dimension. In Minerva Mills (1980) the Court invalidated the 42nd Amendment’s extension of Article 31C immunity to all DPSPs, reasoning that the amendment was a colourable exercise of constituent power — it sought to emasculate the basic structure (judicial review, Fundamental Rights) under the guise of implementing Directive Principles. The Court emphasized that the Constitution does not permit a “colourable” amendment that destroys its own identity.

The doctrine also surfaces in the context of Article 31C. In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) the Court held that a law claiming protection under Article 31C must have a “reasonable nexus” with Articles 39(b) and (c). If the nexus is illusory — for example, a law nationalising an industry unrelated to the distribution of material resources — the law is colourable and loses the shield of Article 31C. The Court thus reviews the substantive connection, not merely the legislative label.

Recent jurisprudence illustrates the doctrine’s continuing relevance. In Indian Hotel & Restaurants Association v. State of Maharashtra (2013) the Supreme Court examined a state law banning dance bars, ostensibly to protect public morality (a DPSP under Article 47). The Court found the law colourable because it targeted a specific class of establishments while allowing similar activities in hotels, revealing a discriminatory purpose that violated Article 14. The judgment reiterated that the “colourable” label attaches when the legislative classification bears no rational relation to the stated Directive Principle.

For the aspirant, the operational checklist is: (1) Identify the legislative entry or constitutional provision invoked; (2) Determine the true object and effect of the statute; (3) Test whether the object falls within the competence or is a disguised infringement of a Fundamental Right; (4) Apply the “reasonable nexus” test for Article 31C claims; (5) Remember that motive is irrelevant — only substance matters.

The Doctrine of Pith and Substance in Resolving Conflicts between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles

The doctrine of pith and substance, borrowed from Canadian federalism, enables courts to ascertain the true character of a legislation when its provisions appear to overlap two constitutional fields — typically a Fundamental Right and a Directive Principle. The leading Indian authority is State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), where the Court held that a law’s “pith and substance” must be examined to decide whether it falls within the legislative competence of the enacting legislature. In the rights‑directive context, the doctrine helps determine whether a law is genuinely a measure to implement a DPSP or a covert violation of a Fundamental Right.

When a state law regulates an activity that implicates Article 19(1)(g) (freedom of trade) but claims to be a social welfare measure under Article 47 (nutrition, public health), the Court applies pith and substance. In State of Karnataka v. R. S. R. R. (1995) the Supreme Court upheld a law prohibiting the sale of arrack, finding its pith and substance to be public health (a DPSP) rather than a restriction on trade. The Court noted that the incidental impact on Article 19(1)(g) was permissible because the dominant purpose was a Directive Principle.

Conversely, in K. A. Abbas v. Union of India (1971) the Court struck down a censorship law that purported to protect “public order” (a DPSP under Article 38) but whose pith and substance was the suppression of political dissent, violating Article 19(1)(a). The Court emphasized that the “dominant purpose” test cannot be used to cloak a law whose real aim is to curtail a Fundamental Right.

The doctrine also interacts with Article 31C. In Minerva Mills the Court observed that a law claiming immunity under Article 31C must have its pith and substance in furthering Articles 39(b) and (c). If the law’s dominant character is something else — for example, a tax measure disguised as land reform — the immunity fails. This ensures that the Article 31C shield is not a blanket cover for any legislation labelled “social welfare”.

Practically, the pith‑and‑substance analysis proceeds in three steps: (i) identify the legislative entries or constitutional provisions invoked; (ii) examine the statute’s text, preamble, and surrounding circumstances to discern its dominant purpose; (iii) weigh the incidental encroachment on a Fundamental Right against the legitimacy of the Directive Principle objective, applying the proportionality standard. The doctrine thus operationalises the harmonious construction mandate of Kesavananda and Minerva Mills.

Key examination points: (1) Pith and substance is a tool of legislative competence, not a standalone ground for striking down a law; (2) It is frequently invoked in Centre‑State disputes but equally applies to rights‑directive conflicts; (3) The “dominant purpose” test is subjective — courts look at the statute as a whole, not isolated sections; (4) A law whose pith and substance is a DPSP may still be invalid if it fails the proportionality test under Article 21 or Article 14.

Article 31C and the Limits of Legislative Immunity for Directive Principles

Article 31C, inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971) and expanded by the 42nd Amendment (1976), provides that laws giving effect to the Directive Principles in Articles 39(b) and (c) shall not be deemed void for contravening Articles 14, 19 or 31. The provision creates a limited “immunity zone” for socio‑economic legislation, but its scope has been sharply delineated by the Supreme Court.

In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Court upheld the original Article 31C (protecting only Articles 39(b) and (c)) as a valid exercise of constituent power, but struck down the 42nd Amendment’s attempt to extend immunity to all Directive Principles. The majority held that such an extension would destroy the basic structure by removing judicial review over a vast swath of Fundamental Rights. The Court thus restored the pre‑1976 position: only laws aimed at the equitable distribution of material resources (39(b)) and prevention of concentration of wealth (39(c)) enjoy the shield.

The “reasonable nexus” test was articulated in Waman Rao (1981) and reaffirmed in Minerva Mills (1980). A law claiming Article 31C protection must demonstrate a direct and rational connection to Articles 39(b) or (c). In State of Karnataka v. R. S. R. R. (1995) the Court denied immunity to a law nationalising a private bus company because its pith and substance was not the distribution of material resources but the regulation of transport services.

Subsequent cases have refined the nexus requirement. In Indian Hotel & Restaurants Association (2013) the Court held that a ban on dance bars, though justified under Article 47 (public health), could not invoke Article 31C because Article 47 is not among the protected clauses. The judgment clarified that the immunity is exhaustive — only 39(b) and (c) qualify.

The 44th Amendment (1978) repealed Article 31 (right to property) and inserted Article 300A, but left Article 31C untouched. Consequently, property‑related laws that satisfy the 39(b)/(c) nexus still enjoy immunity from Articles 14 and 19 challenges, but not from Article 21 (right to life) challenges, as the Court in Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat (1995) held that Article 31C does not protect against Article 21 violations.

For the aspirant, the critical take‑aways are: (1) Article 31C immunity is confined to Articles 39(b) and (c) only; (2) The “reasonable nexus” test is a justiciable standard — courts examine the law’s true object; (3) Immunity does not extend to Article 21; (4) The 42nd Amendment’s expansion was struck down as basic‑structure violation; (5) Any exam question on “legislative immunity for DPSPs” must reference the current, narrowed scope of Article 31C.

  • Trap 1: Assuming Article 31C protects all Directive Principles — it covers only Articles 39(b) and (c).
  • Trap 2: Confusing the “reasonable nexus” test with a mere legislative declaration; the Court reviews the actual substance.
  • Trap 3: Believing Article 31C shields a law from Article 21 challenges — it does not.
  • Trap 4: Treating the collegium system as a constitutional text; it is a judge‑made convention entrenched as basic structure.
  • Trap 5: Arguing that the NJAC judgment permits any executive role in appointments; the Court held that executive primacy violates basic structure.
  • Trap 6: Applying the pith‑and‑substance doctrine to strike down a law solely because it incidentally affects a Fundamental Right; the dominant purpose must be a DPSP.
  • Trap 7: Citing the 42nd Amendment’s expanded Article 31C as good law — it was invalidated in Minerva Mills.

The advanced sections above equip you to analyse the structural interplay between rights, directives and duties with doctrinal precision.

Article 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule: Constitutional Immunity for Agrarian Reforms and the Basic Structure Doctrine

Articles 31A and 31B, inserted by the First Amendment (1951), created a unique constitutional architecture to insulate land reform legislation from judicial review. Article 31A saves five categories of laws — acquisition of estates, takeover of management, amalgamation of corporations, modification of mining leases, and modification of rights of directors — from challenges under Articles 14 and 19. Crucially, the protection applies only if the law provides for compensation at market value when the acquisition concerns land held under personal cultivation within the statutory ceiling limit. Article 31B goes further: it validates, retrospectively, any Act or Regulation placed in the Ninth Schedule, irrespective of inconsistency with any Fundamental Right. The First Amendment placed thirteen state land reform Acts in the Schedule; subsequent amendments expanded it to over 280 entries, covering subjects far beyond agrarian reform — reservation laws, mining regulations, industrial disputes legislation, and even certain tax statutes.

The Supreme Court’s engagement with this immunity has been a running dialogue on the basic structure. In Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1964), the Court upheld the First and Seventeenth Amendments, holding that Article 368 empowered Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights. Golak Nath (1967) reversed this, declaring Fundamental Rights immune from amendment. The Twenty-fourth Amendment (1971) restored parliamentary power, but Kesavananda Bharati (1973) introduced the basic structure doctrine, subjecting constitutional amendments to judicial review. In Waman Rao (1981), the Court drew a clear line: amendments made before 24 April 1973 (the date of Kesavananda) were immune from challenge; those after were open to scrutiny on basic structure grounds. This “doctrine of prospective overruling” protected the first sixty-six Ninth Schedule entries but exposed later insertions.

The definitive judgment came in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine-judge bench. The Court held that any law placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 must be tested against the basic structure, specifically the “rights test” — whether the law destroys the identity of the Constitution by abrogating the core of Part III. The Court rejected the argument that Article 31B creates a “constitution within a constitution”. It clarified that the basic structure includes the supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, and the mandate to build a welfare state under the Directive Principles. A Ninth Schedule law that violates the essence of Articles 14, 19, or 21 — such as a reservation law exceeding the 50% ceiling without extraordinary justification, or a law removing judicial review entirely — can be struck down. The judgment also established the “impact and effect test”: courts examine the practical operation of the law, not merely its form.

Post-Coelho, the Supreme Court has applied this standard in several cases. In K. Krishna Kumar v. State of Telangana (2019), a Ninth Schedule law providing for reservation in promotions was examined for compliance with the Nagaraj criteria (backwardness, inadequacy of representation, administrative efficiency). In Madhav Rao Scindia (2020), the Court reiterated that the Ninth Schedule is not a “dead letter” zone; the Constitution’s identity cannot be altered by legislative fiat. For the aspirant, the key distinctions are: (1) Article 31A is a substantive saving clause with a market-value compensation condition for personal cultivation land; (2) Article 31B is a blanket validation mechanism dependent on the Ninth Schedule; (3) The 24 April 1973 cut-off date is constitutionally entrenched; (4) The “rights test” under basic structure is the governing standard for post-1973 entries; (5) The doctrine does not immunise laws from challenges under Article 32 or 226 if they violate the basic structure.

Reservations in Promotions and Consequential Seniority: The Constitutional Architecture of Articles 16(4A) and 16(4B) after Nagaraj and Jarnail Singh

The Seventy-seventh Amendment (1995) inserted Article 16(4A), enabling the State to make provisions for reservation in matters of promotion to any class or classes of posts in the services under the State in favour of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes which, in the opinion of the State, are not adequately represented in the services under the State. The Eighty-fifth Amendment (2001) inserted Article 16(4B), allowing unfilled reserved vacancies of a year to be carried forward as a separate class of vacancies, not subject to the fifty-per-cent ceiling of that year. These amendments were a direct legislative response to the Supreme Court’s judgment in Indra Sawhney (1992), which had held that reservation under Article 16(4) applies only to initial appointments, not promotions, and that the fifty-per-cent rule is a binding ceiling.

The constitutional validity of these amendments was upheld in M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006), a five-judge bench, but subject to three stringent conditions that the State must satisfy before enacting promotion reservation laws: (i) the SC/ST community must be socially and educationally backward; (ii) it must be inadequately represented in the relevant promotional posts; and (iii) the reservation must not adversely affect the efficiency of administration as mandated by Article 335. The Court held that these are not mere formalities but justiciable requirements; the State must collect quantifiable data to demonstrate backwardness and inadequacy of representation. The judgment also introduced the “creamy layer” concept into SC/ST promotions, a point later revisited.

In Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018), a five-judge bench revisited Nagaraj. The Court unanimously held that the requirement to prove “backwardness” of SC/STs for promotions is contrary to the constitutional scheme — the Presidential Lists under Articles 341 and 342 conclusively identify SC/STs, and their backwardness is presumed. The Nagaraj requirement of quantifiable data on backwardness was therefore struck down as ultra vires. However, the Court affirmed the other two Nagaraj conditions: quantifiable data on inadequacy of representation in the specific promotional cadre, and the Article 335 efficiency-of-administration test. The judgment also clarified that the creamy layer exclusion does not apply to SC/STs in promotions, distinguishing them from OBCs where the creamy layer is mandatory (Indra Sawhney, Ashoka Kumar Thakur).

The interplay of Article 16(4B) with the fifty-per-cent ceiling remains a live issue. In Union of India v. Ramesh Ram (2010), the Court held that carried-forward vacancies under Article 16(4B) are exempt from the fifty-per-cent limit for the year in which they are filled, but the overall representation in the cadre must not breach the ceiling in a manner that destroys the balance of the constitutional scheme. The “roster point” system and the “post-based” versus “vacancy-based” roster debate continues to generate litigation. In Mukesh Kumar v. State of Uttarakhand (2020), the Court held that the State is not bound to make reservations in promotions; it is an enabling provision, not a mandate. However, if the State chooses to exercise it, the Nagaraj-Jarnail Singh conditions are mandatory. For the aspirant, the critical takeaways are: (1) Articles 16(4A) and (4B) are enabling, not obligatory; (2) The Jarnail Singh judgment removed the backwardness proof requirement for SC/STs but retained the inadequacy-of-representation and efficiency tests; (3) Creamy layer exclusion does not apply to SC/ST promotions; (4) Article 16(4B) carved-out vacancies are a distinct class but subject to overall constitutional balance; (5) Quantifiable data must be cadre-specific, not generic.

Examiner's Trap: Conflating the Tests for OBC and SC/ST Promotions
A question asks: "The Supreme Court in Jarnail Singh (2018) extended the creamy layer principle to SC/ST reservations in promotions. Comment."
The statement is false. Jarnail Singh explicitly held that the creamy layer principle, which applies to OBCs under Indra Sawhney and Ashoka Kumar Thakur, does not apply to SC/STs in promotions. The Court reasoned that the Presidential Lists under Articles 341/342 identify SC/STs as a class deemed backward by the Constitution itself; imposing a creamy layer filter would amount to rewriting the Lists, a power reserved for Parliament under Article 341(2)/342(2). The judgment struck down the Nagaraj requirement to prove backwardness for SC/STs but retained the quantifiable data requirement for inadequacy of representation and the Article 335 efficiency test. The trap lies in mechanically applying OBC jurisprudence to SC/STs; the constitutional text and history create a deliberate distinction.
Exam-Day Strategy: The Three-Condition Checklist
When a question on promotion reservations appears, mentally run the Nagaraj-Jarnail Singh checklist: (1) Is the group SC/ST or OBC? (SC/ST = no backwardness proof, no creamy layer; OBC = both required). (2) Has the State collected quantifiable data on inadequacy of representation in the specific promotional cadre? (3) Has the State assessed the impact on efficiency of administration under Article 335? Cite Jarnail Singh for the SC/ST backwardness presumption and Nagaraj for the other two conditions. This structure fetches full marks for doctrinal precision.

Commercial Speech under Article 19(1)(a): The Evolution from State Monopoly to Regulated Marketplace

The constitutional status of commercial speech — advertising, price information, professional solicitation — has undergone a radical transformation. In Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India (1960), the Supreme Court held that commercial advertising is not “speech” within the meaning of Article 19(1)(a) but a mere trade activity protected, if at all, under Article 19(1)(g). The Drug and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954, which prohibited advertisements of certain drugs claiming magical cures, was upheld. The Court reasoned that the freedom of speech and expression is designed to protect the free propagation of ideas, not commercial transactions. This “commercial speech exclusion” doctrine persisted for over three decades.

The turning point came in Tata Press Ltd. v. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. (1995). The issue was whether MTNL, a public sector monopoly, could refuse to accept advertisements for its telephone directory. The Court, per Justice K. Ramaswamy, held that commercial speech is a part of the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by Article 19(1)(a). The judgment relied on the U.S. Supreme Court’s Virginia State Board of Pharmacy v. Virginia Citizens Consumer Council (1976) and the Canadian Irwin Toy (1989) reasoning: the free flow of commercial information is indispensable to the functioning of a free market economy and to the consumer’s right to make informed choices. The Court clarified that the protection extends to truthful, non-misleading commercial speech concerning lawful activities. False, deceptive, or misleading advertising, and advertising of illegal goods or services, remain outside the protection and can be regulated under Article 19(2).

Post-Tata Press, the jurisprudence has refined the boundaries. In Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985, pre-Tata Press but influential), the Court had already recognised that the freedom of the press includes the right to advertise. In Secretary, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting v. Cricket Association of Bengal (1995), the Court extended the logic to sports broadcasting rights. In Hindustan Times v. State of U.P. (2003), the Court struck down a state law imposing a tax on advertisements, holding it a direct burden on Article 19(1)(a). The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 now provide the statutory framework for regulating misleading advertisements, unfair trade practices, and content standards. The Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) code, though self-regulatory, has been given judicial recognition in several High Court judgments as a benchmark for “reasonable restriction”.

The contemporary challenges involve digital advertising, influencer marketing, data-driven targeted ads, and the regulation of online platforms. The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 impose due diligence obligations on social media intermediaries regarding advertisements, including labelling of sponsored content. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), while striking down Section 66A of the IT Act, the Court affirmed that commercial speech on the internet enjoys Article 19(1)(a) protection subject to the narrow grounds of Article 19(2). For the aspirant, the doctrinal arc is: (1) Hamdard Dawakhana — commercial speech excluded; (2) Tata Press — commercial speech included as a facet of Article 19(1)(a) for truthful, lawful, non-misleading information; (3) Regulation permitted under Article 19(2) grounds (public order, decency, morality, defamation, incitement) plus consumer protection statutes; (4) The “commercial speaker” (advertiser) and the “commercial listener” (consumer) both have rights; (5) Digital commercial speech is subject to the same constitutional standard with platform-specific regulatory overlays.

Rights of Prisoners, Undertrials and Detenues: The Article 21 Jurisprudence on Custodial Justice

The expansion of Article 21 into the prison cell is one of the most consequential developments in Indian constitutional law. The foundational principle, articulated in Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration (1978), is that “prison walls do not keep out fundamental rights”. A prisoner retains all Fundamental Rights except those necessarily lost as an incident of incarceration. The Court has read into Article 21 a cluster of custodial rights: right to legal aid (M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra, 1978), right to speedy trial (Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, 1979), right against solitary confinement and bar fetters (Sunil Batra II, 1980), right to meet family and lawyers (Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi, 1981), right to medical care (Parmanand Katara v. Union of India, 1989), and right to compensation for custodial violence (Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa, 1993).

The undertrial crisis has driven much of this jurisprudence. In Hussainara Khatoon, the Court held that detention of undertrials for periods longer than the maximum possible sentence for the alleged offence violates Article 21. It directed the release of thousands of undertrials on personal bond. The Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2005 introduced Section 436A, mandating release of undertrials who have served half the maximum sentence (except for death penalty offences). The Model Prison Manual, 2016 and the Prisons Act, 1894 (as amended by states) now incorporate many of these judicial standards, but implementation remains uneven.

Preventive detention under Article 22 occupies a distinct but overlapping space. The safeguards — communication of grounds, earliest opportunity for representation, advisory board review within three weeks — have been strictly enforced. In A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982), the Court upheld the National Security Act, 1980, but insisted on strict compliance with Article 22(5). In Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab (1994), the Court read down the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, to require that the advisory board’s opinion be communicated to the detenu. The 44th Amendment (1978) reduced the maximum detention without advisory board opinion from three months to two months, but this provision has not been brought into force; the three-month period under the original Article 22(4) continues to operate.

Custodial death and torture have attracted the doctrine of “compensatory jurisprudence”. In Nilabati Behera, the Court awarded monetary compensation to the mother of a youth who died in police custody, holding that the State has a strict liability for custodial violence. The DK Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) guidelines — arrest memo, notification to next friend, medical examination every 48 hours, access to lawyer — were later incorporated into the CrPC (Amendment) Act, 2008 (Sections 41B, 41D, 50A, 54, 55A). The Law Commission’s 273rd Report (2018) recommended a standalone anti-torture law; the Prevention of Torture Bill has lapsed multiple times. For the aspirant, the key propositions are: (1) Article 21 travels with the prisoner; only rights necessarily inconsistent with incarceration are lost; (2) Undertrial detention beyond half the maximum sentence (Section 436A CrPC) is a prima facie Article 21 violation; (3) Preventive detention safeguards under Article 22 are minimal but judicially enforceable; (4) Custodial violence attracts State liability under public law (Article 21) distinct from private law tort; (5) The DK Basu guidelines have statutory force post-2008 CrPC amendments.

Article 32 versus Article 226: Comparative Writ Jurisdiction, Territorial Limits and the Discretionary Principle

The constitutional design creates a dual writ jurisdiction: the Supreme Court under Article 32 and the High Courts under Article 226. While both enforce Fundamental Rights, their scope, reach, and procedural character differ in ways that determine forum selection and litigation strategy. Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right — the “heart and soul” of the Constitution per Dr. Ambedkar. The Supreme Court’s jurisdiction is mandatory; it cannot refuse to entertain a petition that discloses a violation of a Fundamental Right. Article 226 confers a discretionary power on High Courts; they “may” issue writs. This discretion is judicial, not arbitrary, and is exercised on grounds such as availability of alternative remedy, laches, res judicata, or the petitioner’s conduct.

Territorially, Article 32 extends to the whole of India. The Supreme Court can issue writs against any authority within the territory of India, including State governments and Central agencies. Article 226 is limited to the territorial jurisdiction of the High Court, but the cause of action must arise, wholly or in part, within that territory. A High Court can issue a writ against a Central authority if the cause of action arises within its jurisdiction (State of Assam v. Sankar Prasad, 1998). The Supreme Court has original jurisdiction under Article 32; High Courts have original and appellate jurisdiction under Article 226.

The range of writs is identical — habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto — but Article 226 extends to “any other purpose”, allowing High Courts to enforce statutory rights, contractual rights, and even non-justiciable Directive Principles in appropriate cases (Dwarka Nath v. ITO, 1966). Article 32 is confined to Fundamental Rights. This makes Article 226 a broader jurisdictional gateway. However, the Supreme Court has expanded Article 32 through the “continuing mandamus” and “structural injunction” techniques to monitor implementation of complex rights (environment, prison reform, police reform), effectively bridging the remedial gap.

The principle of “alternative remedy” operates differently. Under Article 226, the existence of an efficacious alternative remedy is a ground for declining jurisdiction. Under Article 32, the Supreme Court has held that the existence of an alternative remedy does not oust its jurisdiction, though it may refuse to exercise it if the remedy is adequate and the petitioner has not availed it (Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras, 1950; Khatri v. State of Bihar, 1981). The Supreme Court also entertains Public Interest Litigation under Article 32 with relaxed locus standi; High Courts do so under Article 226 with similar flexibility. The L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) judgment held that the power of judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 is part of the basic structure; tribunals cannot oust High Court writ jurisdiction. For the aspirant, the decision matrix is: (1) If the violation is of a Fundamental Right only and pan-India or involves a Central law — Article 32; (2) If the violation includes statutory/contractual rights, or the cause of action is local — Article 226; (3) If speed is critical (habeas corpus) — both lie, but High Courts are geographically accessible; (4) If the petitioner has an alternative remedy — Article 32 is safer; (5) The Supreme Court’s jurisdiction is a right; the High Court’s is a discretion — frame the prayer accordingly.

  • Trap 1: Assuming Article 31A protects all land reform laws without the market-value compensation condition for personal cultivation land — the condition is mandatory and justiciable.
  • Trap 2: Believing the Ninth Schedule provides absolute immunity post-Coelho — the basic structure “rights test” applies to all post-1973 entries.
  • Trap 3: Applying the creamy layer principle to SC/ST promotions — Jarnail Singh explicitly forbids it; the Presidential Lists create a constitutional presumption of backwardness.
  • Trap 4: Treating Article 16(4A) as a mandate rather than an enabling provision — the State is not constitutionally compelled to provide reservation in promotions.
  • Trap 5: Arguing that Hamdard Dawakhana remains good law on commercial speech — Tata Press overruled it sub silentio; commercial speech is now a facet of Article 19(1)(a).
  • Trap 6: Claiming that prisoners lose all Fundamental Rights — they retain all rights except those necessarily incident to incarceration (Sunil Batra).
  • Trap 7: Asserting that the existence of an alternative remedy bars Article 32 jurisdiction — it does not; the Supreme Court may still entertain the petition, unlike Article 226 where it is a valid ground for refusal.

The Ninth Schedule and Article 31B: The 'Rights Test' and 'Basic Structure Test' Post-I.R. Coelho

Article 31B, inserted by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, provides that any Act or Regulation specified in the Ninth Schedule shall not be deemed void on the ground of inconsistency with Fundamental Rights. Unlike Article 31A, which saves specific categories of laws (agrarian reform, etc.) subject to conditions, Article 31B offers a blanket validation for whatever Parliament places in the Schedule. The constitutional history of this provision is a dialogue between legislative assertion and judicial containment.

The Supreme Court in Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) drew a clear temporal line: laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment) are immune from challenge on the ground of Fundamental Rights violation. This immunity rests on the theory that the basic structure doctrine was not yet enunciated, and Parliament’s constituent power was then considered plenary. However, for laws inserted after 24 April 1973, the Court held they are open to challenge if they damage the basic structure.

The definitive exposition came in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine-judge bench decision. The Court formulated the "Rights Test": a Ninth Schedule law must be tested on the touchstone of the basic structure as reflected in Articles 14, 19, and 21 (the "golden triangle"). The validation under Article 31B does not confer immunity from the basic structure doctrine. The Court clarified that the "impact and effect" test applies — it is not enough that the law facially pursues a legitimate aim; its actual operation must not destroy the constitutional identity. The 42nd Amendment (1976) had attempted to bar judicial review of Ninth Schedule laws entirely by amending Article 31B; this was struck down in Minerva Mills (1980) as violating the basic structure. Post-Coelho, the Ninth Schedule remains a legislative tool, but its entries are subject to a rigorous "basic structure audit" focusing on the substantive violation of equality, freedom, and life.

Practically, this means land reform acts placed post-1973 (e.g., certain state ceiling laws) and non-agrarian laws (e.g., the Tamil Nadu Backward Classes Act, 1993, placed in the Schedule by the 76th Amendment) are justiciable. The burden is on the petitioner to demonstrate that the law, in its effect, abrogates a basic structure feature. The State must then justify it as a reasonable restriction or a measure that does not destroy the constitutional core.

Articles 31A and 31C: Constitutional Immunity for Land Reform and Directive Principle Implementation

Article 31A and Article 31C represent two distinct constitutional strategies to insulate socio-economic legislation from Fundamental Rights challenges. Article 31A, introduced by the First Amendment (1951) and expanded by the Fourth (1955), Seventeenth (1964), and Forty-second (1976) Amendments, saves five categories of laws: (i) agrarian reform (acquisition of estates, rights of tenants, etc.), (ii) takeover of management of property for a limited period, (iii) amalgamation of corporations, (iv) modification of mining leases, and (v) modification of rights of directors/managers of corporations. A critical condition attaches to the first category: where the law acquires land held under personal cultivation within the statutory ceiling limit, it must provide for compensation at market value (proviso to Art. 31A(1)). This proviso, inserted by the Seventeenth Amendment and retained thereafter, is justiciable; the Court can examine whether the compensation provided is illusory or genuinely reflects market value (K. T. Plantation v. State of Karnataka, 2011).

Article 31C, inserted by the Twenty-fifth Amendment (1971), originally had two limbs: (a) a law giving effect to the policy of Article 39(b) and (c) (distribution of material resources, prevention of concentration of wealth) shall not be deemed void for contravention of Articles 14, 19, or 31; (b) such a law "shall not be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy". The second limb — an ouster of judicial review — was struck down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) as violating the basic structure. The Forty-second Amendment (1976) expanded Article 31C to cover all Directive Principles, not just Article 39(b)(c). In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Court struck down this expansion, holding that giving primacy to all DPSPs over Fundamental Rights destroys the balance which is part of the basic structure. Article 31C was thus restored to its pre-1976 form: it protects only laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c), and judicial review of whether a law genuinely falls within that protection remains intact.

The interplay is significant: Article 31A is a category-based shield with a market-value compensation condition for personal cultivation land. Article 31C is a policy-based shield limited to two specific DPSPs. Neither provides absolute immunity. In Waman Rao, the Court held that Article 31C laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 1973 are subject to the basic structure test. The current position is that both provisions are valid but narrowly construed; the State must demonstrate the law falls squarely within the saved category or policy, and the Court retains the power to examine the "true nature and character" of the legislation (Ambika Mills v. State of Gujarat, 1974).

Worked Example: Distinguishing the Immunity Provisions
A State enacts a law acquiring all private forests for conservation, placing it in the Ninth Schedule via a constitutional amendment in 2020. The law provides compensation based on circle rates, which are 40% of market value. The law is challenged. Analyse the validity under Articles 31A, 31B, and 31C.
Step 1: Article 31A. The law acquires "estates" (forests may qualify as "estates" under state definition). However, if any land is held under personal cultivation within ceiling limits, the market-value compensation proviso applies. Circle rates at 40% of market value fail this test. The law is not saved by Art. 31A for such lands.
Step 2: Article 31C. The law aims at conservation, not distribution of material resources (Art. 39(b)) or prevention of concentration of wealth (Art. 39(c)). It does not implement Art. 39(b)(c). Art. 31C shield unavailable.
Step 3: Article 31B / Ninth Schedule. The law was placed in the Ninth Schedule in 2020 (post-1973). Per I.R. Coelho, it is subject to the "Rights Test" — does it violate the basic structure (Art. 14, 19, 21)? The compensation at 40% market value is arbitrary (Art. 14) and violates the right to property (Art. 300A, a constitutional right). The Ninth Schedule validation does not cure this basic structure violation.
Conclusion: The law is vulnerable to being struck down for the lands where compensation is not at market value, and potentially in its entirety if the arbitrariness permeates the statute.
Exam Strategy: The Immunity Hierarchy
When a question involves a socio-economic law challenged under FRs, apply the hierarchy: (1) Does Art. 31A apply? Check category + market-value proviso for personal cultivation land. (2) Does Art. 31C apply? Check if law implements Art. 39(b)(c) ONLY. (3) Is it in Ninth Schedule? If pre-1973 → immune from FR challenge (but not basic structure if amended post-Kesavananda? No, Waman Rao says pre-1973 immune). If post-1973 → apply Coelho "Rights Test" (Art. 14, 19, 21 basic structure). Remember: Art. 31A and 31C are defences the State must plead and prove; the burden is on the State to show the law falls within the saved category/policy.

Article 13(3): The Definition of 'Law' — Constitutional Amendments, Ordinances, and Delegated Legislation

Article 13(3) defines "law" for the purposes of Article 13(2) (which voids laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights). The definition is inclusive: "law includes any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law". "Laws in force" (Art. 13(3)(b)) covers pre-constitutional statutes. The judicial interpretation of this definition determines the reach of Fundamental Rights.

Constitutional Amendments: The question whether a constitutional amendment under Article 368 is "law" under Article 13(2) has a chequered history. Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1964) held amendments are not "law" — they are exercises of constituent power. Golaknath (1967) reversed this, holding amendments are "law" and void if they abridge FRs. The Twenty-fourth Amendment (1971) inserted Article 13(4) and Article 368(3) stating: "Nothing in Article 13 shall apply to any amendment of this Constitution made under Article 368." Kesavananda Bharati (1973) upheld the Twenty-fourth Amendment: constitutional amendments are not "law" under Article 13. However, they are subject to the basic structure doctrine — a judicial innovation outside Article 13. Thus, an amendment violating basic structure is void, but not because of Article 13(2).

Ordinances (Articles 123, 213): An Ordinance promulgated by the President or Governor is explicitly included in "law" under Article 13(3)(a). It can be challenged for Fundamental Rights violation. Its repromulgation without legislative approval has been held a fraud on the Constitution (D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar, 1987; Krishna Kumar v. State of Bihar, 2017).

Delegated Legislation: Rules, regulations, bye-laws, notifications made under statutory power are "law". However, administrative instructions, circulars, office memoranda, and guidelines without statutory force are generally not "law" under Article 13(3) unless they have the "force of law" — i.e., they are binding and enforceable by sanction (Commissioner of Police v. Gordhandas Bhanji, 1952; Suganmal v. State of M.P., 1965). A government resolution directing officers is not "law"; a rule made under a statute is.

Customs and Usages: Only those "having the force of law" — i.e., judicially recognized, certain, reasonable, and not opposed to public policy — are included. Personal law (Hindu, Muslim law) was historically debated; the Supreme Court in Narasu Appa Mali (1951) held uncodified personal law is not "law" under Article 13, but this is now contested. Codified personal law (Hindu Marriage Act, etc.) is statutory "law".

Judicial Decisions: A judgment of the Supreme Court under Article 141 is "law declared" but not "law made" — it cannot be challenged under Article 13(2) as violative of FRs (A.R. Antulay v. R.S. Nayak, 1988). However, a judicial order that acts legislatively (e.g., a direction creating a new offence) may be scrutinized.

Adjudicating Socio-Economic Rights: The 'Reasonableness' Standard, Minimum Core Obligations, and the Separation of Powers Constraint

Directive Principles (Part IV) are expressly non-justiciable (Article 37), yet the Supreme Court has converted many into enforceable facets of Article 21. The doctrinal challenge is to enforce positive State obligations without transgressing the separation of powers or engaging in polycentric policy-making. Indian jurisprudence has evolved a distinct "reasonableness review" model, influenced by but distinct from the South African "minimum core" and "reasonableness" approach (Government of RSA v. Grootboom, 2000; Minister of Health v. Treatment Action Campaign, 2002).

The Reasonableness Standard: In Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), the Court held that the right to livelihood is part of Article 21, but eviction of pavement dwellers is permissible if the procedure is "fair, just, and reasonable". The State's policy choice is not substituted; the Court asks whether the decision is non-arbitrary, proportionate, and based on relevant considerations. In Chameli Singh v. State of U.P. (1996), the right to shelter was read into Article 21, but the Court declined to mandate a specific housing scheme, directing the State to "frame a policy".

Minimum Core Obligations: While India has not formally adopted the "minimum core" doctrine (which requires the State to ensure minimum essential levels of each right immediately), the concept operates implicitly. In Shantistar Builders v. Narayan Khimalal Totame (1990), the Court spoke of "bare necessities of life" — food, clothing, shelter, education. In Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal (1996), the denial of emergency medical care to a poor person was held a violation of Article 21; the State's resource constraint argument was rejected for emergency/core obligations. The PUCL v. Union of India (2001) right to food litigation saw the Court convert DPSPs (Art. 39(a), 47) into enforceable interim orders (mid-day meals, ICDS universalization), monitoring implementation through Commissioners — a structural injunction technique.

Progressive Realisation and Resource Constraints: The State often pleads financial inability. The Court accepts that progressive realisation is inherent in socio-economic rights but demands time-bound plans and non-retrogression. In State of Karnataka v. All India Manufacturers' Organisation (2006), the Court acknowledged budgetary limits but insisted on prioritisation. The "non-retrogression" principle (drawn from ICESCR General Comment 3) means the State cannot deliberately roll back existing protections (e.g., cutting mid-day meal budgets) without compelling justification.

Separation of Powers and Remedial Design: The Court avoids "budgetary mandamus" (directing specific allocations). Instead, it uses continuing mandamus (periodic reporting, monitoring committees), structural injunctions (institutional reform — police, prisons, environment), and declaratory relief coupled with a direction to legislate. The Vineet Narain (1998) "hawala case" and Prakash Singh (2006) police reform judgments exemplify this. The legitimacy rests on the Court acting as a catalyst for executive accountability, not a substitute for the legislature.

Articles 26, 27, and 28: Denominational Freedom, Freedom from Religious Taxation, and Religious Instruction — The Architecture Beyond Essential Practices

While Article 25 guarantees individual freedom of conscience and profession, Articles 26, 27, and 28 constitute the institutional and financial architecture of secularism. Article 26 confers on every "religious denomination or any section thereof" the right to (a) establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes, (b) manage its own affairs in matters of religion, (c) own and acquire movable and immovable property, and (d) administer such property in accordance with law. These rights are subject to public order, morality, and health — but not to the other Fundamental Rights (unlike Art. 25(1)). In Shirur Mutt (1954), the Court defined "denomination" as a collection of individuals with a common faith, organization, and distinctive name. The essential practices test originated here to determine what constitutes "matters of religion" under Art. 26(b).

Article 27 prohibits the State from compelling any person to pay taxes the proceeds of which are specifically appropriated for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion or religious denomination. The distinction between tax and fee is critical: a fee for secular administration of a religious institution (e.g., audit, regulation of trusts) is valid (Ratilal Panachand Gandhi v. State of Bombay, 1954). A levy where the primary purpose is religious promotion is a tax and violates Art. 27. In P.M. A. Metropolitan v. Moran Mar Marthoma (1995), a levy for church renovation was held a tax.

Article 28 regulates religious instruction in educational institutions. It creates a four-fold classification: (1) Wholly State-funded institutions: No religious instruction (Art. 28(1)). (2) State-administered but established under endowment/trust requiring religious instruction: Instruction permitted (Art. 28(2)). (3) Recognized or aided by State: No person can be compelled to attend religious instruction without consent (guardian's consent for minors) (Art. 28(3)). (4) Wholly private, unaided: No constitutional restriction. In DAV College v. State of Punjab (1971), the Court held that a university statute making Guru Nanak's teachings compulsory in affiliated colleges violated Art. 28(3) for aided colleges. Aruna Roy v. Union of India (2002) distinguished "religious education" (study of religions, permitted) from "religious instruction" (ritualistic, dogmatic, prohibited in State-funded schools).

The interplay with Article 29(2) (no denial of admission on grounds of religion in State-aided institutions) and Article 30 (minority right to establish/administer educational institutions) is dense. A minority institution under Art. 30 can provide religious instruction even if aided, but cannot compel students of other communities to attend (Art. 28(3)). The T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002) and P.A. Inamdar (2005) judgments navigated this by holding that aided minority institutions must admit a reasonable percentage of non-minority students (State quota) but retain administrative control; religious instruction for minority students is protected, but Art. 28(3) protects non-minority students from compulsion.

  • Trap 1: Assuming Article 31B (Ninth Schedule) provides absolute immunity for post-1973 laws. Post-Coelho, the "Rights Test" (Art. 14, 19, 21 basic structure) applies fully.
  • Trap 2: Confusing Article 31A's market-value compensation proviso. It applies only to land held under personal cultivation within the ceiling limit. For other acquisitions under Art. 31A, the compensation need not be market value (only "not illusory" per pre-1978 Art. 31 jurisprudence, now Art. 300A reasonableness).
  • Trap 3: Arguing that a constitutional amendment violating Fundamental Rights is void under Article 13(2). Since the 24th Amendment (1971) and Kesavananda, amendments are not "law" under Art. 13; they are tested on basic structure, not Art. 13(2).
  • Trap 4: Treating every government circular or office memorandum as "law" under Article 13(3). Only instruments with statutory force and binding sanction qualify; administrative guidelines without penalty are not "law".
