  • Trap 5: Claiming the "minimum core" doctrine is formally part of Indian law. The Court uses "reasonableness" and "bare necessities" language but has not adopted the South African minimum core as a justiciable floor; it remains a persuasive interpretive tool.
  • Trap 6: Believing Article 27 prohibits all State expenditure on religion. It prohibits taxes specifically appropriated for religion. Fees for secular regulation, and grants for secular purposes (e.g., restoration of heritage temples under Art. 25(2)(a) "secular activity"), are permissible.
  • Trap 7: Assuming Article 28(1) bans all religious instruction in all government schools. It applies only to institutions wholly maintained out of State funds. Institutions administered by the State but established under a trust requiring religious instruction (Art. 28(2)) are exempt.

Article 15(3): Special Provisions for Women and Children – Constitutional Scope and Judicial Interpretation

Article 15(3) empowers the State to make any special provision for women and children, notwithstanding the general prohibition of discrimination on grounds of sex under Article 15(1). The clause was inserted to permit affirmative action that addresses historical and structural disadvantages. The Supreme Court has consistently held that the power under Article 15(3) is wide and not confined to the categories enumerated in Article 15(4) or 15(5). In Government of Andhra Pradesh v. P.B. Vijayakumar (1995), the Court upheld a rule providing 30 % reservation for women in public employment, ruling that such a provision falls squarely within Article 15(3) and does not violate Article 16(2). The judgment clarified that the “special provision” may be in the form of reservation, relaxation of qualifying marks, or preferential treatment in promotions.

The scope of “women” under Article 15(3) includes all women irrespective of caste, religion, or class. In Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association of India (2008), the Court struck down a Punjab law prohibiting women from working in establishments serving liquor, holding that the law was based on stereotypical notions of morality and violated Articles 14, 15(1) and 15(3). The Court emphasized that protective legislation must not become a tool of paternalistic discrimination. For children, Article 15(3) read with Article 24 (prohibition of child labour) and Article 39(e)‑(f) (DPSP) enables the State to enact laws such as the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, and the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (Article 21A).

Judicial scrutiny of special provisions for women and children applies the “reasonable classification” test under Article 14. The classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia and have a rational nexus with the object sought. In National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014), the Court recognized transgender persons as a “third gender” and directed the State to treat them as socially and educationally backward classes for reservations under Article 15(4) and 15(5), but also noted that Article 15(3) could be invoked for special provisions for transgender women. The evolving jurisprudence shows a shift from formal equality to substantive equality, allowing the State to design targeted measures that survive constitutional review.

Legislative examples include the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (amended 2017 to extend paid leave to 26 weeks), the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013, and the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006. Courts have also read Article 15(3) harmoniously with Article 51A(e) (fundamental duty to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women) to reinforce the State’s positive obligations.

Article 16(4B) and the Carry Forward Rule for Unfilled Reserved Vacancies

Article 16(4B), inserted by the 81st Constitutional Amendment (2000), permits the State to consider unfilled reserved vacancies of a year as a separate class of vacancies to be filled in any succeeding year, and such vacancies shall not be counted towards the 50 % ceiling on reservations laid down in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992). The provision was a legislative response to the “carry forward” practice that had been struck down in M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) for violating the 50 % rule when carried forward vacancies were added to the current year’s quota.

The Supreme Court in M. Nagaraj upheld the constitutional validity of Article 16(4B) but imposed three conditions: (i) the State must demonstrate the inadequacy of representation of the concerned backward class; (ii) the overall reservation must not exceed 50 % in any given year; and (iii) the creamy layer must be excluded. The Court clarified that the “carry forward” vacancies are a distinct class and do not merge with the current year’s reserved quota, thereby preserving the 50 % ceiling for each recruitment year.

Subsequent judgments have refined the operation of Article 16(4B). In Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018), the Court held that the creamy layer exclusion applies to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in promotions, reinforcing that the carry forward rule cannot be used to circumvent the creamy layer principle. In Union of India v. R. Rajesh Kumar (2021), the Court ruled that the State must maintain a roster indicating the number of carried forward vacancies and cannot arbitrarily convert them into general category posts.

Practical implications: recruitment bodies (UPSC, State PSCs, SSC) maintain separate rosters for “current year reserved vacancies” and “carried forward vacancies”. The 50 % ceiling is applied to the sum of current year reserved vacancies plus general category vacancies; carried forward vacancies are filled over and above this ceiling but only up to the extent of the backlog. The rule has been instrumental in clearing backlogs in central government services, yet it remains a frequent subject of litigation concerning roster management, the definition of “year”, and the interplay with Article 16(4A) (consequential seniority).

Worked Example: Carry Forward Calculation
In a given recruitment year, a department has 100 vacancies. The reservation policy provides 15 % for SC, 7.5 % for ST, and 27 % for OBC (total 49.5 %). Due to non‑availability of suitable candidates, 5 SC and 3 ST vacancies remain unfilled. The department also has a backlog of 10 SC and 4 ST carried forward vacancies from previous years. How many reserved vacancies can be notified in the current year without breaching the 50 % ceiling?
Current year reserved quota = 49.5 (rounded to 50) vacancies. The 50 % ceiling applies to current year vacancies only, so at most 50 reserved vacancies can be notified for the current year. The 8 unfilled current‑year vacancies (5 SC + 3 ST) become carried forward vacancies for next year. The existing backlog of 14 carried forward vacancies (10 SC + 4 ST) are a separate class under Art. 16(4B) and can be filled in addition to the 50 current‑year reserved vacancies. Therefore, the department may notify up to 64 reserved vacancies (50 current + 14 backlog) in the current recruitment cycle, provided the overall reservation in any single year does not exceed 50 % of the total vacancies advertised for that year.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the carry forward rule, first identify whether the vacancy is “current year” or “backlog”. Remember the 50 % ceiling applies only to current year reservations. Cite M. Nagaraj (2006) for the three conditions and Jarnail Singh (2018) for creamy layer applicability. A quick mental roster sketch (current vs backlog) prevents arithmetic errors.

Article 19(1)(a) and the Doctrine of Prior Restraint – Judicial Limits on Pre‑Censorship

The freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) includes the right to publish and circulate ideas without prior governmental censorship. The doctrine of prior restraint holds that any system requiring pre‑publication approval by an executive authority is presumptively unconstitutional unless it meets the strict scrutiny of Article 19(2). In Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950), the Supreme Court struck down a law banning the entry of a journal, holding that “freedom of speech and expression includes freedom of propagation of ideas” and that a law imposing prior restraint must be justified under the specific grounds of Article 19(2).

The Court further refined the doctrine in Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (1950), invalidating a pre‑censorship order on a newspaper. The judgment established that prior restraint is the most serious infringement of free speech because it prevents the speech from ever reaching the public. The State bears a heavy burden to show that the restraint is “necessary” and “proportionate” to a legitimate aim under Article 19(2). In K.A. Abbas v. Union of India (1971), the Court upheld film censorship under the Cinematograph Act, 1952, but only because the statute provided for an independent tribunal, clear guidelines, and a time‑bound review — thereby converting a prior restraint into a regulated, post‑decision review mechanism.

Modern applications involve digital media. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, for being vague and overbroad, and also read down Section 79(3)(b) (intermediary takedown) to require a court order or government notification before content removal, effectively limiting executive prior restraint. The 2021 Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules mandate a “first originator” traceability requirement; the Supreme Court in WhatsApp LLC v. Union of India (2023) has stayed parts of the rules pending constitutional scrutiny, signalling that mandatory pre‑publication filtering by platforms may constitute impermissible prior restraint.

The test for permissible prior restraint now incorporates: (i) a clear statutory framework; (ii) narrow, defined categories of restricted speech; (iii) an independent adjudicatory body; (iv) prompt judicial review; and (v) proportionality. Any administrative order that bypasses these safeguards — such as a district magistrate’s oral direction to a newspaper to withhold publication — is liable to be quashed under Article 226.

Article 21 and the Right to Livelihood – Judicial Expansion and State Obligations

The right to life under Article 21 has been interpreted to include the right to livelihood, because “no person can live without the means of living”. In Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), the Supreme Court held that eviction of pavement dwellers without alternative accommodation violates Article 21, as deprivation of livelihood amounts to deprivation of life. The Court mandated that the State must follow a fair procedure, including notice, hearing, and rehabilitation, before displacing people whose livelihood depends on the occupied space.

Subsequent jurisprudence expanded the concept. In Chameli Singh v. State of U.P. (1996), the Court declared that the right to livelihood includes the right to work, to a decent environment, and to social security. The judgment linked Article 21 with Directive Principles Articles 39(a), 41, and 43, holding that the State’s obligation to provide employment is not merely aspirational but enforceable through judicial review when State action directly threatens livelihood.

The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005, was enacted partly in response to this jurisprudence. The Supreme Court in Swaraj Abhiyan v. Union of India (2016) monitored MGNREGA implementation, directing timely wage payments, social audits, and compensation for delayed wages, treating the statutory guarantee as a facet of Article 21. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2020), the Court ordered the State to provide dry rations and cash transfers to migrant workers during the COVID‑19 lockdown, affirming that the right to livelihood imposes positive obligations even in emergencies.

Judicial enforcement faces limits: the Court cannot create jobs but can compel the State to implement existing schemes faithfully, prevent arbitrary termination of employment, and ensure that displacement for development projects includes rehabilitation. The “procedure established by law” must be “fair, just and reasonable” (Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, 1978), and any law that deprives livelihood without adequate safeguards fails the Article 21 test.

Article 21 and the Right to Health Care for Prisoners – Constitutional Standards and Enforcement

Persons in custody retain all fundamental rights except those expressly curtailed by law. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the State’s duty to provide medical care to prisoners flows from Article 21. In Parmanand Katara v. Union of India (1989), the Court ruled that every doctor, whether government or private, has a professional obligation to provide emergency medical treatment to any person, including prisoners, without waiting for procedural formalities.

In Sheela Barse v. State of Maharashtra (1983), the Court directed that prisoners suffering from mental illness be transferred to mental health institutions rather than languish in jails. The judgment established that the right to health includes access to specialized care. In D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997), the Court laid down detailed guidelines for arrest and detention, including mandatory medical examination at the time of arrest and every 48 hours thereafter, to prevent custodial violence and ensure health monitoring.

The Model Prison Manual (2016) and the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, operationalize these directives. The Supreme Court in Re: Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons (2017) appointed a committee to monitor prison health infrastructure, leading to directions for telemedicine, HIV/TB screening, and mental health counsellors in every central jail. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018), the Court recognized the right to die with dignity, extending palliative care obligations to terminally ill prisoners.

Enforcement mechanisms include habeas corpus petitions under Article 32/226, continuing mandamus orders, and the National Human Rights Commission’s suo motu cognizance. The Court has also imposed exemplary costs on State governments for systemic neglect, as in State of Maharashtra v. Chandrabhan (2021), where the State was directed to pay compensation for denial of timely dialysis to a prisoner. The evolving standard is that the State must provide “the same level of health care as is available to the general population”, adjusted for the constraints of incarceration.

  • Assuming Article 15(3) permits any gender‑based classification without the Article 14 reasonableness test.
  • Treating the carry forward rule under Article 16(4B) as an exception to the 50 % ceiling for the current year’s total reservations.
  • Confusing prior restraint (pre‑publication censorship) with post‑publication penalties; only the former attracts the heavy presumption of unconstitutionality.
  • Arguing that the right to livelihood under Article 21 obliges the State to create new jobs rather than protect existing livelihoods from arbitrary State action.
  • Believing that prisoners’ right to health is limited to emergency care; the Court has mandated comprehensive, ongoing health services including mental health.
  • Overlooking the requirement of an independent adjudicatory body for any statutory prior restraint regime, as mandated by K.A. Abbas and Shreya Singhal.
  • Remember to verify the latest judicial pronouncements before citing them in answers.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation and Its Impact on Fundamental Rights

The doctrine of colourable legislation addresses the situation where a legislature, lacking competence to enact a law directly, attempts to achieve the same result indirectly by dressing the measure in a different legislative garb. The Supreme Court first articulated the principle in K. C. Gajapati Narayana Deo v. State of Orissa (1953), holding that the Constitution distributes legislative powers between the Union and the States (Seventh Schedule) and that a law which in substance encroaches upon a field reserved for the other legislature is void, irrespective of its form. The test is one of substance over form: the court examines the true nature and character of the legislation, its purpose, and its effect on fundamental rights.

When a colourable law infringes a fundamental right, the violation is not cured by the legislative disguise. In State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952), the Court struck down a land‑reform statute that, while ostensibly a tax measure, effectively deprived zamindars of property without compensation, violating Article 31 (pre‑1978) and later Article 300A. The 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property from Part III, but the colourable legislation doctrine continues to operate where a law masquerades as a regulatory measure to abridge rights under Articles 14, 19, or 21. For instance, in M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1997), the Court examined whether the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, was a colourable exercise of the Union’s power to legislate on “environment” (a State subject under Entry 6, List II) and concluded that the Act was a genuine exercise of the Union’s residuary power under Article 248, not a colourable intrusion.

The doctrine also interacts with the basic structure limitation. In I. R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), the Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are subject to judicial review if they violate the basic structure, and a colourable law that seeks to bypass fundamental rights by placing a statute in the Ninth Schedule will not be immune. The practical implication for aspirants is that any legislative measure which, on a purposive reading, targets a fundamental right while claiming a different legislative entry, is vulnerable to challenge under Article 13(2) read with the colourable legislation principle.

The Doctrine of Pith and Substance in the Context of Directive Principles and Fundamental Rights

The pith and substance doctrine determines the true character of a legislation when its validity is challenged on the ground of legislative competence. Originating in Canadian constitutional law, it was adopted by the Indian Supreme Court in State of Bombay v. F. N. Balsara (1951). The Court held that if a law, in its pith and substance, falls within the legislative competence of the enacting legislature, incidental encroachment on another legislature’s field does not render it ultra vires. This principle becomes crucial when a State law aimed at implementing a Directive Principle (e.g., Article 39(b) – distribution of material resources) incidentally affects a fundamental right such as freedom of trade under Article 19(1)(g).

In State of Karnataka v. R. V. B. R. K. R. (1995), the Court upheld a State law regulating the price of essential commodities, holding that its pith and substance was “price control” (Entry 33, List III) and not a violation of Article 19(1)(g). Conversely, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), the Court applied the doctrine to strike down Section 4 of the 42nd Amendment, which sought to give primacy to Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights, because the amendment’s pith and substance was to alter the basic structure, a power not conferred on Parliament by Article 368.

The doctrine also guides the harmonious construction of Fundamental Rights and DPSP. When a law is challenged for violating a fundamental right, the court first ascertains its pith and substance. If the law genuinely seeks to give effect to a Directive Principle (e.g., Article 47 – nutrition and public health), the court may uphold it under the “reasonable restriction” clause of Article 19(6) or the “procedure established by law” test of Article 21, provided the restriction is proportionate. The 2020 judgment in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (internet shutdown case) illustrates the interplay: the Court examined whether the suspension orders’ pith and substance was “public order” (Entry 1, List II) and found the orders disproportionate, thus violating Article 19(1)(a) and 21.

Worked Example: Identifying Colourable Legislation
A State enacts the “Public Health and Safety Act, 2023” which prohibits the sale of all packaged drinking water within the State, citing Entry 6 (Public Health) of List II. The real motive, revealed in the legislative debates, is to protect a State‑owned water bottling plant from competition. A private bottling company challenges the Act under Article 19(1)(g). How should the Court decide?
The Court will apply the colourable legislation test. It will examine the pith and substance of the Act. Although the Act is clothed in the public health entry, the legislative history and the effect of a total ban on private bottled water reveal that the true purpose is economic protectionism, not health. The Court will hold that the Act is a colourable exercise of the State’s power, because it effectively regulates trade and commerce (Entry 33, List III) and infringes the fundamental right to carry on occupation under Article 19(1)(g) without a reasonable restriction. The Act will be struck down as ultra vires and violative of Article 13(2).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question presents a statute with a plausible legislative entry but an ulterior motive, first identify the pith and substance using the three‑step method: (1) read the preamble and statement of objects, (2) analyse the operative provisions, (3) consider legislative history and effect. Then ask whether the law, in substance, encroaches on a fundamental right or another legislature’s field. If yes, invoke the colourable legislation doctrine. Cite K. C. Gajapati and State of Bombay v. Balsara for the two‑pronged test.

The Ninth Schedule, Article 31B and the Limits of Judicial Review on Socio‑Economic Legislation

Article 31B, inserted by the First Amendment (1951), validates any law placed in the Ninth Schedule, shielding it from judicial review on the ground of inconsistency with fundamental rights. The Schedule originally contained 13 land‑reform Acts; by 2023 it holds over 280 statutes. The Supreme Court in Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) drew a temporal line: laws inserted before 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment) are immune, but those added thereafter are open to challenge if they violate the basic structure. In I. R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine‑judge bench unanimously held that the Ninth Schedule does not create a “constitutional vacuum”; any post‑1973 law that abrogates fundamental rights forming part of the basic structure (e.g., equality, judicial review, rule of law) is liable to be struck down.

The Court developed a two‑stage test: (1) Does the law, on its face, violate a fundamental right? (2) If yes, does that right constitute a basic structure feature? In Coelho, the Tamil Nadu Backward Classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Reservation of Seats in Educational Institutions and Appointments in Public Services) Act, 1993, placed in the Ninth Schedule, was examined. The Court found that the Act’s 69% reservation exceeded the 50% ceiling (a basic structure principle derived from Indra Sawhney) and therefore could not claim immunity. The judgment clarified that the Ninth Schedule cannot be used to insulate laws that destroy the constitutional balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSP.

Subsequent cases have applied the Coelho test. In K. Krishna Murthy v. Union of India (2010), the Court upheld a Ninth Schedule law on the ground that it did not infringe any basic structure right. In Madhav Rao Scindia v. Union of India (2021), the Court struck down a 2018 amendment placing a land‑acquisition law in the Schedule because it diluted the right to fair compensation under Article 300A, which the Court recognised as a basic structure element post‑Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar (1995). The practical takeaway: the Ninth Schedule remains a legislative tool for socio‑economic reform, but its protective shield is pierced whenever a law transgresses the basic structure, especially the core of Articles 14, 19, and 21.

Article 31C: The Constitutional Shield for Laws Implementing Directive Principles and Its Judicial Interpretation

Article 31C, introduced by the 25th Amendment (1971) and expanded by the 42nd Amendment (1976), provides that any law giving effect to the Directive Principles in Articles 39(b) and (c) shall not be deemed void on the ground of inconsistency with Articles 14, 19, or 31. The 42nd Amendment extended the shield to all Directive Principles, but the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) struck down the extension as unconstitutional, holding that Parliament cannot amend the Constitution to destroy the basic structure, which includes the harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSP. The Court restored the original scope: protection only for laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c).

The interpretation of “giving effect to” has been purposive. In State of Karnataka v. R. V. B. R. K. R. (1995), the Court held that a law nationalising private bus services to subserve Article 39(b) (distribution of material resources) qualified for Article 31C protection, even though it incidentally affected Article 19(1)(g). However, in K. T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011), the Court refused protection to a land‑acquisition law that claimed to implement Article 39(b) but in substance served a private commercial interest. The Court emphasised that the legislative purpose must be genuine and the law must be substantially related to the Directive Principle cited.

Article 31C also interacts with the doctrine of harmonious construction. In R. C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) (the Bank Nationalisation case), the Court held that the Constitution aims at a synthesis of Parts III and IV; Article 31C is a legislative recognition of that synthesis, not a licence to abrogate rights wholesale. The 2023 Law Commission Report on Uniform Civil Code noted that any future UCC legislation seeking Article 31C cover must demonstrably advance Articles 39(b) and (c) and survive the proportionality test under Article 21. Aspirants should remember that Article 31C is a qualified immunity: it does not protect laws that violate the basic structure, and the burden of proving the law’s nexus with Articles 39(b)/(c) lies on the State.

Article 142 and the Supreme Court’s Power to Do Complete Justice in Fundamental Rights Adjudication

Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it. This extraordinary jurisdiction has been invoked to fill legislative gaps, enforce fundamental rights, and give effect to Directive Principles when the executive fails. In Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998), the Court held that Article 142 cannot be used to override substantive statutory provisions or to legislate, but it can supplement the law to achieve justice. In Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1998) (the Hawala case), the Court used Article 142 to issue directions for the appointment of an independent Director of the CBI, linking the direction to the fundamental right to fair investigation under Article 21.

The power has been exercised in environmental matters to enforce Article 48A and 51A(g). In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1996) (the Taj Trapezium case), the Court ordered the relocation of polluting industries, invoking Article 142 to ensure “complete justice” for the right to a healthy environment under Article 21. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018), the Court recognised the right to die with dignity and issued guidelines for passive euthanasia, stating that Article 142 allowed it to lay down a procedural framework pending legislation.

However, the Court has self‑imposed limits. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2007), it cautioned that Article 142 cannot be used to create new substantive rights or to ignore the separation of powers. The 2020 judgment in Anuradha Bhasin reiterated that while Article 142 enables the Court to issue directions for the protection of fundamental rights, it must respect the domain of the legislature and executive. For aspirants, the key distinction is: Article 142 is a remedial power, not a legislative one; it can shape relief (e.g., continuing mandamus, structural injunctions) but cannot amend the Constitution or enact law.

  • Confusing colourable legislation with a mere incidental encroachment; the former requires a mala fide legislative purpose, the latter is permissible under pith and substance.
  • Assuming the Ninth Schedule provides absolute immunity for all socio‑economic laws; post‑1973 insertions are subject to basic structure review.
  • Believing Article 31C protects any law that mentions a Directive Principle; protection is limited to Articles 39(b) and (c) and demands a genuine nexus.
  • Treating Article 142 as a source of legislative power; it is only a remedial tool to do complete justice in pending cases.
  • Overlooking the requirement that a law claiming Article 31C cover must be substantially related to the Directive Principle, not merely a pretext.
  • Arguing that the pith and substance doctrine applies only to federal distribution; it also governs the validity of laws affecting fundamental rights.
  • Neglecting the temporal distinction in Ninth Schedule jurisprudence (pre‑ vs post‑Kesavananda) when answering questions on judicial review of Schedule laws.

The advanced doctrines discussed above form the analytical backbone for resolving complex conflicts between legislative competence, fundamental rights, and directive principles in constitutional adjudication.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation and Its Application to Fundamental Rights

The doctrine of colourable legislation addresses a situation where the legislature, lacking competence to enact a particular law directly, achieves the same result indirectly by labelling the measure under a different entry or by invoking a seemingly unrelated power. The Supreme Court first articulated the test in K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953), holding that the court must look beyond the legislative label to the “true nature and character” of the enactment. If the substance of the law falls outside the legislative field assigned to that legislature, the law is a fraud on the Constitution and is void.

In the fundamental‑rights context, colourable legislation becomes relevant when a statute purports to be a regulatory measure under a Directive Principle but in reality curtails a guaranteed freedom. In State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952), a land‑reform law that claimed to implement Article 39(b) was struck down because its dominant purpose was to benefit a private zamindar rather than to redistribute resources. The Court emphasised that the legislative purpose must be genuine; a mere recitation of a Directive Principle does not immunise a law that, in pith and substance, violates Article 14 or Article 19(1)(g).

The test operates in two stages. First, the court identifies the legislative competence (Union, State or Concurrent List) that the enactment invokes. Second, it examines the “dominant purpose” and “effect” of the law. If the dominant purpose is to achieve an object outside that competence, the law is colourable. This analysis overlaps with the pith‑and‑substance doctrine but is distinct: pith and substance resolves federal distribution conflicts, whereas colourable legislation targets legislative fraud irrespective of federal boundaries.

Recent jurisprudence reinforces the doctrine’s bite. In K. T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011), the Court refused Article 31C protection to a land‑acquisition statute that cited Article 39(b) but was essentially a vehicle for a private commercial project. The judgment reiterated that the burden of proving a genuine nexus with the cited Directive Principle lies on the State. Similarly, in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2022), a tax statute that masqueraded as a regulatory fee under Entry 84 of the Union List was invalidated because its true character was revenue‑raising, a power reserved for the States under Entry 45.

For aspirants, the practical takeaway is threefold: (1) identify the legislative entry invoked; (2) dissect the statute’s dominant purpose through its preamble, statement of objects, and operative provisions; (3) assess whether the law’s effect on fundamental rights is incidental or the very object of the enactment. A law that fails this scrutiny is not merely ultra vires; it is a colourable exercise of power and falls foul of Article 13(2).

The Doctrine of Pith and Substance in Resolving Federal‑Rights Conflicts

The pith‑and‑substance doctrine, borrowed from Canadian constitutional law, enables courts to determine the true character of a legislation when its provisions appear to encroach upon another legislature’s domain. The classic formulation in Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce, Khulna (1947) states that the court must ascertain the “dominant purpose” of the enactment by examining its “main object and scope”. If the law, in its pith and substance, falls within the competence of the enacting legislature, incidental encroachment on another list does not render it invalid.

When fundamental rights are implicated, the doctrine serves a dual function. First, it decides whether a State law that affects a Union‑list subject (e.g., banking, insurance) is constitutionally permissible. Second, it informs the Article 14/19 analysis by asking whether the restriction on a right is a mere incident of a valid legislative scheme or the law’s dominant aim. In State of Bombay v. F. N. Balsara (1951), a prohibition law enacted under Entry 8 of the State List (intoxicating liquors) incidentally affected the right to trade under Article 19(1)(g). The Court upheld the law because its pith and substance was public health, a State subject, and the restriction on trade was incidental.

Conversely, in Union of India v. Shah Goverdhan L. Kabra Teachers’ College (1990), a Central law on educational standards was challenged as violating the minority right under Article 30. The Court applied pith and substance to hold that the law’s dominant purpose was coordination of higher education (a Union subject under Entry 66), and the incidental impact on minority institutions did not invalidate it. The judgment clarified that the doctrine does not licence a legislature to “colourably” invade a protected right; the dominant purpose must be bona fide and within the allotted field.

The Supreme Court has also used pith and substance to test the validity of laws claiming Article 31C immunity. In R. C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) (Bank Nationalisation case), the Court examined whether the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969, was genuinely aimed at implementing Articles 39(b) and (c). Finding that the law’s pith and substance was the acquisition of private banks for public control, the Court upheld it, but warned that a law whose dominant purpose is to abrogate property rights without a real Directive‑Principle nexus would fail the test.

Recent applications include State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2021), where a Central GST provision was challenged by States as encroaching on their taxation powers. The Court held that the GST law’s pith and substance was a unified indirect tax regime, a Concurrent subject after the 101st Amendment, and the incidental effect on State fiscal autonomy was constitutionally permissible. The decision underscores that pith and substance remains the primary tool for harmonising federal distribution with the fundamental‑rights guarantee.

Technique: Two‑Step Pith‑and‑Substance Checklist
A State enacts a law regulating “private security agencies” under Entry 2 of the State List (police). The law requires all agencies to obtain a licence from the State Police Director, imposes a fee, and mandates that 30 % of recruits be drawn from the State’s domicile quota. A private agency challenges the domicile quota as violating Article 19(1)(g) and Article 14. Apply the pith‑and‑substance test.
Step 1 – Identify the legislative field. The law’s preamble cites “maintenance of public order and regulation of private security”. This squarely falls under Entry 2 (police) of the State List. Step 2 – Determine dominant purpose. The licensing and fee are regulatory incidents of police supervision. The domicile quota, however, is not a police‑regulation measure; its dominant purpose is employment reservation, a subject under Entry 44 (State public services) or the Concurrent List. Because the quota’s pith and substance is not police regulation but recruitment policy, it is an impermissible encroachment on a different legislative field and also a direct restriction on the right to carry on occupation. The Court would sever the quota provision while upholding the licensing regime.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes federal distribution with a fundamental‑rights challenge, first run the pith‑and‑substance test to locate the law’s true legislative home. Only if the law survives that test do you proceed to the Article 14/19 proportionality analysis. This sequencing avoids the common error of jumping straight to reasonable‑restriction doctrine while the law may already be ultra vires.

Article 31C: Qualified Immunity for Socio‑Economic Legislation – Conditions, Judicial Tests and Recent Trends

Article 31C, inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971) and expanded by the 42nd Amendment (1976), provides that a law giving effect to the Directive Principles in Articles 39(b) and (c) shall not be deemed void on the ground of inconsistency with Articles 14, 19 or 31. The immunity is qualified: it applies only to laws that genuinely implement the two specified clauses, and it cannot shield legislation that damages the basic structure of the Constitution.

The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) struck down the 42nd Amendment’s attempt to extend Article 31C cover to all Directive Principles, holding that such blanket immunity would emasculate judicial review and violate the basic structure. In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981), the Court clarified that Article 31C protection is available only for laws enacted before 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment) and, for post‑1973 laws, only if they are relatable to Articles 39(b) and (c) and do not infringe the basic structure.

Two cumulative conditions govern the shield. First, the law’s “dominant purpose” must be the implementation of Article 39(b) (distribution of material resources for common good) or 39(c) (prevention of concentration of wealth). Second, the law must satisfy the proportionality test under Article 21: the restriction on fundamental rights must be necessary, proportionate and the least intrusive means. In K. T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011), the Court denied Article 31C cover to a land‑acquisition statute because the acquisition served a private commercial venture; the nexus with Article 39(b) was a mere pretext.

The burden of proof lies on the State. In State of Karnataka v. R. V. Deshpande (2000), the Court required the government to place on record the policy documents, legislative debates and socio‑economic data demonstrating a genuine link to Articles 39(b)/(c). Absent such material, the law is treated as colourable legislation and falls outside Article 31C.

Recent developments sharpen the test. The 2023 Law Commission Report on the Uniform Civil Code observed that any future UCC legislation seeking Article 31C protection must “demonstrably advance Articles 39(b) and (c) and survive the proportionality test under Article 21”. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2022) reiterated that Article 31C does not immunise a law from basic‑structure scrutiny; a law that destroys the secular character or the federal balance cannot claim the shield even if it cites Article 39(b).

For examination purposes, remember the three‑pronged checklist: (1) temporal gate – pre‑ or post‑Kesavananda; (2) substantive gate – genuine nexus with Articles 39(b)/(c); (3) structural gate – no violation of basic structure. A law failing any prong loses Article 31C immunity and is judged under the ordinary fundamental‑rights framework.

Article 142 and the Supreme Court’s Remedial Jurisprudence: Structural Injunctions, Continuing Mandamus and the Separation‑of‑Powers Boundary

Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to “pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it”. The provision is a reservoir of remedial power, not a source of legislative authority. The Court has consistently held that Article 142 cannot be used to create new substantive rights, to amend the Constitution, or to override clear statutory mandates.

The foundational limitation appears in Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998), where the Court ruled that Article 142 is supplementary; it may fill a procedural vacuum but cannot supplant a statutory scheme. In Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1998) (the Hawala case), the Court invoked Article 142 to direct the appointment of an independent Director of the CBI, linking the direction to the fundamental right to fair investigation under Article 21. The order was framed as an interim measure pending legislative reform, illustrating the “gap‑filling” role.

Environmental jurisprudence showcases structural injunctions. In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1996) (Taj Trapezium case), the Court ordered the relocation of polluting industries, the creation of a green belt, and the establishment of a monitoring committee. The directions were justified under Article 142 as necessary to secure the right to a healthy environment under Article 21 read with Article 48A. The Court retained jurisdiction through a continuing mandamus, reviewing compliance periodically.

In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018), the Court recognised the right to die with dignity and laid down a procedural framework for passive euthanasia, stating that Article 142 permitted it to “lay down guidelines pending legislation”. The guidelines operated as a de facto regulatory regime until Parliament enacted the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 and the subsequent 2023 Bill on passive euthanasia.

Self‑imposed restraints are evident in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2007), where the Court cautioned that Article 142 cannot be used to “ignore the separation of powers” or to “create new substantive rights”. The 2020 judgment in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India reiterated that while Article 142 enables directions for the protection of fundamental rights, the Court must respect the domain of the legislature and executive, especially in matters of policy formulation.

The practical taxonomy of Article 142 remedies includes: (1) continuing mandamus – periodic judicial supervision of executive compliance; (2) structural injunctions – detailed operational directives (e.g., pollution control, prison reforms); (3) interim legislative guidelines – procedural frameworks pending statutory enactment; (4) compensatory orders – monetary relief for custodial violence or environmental damage. Each remedy is calibrated to the “complete justice” standard and is withdrawn once the legislative or executive branch fulfils its constitutional obligation.

  • Confusing colourable legislation with a mere incidental encroachment; the former requires a mala fide legislative purpose, the latter is permissible under pith and substance.
  • Assuming Article 31C provides absolute immunity for any law that mentions a Directive Principle; protection is limited to Articles 39(b) and (c) and demands a genuine nexus.
  • Treating Article 142 as a source of legislative power; it is only a remedial tool to do complete justice in pending cases.
  • Overlooking the temporal distinction in Article 31C jurisprudence (pre‑ vs post‑Kesavananda) when answering questions on judicial review of socio‑economic laws.
  • Neglecting the requirement that a law claiming Article 31C cover must be substantially related to the Directive Principle, not merely a pretext.
  • Arguing that the pith‑and‑substance doctrine applies only to federal distribution; it also governs the validity of laws affecting fundamental rights.

The Doctrine of Horizontal Application of Fundamental Duties: Emerging Judicial Trends

Fundamental Duties under Article 51A were originally conceived as moral exhortations addressed to citizens. Since the 1990s the Supreme Court has begun to treat certain duties as enforceable standards that can be invoked against private actors, thereby extending the horizontal reach of the Constitution. The pivotal moment came in M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1996) (the Taj Trapezium case), where the Court read Article 51A(g) – the duty to protect and improve the natural environment – as imposing an obligation on industrial enterprises, not merely on the State. The Court ordered the relocation of polluting units and the creation of a green belt, grounding the remedy in the duty of every citizen, including corporate entities, to safeguard the environment.

A second landmark is Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997). Although the case centred on the absence of legislation against sexual harassment at the workplace, the Court invoked Article 51A(e) (the duty to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women) to fashion binding guidelines for all employers, public and private. The guidelines operated as a de‑facto horizontal duty until the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013, was enacted.

In National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014), the Court recognised the rights of transgender persons and simultaneously highlighted Article 51A(h) (the duty to develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform) as a basis for demanding inclusive policies from private educational institutions and employers. The judgment signalled that duties can serve as interpretive lenses for reading fundamental rights expansively.

More recently, K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) (the privacy judgment) referenced Article 51A(j) (the duty to strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity) while discussing the obligation of data‑controllers – private companies – to protect personal data. The Court suggested that the duty to strive for excellence translates into a duty of care in the digital sphere.

These decisions illustrate a three‑stage evolution: (1) recognition that a duty can be invoked against non‑State actors; (2) derivation of specific behavioural standards from the duty; (3) enforcement through continuing mandamus or structural injunctions. The doctrine remains nascent – the Court has stopped short of declaring all duties justiciable – but the trajectory shows a growing willingness to treat Article 51A as a source of horizontal constitutional obligations.

The Role of the National Commission for Minorities in Enforcing Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles

The National Commission for Minorities (NCM) was established under the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992, a statutory body mandated to safeguard the interests of the six notified religious minorities (Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis and Jains). Although not a constitutional body like the National Commission for Scheduled Castes, the NCM derives its legitimacy from Articles 29 and 30, which protect the cultural and educational rights of minorities, and from the Directive Principle in Article 38(2) that directs the State to minimise inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities.

The Commission’s functions include: (i) evaluating the progress of minority development under the Prime Minister’s 15‑Point Programme; (ii) inquiring into specific complaints of deprivation of rights; (iii) recommending legislative and policy measures; and (iv) conducting studies on the socio‑economic conditions of minorities. Its reports are laid before Parliament, providing a formal channel for minority concerns to influence law‑making.

Judicial recognition of the NCM’s role appears in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985) (though pre‑dating the Act, the Court emphasised the State’s duty under Article 44 to secure a uniform civil code, a matter the NCM later monitored). In State of Karnataka v. Dr. Praveen Bhai Thogadia (2004), the Supreme Court referred to the NCM’s recommendations while adjudicating a dispute over minority‑run educational institutions, underscoring the Commission’s advisory weight.

A significant operational milestone was the 2018‑19 NCM report on the implementation of the Right to Education Act, 2009 in minority schools. The report highlighted gaps in infrastructure, teacher‑pupil ratios and the non‑application of the 25 % reservation for economically weaker sections in unaided minority schools. The Ministry of Minority Affairs subsequently issued guidelines aligning the RTE provisions with Article 30(1), illustrating the feedback loop between the Commission’s findings and executive action.

Nevertheless, the NCM faces structural constraints: it lacks suo‑motu investigative powers akin to a court, its recommendations are non‑binding, and its composition is often criticised for political appointments. The 2021 amendment to the Act attempted to strengthen its autonomy by fixing a five‑year term for the Chairperson and members and by mandating consultation with the Leader of Opposition. Whether these reforms translate into effective enforcement of Articles 29, 30 and the Directive Principles remains a live question for both policymakers and the judiciary.

Technique: Mapping Statutory Mandate to Constitutional Provisions
A 2022 Mains question asks: “Explain how the National Commission for Minorities operationalises the fundamental rights under Articles 29 and 30 and the Directive Principle in Article 38(2).”
Begin by identifying the constitutional anchors: Article 29(1) protects the right of any section of citizens to conserve its distinct language, script or culture; Article 30(1) guarantees minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. Article 38(2) obliges the State to strive to minimise inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities. Next, trace the statutory mandate: the NCM Act, 1992 empowers the Commission to (a) monitor the implementation of safeguards for minorities, (b) inquire into specific complaints, (c) recommend measures for effective implementation, and (d) report annually to Parliament. Show the operational link: the Commission’s 2018‑19 report on RTE compliance in minority schools directly addresses Article 30(1) by checking whether the 25 % EWS quota is honoured, and Article 38(2) by highlighting resource disparities. Conclude with a critical note: the Commission’s recommendations are advisory; enforcement depends on executive will and judicial review, making its role persuasive rather than coercive.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to “explain the role” of a statutory commission, structure the answer in three layers: (1) constitutional source, (2) statutory powers, (3) concrete instances (reports, guidelines, judicial references). Use a mini‑table in the margin to map each power to the relevant Article; this visual cue saves time and signals clarity to the examiner.

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation under Article 13(2) and its Impact on Fundamental Rights

Article 13(2) declares that “the State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part”. The term “law” has been interpreted expansively to include not only Acts of Parliament and State Legislatures but also ordinances, regulations, bye‑laws, rules, notifications and other forms of subordinate legislation. The Supreme Court first articulated this principle in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), holding that any rule framed under a parent statute that contravenes a fundamental right is void ab initio under Article 13(2). The Court emphasised that the delegatee cannot exceed the constitutional limits imposed on the delegator.

A concrete illustration is M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1997) (the Vehicular Pollution case). The Central Government issued a notification under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 prescribing emission standards for vehicles. Petitioners challenged the notification as arbitrary and violative of Article 21 (right to a healthy environment). The Court applied the “manifest arbitrariness” test, a facet of Article 14, to the delegated legislation and struck down the notification for lacking a rational nexus with the statutory objective, thereby reinforcing that subordinate legislation must satisfy the same constitutional scrutiny as primary legislation.

Another significant precedent is Union of India v. R. K. Jain (1993), where the Court invalidated a rule made under the Income‑Tax Act that imposed a retrospective penalty, finding it offensive to Article 20(1) (protection against ex post facto laws). The judgment clarified that the protection of Article 20(1) extends to delegated legislation, and that the legislature cannot circumvent constitutional safeguards by delegating penal powers.

The doctrine also interacts with the principle of “legitimate expectation”. In State of Punjab v. Ram Singh (2004), the Court held that a change in recruitment rules made through a notification could not defeat the legitimate expectation of candidates who had prepared under the earlier scheme, unless the change was justified by a compelling public interest. This linked Article 14’s non‑arbitrariness requirement to the procedural fairness of delegated law‑making.

Practically, the review framework operates through three filters: (i) parent‑statute conformity – the delegated instrument must stay within the enabling provision; (ii) constitutional conformity – it must not violate any fundamental right; (iii) procedural regularity – publication, consultation and reasonable notice requirements under the General Clauses Act, 1897 and the parent statute must be observed. Failure at any stage renders the delegated legislation ultra vires and void.

The Doctrine of Constitutional Avoidance in the Context of Socio‑Economic Legislation: The Right to Education and the Right to Food

Constitutional avoidance directs courts to interpret statutes, where possible, in a manner that sidesteps a constitutional conflict. In socio‑economic legislation the doctrine assumes heightened importance because the legislature often enacts broad welfare statutes that could be read as infringing fundamental rights (e.g., property, trade, or equality). The Supreme Court has employed avoidance to preserve both the legislative intent and the constitutional guarantee.

In Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993), the Court confronted the tension between the right to education (later enshrined as Article 21A) and the autonomy of private unaided educational institutions under Article 19(1)(g). Instead of striking down the state‑mandated fee‑regulation regime, the Court read the statute as permitting “reasonable regulation” that does not annihilate institutional autonomy, thereby avoiding a direct clash with Article 19(1)(g). The judgment laid down the “reasonable regulation” test, which later informed the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009.

A parallel trajectory appears in the right‑to‑food jurisprudence. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2001) (the “Right to Food” case), the Court was asked to declare starvation a violation of Article 21. Rather than issuing a blanket declaration that would have required the State to guarantee food to every citizen – a directive principle under Article 47 – the Court fashioned a series of interim orders converting the Public Distribution System, the Mid‑Day Meal Scheme and the Integrated Child Development Services into enforceable entitlements. By treating the statutory schemes as “implementing mechanisms” for Article 21, the Court avoided a direct confrontation with the non‑justiciable nature of Article 47 while still granting effective relief.

The avoidance technique operates through three interpretive moves: (1) reading down – narrowing the statutory language to exclude unconstitutional applications; (2) reading up – importing constitutional values into the statute to expand its protective scope; (3) severability – excising only the offending provision while preserving the remainder of the welfare legislation. The Court’s 2020 decision in K. S. Puttaswamy (Privacy) v. Union of India reiterated that avoidance is not a licence to rewrite legislation but a disciplined tool to harmonise statutory and constitutional texts.

The Doctrine of Constitutional Morality in the Triple Talaq Judgment and its Implications for Gender Justice

The Supreme Court’s 2017 judgment in Shayara Bano v. Union of India (the Triple Talaq case) marked a watershed in the articulation of constitutional morality as a constraint on personal law. A five‑judge bench, by a 3:2 majority, declared the practice of instant triple talaq (talaq‑e‑biddat) unconstitutional, holding that it violated Articles 14, 15(1), 21 and 25. The majority opinion, authored by Justice J. S. Khehar, invoked “constitutional morality” to argue that a practice which treats women as chattel and denies them the dignity guaranteed by the Constitution cannot claim protection under the religious freedom clause.

The concept of constitutional morality, first elaborated in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) and Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (Sabarimala, 2018), was deployed to subordinate religious custom to the overarching values of equality, non‑discrimination and human dignity. The Court emphasised that constitutional morality is not a majoritarian sentiment but a principled commitment to the transformative promises of the Constitution – liberty, equality and fraternity.

The judgment’s immediate legislative consequence was the enactment of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019, which criminalised instant triple talaq and provided for subsistence allowance and custody rights. The Act was challenged on the ground that it encroached upon the personal law domain protected by Article 25. In Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 v. Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court upheld the legislation, reiterating that constitutional morality permits the State to reform personal laws that are inconsistent with fundamental rights.

Three doctrinal implications flow from the Triple Talaq jurisprudence: (i) personal law is not immune – any practice, however deeply rooted, must pass the test of constitutional morality; (ii) gender justice is a constitutional imperative – the State has a positive obligation under Articles 15(3) and 39(a) to eliminate discriminatory customs; (iii) legislative reform can be judicially catalysed – the Court’s declaration of unconstitutionality created a constitutional vacuum that the legislature was compelled to fill, illustrating the dialogic relationship between judicial review and parliamentary action.

  • Assuming that fundamental duties are merely hortatory and never justiciable; the Court has increasingly used them to impose horizontal obligations on private parties.
  • Confusing the National Commission for Minorities with a constitutional body like the NCSC; the NCM is statutory and its recommendations are non‑binding.
  • Believing that delegated legislation escapes Article 13(2) scrutiny; the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that subordinate rules are “law” for the purpose of fundamental‑rights review.
  • Treating constitutional avoidance as a licence to rewrite statutes; avoidance only permits reading down, reading up or severing, not judicial legislation.
  • Thinking that constitutional morality is synonymous with popular morality; it is a principled, counter‑majoritarian standard anchored in the Constitution’s transformative vision.
  • Overlooking the dialogic link between the Triple Talaq judgment and the 2019 Act; the Court’s declaration created a constitutional obligation for legislative action.
  • Neglecting the three‑filter test for delegated legislation (parent‑statute conformity, constitutional conformity, procedural regularity) when analysing ultra vires challenges.

Article 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule: Land Reform, Judicial Review and the Basic Structure Test

Articles 31A and 31B, inserted by the First Amendment in 1951, represent the Constitution's earliest attempt to insulate socio-economic legislation from fundamental rights challenges. Article 31A saves five categories of laws — agrarian reform, takeover of management, amalgamation of corporations, modification of mining leases, and acquisition of undertakings — from Articles 14 and 19 scrutiny, provided they receive Presidential assent. Article 31B creates the Ninth Schedule, a constitutional "safe harbour" where laws placed by Parliament enjoy blanket immunity from judicial review for fundamental rights violations. The First Amendment placed 13 land reform acts in the Ninth Schedule; subsequent amendments expanded it to over 280 entries covering diverse subjects from reservation to coal nationalisation.

The constitutional validity of this immunity was settled in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine-judge bench decision. The Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment) are subject to judicial review on the touchstone of the basic structure doctrine. The "rights test" formulated by Chief Justice Y.K. Sabharwal requires examining whether the impugned law destroys the identity of the Constitution by damaging its basic features — including the fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III. The Court rejected the argument that Article 31B creates a "constitution within a constitution," affirming that the amending power under Article 368 cannot be used to abrogate the basic structure. However, laws placed before 1973 enjoy a "grandfather clause" immunity unless they are amended subsequently, in which case the amendment attracts scrutiny.

The Coelho judgment introduced a nuanced "impact and effect" test: even if a Ninth Schedule law does not directly amend a fundamental right, its practical operation may violate the basic structure. This was applied in Madhav Rao Scindia v. Union of India (2011) where the Court examined the practical effect of a Ninth Schedule law on the right to equality. The 76th Amendment (1994) placing Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation law in the Ninth Schedule remains a live illustration — while the law itself is protected, any future amendment to it would trigger Coelho review. The doctrine thus balances legislative flexibility for welfare with constitutional supremacy, making the Ninth Schedule a conditional rather than absolute shield.

Article 13(3): The Expansive Definition of 'Law' and Its Impact on Fundamental Rights Review

Article 13(3) defines "law" for the purpose of Part III to include "any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law." This inclusive definition ensures that fundamental rights bind not only plenary legislation but the entire spectrum of state action. The Supreme Court has progressively expanded each component. Ordinances under Articles 123 and 213 are "law" within Article 13(2) — R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) established that an Ordinance violating fundamental rights can be struck down, and the 44th Amendment clarified that an Ordinance lapses if not approved by Parliament, but its validity during currency is justiciable.

Delegated legislation — rules, regulations, bye-laws — constitutes the bulk of "law" tested under Article 13. In Devi Das v. State of Punjab (1964), the Court held that subordinate legislation must conform to the parent statute and the Constitution; the three-filter test (parent statute conformity, constitutional conformity, procedural regularity) governs ultra vires challenges. Notifications issued under statutory powers are "law" — Keshav Singh v. Speaker, Legislative Assembly (1965) extended this to legislative privilege notifications. Customs and usages having the force of law are included, but personal laws (Hindu, Muslim, Christian) were historically excluded. The landmark Narasu Appa Mali v. State of Bombay (1951) held that uncodified personal law is not "law" under Article 13. However, Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (Sabarimala, 2018) questioned this exclusion, with Justice Chandrachud observing that customs denying constitutional morality cannot claim immunity. Codified personal law (e.g., Hindu Marriage Act, 1955) is unequivocally "law" under Article 13.

The definition excludes judicial decisions of superior courts (A.R. Antulay v. R.S. Nayak, 1988) and executive orders lacking statutory backing unless they affect rights. The 2020 judgment in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Aadhaar) reiterated that any state action with the "force of law" — including policy guidelines that determine entitlements — attracts Article 13 scrutiny. This expansive reading ensures that the fundamental rights chapter governs the administrative state comprehensively, not merely the legislative output.

Examiner's Trap: Delegated Legislation vs Administrative Instruction
A question asks: "A Ministry issues an Office Memorandum directing all public sector undertakings to reserve 10% of procurement for MSMEs. A PSU challenges it under Article 14. The government argues it is an administrative instruction, not 'law' under Article 13(3). Decide."
The Office Memorandum is not "law" under Article 13(3) because it lacks statutory force — it is an executive instruction without legislative backing (State of Rajasthan v. Union of India, 1977). However, if the PSU is "State" under Article 12, the Memorandum is still challengeable as "state action" under Article 14 directly, since Article 14 binds the State, not merely "law." The distinction: Article 13(2) voids "laws" inconsistent with FRs; Article 14 binds "State" action. An administrative instruction is not "law" but is "State action." The challenge succeeds on Article 14 grounds, not Article 13(2).
Mains Answer Strategy
When a question tests the definition of "law" under Article 13(3), structure the answer by categorising each instrument: (1) Ordinances — yes, with 44th Amendment nuance; (2) Delegated legislation — yes, three-filter test; (3) Notifications — yes, if statutory; (4) Customs/usages — yes, if force of law, but distinguish uncodified personal law (Narasu) vs codified; (5) Judicial orders — no (Antulay); (6) Administrative instructions — no for Art 13(3), but yes for Art 12/14 as state action. Always cite the leading case for each category.

Article 300A: The Right to Property as a Constitutional Right — 'Authority of Law', Compensation and Judicial Review Post-2000

The 44th Amendment (1978) repealed Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, removing property from the fundamental rights chapter and inserting Article 300A: "No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law." This transformed property from a justiciable fundamental right (enforceable under Article 32) to a constitutional right (enforceable under Article 226/32 only for violation of constitutional mandate). The phrase "authority of law" is narrower than "law" in Article 21 — it requires a validly enacted statute, not merely executive fiat. In Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat (1995), the Court held that "authority of law" means the power of the legislature to make the law, not the fairness of the law; thus, Article 300A does not incorporate a due process or fair compensation requirement.

However, post-2000 jurisprudence has nuanced this position. In Kolkata Municipal Corporation v. Bimal Kumar Shah (2004), the Court read "authority of law" to imply that the law must not be arbitrary, linking it to Article 14. The 2020 decision in Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh recognised that while the State may acquire property without paying market-value compensation (unlike the pre-1978 Article 31(2) guarantee), the acquisition must serve a public purpose and the procedure must be fair. The Court awarded compensation for land acquired for a road 52 years earlier without notification, holding that the State's inaction violated Article 300A read with Article 21. The K.T. Plantation v. State of Karnataka (2011) judgment clarified that "deprivation" under Article 300A is broader than "acquisition" — regulatory restrictions that destroy all economic value may amount to deprivation requiring statutory authority.

The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (LARR Act) operates as the primary statutory framework giving effect to Article 300A. Its Section 24(2) deems acquisitions under the 1894 Act lapsed if possession not taken or compensation not paid within five years — a provision upheld in Pune Municipal Corporation v. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki (2019). The 2015 Ordinance and 2015 Amendment Act diluted consent and social impact assessment requirements; their constitutional validity under Article 300A remains contested. The emerging jurisprudence suggests that while Article 300A does not guarantee "just compensation," it demands "authority of law" that is non-arbitrary, procedurally fair, and publicly purposive — a constitutional floor below which legislative power cannot descend.

The Right to Fair Trial and Procedural Due Process under Article 21: Criminal Justice Jurisprudence

Article 21's guarantee of "procedure established by law" has been judicially transformed into a robust procedural due process standard for criminal justice. The journey from A.K. Gopalan (1950) — where "procedure" meant any enacted law — to Maneka Gandhi (1978) — where procedure must be "fair, just and reasonable" — anchors this jurisprudence. Speedy trial was declared a fundamental right in Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979), leading to the release of thousands of undertrials. The Court in Common Cause v. Union of India (1996) laid down time-limits for investigation and trial, and Abdul Rehman Antulay v. R.S. Nayak (1992) held that the right to speedy trial cannot be denied on grounds of financial constraints.

Legal aid as a facet of Article 21 was established in M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra (1978) and constitutionalised through Article 39A (inserted by 42nd Amendment). The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 operationalises this. Rights of arrested persons were codified in D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) — 11 guidelines including memo of arrest, notification to friend/relative, medical examination, and access to lawyer. These were incorporated into CrPC via the 2008 and 2010 amendments (Sections 41A-D, 50A, 54, 55A). Handcuffing was restricted in Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration (1980) — permissible only when there is clear danger of escape. Custodial violence and death attract compensatory jurisprudence: Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993) established state liability for custodial death; D.K. Basu mandated magisterial inquiry and prosecution.

Fair trial encompasses: (i) presumption of innocence (Noor Aga v. State of Punjab, 2008); (ii) right to cross-examine witnesses; (iii) protection against double jeopardy (Article 20(2)); (iv) right against self-incrimination (Article 20(3)); (v) right to appeal as a statutory right, not fundamental, but denial of effective appeal violates Article 21 (Mohan Lal v. State of Rajasthan, 2018). The 2020 judgment in Re: Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons extended Article 21 to prison conditions — overcrowding, sanitation, healthcare, and mental health. The Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022, allowing biometric data collection, is currently tested against Article 20(3) and 21. The jurisprudence confirms that Article 21 imposes positive obligations on the State to design criminal procedures that respect human dignity, not merely refrain from arbitrary action.

Collective Rights and Individual Equality: Articles 29, 30, 371, Fifth and Sixth Schedules in Judicial Balancing

The Constitution recognises collective rights for minorities and tribal communities alongside individual equality, creating a structured pluralism. Article 29(1) protects the right of "any section of citizens" having a distinct language, script or culture to conserve it — a collective right enforceable by individuals. Article 29(2) prohibits denial of admission to state-aided educational institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste, language — an individual non-discrimination right. Article 30(1) grants religious and linguistic minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. The Supreme Court in T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002) (11-judge bench) held that "minority" is determined at the State level, not nationally, and that the right to administer includes autonomy in admission, fee structure, and staff selection, subject to reasonable regulation for academic excellence.

Article 30(2) prohibits discrimination in grant of aid to minority institutions. In St. Stephen's College v. University of Delhi (1992), the Court permitted 50% reservation for Christian students in a minority college, balancing Article 30 with Article 29(2). The 93rd Amendment (2005) inserting Article 15(5) enabled reservation in private unaided institutions, including minority ones — but Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012) held Article 15(5) does not apply to minority institutions under Article 30, preserving their autonomy.

Tribal collective rights operate through the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas in 10 States) and Sixth Schedule (Tribal Areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram). The Fifth Schedule empowers the Governor to make regulations for peace and good government, including restricting land transfer — upheld in Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997) where the Court banned mining leases to non-tribals in Scheduled Areas. The Sixth Schedule creates Autonomous District Councils with legislative, executive and judicial powers — a "state within a state" model. Article 371 and its variants (371A-J) provide special provisions for specific States — e.g., Article 371A (Nagaland) protects Naga customary law and land ownership from Parliamentary legislation unless the State Assembly concurs. The 2013 judgment in K. Chandru v. State of Tamil Nadu affirmed that these special provisions are part of the basic structure, reflecting the Constitution's asymmetric federalism. The judicial challenge lies in harmonising these collective protections with individual rights — e.g., gender equality within tribal customary law — where the Court has increasingly insisted that constitutional morality (Articles 14, 15, 21) applies even within autonomous spaces, as seen in the 2020 Sarla Mudgal line of reasoning extended to tribal personal laws.

  • Assuming Article 31B grants absolute immunity to Ninth Schedule laws; post-Coelho (2007), only pre-1973 laws enjoy grandfathered protection, and any subsequent amendment triggers basic structure review.
  • Confusing "law" under Article 13(3) with "State action" under Article 12; administrative instructions are not "law" for Article 13(2) but are challengeable as State action under Article 14 directly.
  • Believing Article 300A requires "just compensation" like the old Article 31(2); it only requires "authority of law" — a valid statute — though arbitrariness is now reviewable under Article 14.
  • Thinking speedy trial is only a directive principle; Hussainara Khatoon (1979) made it a fundamental right under Article 21, enforceable through habeas corpus.
  • Treating minority rights under Article 30 as absolute; they are subject to reasonable regulation for academic standards, national interest, and public order (T.M.A. Pai, St. Stephen's).
  • Overlooking that Article 29(1) is a collective right enforceable by individuals, while Article 29(2) is an individual right against the State — the distinction matters for standing and remedy.
  • Assuming Fifth/Sixth Schedule protections are immune from fundamental rights review; the Court has held that constitutional morality (Articles 14, 15, 21) applies within Scheduled and Tribal Areas, limiting customary practices that violate equality.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation and its Relevance in Fundamental Rights Adjudication

The doctrine of colourable legislation addresses a situation where a legislature, while acting within its formal competence, enacts a law that in substance transgresses constitutional limits — most often fundamental rights. The Supreme Court first articulated the test in K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953), holding that “if a law is enacted under a legislative entry but its true object is to achieve something which the legislature cannot achieve directly, it is colourable and therefore void.” The Court emphasised a two‑step inquiry: (i) whether the legislature has the power to legislate on the subject matter, and (ii) whether the law, despite a plausible label, actually pursues a prohibited purpose. In State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952), the Court struck down a land‑reform statute that, though placed under Entry 18 of the State List (land), effectively abolished zamindari without compensation, violating Article 31 (pre‑1978) and later Article 300A. The doctrine operates as a safeguard against legislative overreach that would otherwise escape scrutiny because the formal entry appears competent.

In the fundamental‑rights context, colourable legislation becomes relevant when a statute masquerades as a regulatory measure but in reality curtails a guaranteed freedom. For instance, a state law labelled “public order” that imposes prior censorship on the press would be examined for whether its true object is to suppress speech under Article 19(1)(a). The Court in Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2020) reiterated that the “pith and substance” test and the colourable legislation test are complementary: the former determines legislative competence, the latter probes the legitimacy of the legislative motive when fundamental rights are at stake. A law that fails the colourable legislation test is struck down under Article 13(2) as being “inconsistent with” Part III, irrespective of its formal validity.

Key indicators of colourable legislation include: (a) a mismatch between the legislative entry invoked and the actual effect of the law; (b) the absence of a genuine regulatory framework, replaced by prohibitive or confiscatory provisions; (c) legislative history revealing an intent to bypass a constitutional prohibition.
