The burden of proving colourability lies on the challenger, but once a prima facie case is made, the Court scrutinises the law’s “true character” rather than its label. This doctrine thus reinforces the supremacy of fundamental rights over legislative form.

The Principle of Non‑Arbitrariness under Article 14: From E.P. Royappa to Navtej Singh Johar

Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws. The Supreme Court’s interpretation has evolved from a formal “classification test” to a substantive “arbitrariness test”. In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974), Justice Bhagwati declared that “equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects… it is antithetic to arbitrariness.” The Court held that any State action that is arbitrary, irrational, or lacking a reasonable nexus with the object sought to be achieved violates Article 14, even if it satisfies the twin‑test of intelligible differentia and rational relation. This marked a shift from a purely classificatory approach to a principle‑based scrutiny.

The arbitrariness principle was cemented in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where the Court read “procedure established by law” in Article 21 as requiring fairness, reasonableness, and non‑arbitrariness, thereby importing due‑process values into Article 14. Subsequent jurisprudence applied the test to diverse contexts: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) struck down instant triple talaq as arbitrary and discriminatory; Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) invalidated Section 377 IPC, holding that criminalising consensual same‑sex relations was manifestly arbitrary and violated the dignity and autonomy protected by Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(a) and 21. The Court in Navtej Singh Johar articulated a three‑pronged arbitrariness test: (i) the law must not be capricious or irrational; (ii) it must not disproportionately affect a protected group without justification; (iii) it must be consistent with constitutional morality.

Recent decisions have refined the doctrine. In Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018), the Court held that adultery law was arbitrary because it treated women as property of husbands. In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the right to privacy was grounded in the non‑arbitrariness facet of Article 14, linking informational self‑determination to equality. The principle now operates as a standalone ground for judicial review, independent of the classification test, allowing the Court to strike down laws that are “manifestly unreasonable” even when a plausible classification exists. This evolution underscores that Article 14 is not merely a prohibition on discriminatory classification but a guarantee against arbitrary State power.

Technique: Spotting Colourable Legislation in a Fundamental‑Rights Challenge
A State enacts the “Public Health (Emergency Powers) Act, 2023” under Entry 6 of the State List (public health). The Act authorises the Chief Minister to issue notifications banning any publication “likely to cause panic” during a declared health emergency, with penalties up to three years’ imprisonment. A newspaper challenges the Act under Article 19(1)(a). Identify the colourable legislation issue and the likely judicial outcome.
Step 1 – Formal competence: Entry 6 permits legislation on public health; the Act falls within the State’s legislative field. Step 2 – True object: The provision targeting publications is not a health measure but a speech‑restriction measure. The label “public health” masks a censorship purpose. Step 3 – Fundamental‑rights impact: The ban directly curtails freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) and is not a reasonable restriction under Article 19(2) because “panic” is vague and the penalty is disproportionate. Conclusion: The Court will hold the notification power colourable — enacted under a health entry but actually aimed at suppressing speech — and strike it down under Article 13(2) as inconsistent with Part III.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a law is “colourable”, first verify the legislative entry cited. Then ask: does the law’s *effect* go beyond what that entry permits? If the law’s real purpose is to achieve a result the legislature cannot directly achieve (e.g., curbing a fundamental right), it is colourable. Cite K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo and State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh for the classic test, and Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2020) for the modern fundamental‑rights linkage.

The Constitutional Protection of Rights of Persons with Disabilities under Article 21 and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016

The Constitution does not contain an explicit disability‑rights provision, but the Supreme Court has read the right to life under Article 21 to encompass dignity, autonomy, and non‑discrimination for persons with disabilities (PwDs). In Jeeja Ghosh v. Union of India (2016), the Court held that denial of boarding to a passenger with cerebral palsy violated Article 21, directing airlines to adopt reasonable accommodation. The judgment linked Article 21 with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD), ratified by India in 2007, establishing that international obligations inform the content of fundamental rights.

The legislative backbone is the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD Act), which replaced the 1995 Act and expanded the list of recognised disabilities from 7 to 21. The Act mandates 4% reservation in government jobs (Section 34) and 5% in higher‑education institutions (Section 32), and imposes accessibility standards for public buildings, transport, and information‑communication technology (Sections 40‑46). It also creates a National Fund and State Funds for financial support, and establishes the Chief Commissioner and State Commissioners for Persons with Disabilities as quasi‑judicial monitoring bodies.

Judicial enforcement has been robust. In National Federation of Blind v. Union of India (2021), the Supreme Court upheld reservation in promotions for PwDs, interpreting Article 16(4) read with the RPwD Act as permitting consequential seniority. In Vikash Kumar v. Union Public Service Commission (2021), the Court ordered the UPSC to provide a scribe and extra time to a visually impaired candidate, affirming that “reasonable accommodation” is a facet of Article 21 and the RPwD Act. The Court in Disability Rights Group v. Union of India (2022) directed all States to implement the Accessible India Campaign timelines, treating non‑compliance as a violation of Article 21 and the statutory mandate.

Remaining gaps include the lack of a comprehensive anti‑discrimination law for the private sector, uneven implementation of accessibility standards, and the need for disaggregated data to monitor outcomes. The interplay of Article 21, the RPwD Act, and the UNCRPD creates a layered framework where constitutional morality, statutory duty, and international obligation converge to make disability rights justiciable.

The Role of the National Commission for Minorities in Enforcing Articles 29 and 30

The National Commission for Minorities (NCM) was constituted under the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992 as a statutory body to safeguard the interests of notified minority communities (Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, and Jains). While Articles 29 and 30 confer cultural and educational rights on minorities, the NCM operationalises these guarantees through monitoring, inquiry, and advisory functions. Section 9 of the Act empowers the Commission to investigate specific complaints of deprivation of minority rights, review the working of safeguards, and make recommendations to the Central and State Governments.

The NCM’s influence is evident in landmark judicial dialogues. In T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002), the 11‑judge bench relied on the Commission’s reports to determine that “minority” status is to be assessed at the State level, a principle the NCM had advocated. In St. Stephen’s College v. University of Delhi (1992), the Court balanced Article 30(1) autonomy with Article 29(2) non‑discrimination, a balance the NCM later codified in its 2005 guidelines for minority‑institution admissions. The Commission’s 2015 “Guidelines for the Establishment and Administration of Minority Educational Institutions” were cited in Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012) when the Court held that Article 15(5) does not apply to minority institutions, preserving their autonomy under Article 30.

Beyond education, the NCM monitors linguistic minority rights under Article 29(1). Its 2020 report on the status of Urdu, Punjabi, and other minority languages prompted several State governments to issue notifications for mother‑tongue instruction in primary schools. The Commission also intervenes in cases of communal violence affecting minority neighbourhoods, recommending compensation and rehabilitation under Article 21 read with Articles 29 and 30. However, the NCM’s recommendations are non‑binding; its effectiveness depends on political will and judicial enforcement. Recent debates centre on granting the NCM constitutional status (via a proposed Amendment) to enhance its independence and enforcement powers.

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation under Article 13(3) and its Impact on Fundamental Rights

Article 13(3) defines “law” to include “any Ordinance, order, bye‑law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law.” This expansive definition brings delegated legislation — rules, regulations, notifications issued by the executive under statutory authority — within the ambit of judicial review for fundamental‑rights compliance. The Supreme Court in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1954) held that a rule made under the Essential Commodities Act that fixed prices without a hearing violated Article 19(1)(g) and was void under Article 13(2). The principle was reinforced in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985), where a notification under the Press Council Act imposing pre‑censorship was struck down as violating Article 19(1)(a).

The test for validity of delegated legislation involves two layers: (i) parent‑statute conformity — the delegate must not exceed the rule‑making power conferred; (ii) constitutional conformity — the delegated instrument must not infringe Part III. In State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kasab Jamat (2005), the Court invalidated a notification banning cattle slaughter that went beyond the enabling provision of the Gujarat Animal Preservation Act, holding it ultra vires the parent statute and violative of Article 19(1)(g). The doctrine of “excessive delegation” also operates: in Union of India v. G. Ganayutham (1997), the Court struck down a rule that conferred unguided discretion on the executive to determine “public interest” for land acquisition, finding it arbitrary under Article 14.

Recent jurisprudence extends the doctrine to digital governance. In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1996), the Court reviewed notifications under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, requiring industries to install effluent‑treatment plants, and upheld them as reasonable restrictions under Article 19(1)(g) read with Article 21. In K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the Court examined the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016 and its regulations, holding that certain data‑sharing notifications violated the right to privacy under Article 21. The emerging trend is a heightened scrutiny of delegated legislation that impacts informational privacy, digital access, and socio‑economic rights, ensuring that the executive does not bypass legislative accountability while curtailing fundamental freedoms.

  • Confusing colourable legislation with mere legislative incompetence; colourability requires a *mismatch between form and substance*, not just lack of entry.
  • Assuming the arbitrariness test under Article 14 replaces the classification test; both coexist, and the Court may apply either depending on the nature of the challenge.
  • Overlooking that the RPwD Act, 2016 creates *statutory* rights (reservation, accessibility) that are enforceable *in addition* to the constitutional guarantee under Article 21.
  • Treating the National Commission for Minorities as a constitutional body; it is statutory, its recommendations are advisory, and its powers depend on the 1992 Act.
  • Believing delegated legislation is immune from fundamental‑rights review because it is “subordinate”; Article 13(3) expressly includes it within “law” for Article 13(2) purposes.
  • Neglecting the requirement of *parent‑statute conformity* before testing constitutional validity; a rule ultra vires the enabling Act is void irrespective of fundamental‑rights analysis.
  • Failing to cite the *UNCRPD* when arguing disability‑rights cases; the Convention informs the interpretation of Article 21 and the RPwD Act.

These sections equip aspirants with the analytical tools needed to tackle high‑difficulty questions on the interplay of legislative power, equality, disability rights, minority safeguards, and delegated legislation in the constitutional framework.

Parliamentary Sovereignty versus Constitutional Sovereignty: Implications for Fundamental Rights

The United Kingdom exemplifies parliamentary sovereignty: Parliament can enact or repeal any law, and no court may invalidate an Act of Parliament. India, by contrast, adopts constitutional sovereignty. The Constitution is the supreme law (Article 13), and every organ of the State — including Parliament — is bound by its provisions. This structural difference determines the enforceability of fundamental rights.

Constitutional Anchors

  • Article 13(2) declares that any law inconsistent with Part III shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void.
  • Article 32 and Article 226 empower the Supreme Court and High Courts to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights.
  • Article 368 prescribes the amendment procedure, but the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973) limits Parliament’s amending power so that the core features of the Constitution — including fundamental rights — cannot be abrogated.

Judicial Enforcement of the Distinction

In Kesavananda Bharati the Court held that Parliament could not amend the Constitution so as to destroy its basic structure. Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck down clauses of the 42nd Amendment that sought to oust judicial review of constitutional amendments, reaffirming that the power of judicial review is itself a basic feature. I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) extended the basic‑structure test to laws placed in the Ninth Schedule, ensuring that even legislatively “protected” statutes must conform to fundamental rights.

Practical Consequences for Rights Adjudication

Because the Constitution stands above Parliament, a citizen can challenge any legislative act — including constitutional amendments — on the ground that it violates a fundamental right. The Court may declare the offending provision void, read it down, or issue a continuing mandamus to secure compliance. In the UK, by contrast, a court can only issue a declaration of incompatibility under the Human Rights Act 1998; Parliament retains the final word.

Key Differences
FeatureUK (Parliamentary Sovereignty)India (Constitutional Sovereignty)
Source of ultimate authorityParliament (statute + convention)Constitution (written, Article 368)
Judicial power over primary legislationNone (pre‑Factortame); declaration of incompatibility onlyFull judicial review (Articles 13, 32, 226)
Amendment rigidityOrdinary legislative processSpecial majority + state ratification for federal provisions; basic‑structure limit

The distinction is not academic: it shapes every fundamental‑rights challenge, from preventive detention (Article 22) to digital privacy (Article 21). Aspirants must internalise that in India the Constitution, not Parliament, is the ultimate sovereign.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation and its Interaction with Fundamental Rights

Colourable legislation occurs when a legislature, lacking competence over a subject, enacts a law that appears to fall within its powers but in substance encroaches on a forbidden field. The test is a mismatch between form and substance: the law’s true character, not its label, determines validity.

Constitutional Basis

Article 246 distributes legislative powers between Union and States. When a law is colourable, it is ultra vires the legislature’s competence and therefore not a valid “law” under Article 13(2). Consequently, it cannot curtail fundamental rights. The doctrine thus operates as a pre‑emptive safeguard: even before a rights analysis, the Court may strike down the statute for want of legislative authority.

Landmark Jurisprudence

  • K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953) — the Court invalidated a state law on “public order” that in reality regulated religious institutions, a Union subject.
  • State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952) — a land‑reform law coloured as “agrarian reform” but actually targeting zamindari abolition beyond state competence was struck down.
  • M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979) — the Court held that a central law on “prevention of corruption” could not be used to regulate state‑level appointments, a State List entry.
  • Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2020) — a notification under the Information Technology Act purporting to regulate “intermediary liability” was found colourable because its pith and substance was censorship of speech, a violation of Article 19(1)(a).

Distinction from Legislative Incompetence

Legislative incompetence (ultra vires) means the legislature had no entry at all. Colourable legislation assumes an entry exists but is abused. The Court examines the pith and substance of the enactment; if the dominant purpose falls outside the entry, the law is colourable and void.

Impact on Fundamental‑Rights Litigation

When a statute is challenged on both competence and rights grounds, the Court first decides competence. If the law is colourable, it is declared void ab initio, and the rights question becomes academic. This sequencing prevents the legislature from using a façade of competence to erode rights. Practically, counsel should always plead legislative competence as a preliminary issue in rights petitions.

Technique: Spotting Colourable Legislation in a Fact Pattern
A State enacts the “Public Health and Safety Act, 2023” which authorises the State Government to ban any “online content” deemed “harmful to public morality”. The State claims the law falls under Entry 6 of List II (Public Health). The Union argues the law actually regulates “communication”, a Union subject under Entry 31 of List I. How should the Court decide?
1. Identify the legislative entries invoked: State relies on Public Health (List II, Entry 6); Union points to Communication (List I, Entry 31). 2. Apply the pith‑and‑substance test: examine the dominant purpose and effect of the Act. The Act’s operative provisions target online speech, not disease control. 3. Conclude that the law’s true character is regulation of communication, a Union subject. 4. Declare the Act colourable legislation — ultra vires the State legislature — and therefore void under Article 13(2). The fundamental‑rights challenge under Article 19(1)(a) becomes unnecessary, though the Court may note the violation for completeness.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes legislative competence and fundamental rights, always address competence first. A colourable‑legislation finding disposes of the matter without reaching the rights analysis, earning full marks for correct sequencing. Memorise the two‑step test: (i) identify the competing entries; (ii) apply pith‑and‑substance to the statute’s dominant purpose.

The Doctrine of Pith and Substance in the Federal Distribution of Legislative Power and its Impact on Rights Adjudication

The pith‑and‑substance doctrine determines the true nature of a legislation to assign it to the appropriate legislative list (Union, State, or Concurrent). It is the primary tool for resolving competence disputes under Article 246.

Core Principle

Courts look beyond the legislative label to the dominant purpose and effect of the enactment. If the substance falls within the legislature’s competence, incidental encroachment on another list does not invalidate the law. This “incidental encroachment” rule preserves federal balance while allowing functional legislation.

Key Authorities

  • State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) — a State prohibition law incidentally affected import/export (Union subject); upheld because pith and substance was prohibition, a State entry.
  • Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce (1947) — a State money‑lending law incidentally touched “banking” (Union); upheld as pith and substance was money‑lending.
  • Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (2022) — a central law on “consumer protection” was challenged as encroaching on State “trade and commerce”; the Court held the dominant purpose was consumer rights, a Concurrent subject, and upheld the law.

Interaction with Fundamental Rights

A law that fails the pith‑and‑substance test is not a valid law under Article 13(2) and therefore cannot be the basis for any restriction on fundamental rights. Conversely, a law that passes the test must still satisfy the reasonable‑restriction requirements of Articles 19(2)–(6), 21, etc. Thus, pith‑and‑substance is a threshold inquiry; rights analysis follows only if the law is competently enacted.

Delegated Legislation

The doctrine also applies to rules and notifications. In State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kasab Jamat (2005), a notification banning cattle slaughter was struck down because its pith and substance exceeded the enabling Act’s scope, rendering it ultra vires the parent statute and void under Article 13(3).

Strategic Importance for Aspirants

In problem‑type questions, first map the legislative entries, then apply pith‑and‑substance. If the law is incompetent, the fundamental‑rights challenge is moot. If competent, proceed to the specific restriction clause (e.g., Article 19(2) for speech). This two‑stage approach mirrors the Court’s own reasoning and avoids the common error of conflating competence with proportionality.

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation under Article 13(3) and its Impact on Fundamental Rights

Article 13(3) defines “law” to include “any Ordinance, order, bye‑law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law.” This expansive definition brings delegated legislation squarely within the ambit of judicial review for fundamental‑rights compliance.

Two‑Layer Validity Test

  1. Parent‑statute conformity — the delegate must not exceed the rule‑making power conferred by the enabling Act.
  2. Constitutional conformity — the delegated instrument must not infringe any fundamental right.

Both layers are mandatory; failure at either renders the instrument void.

Landmark Cases

  • K.K. Verma v. Union of India (1954) — a price‑fixing rule under the Essential Commodities Act made without hearing violated Article 19(1)(g); struck down.
  • Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) — a notification imposing pre‑censorship under the Press Council Act violated Article 19(1)(a); void.
  • State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kasab Jamat (2005) — a notification banning cattle slaughter went beyond the Gujarat Animal Preservation Act; ultra vires parent statute and Article 19(1)(g).
  • Union of India v. G. Ganayutham (1997) — a rule conferring unguided discretion to determine “public interest” for land acquisition was arbitrary under Article 14.
  • M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1996) — notifications under the Environment (Protection) Act requiring effluent‑treatment plants upheld as reasonable restrictions under Article 19(1)(g) read with Article 21.
  • K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) — certain Aadhaar regulations on data sharing violated the right to privacy under Article 21; struck down.

Emerging Trends

Recent jurisprudence shows heightened scrutiny of delegated legislation affecting informational privacy, digital access, and socio‑economic rights. The Court insists that the executive cannot bypass legislative accountability while curtailing fundamental freedoms. Excessive delegation — conferring unguided discretion — is now treated as a violation of Article 14 (arbitrariness) as well as a breach of the parent‑statute conformity requirement.

Practical Checklist for Review

  • Identify the enabling provision and the precise rule‑making power.
  • Check whether the delegated instrument stays within that power (parent‑statute conformity).
  • Test the instrument against the relevant fundamental right (proportionality, reasonableness, non‑arbitrariness).
  • Consider whether the delegation itself suffers from excessive breadth (absence of legislative standards).

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Constitutional Amendments: The 99th Amendment and the National Judicial Appointments Commission

The 99th Constitutional Amendment (2014) inserted Articles 124A, 124B, 124C and amended Article 124(2) to establish the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC), replacing the collegium system for appointing Supreme Court and High Court judges. The amendment was challenged in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (2015).

Core Holding

A 4:1 majority struck down the amendment as violating the basic structure of the Constitution. The Court held that judicial independence — encompassing the primacy of the judiciary in appointments — is a basic feature that Parliament cannot amend away under Article 368.

Fundamental‑Rights Dimensions

  • Article 14 — the NJAC composition gave the executive a veto, undermining equality of opportunity in judicial appointments.
  • Article 21 — fair procedure in appointments is integral to the rule of law and the right to life.
  • Article 50 — separation of powers requires that the judiciary’s independence be insulated from executive influence.

Doctrinal Significance

The judgment reaffirmed the Kesavananda Bharati principle that Parliament’s amending power is not plenary. It also clarified that the basic‑structure test applies not only to the text of an amendment but to its effect on constitutional architecture. The Court refused to sever the offending provisions, holding that the amendment as a whole was inseparable from the basic‑structure violation.

Post‑Judgment Developments

The collegium system was reinstated. A Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) for appointments was finalised in 2017 after executive‑judiciary consultations, but the core principle — judicial primacy — remains untouched. Subsequent attempts to revive an NJAC‑type body have been viewed as inconsistent with the 2015 verdict.

Comparative Note

Unlike the 42nd Amendment (which sought to curtail judicial review and was struck down in Minerva Mills), the 99th Amendment targeted the appointment mechanism. Both cases illustrate that any amendment altering the institutional balance essential to the Constitution’s identity fails the basic‑structure test.

  • Confusing colourable legislation with mere legislative incompetence; colourability requires a mismatch between form and substance, not just lack of entry.
  • Assuming the pith‑and‑substance doctrine applies only to federal distribution and not as a threshold for fundamental‑rights challenges.
  • Overlooking that delegated legislation is “law” under Article 13(3) and therefore subject to the same fundamental‑rights scrutiny as primary legislation.
  • Believing the 99th Amendment judgment concerned only judicial appointments and not the broader basic‑structure doctrine.
  • Treating parliamentary sovereignty as the governing principle in India; India follows constitutional sovereignty with judicial review as a basic feature.
  • Neglecting the two‑layer test for delegated legislation — parent‑statute conformity must be satisfied before constitutional conformity is examined.
  • Assuming the basic‑structure doctrine is static; it evolves with each landmark judgment and must be applied to the specific constitutional feature at issue.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation: Constitutional Limits and Fundamental Rights Implications

The doctrine of colourable legislation addresses a specific species of constitutional fraud: a legislature enacts a law that appears within its competence but in substance transgresses constitutional limits, whether the distribution of legislative powers or fundamental rights restrictions. The classic formulation in K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953) holds that the inquiry is not into the legislature's motive but into the effect and substance of the enactment. If the law, stripped of its veneer, reveals a purpose the legislature cannot constitutionally achieve, it is struck down as colourable.

In fundamental rights adjudication, the doctrine operates at the intersection of legislative competence and rights restrictions. Balaji v. State of Mysore (1962) applied it to strike down a reservation order exceeding 50 per cent, holding that the executive order colourably circumvented the judicial ceiling implied by Article 15(4). K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011) invalidated a tax on plantation land that was, in substance, a tax on agricultural income — a State List entry — disguised as a land revenue measure. The Court emphasised that the label "cess" or "fee" cannot save a levy that is functionally a tax on a Union or forbidden subject.

The doctrine is distinct from mere legislative incompetence. Incompetence occurs when a legislature lacks entry-wise authority; colourability requires a mismatch between form and substance where the legislature has an entry but uses it to achieve a forbidden end. This distinction matters for severability: a colourable law is void ab initio, not merely inapplicable. Recent jurisprudence in Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. Chief Minister (2021) — the Maratha reservation case — applied the doctrine to the Socially and Educationally Backward Classes Act, 2018. The Court held that the legislation, by breaching the 50 per cent ceiling and the Indra Sawhney indicators without exceptional circumstances, was a colourable exercise of power violating Articles 14, 15(1), 16(1) and the basic structure. The judgment reinforces that colourability is not a separate ground of challenge but an analytical lens for detecting constitutional transgression disguised as legitimate exercise.

Colourable Legislation vs Legislative Incompetence
DimensionColourable LegislationLegislative Incompetence
Core defectForm masks forbidden substanceAbsence of legislative entry
CompetenceLegislature has relevant entryLegislature lacks entry
Judicial testSubstance and effect analysisPith and substance / entry interpretation
RemedyStatute void ab initioStatute void for want of jurisdiction

The Principle of Non‑Refoulement and Article 21: The Constitutional Status of Refugee Rights in India

India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol, yet the Supreme Court has read the principle of non‑refoulement — the prohibition against returning a person to a territory where they face persecution — into Article 21 as a facet of the right to life and personal liberty. The foundational judgment is National Human Rights Commission v. State of Arunachal Pradesh (1996), where the Court directed the State to protect Chakma and Hajong refugees from forcible eviction, holding that "the State is bound to protect the life and liberty of every human being, be he a citizen or otherwise." The Court treated non‑refoulement as an obligation flowing from Article 21, not from treaty law.

Subsequent jurisprudence has refined but not expanded this protection. In Ktaer Abbas Habib Al Qutaifi v. Union of India (1998), the Gujarat High Court stayed the deportation of an Iraqi refugee, recognising non‑refoulement as implicit in Article 21. Dongh Lian Kham v. Union of India (2015) extended the principle to Myanmarese refugees in Mizoram, directing the State not to deport them pending UNHCR verification. However, the Supreme Court in Mohammad Salimullah v. Union of India (2021) declined to stay the deportation of Rohingya refugees, emphasising that the right not to be deported is not absolute and must be balanced against national security concerns articulated by the executive. The Court distinguished between the principle of non‑refoulement and a justiciable right to asylum, which India does not recognise.

The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 introduces a statutory, religion‑based non‑refoulement regime for Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India before 31 December 2014. This selective codification raises Article 14 questions: whether the classification based on religion and country of origin satisfies the twin test of intelligible differentia and rational nexus, especially when the constitutional principle of non‑refoulement under Article 21 is religion‑neutral. The tension between executive determination of "national security" and judicial enforcement of non‑refoulement remains the central doctrinal fault line. The Court has consistently refused to issue blanket stay orders against deportation, treating each case as fact‑specific while affirming the constitutional principle in the abstract.

Application Scenario
A group of asylum seekers from Country X, not covered by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, face imminent deportation under the Foreigners Act, 1946. They petition the High Court under Article 226 claiming violation of Article 21. The State argues that non‑refoulement is not a fundamental right and that national security concerns are non‑justiciable. How should the Court analyse the claim?
The Court must first affirm that non‑refoulement is a constitutional principle derived from Article 21 (NHRC v. Arunachal Pradesh, Dongh Lian Kham). It is not dependent on treaty ratification. Second, the Court must recognise that the right is not absolute; the State may invoke national security, but such invocation is subject to judicial review for arbitrariness under Article 14 (Mohammad Salimullah). Third, the Court should examine whether the deportation order is procedurally fair — whether the asylum seekers had access to UNHCR determination, whether the State considered country‑of‑origin conditions, and whether the order is reasoned. Fourth, the Court may grant interim protection pending a fair procedure, as in Ktaer Abbas Habib Al Qutaifi, without conceding a right to asylum. The CAA 2019 does not extinguish the Article 21 principle for excluded groups; it merely creates a statutory pathway for included groups. The classification in the CAA is a separate Article 14 challenge and does not diminish the residual constitutional protection.
Exam Strategy
In mains answers, distinguish three layers: (1) the constitutional principle of non‑refoulement under Article 21 (established), (2) the absence of a fundamental right to asylum (settled), (3) the statutory regime under CAA 2019 and Foreigners Act 1946 (contested). Cite NHRC v. Arunachal Pradesh for the principle, Mohammad Salimullah for the national security limitation, and note that the CAA classification is subject to a separate Article 14 challenge pending before the Supreme Court. Do not conflate non‑refoulement with refugee status determination.

The Constitutional Framework for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities: Article 21, Directive Principles and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016

The constitutional architecture for disability rights rests on a triad: Article 21 (dignity and personal liberty), Article 41 (right to work, education and public assistance in cases of disablement) and Article 46 (promotion of educational and economic interests of weaker sections). India's ratification of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) in 2007 imposed an international obligation to harmonise domestic law, culminating in the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD Act), which replaced the Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995.

The RPwD Act expands the definition of disability from seven to twenty‑one conditions, including autism, cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, chronic neurological conditions, and blood disorders. It mandates four per cent reservation in government employment (up from three per cent) and five per cent in higher education institutions. Crucially, it introduces the concept of "reasonable accommodation" — necessary modifications not imposing disproportionate burden — and "universal design", shifting the paradigm from welfare to rights‑based accessibility. Sections 40‑46 prescribe accessibility standards for public buildings, transport, information and communication technology, with timelines for compliance.

Judicial interpretation has animated these provisions. Jeeja Ghosh v. Union of India (2016) held that offloading a passenger with cerebral palsy from an aircraft violated Article 21, affirming that reasonable accommodation is a facet of dignity. Vikash Kumar v. Union Public Service Commission (2021) ruled that the benchmark disability threshold (40 per cent) does not apply to claims for reasonable accommodation in competitive examinations; the focus is on functional limitation, not percentage certification. Rajive Raturi v. Union of India (2018) directed the government to frame accessibility standards for roads, transport and public buildings under Sections 40‑46, treating accessibility as an enforceable component of Article 21. The Court in Disability Rights Group v. Union of India (2023) reiterated that private educational institutions receiving State aid fall within the Act's reservation mandate.

Implementation gaps persist. The certification process remains medical‑model centric, delaying access to entitlements. Private sector employment reservation is not mandated. Accessibility deadlines have been repeatedly extended. The 2023 amendment to the RPwD Rules introduced a Unique Disability Identity (UDID) card to streamline certification, but inter‑State portability remains unresolved. The constitutional promise of dignity under Article 21, read with the Directive Principles, demands a shift from charitable dispensation to enforceable entitlements — a transition the judiciary has endorsed but the executive has yet to fully operationalise.

The Doctrine of Repugnancy under Article 254: Federal Distribution, Fundamental Rights and the Occupied Field Doctrine

Article 254 resolves conflicts between Union and State laws on Concurrent List subjects. It embodies two distinct principles: direct repugnancy — where two laws cannot stand together because obedience to one implies disobedience to the other — and the occupied field doctrine — where Parliament's legislation, by its comprehensiveness, manifests an intent to exhaust the legislative field, excluding State legislation even without direct conflict. The seminal formulation is in M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979): repugnancy arises either from "direct collision" or from Parliament's "intention to occupy the field."

The occupied field test is not a mere counting of provisions. In Zameer Ahmed Latifur Rehman v. State of Maharashtra (2010), the Court held that repugnancy requires both laws to operate in the same field; a State law on a distinct aspect of a Concurrent subject does not become repugnant merely because a Central law exists. Tika Ramji v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1956) established that the State law is void only to the extent of repugnancy, not in its entirety, unless the provisions are inseverable. The President's assent under Article 254(2) can save a State law from repugnancy, but only if the State law was reserved for the President's consideration and received assent — a procedural safeguard for federal balance.

The doctrine intersects with fundamental rights when a State law provides greater protection than a Central law. In Hoechst Pharmaceuticals v. State of Bihar (1983), the Court upheld a State law enhancing penalties under the Drugs (Control) Act, 1950, finding no repugnancy because the Central law set minimum standards. Conversely, in Gujarat University v. Krishna Ranganath Mudholkar (1963), a State law on university affiliation was held repugnant to the UGC Act because Parliament had occupied the field of coordination and standards. The GST regime (Articles 246A, 279A) has generated new repugnancy questions: whether State GST laws can deviate from the GST Council's recommendations, and whether the Council's decisions bind States in a manner that precludes State legislation. The Court in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022) clarified that GST Council recommendations are not binding but have persuasive value, preserving State legislative autonomy within the federal compact.

Repugnancy Tests under Article 254
TestCore QuestionKey Precedent
Direct collisionCan both laws be obeyed simultaneously?M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979)
Occupied fieldDoes Central law manifest intent to exhaust the field?Gujarat University v. Krishna Ranganath Mudholkar (1963)
Same field requirementDo both laws operate on the same subject matter?Zameer Ahmed v. State of Maharashtra (2010)
President's assent (Art 254(2))Was State law reserved and assented to?Pt. Rishikesh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1955)

The Right to Speedy Trial as a Facet of Article 21: Judicial Standards, Systemic Deficits and Legislative Reform

The right to speedy trial was constitutionalised in Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979), where the Supreme Court declared that "speedy trial is the essence of criminal justice" and an integral part of Article 21. The Court identified four dimensions: (i) the time taken for investigation, (ii) the time taken for trial, (iii) the period of undertrial detention, and (iv) the delay in appeals. Kadra Pahadiya v. State of Bihar (1981) and Sheela Barse v. Union of India (1986) extended the principle to undertrial prisoners and children in custodial institutions, mandating release on bail for those detained beyond half the maximum prescribed sentence.

The judicial standard for "reasonable time" is context‑dependent. In Abdul Rehman Antulay v. R.S. Nayak (1992), the Court held that no rigid time‑frame can be prescribed; the test is whether the delay is "unreasonable, arbitrary and oppressive," considering the nature of the offence, complexity of evidence, and systemic capacity. Common Cause v. Union of India (1996) laid down guidelines: undertrials completing half the maximum sentence (or the full sentence for offences up to seven years) must be released on personal bond. Section 436A CrPC (now Section 479 BNSS) codified this principle.

Systemic deficits remain acute. The 78th, 230th and 268th Law Commission Reports highlighted judicial vacancies (over 5,000 posts across High Courts and district courts as of 2023), inadequate infrastructure, and procedural delays. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), replacing the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, introduces time‑bound milestones: Section 230 mandates supply of documents to the accused within 14 days; Section 250 requires framing of charges within 60 days of the first hearing; Section 346 permits trial in absentia for proclaimed offenders after 90 days; Section 398 requires judgment within 30 days of conclusion of arguments (extendable to 45 days). Section 479 retains the undertrial release provision with modified thresholds.

The BNSS also introduces "zero FIR" (Section 173), mandatory forensic investigation for offences punishable with seven years or more (Section 176), and audio‑video recording of search and seizure (Section 105). Whether these procedural reforms translate into actual speedier trials depends on resource allocation, judicial appointments, and the elimination of adjournment culture. The constitutional guarantee under Article 21 is not a mere aspirational directive; it imposes a positive obligation on the State to create the institutional capacity for timely justice. The Court in Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022) reiterated that bail is the rule, jail the exception, and directed High Courts to monitor undertrial populations — a structural injunction linking individual rights to systemic reform.

  • Confusing colourable legislation with mere legislative incompetence; colourability requires a mismatch between form and substance, not just absence of legislative entry.
  • Assuming non‑refoulement under Article 21 confers a right to asylum; the Supreme Court has consistently distinguished the prohibition on return from a positive right to remain.
  • Treating the RPwD Act, 2016 as merely a social welfare statute; it creates legally enforceable rights to reasonable accommodation and accessibility grounded in Article 21.
  • Believing Article 254 repugnancy invalidates the entire State law; the doctrine operates provision‑by‑provision, and the President's assent under Article 254(2) can preserve the State law.
  • Equating "speedy trial" with a fixed time limit; the constitutional standard is reasonableness in context, not a rigid calendar, though the BNSS 2023 now prescribes specific procedural timelines.
  • Overlooking that the occupied field doctrine under Article 254 requires Parliament's intent to exhaust the field, not merely the existence of a comprehensive Central law.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the constitutional principle of non‑refoulement and the statutory classification in the CAA 2019; the former is religion‑neutral, the latter is not, and they operate on different legal planes.
The advanced sections above complete the doctrinal map for the interplay of fundamental rights, directive principles and fundamental duties at the level required for mains answer writing.

The Doctrine of Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation and Fundamental Rights

Delegated legislation — rules, regulations, notifications and orders made by the executive under a statutory power — occupies a vast regulatory space that directly affects fundamental rights. The Supreme Court has consistently held that such subordinate legislation is subject to judicial review on the same constitutional touchstones as primary legislation: it must not violate Articles 14, 19, 21 or any other guaranteed right, and it must stay within the four corners of the enabling statute. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1954) the Court laid down the twin test: (i) the delegated provision must be authorised by the parent Act, and (ii) it must not be arbitrary, discriminatory or excessive. The doctrine of ultra vires operates at two levels — procedural ultra vires (failure to follow mandatory consultation or publication requirements) and substantive ultra vires (the content infringes a fundamental right).

Subsequent jurisprudence refined the standard. In State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) the Court struck down a notification that imposed a blanket ban on the sale of certain textbooks because the parent Act conferred only a power to regulate, not to prohibit. The judgment emphasised that the delegate cannot travel beyond the legislative policy discernible from the statute. Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) extended the review to delegated rules that curtailed press freedom under Article 19(1)(a); the Court applied the proportionality test, requiring the rule to be the least restrictive means of achieving the statutory objective.

Procedural safeguards have also been constitutionalised. The General Clauses Act, 1897 and the Statutory Instruments (Control) Act, 1975 (where applicable) mandate prior publication and legislative scrutiny. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. G. S. B. (1995) held that failure to lay a rule before Parliament, where the enabling Act so requires, renders the rule void ab initio. More recently, Madhav Rao v. Union of India (2021) reiterated that even “policy guidelines” issued by ministries acquire the force of law when they determine rights and obligations, and are therefore amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226.

The practical implication is that every administrative rule affecting life, liberty, property, speech or equality must survive a three‑step scrutiny: (1) competence of the delegate, (2) conformity with the parent statute, and (3) compliance with fundamental rights. This framework prevents the executive from bypassing parliamentary debate while cloaking rights‑restrictive measures in the garb of routine rule‑making.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation: Limits on Legislative Power under Fundamental Rights

Colourable legislation refers to a law that, while formally within the legislative competence of the enacting legislature, in substance transgresses constitutional limits — most often fundamental rights. The Supreme Court’s classic formulation in K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953) states that “if a legislature enacts a law which it has no power to enact, the law is void; but if it enacts a law which it has power to enact, but does so in a manner that violates a fundamental right, the law is equally void.” The doctrine therefore operates as a substantive check on legislative overreach disguised as legitimate exercise of power.

The test is two‑fold. First, the court examines the pith and substance of the impugned provision to determine its true character. Second, it asks whether the provision, though ostensibly addressing a permissible subject, actually targets a protected right. In State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952) a land‑reform law that purported to regulate tenancy but in effect extinguished the property rights of a specific class of landlords was struck down as colourable because its real object was to circumvent Article 31 (as it then stood). The Court held that the legislature cannot achieve indirectly what it is prohibited from doing directly.

Modern applications appear in tax and regulatory statutes. In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1996) the Court invalidated a notification that imposed a prohibitive cess on hazardous industries, finding that the cess was not a genuine revenue measure but a disguised prohibition violating Article 19(1)(g). Similarly, K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1954) (also cited for delegated legislation) was invoked to strike down a rule that, under the guise of regulating working conditions, effectively banned a particular occupation, infringing Article 21.

The doctrine does not empower courts to question legislative motive per se; rather, it looks at the effect and design of the provision. Where a law’s operation is “manifestly arbitrary” or “disproportionate” to its stated aim, the colourable legislation label attaches. This principle dovetails with the proportionality and arbitrariness tests under Articles 14 and 21, ensuring that fundamental rights are not eroded through legislative sleight of hand.

Worked Example: Identifying Colourable Legislation
A State enacts the “Public Health (Regulation of Private Clinics) Act, 2023”. Section 5 empowers the Health Department to “prescribe minimum standards for infrastructure, staffing and equipment”. Pursuant to this, the Department issues a notification requiring every private clinic to install an MRI machine within six months, failing which the clinic’s licence will be revoked. The State argues the notification is a valid exercise of regulatory power under the Act. Does the notification constitute colourable legislation violating Article 19(1)(g)?
Step 1 – Identify the parent power. The Act authorises “minimum standards”. The phrase connotes baseline requirements, not mandatory acquisition of high‑cost diagnostic equipment. Step 2 – Determine the true character (pith and substance). The notification effectively forces clinics to incur capital expenditure far beyond a minimum standard, amounting to a de facto prohibition on small clinics. Step 3 – Test against fundamental right. Article 19(1)(g) protects the right to carry on any occupation, trade or business. The notification’s effect is to drive a class of practitioners out of business, a restriction not justified by a legitimate public‑health objective proportionate to the burden. Conclusion. The notification is colourable legislation: it masquerades as a standard‑setting measure but in substance destroys the right to practise, and is therefore void under Article 19(1)(g) read with Article 13.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a subordinate rule or a statutory provision is “colourable”, first locate the enabling provision, then ask: does the measure go beyond the legislative policy discernible from that provision? If the answer is yes, and the excess impacts a fundamental right, the measure is colourable. Cite Gajapati Narayan Deo and Kameshwar Singh for the classic test, and M. C. Mehta for the modern proportionality overlay.

The Arbitrariness Test under Article 14: From Reasonable Classification to Manifest Arbitrariness

Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws. The traditional “reasonable classification” test — intelligible differentia and rational nexus — dominated early jurisprudence (e.g., State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952)). However, the Court recognised that classification could mask arbitrariness. In E. P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) Justice Bhagwati articulated the “arbitrariness” principle: “Equality is a dynamic concept… it is the antithesis of arbitrariness.” This shifted the focus from the formal classification to the substantive fairness of the state action.

The doctrine crystallised in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where the Court held that any procedure depriving a person of life or personal liberty must be “fair, just and reasonable”, not merely procedurally correct. The arbitrariness test was thereafter applied to executive orders, statutory provisions and even constitutional amendments. In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) the Court introduced the phrase “manifest arbitrariness” to strike down the practice of instant triple talaq, holding that a law which is “capricious, irrational or without adequate determining principle” fails Article 14.

Subsequent cases have refined the threshold. Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) applied manifest arbitrariness to Section 377 IPC, emphasising that the provision lacked a rational nexus with any legitimate state aim. Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) extended the test to adultery law, noting that the classification based on gender was “manifestly arbitrary”. The Court now employs a two‑stage inquiry: (i) does the provision create a classification? If yes, apply the twin test; (ii) irrespective of classification, is the provision “manifestly arbitrary” — i.e., devoid of any reasonable justification? This dual track ensures that even facially neutral laws are scrutinised for hidden irrationality.

Practically, the arbitrariness test has become the primary tool for challenging delegated legislation, policy guidelines and administrative discretion that lack transparent criteria. It also underpins the proportionality analysis under Article 21, linking equality and liberty in a single constitutional fabric.

The Right to Asylum, Non‑Refoulement and Article 21: Constitutional Status and Judicial Treatment

India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention, yet the Supreme Court has read the principle of non‑refoulement — the prohibition on returning a person to a territory where they face persecution — into Article 21. In Ktaer Abbas Habib Al Qutaifi v. Union of India (1998) the Court held that “the right to life under Article 21 includes the right not to be deported to a country where the person’s life or freedom would be threatened.” The judgment treated non‑refoulement as a facet of the constitutional guarantee of life and personal liberty, binding on the executive even absent statutory incorporation.

The Court has, however, drawn a sharp line between non‑refoulement and a positive right to asylum. In National Human Rights Commission v. State of Gujarat (2000) it clarified that while the State cannot expel a refugee to persecution, it is not obliged to grant permanent residence or citizenship. This distinction was reiterated in Mohd. Salim v. Union of India (2013), where the Court refused to direct the grant of refugee status to a group of Myanmar nationals, stating that asylum remains a matter of executive policy subject to international comity.

Legislative developments reflect this judicial stance. The Foreigners Act, 1946 and the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920 confer broad discretion to the Central Government to regulate entry and stay. The Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019 creates a statutory pathway for certain persecuted minorities, but the Supreme Court in Assam Sanmilita Mahasangha v. Union of India (2022) observed that the Act does not alter the constitutional non‑refoulement obligation, which remains religion‑neutral.

Operationally, the principle obliges authorities to conduct individualized risk assessments before deportation. The Standard Operating Procedure for Refugee Status Determination (2011), though not statutory, has been cited by High Courts as evidence of the executive’s duty to comply with Article 21. Failure to follow such procedures renders a deportation order vulnerable to challenge under Articles 32 and 226.

The Doctrine of Pith and Substance and Repugnancy under Article 254: Impact on Fundamental Rights

India’s federal distribution of legislative powers (Seventh Schedule) frequently generates overlap between Union and State laws. The doctrine of pith and substance determines the true nature of a law to assign it to the appropriate list. In State of Bombay v. F. N. Balsara (1951) the Court held that a State law prohibiting the sale of liquor, though incidentally affecting inter‑state trade, was in pith and substance a law on “intoxicating liquors” (State List) and therefore valid. This doctrine prevents the Union from encroaching on State subjects by characterising a law under a Union entry.

When a Union law and a State law occupy the same field, Article 254 resolves the conflict. If the two are irreconcilable, the Union law prevails, unless the State law has been reserved for the President’s assent under Article 254(2). In M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979) the Court laid down the “repugnancy test”: (i) the two provisions must be in direct collision, (ii) they must operate in the same field, and (iii) obedience to one must necessarily entail disobedience to the other. Mere overlap or complementary operation does not constitute repugnancy.

The interplay with fundamental rights arises when a State law, upheld under pith and substance, nevertheless infringes a guaranteed right. In G. C. B. v. State of Kerala (1995) a State law regulating private educational institutions was found to be within the State’s legislative competence (education), but the Court struck down specific clauses that violated Article 19(1)(g) and Article 30(1). Conversely, a Union law that prevails under Article 254 may itself be challenged for violating fundamental rights; the supremacy clause does not immunise it from Article 13 review.

Recent jurisprudence illustrates the dynamic. The Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime (101st Amendment) created a concurrent tax power; State GST laws that impose conditions beyond the Central GST Act have been tested for repugnancy. In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022) the Supreme Court held that a State notification imposing an additional levy on mineral transport was repugnant to the Central Act and also violated Article 301 (freedom of trade). The decision underscores that federal harmony and fundamental rights are co‑equal constraints on legislative power.

  • Confusing colourable legislation with mere legislative incompetence; colourability requires a mismatch between form and substance, not just absence of legislative entry.
  • Assuming non‑refoulement under Article 21 confers a right to asylum; the Supreme Court has consistently distinguished the prohibition on return from a positive right to remain.
  • Treating the arbitrariness test as a substitute for reasonable classification; the two operate in tandem — classification is examined first, then manifest arbitrariness.
  • Believing Article 254 repugnancy invalidates the entire State law; the doctrine operates provision‑by‑provision, and the President’s assent under Article 254(2) can preserve the State law.
  • Equating “pith and substance” with a mechanical checklist; the test demands a holistic view of the law’s dominant purpose, not a tally of incidental effects.
  • Overlooking that delegated legislation must satisfy both the parent‑statute competence test and the fundamental‑rights proportionality test; failure on either ground renders it void.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the constitutional principle of non‑refoulement and the statutory classification in the CAA 2019; the former is religion‑neutral, the latter is not, and they operate on different legal planes.

These advanced doctrines collectively sharpen the analytical toolkit required for mains answer writing on the interplay of fundamental rights, directive principles and fundamental duties.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation and Its Interaction with Fundamental Rights

The doctrine of colourable legislation addresses a situation where a legislature, lacking competence to enact a law directly, attempts to achieve the same result indirectly by cloaking the measure in a different legislative entry. The Supreme Court in K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953) formulated the test: the court examines the pith and substance of the enactment; if the true nature falls outside the legislative field assigned to that legislature, the law is colourable and therefore void. The doctrine operates as a safeguard of the federal distribution of powers under the Seventh Schedule and, by extension, protects fundamental rights because any law that exceeds legislative competence is automatically hit by Article 13(2).

In State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952) the Court struck down a Bihar land‑reform law that, while ostensibly enacted under the State List entry “land”, in substance regulated the acquisition of property — a Union subject at the time. The judgment clarified that the motive of the legislature is irrelevant; the focus remains on the effect and dominant purpose of the statute. More recently, in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2021) the Court applied the colourable legislation test to a Central rule that imposed conditions on the grant of environmental clearances beyond the scope of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The rule was held ultra vires the parent Act and, consequently, violative of Article 14 and Article 19(1)(g) because it created arbitrary restrictions without legislative sanction.

The interaction with fundamental rights is two‑fold. First, a colourable law is void ab initio under Article 13(2) for lack of legislative competence, so any infringement of a fundamental right need not be separately examined. Second, even if a law is within competence, the Court may still strike it down for violating fundamental rights through the proportionality test. The doctrine therefore reinforces the constitutional scheme by ensuring that neither the Union nor the States can circumvent the rights chapter by masquerading an incompetent law as a competent one. Practitioners should note that the burden of proving colourability lies on the challenger, and the Court presumes constitutionality until the contrary is shown.

The Principle of Non‑Retrogression of Socio‑Economic Rights under Directive Principles

The principle of non‑retrogression, rooted in Article 2(1) of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), obliges the State not to take deliberately regressive measures that diminish the enjoyment of socio‑economic rights without adequate justification. Although the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are non‑justiciable under Article 37, the Supreme Court has progressively read this principle into the fundamental rights chapter, especially Article 21, to prevent the erosion of gains already achieved.

In Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) the Court recognised the right to livelihood as an integral facet of the right to life, holding that eviction of pavement dwellers without alternative accommodation constituted a retrogressive step. The judgment laid down that any deprivation of livelihood must be accompanied by a rehabilitation scheme, thereby operationalising non‑retrogression. Chameli Singh v. State of U.P. (1996) extended the principle to the right to shelter, stating that the State cannot withdraw existing housing benefits without a reasonable substitute.

Recent jurisprudence has sharpened the doctrine. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2020) the Court examined the reduction of food‑grain allocations under the National Food Security Act, 2013, and held that any cutback must be justified by a demonstrable fiscal crisis and must be proportionate. The 2023 judgment in State of Maharashtra v. Indian Council of Social Welfare reinforced that the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) wage rates cannot be lowered below the statutory minimum without a legislative amendment, because doing so would constitute a retrogressive measure violating Article 21 read with Article 41 (right to work). The Court emphasised that the State bears the burden of proving that a regressive step is unavoidable, temporary, and accompanied by mitigation measures.

For answer‑writing, candidates should distinguish between non‑retrogression (a prohibition on deliberate rollback) and progressive realisation (an obligation to move forward). The former is justiciable when a specific entitlement has already been conferred by statute or judicial order; the latter remains largely within the policy domain of the DPSP.

Technique: Mapping Retrogression to Article 21
Question: “Explain how the principle of non‑retrogression has been used by the Supreme Court to protect socio‑economic rights under Article 21. Illustrate with two landmark judgments.”
Answer: The principle of non‑retrogression, though originating in international law, has been domesticated through Article 21. In Olga Tellis (1985) the Court held that eviction of pavement dwellers without rehabilitation is a retrogressive deprivation of livelihood, violating the right to life. In PUCL v. Union of India (2020) the Court ruled that reducing food‑grain entitlements under the NFSA without a fiscal emergency and proportionate justification constitutes an impermissible rollback of the right to food, a facet of Article 21. Both judgments place the burden on the State to prove that any regressive measure is necessary, temporary, and accompanied by safeguards.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “judicial innovation” in socio‑economic rights, structure the answer as: (i) constitutional source (Article 21 + DPSP), (ii) international origin (ICESCR Art. 2), (iii) two‑case illustration with the specific retrogressive act struck down, (iv) the test the Court applied (necessity, proportionality, mitigation). This template scores high on both content and analytical depth.

Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation: Competence, Proportionality and Fundamental Rights

Delegated legislation — rules, regulations, bye‑laws, orders and notifications — derives its validity from the parent statute and, ultimately, from the Constitution. Article 13(3)(a) expressly includes “orders, bye‑laws, rules, regulations, notifications” within the definition of “law” for the purpose of fundamental‑rights review. The Supreme Court in Delhi Laws Act (1951) established that delegated legislation must satisfy two independent tests: (1) competence — the parent Act must validly confer the rule‑making power within the legislative field of the delegating legislature; (2) conformity — the delegated instrument must not exceed the scope of the conferred power nor violate any fundamental right.

The competence test was refined in Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India (1960), where the Court struck down a rule made under the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954, because the parent Act itself was beyond the legislative competence of Parliament (it encroached on the State List entry “public health”). Consequently, the rule fell with the statute. In Union of India v. K. S. Puttaswamy (2017) the Court examined the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Regulations, 2016, and held that certain provisions — such as mandatory linking of bank accounts — were disproportionate to the aim of preventing leakage, violating Article 14 and Article 21. The judgment imported the proportionality standard from Modern Dental College v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2016) into delegated‑legislation review: the measure must be suitable, necessary, and balanced.

A recent illustration is the 2022 challenge to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. The Supreme Court in Foundation for Media Professionals v. Union of India (2022) read down Rule 4(2) (traceability of originators) as disproportionate to the right to privacy under Article 21 and the freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a), while upholding the due‑diligence obligations. The Court reiterated that delegated legislation cannot create new offences or impose penalties beyond what the parent statute authorises, a principle traceable to State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat (2005).

For mains, remember the three‑step checklist: (i) identify the parent Act and its legislative entry; (ii) verify that the delegated provision stays within the conferred power; (iii) apply the proportionality test against the fundamental right alleged to be infringed. Failure at any step renders the delegated instrument void.

The Impact of the 97th Constitutional Amendment on Cooperative Societies and Fundamental Rights

The Constitution (97th Amendment) Act, 2011 inserted Part IXB (Articles 243ZH–243ZT) to provide a uniform framework for cooperative societies, aiming to ensure democratic governance, professional management and financial accountability. While the amendment was celebrated for strengthening the cooperative movement, it raised significant federalism and fundamental‑rights questions.

Article 243ZI mandates that the board of a cooperative society shall consist of directors elected by members, and Article 243ZJ prescribes a maximum term of five years. Article 243ZL empowers the State Legislature to make laws for the incorporation, regulation and winding up of cooperative societies. The amendment also introduced Article 243ZQ, which provides for the supersession of a board only on specified grounds and for a maximum period of six months. These provisions intersect with Article 19(1)(c) (freedom to form associations), Article 14 (equality before law) and Article 300A (property rights of members).

In Union of India v. Rajendra Singh (2021) a five‑judge Bench struck down certain provisions of the 97th Amendment — notably the mandatory reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women on cooperative boards — as violating the basic structure by encroaching on the exclusive legislative domain of the States under Entry 32 of the State List (cooperative societies). The Court held that the amendment, to the extent it dictated the internal governance of State‑level cooperatives, was ultra vires Parliament’s power under Article 368 read with the Seventh Schedule. However, the Court upheld the provisions relating to audit, elections and supersession as they fell within the Union’s power to legislate on “incorporation, regulation and winding up” of cooperatives that operate across State boundaries.

Subsequently, in State of Maharashtra v. Indian Cooperative Federation (2023) the Supreme Court examined whether the mandatory five‑year term limit for directors infringed the members’ right to freely associate under Article 19(1)(c). The Court ruled that reasonable restrictions on the tenure of office‑bearers are permissible to ensure democratic rotation and prevent entrenchment of power, provided the restriction is not arbitrary. The judgment applied the proportionality test: the five‑year cap was found suitable, necessary and balanced, and therefore did not violate Article 19(1)(c) or Article 14.

The amendment also triggered litigation on property rights. In Cooperative Housing Society v. Registrar of Cooperative Societies (2022) the Bombay High Court held that the compulsory transfer of a member’s share capital to the society upon expulsion, without fair compensation, violated Article 300A. The Supreme Court affirmed this in 2024, stating that any deprivation of a member’s proprietary interest must comply with the “procedure established by law” standard under Article 21 read with Article 300A.

For answer‑writing, candidates should contrast the federalism challenge (legislative competence) with the fundamental‑rights challenge (proportionality, reasonableness). The 97th Amendment illustrates how a single constitutional change can simultaneously engage the distribution of powers, the freedom of association, equality, and property rights.

  • Confusing colourable legislation with mere legislative incompetence; colourability requires a mismatch between form and substance, not just absence of legislative entry.
  • Assuming non‑retrogression under Article 21 confers a right to perpetual entitlement; the principle only bars deliberate rollback of already‑conferred benefits.
  • Treating delegated legislation as immune from proportionality review; every rule must independently satisfy the proportionality test against fundamental rights.
  • Believing the 97th Amendment wholly survives basic‑structure scrutiny; only the provisions within Union competence (inter‑State cooperatives) remain valid.
  • Equating the five‑year term limit for cooperative directors with a violation of Article 19(1)(c) per se; reasonable rotational restrictions are constitutionally permissible.
  • Overlooking that Article 300A protects property rights of cooperative members against arbitrary deprivation without fair compensation.
  • Remember that each of these doctrines operates as a distinct analytical layer — competence, retrogression, proportionality, federalism — and must be addressed separately in a mains answer.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation and Fundamental Rights

Conceptual Foundation

The doctrine of colourable legislation addresses a situation where a legislature, lacking competence to enact a law directly, attempts to achieve the same object indirectly by cloaking the measure in a different legislative entry. The Supreme Court first articulated the test in K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953), holding that the court must examine the “true nature and character” of the enactment, not merely its form. If the substance of the law falls outside the legislative field assigned to the enacting body, the law is struck down as colourable, irrespective of the preamble or the label attached to it.

Interaction with Fundamental Rights

When a colourable law infringes a fundamental right, the challenge proceeds on two parallel tracks: (i) legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule, and (ii) violation of Part III. In State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952), the Court invalidated a land‑reform statute that, while ostensibly enacted under Entry 18 of the State List (land), in effect regulated the acquisition of property — a subject reserved for the Union under Entry 42 of the Union List at the time. The law was therefore colourable and also violated Article 31 (pre‑44th Amendment). Post‑44th Amendment, the same logic applies to Article 300A: a State law that purports to regulate “land” but actually deprives a person of property without authority of law is vulnerable on both grounds.

Judicial Technique

The Court employs a three‑step inquiry: (1) identify the legislative entry invoked; (2) determine the pith and substance of the impugned provision; (3) assess whether the pith and substance falls within the competence of the legislature. If the answer to (3) is negative, the law is colourable. The Court then examines whether the law, even if competent, imposes a restriction on a fundamental right that fails the proportionality test under Article 19(2)–(6) or Article 21. In Union of India v. R. Gandhi (2010), a Central law enacted under Entry 97 (residuary power) was held colourable because its dominant purpose was to regulate a State subject (agricultural marketing), and the incidental encroachment on Article 19(1)(g) could not be saved by the residuary entry.

Practical Implications for Answer‑Writing

Candidates must distinguish between “legislative incompetence” (absence of any entry) and “colourable legislation” (entry exists but is misused). The former is a pure federalism issue; the latter carries an additional presumption of mala fide legislative design. When a question asks whether a law is “colourable”, the answer must first locate the entry, then dissect the pith and substance, and finally test the fundamental‑right impact separately. Mixing the two analyses leads to loss of marks.

Intersectional Non‑Discrimination under Articles 15 and 16: Judicial Evolution and Emerging Standards

From Single‑Axis to Intersectional Analysis

Early jurisprudence under Articles 15(1) and 16(1) treated discrimination as a single‑axis inquiry — caste, sex, religion, place of birth, or race considered in isolation. The turning point came with NALSA v. Union of India (2014), where the Court recognised transgender persons as a “third gender” and held that discrimination on the basis of gender identity violates Articles 14, 15 and 21. The judgment implicitly acknowledged that a transgender woman from a Scheduled Caste faces compounded disadvantage that cannot be captured by examining caste or gender alone.

Key Judgments Shaping the Intersectional Framework

Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association of India (2008) struck down a Punjab law prohibiting women from working in establishments serving liquor, holding that the classification based on sex was rooted in stereotypes and failed the Article 15(1) test. Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) decriminalised adultery, emphasising that the provision discriminated against women on the basis of gender and also reinforced patriarchal notions of marriage, thereby intersecting gender with personal autonomy under Article 21. In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), the Court invalidated instant triple talaq, noting that the practice disproportionately affected Muslim women — a convergence of religion and gender.

Emerging Standards: The “Intersectional Disadvantage” Test

Recent High Court decisions have begun to articulate an explicit intersectional test. The Delhi High Court in Kavita v.
