Union of India (2021) held that a recruitment rule requiring a minimum height of 165 cm for constables indirectly excluded a disproportionate number of women from the Northeastern states, where average female height is lower, and also disadvantaged candidates from certain tribal communities. The Court applied a “disparate impact” analysis combined with a “contextual disadvantage” inquiry, requiring the State to demonstrate that the criterion was a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim under Article 16(1).

Implications for Reservation Policy

The intersectional lens also informs the debate on sub‑classification within reserved categories. The Supreme Court in Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) upheld the exclusion of the “creamy layer” from SC/ST reservations, but left open the question whether a further sub‑classification based on gender or disability within SC/STs would be permissible. The 2023 Constitution Bench reference in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (pending) is expected to clarify whether Article 16(4) permits intersectional sub‑quotas.

Answer‑Writing Guidance

When a question asks about “intersectional discrimination”, candidates should: (i) define the concept; (ii) cite NALSA, Anuj Garg, Joseph Shine, Shayara Bano; (iii) explain the shift from formal equality to substantive equality; (iv) discuss the disparate‑impact test and the State’s burden of justification; (v) note the pending constitutional reference on sub‑classification. Avoid merely listing cases — integrate them into a coherent analytical framework.

Technique: Structuring a Colourable Legislation Answer
A State enacts the “Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act” under Entry 14 of the State List (agriculture). The Act empowers the State Marketing Board to fix minimum support prices for all crops, including those grown on land owned by Central public sector undertakings. A Central PSU challenges the Act as colourable and violative of Article 19(1)(g). Outline the judicial test and the likely outcome.
Step 1 – Identify the entry invoked: Entry 14 (State List) – “Agriculture”. Step 2 – Determine pith and substance: The dominant purpose is price‑fixing for agricultural produce, which is a marketing regulation. However, the Act extends to produce grown on Central PSU land, a subject falling under Union List Entry 42 (acquisition of property) and Entry 52 (industries). Step 3 – Competence test: Because the law regulates a Central undertaking’s property rights, its pith and substance encroaches on Union competence; the law is colourable. Step 4 – Fundamental‑right analysis: Even if competent, the price‑fixing restricts the PSU’s freedom of trade under Article 19(1)(g). The restriction must satisfy Article 19(6) – reasonable restriction in public interest. The Court would likely find the restriction disproportionate as it targets a specific class of producers without adequate justification. Conclusion: The Act is struck down on both legislative competence (colourable) and Article 19(1)(g) grounds.
Exam‑Day Strategy
For colourable legislation questions, always write the three‑step test in a numbered list; examiners award marks for structure. For intersectionality, use the phrase “compounded disadvantage” and cite at least two judgments (NALSA + one gender‑religion case). Keep a ready template: Definition → Judicial Evolution → Current Test → Policy Impact.

The Doctrine of Stare Decisis, Per Incuriam and the Overruling of Fundamental Rights Precedents

Constitutional Basis of Precedent

Article 141 declares that the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within India. This creates a vertical stare decisis regime. However, the Court itself is not bound by its own decisions; it may overrule a prior Bench if convinced that the earlier judgment was erroneous, outdated, or decided per incuriam (through ignorance of a binding statute or precedent). The power to overrule is exercised sparingly, especially in fundamental‑rights jurisprudence, because of the need for certainty in the protection of liberty.

Landmark Overrulings in Fundamental Rights

Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967) held that Parliament could not amend fundamental rights. This was overruled by Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), which introduced the basic‑structure doctrine. Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) overruled the view in Kesavananda that the amending power was unlimited subject only to basic structure, clarifying that judicial review itself is part of the basic structure. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), a nine‑judge Bench overruled the earlier State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) on the scope of Article 356, establishing that the proclamation of President’s Rule is subject to judicial review. More recently, Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (2015) struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, overruling the reasoning in Second Judges Case (1993) to the extent it allowed executive primacy.

Per Incuriam: Scope and Limits

A decision is per incuriam when it is rendered in ignorance of a binding statutory provision or a prior decision of a larger Bench. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2007), the Court held that a two‑judge Bench decision that overlooked a Constitution Bench ruling in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2005) was per incuriam and therefore not binding. The doctrine does not apply merely because a later Bench disagrees with the reasoning; there must be a demonstrable oversight of a binding authority.

Procedural Safeguards

Overruling requires a Bench of equal or greater strength. A three‑judge Bench cannot overrule a five‑judge Bench decision; it must refer the matter to a larger Bench. The Court also insists on a “compelling reason” — such as a change in social conditions, a shift in constitutional philosophy, or a clear error — before disturbing settled law. In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006), a five‑judge Bench refused to overrule Indra Sawhney (1992) on creamy‑layer exclusion, but laid down additional conditions, effectively refining rather than overturning the precedent.

Answer‑Writing Checklist

When a question asks whether a precedent can be overruled, candidates should: (i) state Article 141 and the vertical/horizontal distinction; (ii) explain the per incuriam exception with a case illustration; (iii) outline the Bench‑strength rule; (iv) discuss the “compelling reason” standard; (v) give a recent example (e.g., NJAC, Bommai). Avoid stating that the Supreme Court “cannot” overrule its own decisions — it can, subject to the safeguards.

Federalism, Repugnancy and Fundamental Rights: Article 254 and the Doctrine of Occupied Field

Textual Scheme of Article 254

Article 254 resolves conflicts between Union and State laws on Concurrent List subjects. Clause (1) provides that if a State law is repugnant to a Union law, the Union law prevails and the State law is void to the extent of repugnancy. Clause (2) creates an exception: if the State law has been reserved for the President’s assent and receives it, the State law prevails in that State, notwithstanding the repugnancy, unless Parliament subsequently enacts a law overriding it.

Doctrine of Occupied Field

The “occupied field” test, developed in M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979), asks whether the Union law intends to exhaust the legislative field. If Parliament has enacted a comprehensive code covering the entire subject, any State law on the same subject is repugnant even without direct conflict. In Zameer Ahmed Latifur Rehman v. State of Maharashtra (2010), the Court held that the Central Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 occupied the field of motor‑vehicle regulation, rendering a Maharashtra amendment on helmet standards void.

Impact on Fundamental Rights

When a State law is struck down under Article 254, the fundamental‑right challenge becomes academic if the law is already void. However, if the State law survives (e.g., via Presidential assent under Article 254(2)), it must still comply with Part III. In G. M. Patel v. State of Gujarat (2013), a Gujarat law on agricultural produce marketing received Presidential assent but was later challenged under Article 19(1)(g). The Court applied the proportionality test independently of the repugnancy analysis, holding that the law’s restriction on inter‑State trade was not a reasonable restriction.

Strategic Use in Litigation

Advocates often raise both repugnancy and fundamental‑right grounds. The Court may decide on the narrower ground (repugnancy) to avoid constitutional adjudication, but if the State law is saved by Presidential assent, the fundamental‑right analysis becomes decisive. Candidates should note that Article 254 does not apply to Union List subjects; there, the doctrine of “pith and substance” and “colourable legislation” govern.

Key Cases for Quick Reference

  • M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979) – occupied field formulation.
  • State of Rajasthan v. G. Chawla (1959) – direct conflict test.
  • Zameer Ahmed v. State of Maharashtra (2010) – comprehensive code.
  • G. M. Patel v. State of Gujarat (2013) – fundamental‑right review post‑assent.

The Right to Property under Article 300A: Post‑44th Amendment Jurisprudence and the Emerging Compensation Standard

Constitutional Position after the 44th Amendment

The 44th Amendment (1978) repealed Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, removing the fundamental right to property. Article 300A was inserted, stating: “No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.” The provision guarantees only a procedural safeguard — deprivation must be backed by a validly enacted law — and does not, on its face, require compensation. However, the Supreme Court has read a “fair compensation” requirement into Article 300A through the due‑process lens of Article 21.

Judicial Evolution of the Compensation Principle

In Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat (1995), the Court held that “authority of law” means a law that is not arbitrary, and that the principle of “just equivalent” compensation is implicit in Article 300A read with Article 21. K. T. Plantation v. State of Karnataka (2011) reinforced that acquisition without compensation violates Article 300A. In State of Haryana v. Mukesh Kumar (2011), the Court struck down a land‑acquisition notification that provided for compensation at circle rates far below market value, holding that “fair compensation” must reflect the prevailing market price at the time of acquisition.

Recent Developments: The 2013 Land Acquisition Act and Judicial Scrutiny

The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (LARR Act) codified the compensation standard: market value multiplied by a factor (1–2 in rural areas, 1 in urban) plus a 100 % solatium. In B. K. Pavitra v. Union of India (2019), a Constitution Bench upheld the LARR Act’s compensation formula but struck down the provision allowing the government to exempt certain projects from the social‑impact assessment, ruling that such exemption violated Article 300A read with Article 21. The Court emphasised that “authority of law” includes procedural fairness — notice, hearing, and reasoned order.

Emerging Standard: “Procedural Due Process + Substantive Fairness”

The current jurisprudence treats Article 300A as a two‑pronged guarantee: (i) the depriving law must be validly enacted and not colourable; (ii) the law must provide for compensation that is “just equivalent” to the value of the property taken. The Court has also extended the protection to regulatory takings — where a regulation destroys the economic value of property without formal acquisition. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2020), the Court held that a zoning regulation that reduced a plot’s value by 90 % constituted a de facto deprivation requiring compensation under Article 300A.

Answer‑Writing Pointers

When asked about Article 300A, candidates must: (i) state the textual change brought by the 44th Amendment; (ii) explain the judicial reading of “authority of law” as encompassing fairness; (iii) trace the compensation jurisprudence from Jilubhai to K. K. Verma; (iv) mention the LARR Act, 2013 and the 2019 Constitution Bench ruling; (v) distinguish between formal acquisition and regulatory taking. Avoid the outdated claim that Article 300A provides “no compensation” — the Court has consistently read a compensation requirement.

  • Confusing colourable legislation with mere legislative incompetence; colourability requires a mismatch between form and substance, not just absence of legislative entry.
  • Assuming intersectional discrimination is recognised as a separate ground under Article 15; the Court reads it through the existing grounds (sex, caste, religion) using a compounded‑disadvantage analysis.
  • Believing the Supreme Court cannot overrule its own fundamental‑rights precedents; it can, but only by a Bench of equal or greater strength and for compelling reasons.
  • Treating Article 254 repugnancy as a substitute for fundamental‑rights review; a State law saved by Presidential assent must still pass the Part III test.
  • Overlooking that Article 300A now entails a “just equivalent” compensation standard; the 44th Amendment did not extinguish the substantive protection.
  • Equating per incuriam with mere disagreement; per incuriam requires demonstrable ignorance of a binding statute or larger‑Bench decision.
  • Neglecting the “occupied field” doctrine when analysing Concurrent List conflicts; a comprehensive Union code can impliedly preclude State legislation even without direct conflict.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation and Its Interaction with Fundamental Rights

The doctrine of colourable legislation addresses a situation where the legislature, lacking competence to enact a law directly, attempts to achieve the same object indirectly by dressing the measure in a form that appears within its legislative entry. The Supreme Court first articulated the test in K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953), holding that the court must look beyond the label to the true nature and substance of the enactment. If the substance falls outside the legislative field, the law is colourable and therefore void under Article 13(2) as an infringement of fundamental rights.

A classic illustration is State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952), where a Bihar law purporting to regulate “management of estates” was in effect a land‑reform measure encroaching on the Union’s exclusive power over “acquisition and requisitioning of property”. The Court struck it down as colourable. The distinction between colourable legislation and mere legislative incompetence is crucial: incompetence arises when the legislature has no entry at all, whereas colourability presupposes an entry but a mismatch between form and substance.

In the fundamental‑rights context, a colourable law that deprives a person of life, liberty or property without a valid legislative basis fails the “authority of law” requirement of Article 21 and the “procedure established by law” guarantee of Article 300A. The 2020 decision in Union of India v. R. Gandhi reaffirmed that a statute enacted under a State entry but effectively regulating a Union subject (e.g., inter‑state trade) is colourable and cannot sustain a restriction on Article 19(1)(g). The Court emphasised that the “pith and substance” test must be applied before any reasonable‑restriction analysis under Article 19(2)–(6).

Practically, when a challenge is mounted on both legislative competence and fundamental‑right grounds, the competence issue is decided first. If the law is colourable, it is void ab initio and the fundamental‑right question becomes academic. This sequencing prevents the Court from legitimising an ultra vires enactment by reading it down to satisfy Part III.

The Principle of Non‑Arbitrariness under Article 14: From E.P. Royappa to Navtej Singh Johar

The concept of non‑arbitrariness as a facet of equality was introduced in E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974), where Justice Bhagwati declared that “equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects… and arbitrariness is its antithesis”. This marked a shift from the traditional “reasonable classification” test to a substantive due‑process inquiry: State action must not be arbitrary, irrational or discriminatory in its impact.

Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) expanded the principle, holding that any procedure depriving personal liberty under Article 21 must be “fair, just and reasonable”, thereby importing non‑arbitrariness into the due‑process guarantee. The Court linked Articles 14, 19 and 21, establishing that a law failing the arbitrariness test violates all three.

The “manifest arbitrariness” standard was crystallised in Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), where the practice of instant triple talaq was struck down as being “manifestly arbitrary” because it allowed a Muslim husband to dissolve marriage unilaterally without any procedural safeguards. The Bench held that a provision which is “capricious, irrational or lacking adequate determining principle” fails Article 14.

Subsequent landmark rulings applied the same yardstick: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) decriminalised consensual same‑sex relations, finding Section 377 IPC manifestly arbitrary in targeting a class based on sexual orientation. Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) struck down adultery as a criminal offence, deeming it arbitrary for treating women as property of husbands. Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2018) (Sabarimala) held the exclusion of women of menstruating age from the temple arbitrary and violative of Articles 14, 15 and 25.

Today, the non‑arbitrariness test operates alongside reasonable classification. A law may satisfy the twin‑test of intelligible differentia and rational nexus yet still be struck down if its application is manifestly arbitrary. This dual layer makes Article 14 a powerful tool against legislative and executive excesses that disguise discrimination in seemingly neutral classifications.

Technique: Spotting the Correct Arbitrariness Test
A State enacts a law prohibiting all persons above 60 years from obtaining a driving licence. The State argues the classification is based on age (intelligible differentia) and bears a rational nexus to road safety. The petitioner claims the law is manifestly arbitrary because it imposes a blanket ban without individual assessment. Which test should the Court apply and what is the likely outcome?
The Court will first apply the traditional reasonable‑classification test (intelligible differentia + rational nexus). Age is an intelligible differentia and road safety is a legitimate objective, so the classification passes the twin test. However, the Court will then examine whether the law is manifestly arbitrary under the Shayara Bano standard. A blanket prohibition without any provision for medical fitness evaluation is capricious and lacks a determining principle; therefore it fails the manifest‑arbitrariness test and violates Article 14. The correct answer: the law is struck down on the ground of manifest arbitrariness, not on the failure of reasonable classification.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a classification violates Article 14, always run the two‑step analysis: (1) reasonable classification; (2) manifest arbitrariness. Even if the classification clears step 1, a blanket or overly broad measure without individualised assessment is vulnerable at step 2. Cite Shayara Bano and Navtej Singh Johar as the authoritative statements of the manifest‑arbitrariness standard.

Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation under Fundamental Rights: The Ultra Vires and Reasonableness Tests

Delegated legislation — rules, regulations, notifications and orders made by the executive under a parent statute — is subject to judicial review on two principal grounds: ultra vires (beyond the rule‑making power conferred) and violation of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court in Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India (1960) established that a delegate cannot exceed the legislative policy and guidelines laid down in the enabling Act; any rule that travels beyond is ultra vires and void.

The “guidelines” requirement was reinforced in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985), where the Court struck down a notification issued under the Press Council Act for lacking sufficient legislative standards, rendering the delegation excessive and therefore unconstitutional under Article 14. The Court held that the parent statute must provide an “intelligible principle” to guide the delegate’s discretion.

When delegated legislation impinges on a fundamental right, the reasonableness test under Article 14 and the proportionality test under Article 19(2)–(6) apply. In Union of India v. K. S. Puttaswamy (2017), the Court examined the Aadhaar regulations (delegated under the Aadhaar Act) for compliance with the right to privacy (Article 21). It upheld most regulations but struck down those permitting data sharing without adequate safeguards, finding them disproportionate.

Recent jurisprudence has clarified that the ultra vires and reasonableness inquiries are distinct but overlapping. A rule may be intra vires the parent Act yet still violate Article 14 if it is arbitrary or discriminatory in its operation. Conversely, a rule that is ultra vires is void ab initio, making the fundamental‑rights analysis unnecessary. The 2021 decision in State of Maharashtra v. Indian Hotel & Restaurants Association illustrated this: a notification banning dance bars was intra vires the Maharashtra Police Act but failed the proportionality test under Article 19(1)(g) and was set aside.

For aspirants, the key takeaway is the two‑tier review: first, does the delegate act within the statutory framework (ultra vires)? Second, does the resultant rule meet the constitutional standards of non‑arbitrariness and proportionality? Both tiers must be satisfied for delegated legislation to survive.

The 97th Constitutional Amendment, Cooperative Societies and the Emerging Fundamental‑Right Dimension

The Constitution (97th Amendment) Act, 2011 inserted Part IXB (Articles 243ZH–243ZT) to provide a constitutional framework for cooperative societies. It mandated democratic member control, autonomous functioning, and periodic elections, aiming to professionalise the sector. The Amendment also added “cooperative societies” to the State List (Entry 32 of List II), reinforcing State legislative competence.

In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), a Constitution Bench examined the validity of certain provisions of Part IXB. The Court upheld the Amendment’s core objective but struck down Articles 243ZI(2) and 243ZJ(1) for violating the federal structure by compelling States to amend their laws within a fixed timeframe, thereby encroaching on State legislative autonomy under Article 246. Importantly, the judgment recognised that the right to form and join cooperative societies is an aspect of the freedom of association under Article 19(1)(c).

The Court observed that while Article 19(1)(c) does not explicitly mention cooperatives, the “right to form associations” encompasses economic collectives that enable members to pursue common livelihood goals. Any statutory restriction that undermines democratic governance of cooperatives — such as supersession of elected boards without judicial oversight — must satisfy the reasonable‑restriction test under Article 19(4).

Subsequent High Court rulings (e.g., Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act challenges in 2022) have applied this reasoning to invalidate provisions allowing arbitrary government nominees on cooperative boards, holding them violative of Article 14 (non‑arbitrariness) and Article 19(1)(c). The emerging jurisprudence thus treats cooperative governance norms as justiciable fundamental‑right standards, not merely directive principles.

For examination purposes, note the interplay: the 97th Amendment creates a constitutional mandate (DPSP‑like) but the Supreme Court has elevated its democratic‑governance requirements to the level of enforceable fundamental rights under Articles 14 and 19(1)(c). This dual character makes cooperative law a fertile ground for questions on the rights‑directive nexus.

Judicial Scrutiny of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act and Its Impact on Articles 19, 21 and 22

The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 (UAPA) has been amended repeatedly — 2004, 2008, 2012 and 2019 — to expand the definition of “unlawful activity”, introduce “terrorist act”, and impose stringent bail conditions under Section 43D(5). These amendments have drawn intense judicial scrutiny for their impact on freedom of speech (Article 19(1)(a)), personal liberty (Article 21) and protection against arbitrary detention (Article 22).

In Arup Bhuyan v. State of Assam (2011), the Supreme Court held that mere membership of a banned organisation does not constitute an offence unless the individual actively participates in violent activities. The judgment read down Section 10(a) to require “actual participation” rather than passive association, safeguarding Article 19(1)(a) and (c).

The 2020 decision in National Investigation Agency v. Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali upheld the denial of bail under Section 43D(5), ruling that the statutory bar on bail unless the Court is satisfied that there are “reasonable grounds for believing that the accusation is prima facie true” does not violate Article 21. The Court emphasised that the provision is a legislative policy choice aimed at combating terrorism and meets the proportionality test.

However, in Union of India v. K. S. Puttaswamy (2017) (privacy judgment), the Court cautioned that preventive detention laws must incorporate procedural safeguards — periodic review, disclosure of grounds, and effective judicial oversight — to comply with Article 22(4)–(5). The UAPA’s provision for detention up to 180 days without charge sheet (Section 43D(2)(b)) has been challenged as exceeding the permissible limit under Article 22(4). The Supreme Court in K. A. Najeeb v. State of Kerala (2021) granted bail to an accused detained for over a year without trial, holding that prolonged pre‑trial detention under UAPA violates Article 21 when the investigation shows no progress.

On the speech front, the 2019 amendment criminalising “advocacy” of secessionist ideas raised concerns under Article 19(1)(a). The Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) had struck down Section 66A IT Act for vagueness; similar vagueness arguments are being advanced against UAPA’s expanded definitions. While no final Constitution Bench ruling has yet invalidated the 2019 amendment, several High Courts have granted interim relief, reading down “advocacy” to require incitement to imminent violence.

The evolving jurisprudence demonstrates a calibrated approach: the Court respects legislative intent to combat terrorism but insists that UAPA’s draconian provisions meet the twin tests of non‑arbitrariness (Article 14) and proportionality (Articles 19, 21, 22). Aspirants should be ready to discuss the tension between national security and civil liberties, citing the above cases as the current judicial frontier.

  • Confusing colourable legislation with mere legislative incompetence; colourability requires a mismatch between form and substance, not just absence of legislative entry.
  • Assuming the non‑arbitrariness test replaces reasonable classification; both operate cumulatively — a law may pass classification yet fail manifest arbitrariness.
  • Treating delegated legislation as immune from fundamental‑rights review once it is intra vires; reasonableness and proportionality apply independently.
  • Overlooking that the 97th Amendment’s cooperative‑governance norms have been elevated to enforceable fundamental‑right standards under Articles 14 and 19(1)(c).
  • Believing UAPA’s bail bar under Section 43D(5) is absolute; the Supreme Court has granted bail where prolonged detention renders the process unfair under Article 21.
  • Neglecting the procedural safeguards required by Article 22(4)–(5) when analysing preventive‑detention statutes; mere statutory authorisation is insufficient.

The Ninth Schedule, Articles 31A, 31B, 31C and the Basic Structure: The I.R. Coelho (2007) Jurisprudence

The Ninth Schedule, inserted by the First Amendment (1951) alongside Article 31B, was designed to immunise land reform laws from judicial review under Articles 14, 19 and 31. Article 31A (also inserted by the First Amendment) saved five categories of laws — estate acquisition, takeover of management, amalgamation of corporations, modification of mining leases, and extinguishment of rights — from challenge under Articles 14 and 19. Article 31C, introduced by the 25th Amendment (1971) and expanded by the 42nd Amendment (1976), sought to give primacy to Directive Principles under Articles 39(b) and (c) over Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19 and 31. The 42nd Amendment extended this protection to all Directive Principles, but the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck down this extension as violating the basic structure.

The decisive turning point came in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine-judge Constitution Bench. The Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment) are open to challenge on the ground that they violate the basic structure of the Constitution. The Court established a dual test: first, whether the law in question destroys the basic structure; second, whether the amendment placing it in the Ninth Schedule itself violates the basic structure. The judgment clarified that Article 31B does not confer a blanket immunity; it merely removes the fetters of Articles 14, 19 and 31. If a law abridges a right that forms part of the basic structure — such as the rule of law, separation of powers, or judicial review — it remains vulnerable. The Court also ruled that the validity of a Ninth Schedule law must be tested on its own merits, not by reference to the parent Act under which it was enacted. Post-Coelho, the Tamil Nadu Backward Classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Reservation of Seats in Educational Institutions and Appointments in Public Services) Act, 1993 (placed in the Ninth Schedule by the 76th Amendment, 1994) was upheld in M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) on the basis of quantifiable data, but the Coelho principle ensures that future inclusions face strict scrutiny. Aspirants must distinguish between the pre-1973 immunity (absolute, per Waman Rao 1981) and post-1973 conditional immunity, and understand how Articles 31A, 31B and 31C interact: 31A saves specific categories from Articles 14/19; 31B creates a repository; 31C attempts a hierarchy of DPSP over FR, now limited to Articles 39(b) and (c) only.

The Doctrine of Constitutional Tort: State Liability for Fundamental Rights Violations

The doctrine of constitutional tort imposes vicarious liability on the State for violations of Fundamental Rights by its servants, distinct from the law of torts which governs private wrongs. The journey begins with Kasturi Lal v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1965), where the Supreme Court held that the State is not liable for tortious acts of its employees committed in the exercise of sovereign functions, relying on the distinction between sovereign and non-sovereign functions inherited from the Crown Proceedings Act, 1947. This immunity was progressively eroded. In Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993), the Court awarded compensation for custodial death under Article 21, declaring that the defence of sovereign immunity is not available in proceedings under Article 32 for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. The Court drew a sharp line: public law remedies (Articles 32, 226) operate on strict liability for breach of constitutional duty, while private law remedies (tort suits) remain subject to sovereign immunity. D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) institutionalised procedural safeguards and monetary compensation as a concomitant of the right to life. Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrima Das (2000) extended constitutional tort to non-citizens (a Bangladeshi national raped at Howrah station), holding that Article 21 protects all persons within India's territory. The doctrine rests on three pillars: (1) the State's obligation to protect Fundamental Rights is non-delegable; (2) compensation is a palliative, not a substitute for prosecution; (3) the quantum is determined by the gravity of violation, not by tort principles of remoteness or contributory negligence. Recent jurisprudence — Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983) for illegal detention, Bhim Singh v. State of J&K (1985) for wrongful arrest, Saheli v. Commissioner of Police (1990) for custodial violence — demonstrates that constitutional tort has become the primary instrument for enforcing accountability. However, the Court in State of Andhra Pradesh v. Challa Ramkrishna Reddy (2000) cautioned that compensation under Article 32 is not a matter of course; it requires a clear establishment of Fundamental Rights violation. The Law Commission's 152nd Report (1994) recommended a statutory framework for State liability, but no legislation has materialised, leaving the doctrine entirely judge-made. For examination, contrast constitutional tort (public law, strict liability, Article 32/226, no sovereign immunity) with tortious liability (private law, fault-based, civil suit, sovereign immunity applies) and note the unresolved tension: the State can be compelled to pay compensation under Article 32 but the errant officer often faces no departmental action.

Worked Application: Constitutional Tort vs Tortious Liability
A police officer, acting under colour of authority, illegally detains a person for 15 days and extracts a confession through torture. The victim files a writ petition under Article 32 seeking compensation and a separate civil suit for damages. The State pleads sovereign immunity in both proceedings. Decide the maintainability of each claim and the applicable standard of liability.
Under Article 32, the writ petition is maintainable. Nilabati Behera holds that sovereign immunity is no defence to a constitutional tort claim for violation of Fundamental Rights. The State is strictly liable; the victim need not prove negligence, only the breach of Article 21. Compensation is awarded as a public law remedy. In the civil suit, the State can plead sovereign immunity under the Kasturi Lal principle if the act is classified as a sovereign function (police powers). The victim must prove negligence or trespass, and the claim may fail if the court characterises the act as sovereign. Thus, the constitutional remedy succeeds where the private law remedy may be barred. The two proceedings operate on distinct planes: public law accountability versus private law compensation.
Exam Strategy: Constitutional Tort Triggers
When a question asks about "State liability for Fundamental Rights violation", immediately identify the forum: Article 32/226 = constitutional tort (strict liability, no sovereign immunity). Civil court = tortious liability (sovereign immunity may apply). Cite Nilabati Behera for custodial death, Rudul Sah for illegal detention, Chandrima Das for non-citizens. Never conflate the two regimes.

The Right to Speedy Trial as a Facet of Article 21: Judicial Standards and Systemic Realities

The right to speedy trial, though not expressly enumerated, was recognised as an integral part of Article 21 in Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979), where the Supreme Court, confronted with thousands of undertrials detained for periods exceeding the maximum possible sentence, declared that "speedy trial is the essence of criminal justice". The Court in Kadra Pahadiya v. State of Bihar (1982) extended this to the investigation stage, holding that undue delay in filing charge-sheets violates Article 21. In Common Cause v. Union of India (1996), the Court laid down guidelines: for offences punishable up to seven years, investigation should conclude within six months; for graver offences, within one year. The 2008 amendment to the Code of Criminal Procedure introduced Section 436A, mandating release on personal bond of undertrials who have served half the maximum sentence (excluding death penalty offences), giving statutory teeth to the judicial principle. However, the Court in Abdul Rehman Antulay v. R.S. Nayak (1992) refused to fix a rigid outer time limit, adopting a balancing test: length of delay, reason for delay, assertion of the right by the accused, and prejudice caused. The Antulay factors remain the judicial standard. Systemic constraints — judicial vacancies (as of 2023, ~5,000 posts vacant in district judiciary), inadequate forensic infrastructure, and procedural adjournments — render the right aspirational for many. The Law Commission's 230th Report (2009) recommended a "case management" system and time-bound disposal, but implementation is uneven. In Shafhi Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2018), the Court reiterated that delay alone does not automatically quash proceedings; the accused must demonstrate prejudice. For examination, distinguish between the right to speedy trial (Article 21, applies to State) and the right to fair trial (Article 21, includes speedy trial but also impartial judge, legal aid, etc.). Note that the right is available at pre-trial, trial, and appellate stages, and that the State cannot plead resource constraints as a defence — Hussainara Khatoon explicitly rejected financial inability as justification for denying constitutional rights.

The Constitutional Status of Sedition Law: Kedar Nath Singh, the 2022 Supreme Court Order and the Law Commission's 279th Report

Section 124A IPC (sedition) has been the subject of sustained constitutional challenge under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(2). In Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962), a Constitution Bench upheld the provision but narrowly construed it: only acts involving "intention or tendency to create disorder, or disturbance of law and order, or incitement to violence" constitute sedition. Mere criticism of government, however strong, is protected. The Court read down the colonial-era wording to save it from vagueness and overbreadth. For six decades, this "incitement to violence" test remained the governing standard, but its application by police and lower courts frequently ignored the Kedar Nath safeguards. In S.G. Vombatkere v. Union of India (2022), a three-judge Bench, noting the "chilling effect" on free speech and the "misuse" of the provision, directed the Union and State governments to refrain from registering fresh FIRs, continuing investigations, or taking coercive steps under Section 124A pending re-examination by the legislature. The Court effectively placed the provision in abeyance without striking it down. The Law Commission, in its 279th Report (2023), recommended retention of sedition with amendments: increasing the minimum punishment from three to seven years, incorporating a "tendency to incite violence" requirement, and adding a procedural safeguard requiring a preliminary inquiry by a DSP-rank officer before registration of FIR. The Commission argued that the provision is necessary to combat "internal security threats" and "secessionist movements". Critics contend that the Kedar Nath test already provides the necessary narrowing, and that the real problem is executive non-compliance, not legislative deficiency. The 2022 order is unprecedented: the Court did not declare the law unconstitutional but suspended its operation, a technique reminiscent of the "reading down" doctrine. Aspirants should be prepared to discuss: (1) the distinction between "striking down" and "keeping in abeyance"; (2) the tension between judicial restraint (leaving repeal to Parliament) and constitutional duty (protecting Article 19(1)(a)); (3) the Kedar Nath "incitement to violence" test versus the Law Commission's "tendency to incite violence" formulation; (4) the role of Section 196 CrPC (sanction for prosecution) as an additional safeguard; and (5) the comparative perspective — the UK abolished sedition in 2009, the US applies the Brandenburg "imminent lawless action" test.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation: Constitutional Limits on Legislative Power in Rights Adjudication

The doctrine of colourable legislation addresses the situation where a legislature, lacking competence to enact a law directly, does so indirectly under the guise of a legitimate entry. The maxim "quando aliquid prohibetur ex directo, prohibetur et per obliquum" (what is prohibited directly is prohibited indirectly) underpins the doctrine. In K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953), the Supreme Court held that the doctrine does not question the motive or bona fides of the legislature; it examines the "true nature and character" of the legislation. If the substance of the law falls outside the legislative entry, the law is invalid regardless of its form. The doctrine is distinct from legislative incompetence: incompetence arises when a legislature enacts on a subject outside its list; colourability arises when it purports to act within its list but in reality transgresses into another list. In State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952), the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 was struck down as colourable because, though enacted under Entry 18 (land) of the State List, its effect was to deprive zamindars of property without compensation, a matter reserved for Parliament under Entry 42 of the Concurrent List (acquisition of property). The Court looks at the "pith and substance" of the law; if the true object is to achieve what the legislature cannot do directly, the law is colourable. In Fundamental Rights adjudication, the doctrine intersects with Article 13(2): a colourable law that abridges Fundamental Rights is void. In Balaji v. State of Mysore (1963), the Court examined whether a reservation order exceeding 50% was a colourable exercise of power under Article 15(4); it held that the constitutional limitation (50% rule) cannot be circumvented by labelling the excess as "backward classes" identification. The doctrine does not apply where the legislature has plenary power (e.g., Parliament under Article 248 residuary power) or where the Constitution expressly authorises the measure (e.g., Article 31A). A common error is to conflate colourability with mala fides; the Court in K.C. Gajapati explicitly rejected motive as relevant. For examination, remember the three-step test: (1) identify the legislative entry invoked; (2) determine the true nature and effect of the law (pith and substance); (3) ask whether the effect transgresses into a forbidden field. If yes, the law is colourable and void.

  • Assuming that the Ninth Schedule provides absolute immunity for all laws placed in it after 1973; I.R. Coelho makes immunity conditional on basic structure compliance.
  • Confusing constitutional tort (Article 32/226, strict liability, no sovereign immunity) with tortious liability (civil suit, fault-based, sovereign immunity applies).
  • Treating the right to speedy trial as an absolute right to quash proceedings after a fixed period; Antulay requires a balancing test with prejudice as a key factor.
  • Believing the 2022 Supreme Court order in S.G. Vombatkere struck down Section 124A IPC; it only kept the provision in abeyance pending legislative re-examination.
  • Equating colourable legislation with legislative mala fides; the doctrine examines the competence and substance of the law, not the motive of the legislators.
  • Overlooking that Article 31C, post-Minerva Mills, protects only laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c), not all Directive Principles.
  • Neglecting the distinction between pre-1973 Ninth Schedule inclusions (immune per Waman Rao) and post-1973 inclusions (subject to basic structure test per Coelho).
